News.title: One of the five men arrested near RAF Fairford called 999 himself
News.content:
One of five men arrested near RAF Fairford in the early hours of Sunday morning had dialled 999 himself, the BBC understands.

The suspect called the police at 00:45 BST, almost an hour before a female farmer also dialled 999 after seeing men in balaclavas.

The five were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later terrorism offences after three vans were spotted, sparking a major security incident around the Gloucestershire base which the US military operates.

They were released on bail on Monday in what police described as an "investigative decision" "grounded in experience and strategy".

Police say a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of the vans.

Police were alerted to "three suspicious vehicles" in Whelford, a village which lies directly east of the base, by the farmer.

She told the BBC it was "pure luck" she had spotted them, having arrived home to find the road blocked and a "large group of hooded and masked men".

"I believe that my 999 call foiled whatever plans they had," she said.

A bomb disposal team arrived on scene shortly afterwards and a 400m (1,312ft) cordon was put in place.

But Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, told reporters on Tuesday that the police response that morning had been due to "a range of information".

Police cordons near the base are expected to be completely lifted on Wednesday, while residents from the 85 homes evacuated on Sunday have been allowed to return to their properties.

The five men are all UK nationals aged between 23 and 25. Four of them live in Westminster and one in Camden, and searches of their homes are now complete.

Taylor previously said their bail was "subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others" as they remained under investigation.

"The safety of the public is at the forefront of our investigative decision-making, and this was certainly the case yesterday," he said on Tuesday.

"I understand why this development was surprising to some, but I would like to reiterate that this is an investigative decision and one which is grounded in experience and strategy."

The RAF base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force for decades.

In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday told journalists he was "disappointed" the five men had been released on bail.

News.title: How did the RAF Fairford incident go from 'suspected bomb plot' to police bail?
News.content:
On Sunday morning, the world was watching as drama unfolded in the village of Whelford.

Before sunrise, residents were called from their beds and told to evacuate as a huge police operation unfolded in the village, which is next door to RAF Fairford, a base used by the US Air Force.

One villager managed to take a picture of five men sitting on the ground, stripped to the waist, handcuffed and under armed guard.

They were arrested for offences under the Explosives Act. But now counter-terrorism detectives say no explosives were found in their three vans, only an "accelerant" - petrol.

What some newspapers called a "suspected bomb plot" ended in the suspects being bailed. So what was going on?

The US President Donald Trump asserted that the men had been trying to do "big damage" to the base. "We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," he declared.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "What could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It's one that clearly involved the hands of a foreign actor."

But in a veiled criticism of that, the head Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK Laurence Taylor said that the worry that a lot of people had been experiencing had been "heightened by the international commentary".

He also defended his detectives' decision to give the suspects police bail with "very strict conditions". This had been criticised by President Trump.

Taylor said it was an "investigative decision and one which is grounded in experience and strategy".

This suggests there were good tactical reasons for releasing the men on bail, perhaps to encourage their cooperation.

News.title: Household energy bills forecast to see biggest rise in four years
News.content:
Household energy prices are set to soar in January, with a typical annual bill forecast to jump by Â£276, figures shared with the BBC reveal.

The 16% predicted increase would hit millions of households at the coldest time of year, and would mark the biggest rise in bills for four years.

The forecast from consultancy Cornwall Insight comes a day before prices go up under regulator Ofgem's October price cap and puts increased pressure on the government to support those who will struggle to pay.

Meanwhile, the boss of supplier EDF Simone Rossi has warned the UK is "walking into a second energy crisis" and called for an extension to the VAT cut on electricity which kicks in on Thursday.

News.title: Burnham vows to end existing pension triple lock in 2030 to help fund care
News.content:
Before turning to the pension triple lock changes, Burnham accepted he may "pay a political price" by trying to make the reforms but argued "someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off".

The triple lock was introduced in 2010 by the coalition government and designed to ensure the value of the state pension was not overtaken by the increase in the cost of living or the incomes of working people.

It means the state pension rates rise every April by either inflation, earnings growth or 2.5% - whichever is the highest.

Burnham said this will stay in place until 2030, at which point he would like to "adjust it".

He said: "The state pension will continue to rise every year at least by prices or 2.5%. And it will hold its value relative to earnings over time so that pensioners will always share in the rising prosperity of the nation.

"But this change will generate significant savings which we will use to build up our national care service.

"Some may not realise it but older people with nothing more than the state pension, or only a little more, can find themselves paying care charges today from that small income. Under my plan, this will no longer happen."

Officials have suggested the change could save Â£15bn a year by 2040.

Jonathan Cribb, deputy director at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said savings "are likely to be relatively small in the first few years, but rise substantially over time".

He also said "we should not expect this reform to save enough that it could fund universal social care in the next parliament".

Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union, told the BBC she believed the government should have "pulled another lever", such as a wealth tax, rather than making changes to the triple lock.

The political backlash was immediate.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said "more tax rises are inevitable" under Labour's plan, while Reform UK's Nigel Farage accused the PM of "launching an offensive against our elderly".

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said families "cannot wait until after another election and it can't be funded from the pockets of our poorest pensioners".

News.title: Chris Mason: Burnham delivers deeply political speech with a personal core
News.content:
What stood out in this speech was its breadth. His pitch could, very broadly, be divided into the short term - what he hopes to achieve before a general election; and the long term - the prospectus he is beginning to assemble to put to the country when polling day comes around inside the next three years.

The biggest ideas have the longest timeframe and, perhaps, the greatest need for a lengthy debate in their gestation.

Take the headline grabber: revamping social care in England. Previous attempts to do so, by both Labour and the Conservatives, haven't survived the intensity of a general election campaign, having been announced close to an election.

The aim of Burnham's plan is to seed a conversation now about what a new system might look like â the idea being that the argument is won in advance.

Let's see. The debate is only just beginning.

The plan to fund this by making increases in the state pension from 2030 less generous than they are now was more detailed than some expected at this stage.

The triple lock means the state pension currently increases annually in line with inflation, average wage growth or 2.5%, whichever is highest.

But from April 2030, if Labour win the next election, the annual earnings link will be dropped. It would, Labour figures say, be increased further if needed, to ensure that it stays above 30% of the full time average wage.

Knowing they would face blunt criticism about binning the existing triple lock â note the reaction of the Unite union and Labour's political rivals â it would appear the prime minister was keen to offer as much of what he hopes will be reassuring detail to many.

Also going into the next Labour manifesto, he said, a change in the Westminster voting system and â after a review to come â the idea of a closer relationship with the European Union.

How much closer, with what trade offs and prompting what reaction, we don't yet know.

And from the longer term stuff to the here and now â including housing reform in England, more public control of the water industry and the electricity grid.

There was an energy and sense of urgency to Burnham's pitch and without question he has created a battalion of dividing lines with Labour's political opponents which are likely to dominate the debate ahead.

His cabinet and many in his party are relishing the battle of ideas the prime minister has set up and is enthusiastically leaning into.

It was noteworthy that beyond a broad reference to Labour's opponents on the Right, the party's rivals didn't get a mention in a speech lasting more than an hour.

The question is: does he and his government have the capacity to deliver?

And do they have the capacity to convince you, the voter, they have a vision you regard as coherent, appealing and affordable?

You hardly need reminding of the backdrop that contributed to thwarting many of his recent, many predecessors: a persistently sclerotic economy and a persistently turbulent international picture, for starters.

Neither will make turning all of this into a reality straightforward.

News.title: 'Mum sent them £140,000': How to spot the signs a loved one is being scammed
News.content:
Head over heels in love with a man she met online, Helen's mother hollowed out a book and put Â£10,000 cash inside. She then posted it to a Shanghai Hospital where he awaited a life-saving operation.

Once he was better they would be together - but the demands kept coming. Then a new man came on the scene - he'd been kidnapped and if she didn't pay the ransom he would be killed.

In total she sent Â£140,000 to romance scammers.

The first time Helen knew something was wrong was when her mum accidentally sent messages intended for the criminals to her. Then she became more secretive.

"It became obvious to me something was going on again," she says.

Here's how to spot the signs a loved one is being scammed and how to help them.

News.title: The intricate web Man City spun to con the Premier League
News.content:
"To cheat, trick, deceive, delude with false pretences; to impose upon, take in, hoax."

That is the Oxford English definition of the word "sham".

And that word appears eight times in the independent commission's ruling published on Tuesday, which found Manchester City guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of financial rules, and all but one in relation to a failure to co-operate with the investigation.

The 40-page document makes fascinating reading.

It catalogues how the club's owners, Abu Dhabi United Group, knew from the 2009-10 season that there would be major overspends if the club was to reach the level they wanted to get to.

So, the ruling says, City found a way to boost sponsorship income. Season, after season, after season.

For nine seasons, in fact.

The report shows how the club's owners were topping up the value of the deals.

The so-called Disguised Funding Scheme is the central plank in a series of charges that Manchester City have been found guilty of by the Premier League.

This scheme managed to hide more than Â£830m of sponsorship funding, while other devices hid Â£90m in expenses.

We break down the key findings from the document.

News.title: Village team triumphs in FA Cup row replay
News.content:
Speaking before the game, Danny Self, joint first team manager at Mulbarton, said: "There's all the emotions, you ask questions and you're frustrated.

"Then you ask can we appeal this and you're told you can't.

"Whether we agree or disagree, we are where we are and we've just got to prepare for it."

Dan Robathan, a retired Premier League and FIFA referee, defended the original matchday official.

He said: "There's a misconception that when we make a decision, that we don't care which is so far from the truth.

"It hits you quite personally and you don't want to have a negative effect on a game.

"But you're trying to process all that at once and I can only assume he's got confused with the law in that moment."

The village club, around six miles (10km) south of Norwich, has risen through local leagues in recent years and is competing at step four of the non-league pyramid for the first time this season.

The tie against Gloucester in the next round is scheduled for the weekend of Saturday 3 October.

Gloucester play at step three of non-league, in Southern League Premier Division South. The winner will claim Â£5,625 in winnings and the losers Â£1,875.

Despite losing tonight's tie, Woodford also collect Â£1,125 from the prize fund.

News.title: Antisemitism on the rise at universities, charity warns
News.content:
Cases of antisemitism affecting university students and staff in the UK increased in the last academic year, according to a charity that monitors antisemitic incidents.

The Community Security Trust (CST) said it had recorded 95 "university-related" incidents in the 2025-26 academic year - up from 83 the year before.

It said the number had fallen from its peak in the year after Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023 and the war in Gaza began, but remains "substantially higher" than before that point.

Universities UK (UUK) represents more than 140 institutions and said its members needed to "protect Jewish students and staff", adding that the findings were a "serious concern".

Lucy Powell, education secretary in England, said the findings in the CST report were "deeply troubling".

"We expect universities to take a zero-tolerance approach to antisemitism, and are providing training to help university staff identify and respond to incidents swiftly," she said.

The CST defines an antisemitic incident as "university-related" if it concerns a student, member of staff or academic at a UK university "in their academic or student capacity" - including on campus and online.

In 2022-23, the last academic year before the 7 October attack, the CST recorded 53 incidents. That grew to 272 in 2023-24.

A report from the charity examining the past two academic years says reported incidents fell in 2024-25 and but grew again in 2025-26.

News.title: Three teenagers die after car enters river
News.content:
Three teenagers have died after a car entered the River Wear.

Northumbria Police said just before 13:30 BST a black Audi A3 came off the road at Panns Bank near Wearmouth Bridge, in Sunderland, and entered the water.

Four people were in the car at the time and a 17-year-old boy managed to reach safety. He is currently in hospital with non-serious injuries, and has subsequently been arrested in connection with the incident, the force said.

The bodies of two teenage boys and a teenage girl have been recovered from the water.

No other vehicles are believed to have been involved.

Ch Supt Scott Cowie, area commander for Sunderland, said it was "a truly tragic incident".

"Our thoughts are with their families, friends and all those impacted by what has happened," he said.

He added the investigation was at an early stage and the force was working to establish the circumstances.

News.title: Huel ad banned for suggesting its products could replace all conventional food
News.content:
An advert for Huel meal replacement shakes has been banned by the advertising watchdog for encouraging or condoning "irresponsible" dietary practices.

The ad featured Huel brand ambassador Spencer Matthews sharing an anecdote of a person he met who "only eats Huel" and who won a 260km race "by miles".

The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) said that viewers could assume from the ad that replacing all conventional food with Huel was "nutritionally appropriate" and was compatible with elite physical performance.

Huel said Matthews' anecdote was not "a recommendation or instruction" and the purpose of the ad was to challenge the misconception that Huel could replace every meal".

The video, which appeared as a sponsored Instagram post and YouTube pre-roll ad, featured Matthews speaking to Huel founder Julian Hearn in the style of a podcast.

The Instagram post included the caption: "Here's how our founder uses Huel. Spoiler alert it's not for every meal."

In the video Hearn said that he has Huel products for breakfast and lunch during the working week, but has a "traditional meal" when he goes home.

In response, Matthews said that when he was competing in an ultramarathon, he met a man who "only eats Huel".

Matthews said he was initially sceptical that the man would be able to manage the race, but then said: "He won it by miles, like literally just left us all in the dirt."

Hearn replied: "In an ideal world, you should have nutritionally complete whole food.

"Most people either don't do that or can't have the time to do that, and therefore that's where Huel fits in the gap."

News.title: Student: Uni strikes 'not what we signed up for'
News.content:
A student has said she feels "shorthanded" as staff at University of Nottingham are to go on strike for three months.

The University and College Union (UCU) said its members would strike on Wednesday and Thursday and would then carry out "sustained strike action" from 5 October to 11 December over the Future Nottingham restructuring plans.

A spokesperson for the University of Nottingham said it was "disappointed" by the timing of industrial action, adding many students would be "unaffected" by the strikes.

Zoe Monroe, who studies English literature with creative writing, told the BBC the strikes were not what students had signed up for.

The university said previously the proposals could involve programme closures and academic restructure.

It added it had reviewed and considered all Future Nottingham counterproposals, which would now go to the University Council for a decision.

The university had suspended music and language courses and planned hundreds of job cuts earlier this year to deal with "significant financial challenges".

Union members from UCU, Unison and Unite voted in July in favour of a motion of no confidence in the vice-chancellor and other senior leaders after a "complete breakdown of trust".

The first two days of action have been planned to coincide with the university's council meeting at which the final business case for cuts will be considered.

The strike will also include action short of a strike, such as only working to contract and not covering for absent colleagues, the UCU said.

News.title: Prince William and Catherine's surprise visit to Kevin Sinfield's charity run
News.content:
The Prince and Princess of Wales made a surprise visit to support rugby league star Sir Kevin Sinfield, on the third day of his endurance challenge to raise funds for Motor Neurone Disease (MND) charities.

"What you're doing is so inspiring â the unity that you're building," Catherine told Sir Kevin.

Prince William and Catherine caught up with Sir Kevin in Wakefield, West Yorkshire, as he carries out what he says will be his final fundraising challenge.

Sir Kevin is aiming to complete seven ultra marathons in seven days, running between Hull and Manchester, in a challenge inspired by his former teammate Rob Burrow, who died from MND in 2024.

News.title: Man City guilty of 'sham' contracts and misleading accounts
News.content:
Manchester City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than Â£830m, the Premier League says.

The League confirmed that City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

An independent commission found that, during that time period, the club arranged the "sham contracts" as well as "relying on sham agreements to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs".

The club continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal.

News broke last week that City had been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching, but on Tuesday the Premier League published a redacted version of the commission's report.

The commission's report said the charges "concerned well over 100 alleged individual breaches of Premier League rules across four broad charge categories".

It also found the club guilty of all charges except one relating to non-cooperation with the Premier League investigation and said that "a number of important club witnesses gave false evidence in key respects and that some knowingly gave untrue and dishonest evidence".

The sham commercial deals were described as being part of a "disguised funding scheme" to the scale of Â£830.69m.

City recorded Â£360m in sponsor fees in the three seasons they won the Premier League - 2011-12, 2013-14, and 2017-18. Only Â£43m of it was legitimate - the rest came from their owners and was disguised.

"The relevant sponsorship agreements were found to be shams, or at minimum did not reflect their economic substance," the commission said.

It also describes "deliberate or reckless conduct intended to circumvent the Premier League rules" and that the "sham" scheme devised by City allowed the club "to avoid recording what would otherwise have been the largest single-season loss in Premier League history in 2009-10".

The commission highlighted the scale of evidence it had to consider by pointing out that the index alone ran to more than 750 pages, while the core bundle of documents "ran to many tens of thousands of pages".

City are owned by the Abu Dhabi United Group, who took over the club in 2008 and are referred to as "ADUG" in the commission's report.

News.title: Burnham to fight next election on pledge to change voting system
News.content:
Andy Burnham has promised that Labour will fight the next general election on a pledge to change the UK's voting system.

In his first party conference speech as prime minister, he announced plans for a national commission to explore options for electoral reform.

He invited other parties to work with the commission to ensure "everyone's vote counts, and everyone's voice is heard".

He has previously supported moves towards a proportional representation (PR) model, telling last year's conference that "PR's time has come".

Westminster's first-past-the-post system, under which candidates with the most votes in each seat are elected, has been called into question as the UK political landscape has fragmented in recent years.

Debate over the system has intensified since Labour amassed a huge parliamentary majority with a 34% vote share in 2024.

Around 100 Labour MPs recently supported a parliamentary amendment in favour of setting up a commission to examine alternative options, a move Burnham himself supported last year when mayor of Greater Manchester.

In his speech Burnham told delegates: "We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No 10 to a divisive government on less than 30% of the vote or less."

He added: "We can't succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times."

News.title: No 'deliberate' contact to stop car in A66 crash
News.content:
No evidence of "tactical contact" or the use of a stinger has been found before the A66 crash which killed five young men and two police officers, an initial investigation has revealed.

The crash between a Volkswagen Passat and a marked Cleveland Police vehicle happened at South Bank, near Middlesbrough, on 22 August and followed a police pursuit which was abandoned.

The initial investigation by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said there was no evidence police had initiated contact with the Passat.

However, director of engagement, Emily Barry, said it will take the IOPC months to conclude its full investigation due to the amount of information to review.

PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, who had not been following the Passat, were killed.

The five people in the Passat were Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, and 17-year-olds Theo Rae and Cole Robert Worthy.

Two North Korean soldiers captured fighting for Russia against Ukraine are now in South Korea.

The move has raised questions ​over how they will be investigated, protected and resettled, and the legal basis for their transfer.

The soldiers are expected to undergo questioning and security screening before the South Korean authorities decide whether to grant them protection and begin the resettlement process.

Seoul's Unification Ministry said on Monday their cases would be reviewed under relevant laws and past practices, suggesting that the North Korean Defectors Protection and Settlement ⁠Support Act would apply.

Under the law, the National Intelligence Service (NIS) investigates applicants in temporary protective custody, verifying their identities, reasons for leaving North Korea and security-related matters.

The investigation and temporary protection may last up to 90 days, with a possible extension in unavoidable circumstances.

The soldiers’ military backgrounds and firsthand knowledge of North Korea’s deployment to Russia could result in more extensive debriefing.

Those granted protection usually receive resettlement training before entering South Korean society.

open image in gallery Russia's President Vladimir Putin (R) and North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un (C) leave after their meeting in Beijing on September 3, 2025 ( AFP/Getty )

Yu Yong-weon, an opposition lawmaker who met the soldiers in Ukraine in February 2025, said they had served in North Korean special forces and ⁠could provide information on Pyongyang's training, military capabilities and participation in the war.

Do they receive protection?

The unification minister normally determines whether a North Korean arrival qualifies for protection, although the NIS director can make the decision on national security grounds.

Yu told Reuters the sensitivity of the case could also keep them out of public view longer than other North Korean arrivals.

Their physical and ⁠psychological condition is also likely to be assessed.

Yu said when he met them they were being held separately at a Ukrainian detention facility and the ​prolonged isolation and uncertainty ⁠may have affected their mental health.

Did Ukraine have the right to transfer them?

The Third Geneva Convention requires prisoners of war to be released and repatriated without delay after active hostilities end. That does not necessarily prohibit earlier release or transfer to a third country.

South Korea and Ukraine have not disclosed the legal basis for their transfer, including whether it formally ends the soldiers’ POW status.

open image in gallery North Korean leader Kim Jong Un speaks during the opening ceremony of the Memorial Museum of Combat Feats at the Overseas Military Operations honouring North Korean troops killed while fighting for Russia in the war against Ukraine, in Pyongyang, North Korea ( Reuters )

Peter ‌Ward, a research fellow at the Sejong Institute, said repatriation was a basic principle governing POWs ‌but should not apply where it could damage their welfare or human rights.

"There is ample basis under humanitarian and human rights law for these POWs to be transferred to a third country of their choice so long as that third country of their choice is prepared to take them," Ward said.

Lee Shin-wha, a Korea University professor and former envoy for North Korean human rights, said the transfer could still generate legal and ⁠diplomatic friction because international law treats North Korea as a separate state, while South Korea considers North Koreans as its citizens.

Their stated wish to come to the South and the risks they could face in the North provide grounds for accepting them, she said.

Could they have been returned to North Korea?

International human rights law would weigh against returning the soldiers if they faced a real risk of torture, persecution or other serious mistreatment.

The principle of non-refoulement prohibits sending people to a country where they face such risks.

Lee said repatriation was the general rule for POWs, but international practice also recognised voluntary repatriation and barred returns that could lead to persecution or torture.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has praised soldiers who committed suicide while fighting against Ukrainian forces in Russia's Kursk region where the pair were captured.

The two men repeatedly ‌expressed a desire to go to South Korea, including in media interviews and during a meeting with Yu.

Ward said North Korea had little basis ​under international law to demand their return.

How has South Korea responded?

South Korea, which is a major arms producer, has ‌faced pressure from some Western countries and Kyiv to provide Ukraine with lethal ⁠weapons but has so far focused on non-lethal aid including demining equipment.

President Lee Jae Myung announced a $100 million support package for Ukraine at a NATO ⁠summit in July, while his government reiterated that lethal weapons were excluded. Seoul also pledged continued humanitarian assistance and support for reconstruction.

At their July summit, Lee and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskiy agreed that the North Korean ‌POW issue should be handled in accordance with the ​soldiers’ free will, international law and humanitarian principles.

South Korea ‌demanded an apology from Ukraine after Zelenskiy disclosed the transfer at the ​UN General Assembly last week, saying Kyiv had breached an agreement to keep it confidential.

Seoul said confidentiality was necessary to protect the soldiers and relatives in North Korea.

Kyiv has said no secrecy agreement existed.

The Right Livelihood Award was awarded Wednesday to two women and two women-led organizations challenging authoritarian rule, violence and discrimination against women, and the harms caused by artificial intelligence, the Stockholm-based foundation said.

The recipients of the international award are a Pakistani lawyer, an Ethiopian-born AI researcher, a Georgian legal rights group and a network of women farmers across Southern Africa.

The annual prize was created in 1980 by Swedish-German philanthropist Jakob von Uexkull, who wanted to honor work that contributes to a more just and peaceful world. It is traditionally announced shortly before the Nobel Prizes, which will be announced starting next Monday.

Right Livelihood said this year's recipients were being awarded for their “resistance to systems that push people to the margins, and a shared insistence on putting people back at the center.” They were chosen from 200 nominations from 72 countries.

“A system built to serve the few was never going to hold. This year, we honor women who refused to wait for permission,” Ole von Uexkull, the nephew of the prize founder and the organization’s executive director, said. “They are rewriting the rules that autocrats, patriarchs and Silicon Valley’s most powerful men assumed were theirs to write alone."

Here is a look at the recipients:

A Pakistani lawyer who works to protect vulnerable communities

Jalila Haider, a human rights lawyer who defends some of Pakistan’s most vulnerable communities from state repression, discrimination against women and ethnic violence, was awarded the prize “for breaking barriers, as the first female lawyer from her Hazara community, to challenge ethnic, state and patriarchal persecution, guided by the conviction that no human being is illegal."

By combining legal work with efforts to help communities advocate for themselves, “Haider has secured justice for thousands targeted or ignored by those in power, specifically ethnic, gender and religious minorities, as well as refugees,” the organization said. Haider's law firm has also helped more than 600 political activists and human rights defenders regain the right to travel freely.

A Southern African women farmers’ group defending land rights

Also awarded was the Rural Women’s Assembly “for organizing rural women across Southern Africa into a united force defending land, seed and bodily autonomy against corporate and patriarchal dispossession."

The Rural Women’s Assembly is a self-organized, movement of more than 178,000 small-scale farmers across 11 Southern African nations. It has established 24 sites where farmers reproduce and preserve seeds for future planting and documented hundreds of local seed varieties, helping protect the practice of saving and exchanging traditional seeds, the Swedish foundation said.

A Georgian human rights group working to safeguard democracy

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association won the prize “for building and safeguarding Georgian democracy and sustaining civic power in the face of an autocratic crackdown."

The group was founded in 1994 by volunteer lawyers who helped draft the country’s first postindependence constitution.

According to Right Livelihood, it has secured major legal victories that reshaped national policy, including protections for people with disabilities, free education for all children and compensation for victims of Soviet-era repression.

A researcher who exposes harms that AI is already causing

Right Livelihood also honored AI researcher Timnit Gebru “for challenging concentrated power in artificial intelligence and pioneering digital technology rooted in justice, lived experience and human agency.”

Gebru, who was born in Ethiopia to a family of Eritrean origin, is the founder of the Distributed AI Research Institute.

Right Livelihood said her work challenges the control that a small number of powerful companies exercise over AI and exposes harms that AI systems are already causing, particularly to communities facing discrimination and exclusion.

Medication prices are soaring in Iran and some treatments have become hard to find, leaving patients and their families scrambling as a U.S. blockade and stepped-up sanctions squeeze the country's pharmaceuticals industry.

Some medicines have more than tripled in price, further squeezing Iranians' finances seven months into the country's war with the United States and Israel. Prices for food and other goods have skyrocketed even as unemployment has risen and the currency, which hit a record low this week, has lost half its value.

The war has become an economic endurance test. Iran has tried to push world energy prices higher with attacks on the region's oil shipping routes; the United States, in turn, has aimed to wreck Iran's economy by blockading its ports since June and slapping it with increasingly tough sanctions.

Iran's pharmaceutical industry is vulnerable because of its reliance on imports. So far there has been little sign of major shortages of medicines at Iran's hospitals, but the difficulties are showing at pharmacies.

Gholamreza Rahmani, a Tehran welder, and his wife recently scoured several pharmacies over two days hoping to fill prescriptions for four medicines for their 12-year-old daughter, who was having stomach troubles. “Each one would have one or two items, not all of them,” he said, noting that they couldn't find one of the medicines anywhere. The search cost him two days of wages because he couldn't go to work.

“My daughter’s illness and the loss of income are like scissors, cutting from two sides,” he said.

Iran's pharmaceutical industry needs imports

Iran produces more than 80% of its medicines domestically, according to official statistics, but many of those rely on imported raw materials. Before the war, most medicines and pharmaceutical components were brought in by sea, but the American naval blockade has cut off shipping, Bahman Sabour, a member of the Tehran Pharmacies Association, told local media.

Medical importers switched to more expensive air routes. But that access has been threatened by new U.S. sanctions on a number of Iranian airlines, which led to some international flights being halted.

U.S. sanctions don't directly target medicines, but financial sanctions in place for years also hurt the pharmaceutical supply because international banks and companies often will be overly cautious and refuse transactions because they fear running afoul of sanctions, said Reza Majdzadeh, a professor at the School of Health and Social Care at the University of Essex in England.

“A medicine may be perfectly legal to sell to Iran, but a bank may refuse to process the payment,” he said. “A pharmaceutical or shipping company may simply decide that dealing with Iran is not worth the risk. ... The transaction is legal on paper, but it does not happen in the real world.”

The Iranian government hasn't said how much medicine production has fallen. But officials say it has been hurt because airstrikes damaged more than 40 pharmaceutical factories, including some producing cancer treatments.

Also, cash-strapped pharmacies sometimes struggle to keep their shelves stocked. Insurance companies have fallen behind by as much as nine months on payments to pharmacies for drug coverage because of the “current situation,” said Mohammad Jamalian, a member of parliament’s health committee.

Sabour, of the pharmacies’ association, said insurance companies owe pharmacies about $270 million.

Supplies are also strained because medicines are smuggled to neighboring Afghanistan, Pakistan and Iraq, where prices are higher, state media reported.

Pharmacy prices are spiking

“The price of almost everything has gone up, in some cases doubling, quadrupling, or even increasing sixfold,” said Mina Mohammadian, a salesperson at a pharmacy in Tehran.

Mehdi Pirsalehi, head of the government agency that sets drug prices, said last week that the prices of 2,000 types of medicines were “amended” over the past six months because of inflation and currency issues.

Ali Fallah, a Tehran resident, said the ointment he buys for inflammation has quadrupled in price in three months — from 750,000 rials, or about $0.35, to 3.25 million rials, or roughly $1.46. The minimum daily wage for an unskilled worker in Iran is about 7.5 million rials, or about $3.50.

“I honestly don’t know where this situation is heading,” Fallah said.

Tablets essential for patients undergoing kidney dialysis, for example, have climbed by nearly 350% in recent months. So have over-the-counter painkillers like acetaminophen, if it can be found at all.

The government appears to be ensuring hospitals are supplied

An employee at one public hospital said there are shortages of key specialized psychiatric medicines to treat bipolar disorders and acute psychosis, and more common medications for anxiety and panic disorders. Doctors have had to use electro-convulsive therapy on patients more often because the relevant drugs weren't available or were of inferior quality, she said.

“The side effects for patients are really a lot,” she told The Associated Press by phone from a major Iranian city. She spoke on condition that she and her location would not be identified for security reasons.

Azita Hassanpour, a part-time teacher, said that her mother, who has cancer, has been able to get her chemotherapy treatments, but sometimes they are delayed because the medicines aren't as available as they were before the war. Hassanpour is also concerned because her mother hasn't been able to get her annual flu shot, with authorities trying to track down new vaccine sources.

“I am worried that I may lose her because of flu. I weep out of her sight every night,” Hassanpour said.

Hadi Ahmadi, a spokesman of the Iranian Pharmacists Association, told local media Saturday that about 700,000 flu vaccine doses were imported from China and another half million doses are expected soon. But a jab this year is going for 22 million rials, or roughly $9, which is almost double last year’s price, though authorities have promised to provide it to high-risk patients free of charge.

___

Radjy reported from New York.

Scientists had warned the government not to build along Venezuela’s coastal strip of La Guaira.

The area’s seaside Caribbean communities, not far from Caracas, were near a major fault line and a mountain range that had unleashed repeated, destructive natural disasters. The soil was poor, a type of silt that would only amplify shaking in an earthquake.

Ignoring the advice, the government threw up exactly the wrong kind of buildings for that location: tall concrete apartment complexes.

It was all a recipe for destruction, according to an Associated Press investigation that relied on interviews with dozens of engineers, seismologists and former government officials.

The people of La Guaira never stood a chance on June 24 when powerful, back-to-back quakes struck.

“They were defying nature” when government officials decided to build there, said Carlos Valdés, head of the seismology department at the Institute of Geophysics of the National Autonomous University of Mexico.

The quakes killed more than 6,500 people and left over 17,000 homeless. The government of acting President Delcy Rodríguez has done little to quell the rage of those who survived the quakes in the three months since that June evening — and she has failed to address why so many buildings collapsed and so many died.

The answer, in fact, can be traced back to 2010 and decisions made after mudslides and heavy rain displaced more than 100,000 people across the country, experts and former government officials told the AP.

That’s when the Venezuelan government raced to ease a humanitarian crisis by constructing scores of apartments on the strip of land flanked by crystalline waters of the Caribbean Sea to the north and lush mountains to the south.

The setting was idyllic. The land beneath it was not.

An area prone to natural disasters and earthquakes

When Venezuela was rocked by the 7.2- and 7.5-magnitude earthquakes, at least 14 apartment towers in La Guaira fell nearly at the same time, pancaking one floor on top of another, trapping hundreds inside. Fires broke out as gas tanks exploded. People screamed for help. Few survived. Bodies were recovered from what used to be bedrooms, stairs, hallways and kitchens. Many were found hugging.

The area, in northern Venezuela, is no stranger to natural disasters.

A deadly 6.6-magnitude earthquake hit the area in 1967, prompting among other actions the design of quake-resistant construction guidelines and the creation of the Venezuelan Foundation for Seismological Research, a counterpart of the U.S. Geological Survey. Similar to June’s earthquakes, it destroyed buildings in La Guaira's parish of Caraballeda and Venezuela’s capital, Caracas.

But no disaster had devastated La Guaira like the floods and mudslides that killed tens of thousands of people in 1999. After the tragedy, President Hugo Chávez’s government chose engineer and then-science minister Carlos Genatios to helm a reconstruction plan.

His team worked with local and international experts to develop a hazard-mitigation program for the state, which included land-use restrictions along the coastal strip primarily to reduce the dangers associated with rains and, to a somewhat lesser extent, earthquakes, Genatios told AP in an interview.

“There are areas, tracts of land, that should not have been used because they are prone to flooding during major surges; in such places, one should place very lightweight structures, parks, sports courts or similar facilities that do not cause major damage and, above all, do not result in fatalities,” Genatios said.

Genatios said scientists warned officials that the area’s history of mudslides and floods would enhance the risks posed by earthquakes. That’s because any buildings would be constructed on the loose, rocky soil that had been deposited there over centuries by floods and mudslides.

The area was also near the major San Sebastian Fault line that runs off the coast and right underneath La Guaira state.

The government disregarded the dangers. In 2011, at Chávez’s direction, it kicked off a massive push to expand public housing to assist people who had been displaced by torrential rains that led to deadly floods and mudslides in late 2010. The government had relocated the displaced — many among them supporters of Chávez’s self-described socialist movement — to public schools, government buildings, military facilities and even the presidential palace.

The government lacked enough land to build its projects, which led to expropriations and to Chávez himself encouraging Venezuelans to help the state compile a list of abandoned lots. As buildings went up, trade and watchdog organizations raised concerns about the projects’ compliance with construction standards, including seismic-resistant design requirements, and the quality of materials used such as cement and steel.

The rise of apartment complexes

Housing towers reminiscent of East Germany’s prefab communist era high-rises were built in Caraballeda as part of the Great Housing Mission Venezuela program. Each tower became known as an “O-P-P,” a shortened version of “O-P-P-P-E,” the Spanish acronym of the office Chávez tasked with carrying out the program. All but four of the 43 towers erected in the state of La Guaira were in Caraballeda.

A state-owned newsletter published a photo of one of the towers with the caption that proclaimed it “proudly stands as a symbol of revolutionary justice.”

People assigned apartments in Caraballeda were delighted when they finally received the keys. Many had lived with relatives or in shelters after being displaced by the 2010 torrential rains. Adults and children finally had bedrooms of their own. Bathrooms came with doors. The beach was a short walk away.

However, they noticed problems right after moving in: Potable water service was essentially nonexistent; elevators stopped working; and trash chutes were breeding grounds for rats and cockroaches.

And they were unaware of the risks during an earthquake. Apartment complexes that were between 10 and 20 floors could end up swaying at the exact same rate as the seismic waves, in a phenomenon known as resonance. The syncing results in the building swaying farther and longer, putting additional pressure on columns and increasing the likelihood of damages and collapse, experts said.

It is unknown whether government contractors followed Venezuela’s building codes. It is also unknown whether officials conducted soil studies before construction began, or whether those studies were ignored. The government has not made public blueprints, soil studies, inspection records or the “descriptive memorandum,” a document that should include engineering and architectural specifications.

Francisco “Farruco” Sesto, who headed the office responsible for Chávez’s housing mission, did not respond to an interview request from AP.

Less than two weeks after the earthquakes, he told an influencer affiliated with the government that land chosen for public housing projects underwent soil studies. He did not show proof to back that assertion, but he did push back on post-earthquake criticism, claiming it is part of an “insidious, malicious campaign” against the housing mission, and he seemingly tried to shift responsibility to the private sector.

“I want to point out that the vast majority of homes built by the state are actually constructed by the private sector as well,” Sesto said. “The state acts as the great organizer — the great planner, if you will … Who performs these soil studies? Primarily, specialized private companies.”

Engineers feared the powerful blow June's quakes delivered

Venezuelans were shocked to see the collapsed buildings by the sea. Scientists were devastated, too, but not surprised. The earthquakes were not just powerful. They dealt the very type of blow engineers fear most — a near-fault pulse.

“It was truly instantaneous — very, very, very violent, very fast,” said Central University of Venezuela geologist Michael Schmitz, who was formerly affiliated with the country’s earthquake-monitoring agency.

Schmitz explained that when the fault shifted, seismic energy stacked up at the front of the rupture as it moved eastward, delivering “a very strong blow to the building’s base.” That pulse, he said, “abruptly knocked the support out from under the building, leaving it unable to dissipate the energy in the way it was designed to do.”

In contrast, buildings on the opposite side of the mountain range, in Caracas, that also have sediment amplification withstood the earthquakes because they were able to sway to dissipate the energy.

Study revealed the quake was particularly devastating

Eduardo Miranda, a Stanford University professor of civil and environmental engineering, and a team of researchers visited Venezuela days after the quake to see if they could determine why the earthquakes had been so devastating.

Without any local instruments or data to determine the intensity of the shaking, Miranda and his team of scientists turned to analyzing video captured by two security cameras near a bowling alley in Caraballeda, the most affected community in La Guaira. The video footage is dramatic: In less than a second, eight buildings collapse simultaneously.

By carefully tracking the motion frame by frame, the team was able to reconstruct how the earthquake produced the motion seen on camera, according to a paper produced by Miranda’s team that was shared with AP.

That analysis revealed one of the largest ground motions ever documented in the world and has provided the only quantitative information of the ground motion of the quake near the rupture. Miranda said it would have been difficult for structures meeting safety standards in Japan, which has among the strictest building codes, to have survived what happened June 24.

The paper under peer review for publication in The Seismic Record, the online journal of the Seismological Society of America, determined that buildings in Caraballeda were pushed so far in one direction for so long that they hit their breaking points, Miranda said.

“The number one reason for the large impact in La Guaira is definitely how strong the ground motion was,” Miranda said in an interview. “Typically, collapses are the result of a number of factors, but that’s an overwhelming main factor of the problems that were there.”

Miranda has yet to share the study’s results with the Venezuelan government, but his team has made officials aware of the analysis.

“It’s clear that they need to raise the level of design,” he said.

Experts worry the government may make the same mistakes again

Styrofoam found among the rubble prompted many residents to accuse the government of using substandard materials to reduce costs. Their accusations were also based on well-documented corruption schemes in which officials and contractors colluded to overbill the state, use cheaper materials than reported and pocket the difference.

The government has not provided any information regarding on-site forensic analyses that experts say are crucial to determine the causes and responsibilities, but its cleanup work, including dynamiting damaged buildings, is underway and so is a rebuilding effort.

The government has estimated that more than 17,000 people were displaced by the earthquakes. Thousands of them have since lived in shelters, encampments or sidewalks near their former homes. Some have also been given homes in public housing buildings in Caracas. The government, however, has also promised to rebuild La Guaira, announcing weeks after the earthquake that it had already located land in that state where construction could soon begin.

Experts said they hope the Venezuelan government doesn’t simply repeat the mistakes of 15 years ago and instead takes a careful and considered approach to its rebuilding efforts. They also said that the additional design and construction work needed to build high-rises capable of resisting earthquakes in the region will likely dissuade the state and some private investors from developing certain areas.

“The question here is: at what cost?” Valdés said. “I would put it another way: how much is a life worth?”

___

Burke reported from San Francisco. Michael Biesecker contributed from Pittsburgh, and Ryan Manzuk and Marshall Ritzel from New York.

Former NFL star wide receiver Antonio Brown is scheduled to be in a Miami courtroom Wednesday to accept a plea deal will let him avoid prison time on a reduced charge in an attempted murder case, according to his attorney.

Defense attorney Mark Eiglarsh has said Brown will plead no contest to aggravated assault and be sentenced to probation. He also said adjudication will be withheld, meaning Brown will not be considered a convicted felon.

Brown could have faced up to 30 years in prison if convicted of the original charge. Eiglarsh has said the agreement with prosecutors was too good to turn down. The Miami-Dade State Attorney’s Office said previously that details would be clarified at the hearing.

Brown is accused of grabbing a handgun from a security staffer after a celebrity boxing match in Miami on May 16, 2025, and firing two shots at a man he was in a fistfight with earlier, according to an arrest warrant. Zul-Qarnain Kwame Nantambu told investigators that one of the bullets grazed his neck.

Brown has said on social media that he was defending himself from an attack and others were trying to steal jewelry from him.

Florida’s Stand Your Ground law allows people who believe they face death or serious injury to use deadly force to defend themselves without a duty to retreat.

Richard Cooper, an attorney for Nantambu, has called the plea deal a fair one. He has said Nantambu forgives Brown and would not cooperate with law enforcement.

Brown, 38, spent 12 years in the NFL and was an All-Pro wide receiver who last played in 2021 for Tampa Bay, including winning a Super Bowl with quarterback Tom Brady.

Over the course of his career, much of it spent with Pittsburgh, he had 928 receptions for more than 12,000 yards and accounted for 88 total touchdowns, including punt returns and one pass.

During a 2021 game with Tampa Bay against the New York Jets, Brown took off his jersey, shoulder pads and gloves and ran off the field, leading to his release by the Buccaneers and effectively ending his career.

Brown has dealt with several legal problems over the years. He previously was accused of battery of a moving truck driver, several domestic violence charges, failure to pay child support and other incidents.

Brown was extradited in November 2025 from Dubai, where he has business interests, after an arrest warrant on the attempted murder charge was issued in June of the same year.

Tennessee is preparing to put to death Christa Gail Pike for a 1995 murder she committed at age 18 in what would be the state's first execution of a woman in at least 200 years.

Pike, now 50, is scheduled to be executed Wednesday morning by lethal injection at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. Pike and her boyfriend were convicted of stabbing and beating 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, their classmate at a job training facility in Knoxville.

The case garnered widespread attention at the time in part because a pentagram that was carved on Slemmer's body and other elements of the crime stoked fears of Satan worship during the “satanic panic” of the 1980s and 1990s. As the execution date drew near, it renewed debate over the death penalty for young offenders.

Pike does not deny committing the killing, but her supporters argue the state should consider Pike’s age at the time, mental illness and a history of severe sexual abuse that included being raped from the time she was a toddler. Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike’s death sentence is an outlier because other 18-year-olds sentenced to death in Tennessee have had their sentences vacated.

The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday denied a request from Pike's attorney's to halt the execution. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee on Monday denied Pike clemency.

“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in a statement included in her clemency petition. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.”

Slemmer’s mother wants the lethal injection to go forward, saying she has waited decades to see Pike’s sentence carried out.

“Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run,” May Martinez said in a telephone interview.

Martinez said a group helped raise money so she and her husband could travel from Florida to witness the execution.

The 1995 killing rocked the city of Knoxville. Prosecutors said Pike, fearing Slemmer was trying to steal her boyfriend, lured her to a wooded area on Jan. 12, 1995. Pike cut Slemmer with a box cutter and beat her with a large chunk of asphalt. Shipp, Pike’s boyfriend, has admitted that he was the one who carved a pentagram, a star-shaped symbol associated with Satanism, into her body.

Shipp was 17 when the crime happened and received a sentence of life in prison with the possibility of parole. Pike was the only one sentenced to death.

Tennessee has not executed a woman for at least 200 years, according to Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. Older records can be spotty, though, so it’s difficult to know precise details about the last woman who was put to death there.

It's a rarity across the U.S. Since 1976, 18 women have been put to death in the country, representing about 1% of all executions, according to the center.

Most recently, Missouri in 2023 executed Amber McLaughlin for a 2003 killing, in what is believed to be the first execution of a transgender woman in the U.S. In 2021, the federal government executed Lisa Montgomery, marking the first time in nearly seven decades that the U.S. government put a female inmate to death.

___

Chandler reported from Montgomery, Alabama.

It’s 1:50am and I’m in a queue down some stairs into what I think is a gay club, but can’t yet be sure.

Ahead are several Turkish men. Within this giant complex are two nightclubs; across the street, a huge mosque casts a shadow over the venue. On the ground floor, down a long corridor, is a straight club. The basement supposedly hosts a gay club.

I’m slightly confused though: surely, these would be closed, dead, or more discrete following recent intense events. It’s a queue I didn’t expect to be in.

Arriving in Istanbul the weekend after the sweeping crackdown on LGBTQ+ clubs, individuals, groups, activists and protesters, I felt a mix of trepidation and defiance.

open image in gallery Gary Nunn on street near Istanbul’s busiest gay bar ( Gary Nunn )

I’ve been coming here annually for 20 years, always as an openly gay man, never hiding who I am. In 2006, mum bought a house in Yalikavak, outside of Bodrum in Turkey. It was intended as a retreat for her and her two kids, irrespective of who they are or who they love. My mum and I were both feeling deeply concerned about the homophobic raids ahead of our trip.

Last September I was at a busy gay bar, Haspa Club, near Bodrum, watching a non-binary belly dancer. I've partied at big gay clubs in Istanbul, where you sometimes transit to get to Bodrum, which is what I’m doing now.

Yet, in Istanbul on Saturday night, it feels like I needn’t have worried. Stay Club is packed full of smiling, dancing, openly gay men and the occasional woman. Some men snog, others grind, few seem deterred. The only hint of nervousness is when staff quickly ask me to put my phone away as I sneak in a photo, which I immediately respect. I ensure nobody’s identifiable in the picture.

I had an inkling it might be like this from two gay bars I visited before the club. One – Sahara Bar – which I visited at peak time (1am Saturday) was as dead as I predicted; just six people in the whole place which, on Google maps, looks erstwhile pumping.

Yet the other bar – Ex Bar – was rammed. It’s Bear Week in Istanbul and nothing, not even intimidating, gun-carrying Turkish police, will prevent the Turkish community of larger, hirsute men from enjoying their special week, which has a packed itinerary of events.

open image in gallery Stay Club Istanbul was packed on a Saturday night ( Gary Nunn )

One man is asked to stop filming bears partaking in a traditional Turkish-style dance, holding hands in a circle, arms horizontally outstretching in time to the dramatic quintessentially Anatolian rock music. I’m invited to join, and take the large hands of two grinning bears for the dance. This is more the Turkey I know and love. There are three rooms of bears and non-bears, dancing like this, and also kissing, smoking, riotously singing and flirting.

Many bears leave Ex Bar to venture to Stay Club, where male gogo dancers on podiums entertain the crowds.

Shouting over the music, partygoer Mustafa* tells me: “They raided this club last week. They checked all our IDs.”

“It’s just politics,” he says, shrugging. “They want to enforce Islam.”

Another reveller I speak to is less nonchalant. Ahmet*, 31, a flight attendant for Turkish Airlines, says he was rattled by a police raid at Ex Bar at 1am the previous Saturday. “They checked all our IDs then sent us home and the bar closed,” he says. “It’s the first time in my life this happened. I was really upset.”

In Cheeky Club, a late night gay venue, the downstairs dancefloor is open but upstairs – usually a darkroom for discrete sexual activity – has closed since the raids.

I wasn’t naive about visiting Turkey; I knew about its conservative streak – partly Islam, partly its longstanding right wing leader, President Erdogan. His government banned Pride events in 2015 and has called gay people like me “deviants”. The country left Eurovision in a huff in 2012, and has since stated it refuses to rejoin because the contest contravenes traditional values, naming Conchita Wurst’s 2014 win as an example.

The recent crackdown is part of a campaign dubbed “My Family is Safe”, which the government alleges protexts “family values and public order” from "obscenity." It’s part of their “Decade of the Family” initiative to address declining birth rates.

open image in gallery Police wait outside a ‘gay-friendly’ hamam ( Gary Nunn )

It interrupts the more on-the-ground laissez-faire attitude towards gay people I’ve experienced in Bodrum and Istanbul, in a country where homosexuality isn’t illegal.

Istanbul has long been known amongs LGBTQ+ people as a thriving hive of homosexual activity. It’s the city where Europe meets Asia and traditional values sit harmoniously alongside distinctly more metropolitan modern ones. It’s the reason I love it.

Similarly, Bodrum has long been a stop on the LGBTQ+ Atlantis cruise, as it was on the one I took in 2022. I told fellow gays on the ship about Bodrum’s live-and-let-live attitude. Nobody reported any problems.

Then, in July, ports in Turkey then Egypt blocked the same LGBTQ+ cruise from docking there, citing "behaviours incompatible with … our moral values."

A disturbing change was underway for British tourists like me who’d mostly felt safe here.

On 13 September, Turkish authorities raided LGBTQ+ organisations, bars, businesses and homes across the country, arresting 162 people.

Two days later, 126 LGBTQ+ activists protesting the raids were detained in Istanbul and the capital, Ankara.

On the Sunday night I visit, outside Istanbul’s “gay-friendly hamam” Firuz Ağa Hamami, a police van waits menacingly the entire night. Inside, gay hamam visitors discuss the raids. One claims the police van is there to protect against gangland violence.

Another – a visitor from Egypt – disagrees. He says police filmed him the night before entering the hamam. He’s still back tonight, but isn’t happy. “This was the wrong week for me to visit Istanbul,” he says. “Police raids shut my favourite gay club – and I’m not attracted to bears.”

Back at my accommodation, Novelty Hotel, Istanbul, I meet a Kurdish man who cannot be out in his country. For him, Istanbul remains the place he escapes to for gay liberation.

The crackdown has led to global pro-LGBTQ+ protests in solidarity and Lord Michael Cashman calling for action in the House of Lords.

open image in gallery Turkish police push back journalists away from people demonstrating outside Istanbul's courthouse to protest over the arrest and growing targeting of LGBTQ+ activists ( AFP/Getty )

At the time of writing, arrests targeting the LGBTQ+ community have grown to include journalists, making me doubly cautious.

Yet I’m also defiant. Some are choosing to take their pink pound elsewhere. As Aidy Smith wrote following the cruise ban: “The [same sex] couple weighing up a package holiday to Bodrum next summer will remember this, as will their friends.” This week, Uncloseted Media’s Spencer Macnaughton wrote: “In 2024, when I flew to Turkey for a hair transplant, I wasn’t too concerned going there as an openly gay man … today, there’s no way in hell I’m travelling back to Istanbul for a touch-up.”

Part of me feels like I’d be doing a disservice to the LGBTQ+ people on the ground in Turkey by boycotting their country at a time they most need international solidarity.

Two bears on Saturday night brought this home for me. “Don’t worry, you’re always safe here,” one said, patting my back. “It’s just cultural stuff.” The other sounded almost triumphant in his resilience. “Last week they raided here, torch lights shining in our eyes, demanding IDs, sending us all home.”

“But look around,” he said, gesticulating to the pumping club. “Tonight, we are all back.”

*names changed

Yes, for sure [this is as good as I’ve felt in an England shirt. My football IQ, I’m getting better and better, smarter and smarter. I need time to really feel at home, to feel comfortable and once I have that I don’t look back.

News.title: How vaccines and antibiotics can beat some cancers
News.content:
At least one in eight cancers worldwide are caused by viruses and bacteria, according to a new study published in The Lancet.

An estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024 – out of a total of 20 million recorded worldwide – were caused by common infections, almost all of which could have been prevented with treatments such as antibiotics or vaccines.

Almost half of infection-linked cancers, around 760,000 cases, were caused by H. pylori, a bacterium that infects the stomach, researchers from the International Agency for Research on Cancer found.

The pathogen, which is typically ingested through contaminated food and water and is carried by around 60 per cent of the world’s population at any given time, can remain relatively undetected in the gut for between 20 and 40 years without causing any symptoms.

If left untreated, it can trigger chronic inflammation in the stomach and cellular mutations that, in some cases, lead to gastric cancer.

Cases of stomach cancer linked to H. pylori are particularly common in East Asia, where roughly 80 per cent of the population carries the bacterium. This is due in part to the prevalence of a more aggressive strain of the pathogen, known as CagA, which is endemic to the region.

East Asian diets – which typically include salty, pickled or smoked foods – can also damage the stomach’s protective lining and accelerate the inflammatory processes that can contribute to stomach cancer, researchers have found.

While H. pylori infection is treatable with a course of antibiotics, its symptoms often mimic those of other digestive problems and can be difficult to distinguish without testing.

This means the infection can remain undetected for years, allowing inflammation and damage to progress.

News.title: ‘Pooled’ TB testing could save money and improve diagnosis, study finds
News.content:
Mixing phlegm samples from multiple patients in “pooled tests” for tuberculosis could halve costs and help find millions of missing cases, according to a major new study.

While most advances in fighting TB come with a large price tag, the shift in strategy could dramatically boost access to diagnosis and save money, experts said.

TB is the deadliest single infection globally, killing around 1.3m people every year, despite being both preventable and curable.

The gold standard in diagnosis is rapid molecular testing, which detects genetic material from the bacteria causing TB in patient sputum samples within hours. But each sample needs a specialist diagnostic cartridge that costs around US$8, beyond the budget of many poorer countries even before recent aid cuts.

In a pooled test, samples from multiple individuals are tested in one cartridge. If the result is negative then all of them are reported to be negative, but if the result is positive each is re-tested individually.

Results published in The Lancet Global Health found the strategy, with up to four patients in each pool, used half as many cartridges as individual testing – 7,028 compared to 14,362. It detected 84.9 per cent of people with TB compared with 88 per cent for individual testing.

The study involved more than 14,000 people whose symptoms suggested TB in Bangladesh, Brazil, Cameroon, Kenya, Malawi, Nigeria and Vietnam.

News.title: UK borrowing costs hit highest level since 2007
News.content:
Britain’s borrowing costs hit their highest level since 2007 after Middle East tensions pushed oil prices above $108.

Yields on 10-year gilts, which determine the price the treasury pays to borrow money, rose above 5.43pc on Monday, before edging back to 5.42pc.

These are levels not seen in almost two decades, underlining the challenge facing John Healey as he prepares for next month’s Budget.

The Chancellor is coming under pressure to slash spending or raise taxes to bring Britain’s borrowing costs under control, against a backdrop of growing debt and rising inflation.

The surge in 10-year gilt yields pushes them above the 19-year high of 5.41pc recorded earlier this month, threatening to put a dent in Mr Healey’s fiscal headroom – a self-imposed guardrail to guide public spending.

Economists said high costs reflect the scale of Britain’s near-£3tn national debt and the rise in inflation facing the country.

“The uncomfortable truth for the PM and his Chancellor, John Healey ... is that the wide spread of gilt yields over peers is fair, in our view, given the UK’s dire fiscal position and the inflationary pressures stemming from high energy prices,” said Elliott Jordan-Doak, at Pantheon Macroeconomics.

“Gilt yields will fall if energy prices drop, but investors will continue to be driven by the economics and the Government’s willingness to take tough fiscal decisions, both of which point to yields staying high.”

UK borrowing costs are growing amid a wider bond market sell-off after Donald Trump rejected a peace deal with Iran over the weekend, pushing oil prices higher.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose by 3pc to just over $108 a barrel on Monday, adding to global inflation pressures. Bond traders reacted by demanding higher yields from governments to lend them money.

The yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds rose to above 5.24pc, the highest level since 2007.
