‘Beyond that, it was about dealing with each player as an individual. Some went on loan, some left, some stayed. Liam Williams went back to Wales. Will Skelton went to La Rochelle. When an organisation is in a situation like that, you have to focus on the people. Make sure each person is treated as well as possible and kept informed with clear communication.’

In 2019, the Saracens players gathered away from the club to privately discuss the future. The senior core pledged to stay and fight. The likes of Farrell, Itoje and Wray all committed to play in the second division and won immediate promotion back to the Premiership.

City might find it harder to retain the likes of Erling Haaland, Rayan Cherki and Ruben Dias in their primes – even if getting back to the top flight should be a formality for a side still fighting at the top of European football.

When Juventus were forcibly relegated in the 2006 Calciopoli scandal, they lost Fabio Cannavaro, Zlatan Ibrahimovic, Patrick Vieira and more to their rivals. But there are still ways that City can retain their stars.

‘The players got together down the pub or the golf club,’ said Wray. ‘We said: “This isn’t great… what are we going to do?”

‘People were at different stages of their careers. Ben Spencer was knocking on the England door and needed to play in the Prem, so he had to leave. That was really sad and emotional. Ben Earl and Max Malins were young and needed to play but didn’t want to leave Saracens, so they went on loan to Bristol.

There may still be ways for City to retain their players if they only drop down one division - young Saracens stars Ben Earl and Max Malins spent a season on loan at Bristol

Saracens won promotion back to the top flight immediately, and two seasons later were champions of England again

'The established England boys who wanted to get picked for the Lions had the right feedback from Eddie Jones and the coaches so they stayed. I suppose if they were told: “Right, if you don’t play in the PREM then you don’t get picked,” then things might have been different.

‘I wasn’t going to turn around on the club and walk away. That’s not really in my nature. A lot of us had been playing together since we were 14. How that compares to Manchester City, I don’t really know. It’s a different team, a different sport, a different culture and it’s still not done. There are too many variables at the moment to have a direct comparison.

‘Nigel Wray (the Saracens chairman who retired after the scandal, and is no relation to Jackson) was the most caring man in the room, always there for me, never forgot the kids' birthday. All these things matter, so we weren’t going to turn around and throw in the towel.

‘It’s hard for any club to sustain success over 20 years but now the club is back with fresh energy under Brendan Venter. We ended up coming back and reaching the final. The journey back from there was one of the proudest things I’ve been part of.’

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel admits he has a 'bad conscience' for not checking on England's Man City stars amid guilty verdict on financial 'sham' - and suggests why Jude Bellingham could be his next England captain
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel admitted that he regretted not checking in with the Manchester City players in his England squad before kick-off against Czechia, just hours after the Premier League confirmed a guilty verdict against the club for serious financial breaches.

Daily Mail Sport reported on Friday that the top-flight side had been found to have committed significant breaches of financial regulations between 2009 and 2018, with the Premier League's official confirmation released alongside a bombshell statement on Tuesday.

But despite the seismic news likely rocking players including starters in Prague Elliot Anderson and Marc Guehi, and Nico O'Reilly, who travelled with the squad, Tuchel revealed after the whistle that the over 115 charges had not been on his mind.

'I have a bad conscience now,' he told BBC Radio 5 Live when asked if he had spoken to Guehi, Anderson, and O'Reilly. 'I did not actually because I am just focused on everything we have to deal with here and to prepare the team.'

Supporters wondered what had captured the attention of Guehi and O'Reilly in particular after they were snapped at the Fortuna Stadium listening to audio on one of their mobile phones.

While it has not been confirmed what the players were listening to - if anything - club chief executive Ferran Soriano released a video shared with the organisation's 1,000-strong staff doubling down on the club's innocence amid a Premier League 'conspiracy theory'.

Thomas Tuchel admitted that he had a 'bad conscience' for focusing solely on England's Nations League tie

His squad contains a number of Man City stars including Marc Guehi and Nico O'Reilly

Premier League CEO Richard Masters claimed Man City's breaches, which included over £900m-worth of 'sham' deals and deliberate attempts to frustrate the league's investigations, showed the club had ‘systematically broken Premier League rules for nearly a decade’.

After the final whistle in Prague, Tuchel also suggested that Jude Bellingham might follow Harry Kane as England's next captain.

Bellingham took the armband when he replaced skipper Kane 20 minutes from the end of last night's 2-0 Nations League win over the Czech Republic in Prague.

Asked afterwards if that was a glimpse into the future, the England manager said: 'If you are the captain at the end of these matches, you can for sure be the permanent captain.

'It's a reward. It's good. I think he loves to be with us at the moment. That's what I feel.

'We had a small talk today about his role and said maybe 30 minutes is enough because he hasn't played in this quick turnaround throughout this season.

'He has done it before, but not in this season, so we didn't want to be the first ones to try that.

'But even in this little encounter you can see that he's confident and happy to even help from the bench.'

Tuchel also revealed that Bellingham reported a slight niggle at the end of the game. England play in Croatia on Saturday and then at home to last night's opponent next Tuesday.

'Hopefully it's nothing serious and he's available for selection,' said Tuchel.

Sports.title: Man United suffer ANOTHER blow as Noussair Mazraoui is forced off injured on Morocco duty - days after star man Bruno Fernandes pulled out of Portugal squad with 'complicated' shin problem
Sports.content:
Manchester United's injury woes over the international break continued on Tuesday night as Noussair Mazraoui was forced off during Morocco's 2-0 win over Lesotho.

At the weekend, Red Devils captain Bruno Fernandes was forced to pull out of Portugal's squad to play Norway with what his manager Jorge Jesus described as a 'complicated' shin problem, in the latest injury blow to Manchester United.

Michael Carrick, who was already without key first-team players Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo, Amad Diallo, Benjamin Sesko and Patrick Dorgu before Fernandes' injury, will now be sweating over Mazraoui's availability after the full-back hobbled off against Lesotho.

As the Moroccan dived in for a tackle in the 68th minute of the Africa Cup of Nations qualifier, he landed awkwardly and immediately signalled towards the bench, appearing in a lot of discomfort.

After holding his lower back in pain, Mazraoui managed to sit upright before being assessed by medical staff and eventually left the field, with Paris Saint-Germain star Achraf Hakimi replacing him.

England duo Rashford and Mainoo were both forced to withdraw from Thomas Tuchel's Nations League squad last week after picking up minor injuries during United's disappointing 1-1 draw with Fulham before the international break.

Man United's Noussair Mazraoui was forced off with injury during Morocco's win over Lesotho

The Morocco full-back landed awkwardly and immediately signalled to the bench after a tackle

While Carrick will hope the pair are available to face Spurs in United's next match at Old Trafford on October 10, there are concerns over Fernandes' fitness after Portugal boss Jesus admitted he has been 'playing with pain' since the start of the season.

‘In the game against Wales, we went in with all the available players but Bruno Fernandes came off with a complicated problem,’ he said during Portugal's press conference on Saturday, before the United captain withdrew from the squad.

‘We’ll see what happens until tomorrow. Experience tells me that on the third day not all players manage to recover but that’s the same for Norway as for us. However, the player who comes in gives as many guarantees as the one who might come off, that’s what I’ll base my decision on.

‘The medical team identified these two players as the most concerning, Nuno Mendes could be available for the game.

‘The other case [Fernandes] involves treatment and recovery time. He’s coming off an injury at United, and he told me he’s been playing with that pain for the last three games, which is hindering him.

‘It was one of the factors that prevented Bruno from playing at his best against Wales.’

It comes days after United's star man Bruno Fernandes missed Portugal's clash with Norway

Carrick has endured a difficult start to the season since being appointed Manchester United's permanent manager in the summer, winning just once in five matches despite facing Fulham, who were bottom of the league before hosting the Red Devils, as well as newly promoted sides Hull City and Ipswich Town.

After a slow start, Carrick faces a huge eight days when his players return from international duty in October, with bottom-of-the-table Tottenham, Champions League stalwarts Atletico Madrid and fierce rivals Leeds United all awaiting the Red Devils during that period.

Sports.title: 'There's no penalty strong enough!': Former Man City chairman David Bernstein sends warning after club found guilty of £900m 'sham' in 'worse than expected' verdict
Sports.content:
Former Manchester City chairman David Bernstein has admitted that confirmation that his old club is guilty of the most serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules on Tuesday is 'worse than expected'.

Man City were found to have disguised payments totalling over £900m over a nine-year period during which time the club won nine trophies, including their first-ever Premier League title in a damning 40-page verdict handed out by the league on Tuesday.

Following a lengthy investigation by an Independent Commission, City were also deemed to have failed to co-operate with the Premier League - with witnesses called on behalf of the club accused of 'dishonesty' during the hearing itself.

After Daily Mail Sport first reported that the charges had been upheld on Friday, Bernstein had suggested that the club should be stripped of its titles if guilty.

But in the wake of Tuesday's bombshell ruling release, he was left aghast and wondering if there could be a penalty 'strong enough' to sanction the club he has supported since boyhood.

'We knew it wasn't going to be good, but it looks worse than I thought it would do,' Bernstein said of the Premier League's incendiary statement on talkSPORT. 'I can't go through all the charges individually, but they include producing false documentation and duplicate contracts and so on, which has been done systematically over a number of years - you can't have anything much more severe than that.

👀 "Looks worse than I thought!"



😤 "The directors would have to stand down!"



Former Man City Chairman, David Bernstein, calls for the Man City board of directors to be suspended! pic.twitter.com/a1wAVbMYH0 — talkSPORT (@talkSPORT) September 29, 2026

Former Manchester City chairman David Bernstein has admitted that the verdict on his old club was 'worse than expected'

Chief executive Ferran Soriano (left, with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak) has doubled down on the club's 'innocence'

'I would be very careful with the language I use, but if this was a commercial situation, I would say this is very close to something fraudulent.

'The wording couldn't be more damning, and I've got to give some credit to the Premier League and the people who did all this for coming up with such a detailed scenario,' he added, stressing that it would not have been easy, but that it 'had to be done'.

Following the release of the Premier League's public verdict, Man City responded with their own statement which stated they had been 'surprised and disappointed' by what the club referred to as the 'opinion' of the commission.

In a video circulated to Man City's 1,000-strong staff, chief executive Ferran Soriano railed against the Premier League's 'conspiracy theories' against City and vowed that the club would stop at nothing to defend its innocence.

Man City have until Friday, October 2 to appeal before a decision is taken over how the club will be sanctioned, but Bernstein remained convinced that a drawn-out appeal process followed by a heavy punishment would represent the worst-possible scenario.

'If it drags on for a year or two, heaven forbid, I think that would be the worst thing for everybody,' he continued. 'But all I would say is that (a punitive financial fine) is not sufficient now.

'If these charges stand now, and let's say the appeal does not happen or fails, then I'm afraid for the club I love, that they've got to come out of the Premier League. This is beyond awful.

'I can't think my penalty is strong enough for this. This is absolutely terrible.'

Bernstein also added that he would be interested to see if those at the very top of the Man City hierarchy would be penalised.

'The directors of the club, including the chief executive, who's been there for years and worked through this period, are responsible for the running of the club in every respect,' he noted. 'If this was a public company, I think the directors, with something as serious as this, (would) have to stand down or be suspended, pending the outcome.'

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said in a statement that he believed the commission's verdict had 'vindicated' the league's pursuit of the charges, a process which began nearly three years ago.

‘It is a key responsibility of the Premier League to ensure that the Rules, approved by the clubs themselves, are upheld to protect the integrity of the competition,’ he said. ‘It is paramount that the League remains competitive and fair for all clubs and for the fans. We take that role extremely seriously.

‘This disciplinary case, and this decision, are the most significant in Premier League history. There are elements of the case that remain to be decided, including, importantly, what sanction must follow for these breaches. Now we have the Commission’s decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the League, our clubs and fans.’

The panel found City arranged ‘sham contracts (which misrepresented the true agreement between the parties) with a number of its commercial partners, as well as relying on ‘sham’ agreements with others, to artificially inflate the club’s revenues and reduce its costs’.

It added that the panel, whose hearing concluded in December 2024, had found that the club had falsely altered the financial picture at the Etihad to the tune of £900m.

The Premier League said that City was actually ‘significantly in breach of both the Premier League’s and UEFA’s spending limits’ during the time period in question - 2009-2018 - when it won eight major trophies.

Deals with a number of sponsors were part of ‘a disguised funding scheme, whereby those companies were only required to pay a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees’, the statement added, saying that ‘the remainder was funded by Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club’.

The panel also found further ‘sham’ arrangements, funded by ADUG, which allowed City to record lower operating expenses than it incurred, along with a ‘”sham” circular arrangement with Fordham, an entity that purchased the club’s players’ image rights, that was funded by ADUG’.

The result was that the club had ‘filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators’.

Had City reported accurately ‘it would have been in breach of both the League’s and UEFA’s spending limits by a very substantial amount’.

The panel also found that City committed multiple breaches of its duties of co-operation and good faith in that it failed to assist the Premier League’s four-year investigation, triggered by the emergence of club emails obtained by a hacker.

Instead, City had ‘made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the Premier League investigation’.

In Man City's statement shared in the wake of the release, the club claimed that it had 'irrefutable evidence' that proved its innocence.

‘The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted,' the statement continued. 'Manchester City will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.’

Sports.title: OLIVER HOLT: Man City have been exposed as the most famous cheats in English sporting history. The gory details revealed by the Premier League leave no doubt - nothing less than relegation will suffice for this sinister, dishonest club
Sports.content:
OLIVER HOLT: Man City have been exposed as the most famous cheats in English sporting history. The gory details revealed by the Premier League leave no doubt - nothing less than relegation will suffice for this sinister, dishonest club

Oliver Holt Chief Sports Writer

The Premier League shoved the owners of Manchester City into a beam of light on a dark stage on Tuesday evening. And the club that has dominated English football for much of the last 20 years stood there, defrocked and unmasked. Guilty of all charges, the League said. But that was not all it said.

In fact, it was the tone of the League’s statement that was the most startling thing about it. They are often circumspect and dull, these offerings. Not this time. This time, it was angry and it was vengeful.

It gloried in the gory details of the industrial-scale cheating it said City had indulged in for year after year as it duped the rest of football with a ‘disguised funding scheme’.

The anger was in the vocabulary, too. ‘Sham contracts,’ the Premier League statement hissed as it outlined the tactics of the Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club.

‘Sham commercial deals,' it added later. Sham, sham, sham. Some had been expecting a conciliatory move from the League in the wake of its victory but this was anything but that.

To read that statement was to see the Premier League dancing on the grave of the club that had come to embody its excellence and its appeal. All the exasperation and all the frustration of years of obstruction and intransigence from City’s Abu Dhabi owners as they fought the 115 charges ranged against them came spilling out on that page.

This was an end to patience. This was an end to keeping one’s counsel. This was an end to diplomacy.

After the accusation, this was the confrontation. The most eye-catching part of it was the revelation of the extent of City’s wrongdoing. This was the juiciest steak the Premier League had to offer and they tossed it out into the public domain with uncommon relish.

‘The purpose of these schemes,’ its statement said, ‘was found to have been to artificially inflate the club’s revenues, and reduce its costs, by more than £900million during the affected period, to appear to comply with financial rules.’

The Premier League have accused Manchester City of 'artificially (inflating) the club’s revenues, and (reducing) its costs, by more than £900million'

To read that statement was to see the Premier League dancing on the grave of the club that had come to embody its excellence and its appeal under (from left) Khaldoon Al Mubarak, Txiki Begiristain and Ferran Soriano

This is English football’s civil war in all its ugliness and its violence and its ferocity. The League’s statement hinted at what is to come. City have until Friday to launch an appeal, which they will almost certainly do but when that is done, it appears the League will press for severe sanctions to quell the inferno of City’s misdemeanours.

The level of City’s duplicity, outlined by the Premier League, laid bare the extent of the advantage that they had gained over the period involved. The punishment will have to fit that. It is harder to see City escaping relegation than it was on Tuesday morning. Anything lesser than that, the League will surely believe, will not be enough to deal with the crimes uncovered.

In the hours that followed the release of the statement, television screens showed reruns of City’s moments of triumph – Phil Foden holding aloft the Premier League trophy on one of the club’s many open-top bus rides, Pep Guardiola and City’s chairman, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, standing together on the pitch at the Etihad Stadium, holding up six fingers to signify the number of leagues Guardiola won.

The footage did not speak of triumphs any more, though. It spoke of subterfuge and shame. Those scenes of jubilation, it now appears, were dishonestly earned. Those trophies were dishonestly won. The club had cheated and cheated and cheated to get to a position where it was held up as the exemplar of all that was good in the game.

The more we know, the worse this feels. The more we know, the more stupid we seem that we were duped, that we believed.

This is moving into Lance Armstrong territory now. This is Chicago Black Sox territory. City, a team once famous for hitting new heights of dominance, are now the most famous cheats in English sporting history.

Their owners are still sticking to their story, even in the face of the findings of the independent commission and the details now provided by the Premier League. Their response has not been humility or contrition. Their response has been, actually, the sinister language of threat and reprisal.

City’s owners are serious people. Al Mubarak, many say, is the equivalent of the prime minister of the UAE. Others equate his role to cabinet secretary. He wields much power and he is the guardian of much wealth. No one takes him on like this and now that someone has, he is fighting to the end.

For now, City are sticking to Al Mubarak’s insistence that they have ‘irrefutable evidence’ that proves their innocence.

It is a curious defence. If the evidence is irrefutable, why has it not been presented already? Why has it been hidden away? Were these men not so powerful and astute, it would be tempting to say that their stance is becoming faintly comical.

The more we know, the more stupid we seem that we were duped, that we believed. Some would say this whole affair is moving into Lance Armstrong territory now

City are sticking to Al Mubarak’s insistence that they have ‘irrefutable evidence’ that proves their innocence. If the evidence is irrefutable, where is it?

‘Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission,’ a City statement said. ‘The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.

'The club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.’

Relentless? That is redolent of Al Mubarak’s notorious assertion more than a decade ago, when City were fighting UEFA, that he would rather spend £30m on the best 50 lawyers in the world and sue UEFA for the next 10 years than lose the Financial Fair Play case in which they were adversaries.

I wonder if some of those who have lionised Al Mubarak for his statements will reconsider now. They said they would when it came to a point when City’s guilt was outlined for all to see. Well, it is out there now. It is there in all its sad and ugly detail. Perhaps some of City’s fans will start to realise now that they, too, have been deceived.

City’s owners, though, will not back down. It is not their style. After months and years of shadow-boxing, the gloves are off. And City stand alone in the ring.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's £150m mega-fight is back ON: Heavyweight rivals set to meet in London face off TOMORROW after Gypsy King claimed rival 'tried to pull out' amid Eddie Hearn's feud with Dana White
Sports.content:
It's on. At last. Finally. Confirmed by the almighty Turki.

Reconfirmed by the late, late word sent out that the face to face stare down between our two heavyweight titans will definitely take place at a press conference launch this Wednesday.

The fight that almost got away. AJ versus the Gypsy King. So close to being another of boxing's lost jewels that we almost gave up hope.

May the lords of the rings be praised.

Whether or not Dana White, the American interloper from UFC cage fighting who is demanding a share of the action, is present despite the protestations of Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn, who won the battle for this fight to take place if not at Wembley but not as far, far west of London as New York.

Anthony Joshua v Tyson Fury has been rescued for the British fight fans, by Cardiff. Although like the 70-odd thousand in the Principality Stadium the TV majority will have to stay awake into the wee small hours on the Friday night of December 11.

Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury will face each other down at a press conference on Wednesday

Fury and Joshua's fight is due to take place on December 11 in Cardiff with the showdown set to begin at 2am so Netflix subscribers can stream it at peak time in America

Fury against Joshua was almost the fight that got away, with the heavyweights now set to sort out differences that should have been settled a decade ago

First bell about 2am so that the tens of millions of Netflix subscribers can stream at peak time in America.

Assuming they buy into this as being a mega fight for all time. Or are satisfied that it is a spectacle unto itself.

Maybe a world heavyweight title adding spice to the occasion. Maybe not. Maybe just two good old Brits sorting differences that should have been settled a decade ago.

And why not? Fury and Joshua may be past their prime but they are not yet the walking dead.

They have enough fight left in their late 30s to put on a show.

And a future to fight for. For the winner there can be challenges to meet from the new generation of champions and a few million dollars more to add to the 75 million each will receive as an early Christmas present.

Always assuming no more spanners are thrown into these on-off-on works.

Good luck to both. Even more so to the Welsh constabulary who will have to deal with all those fans spilling out into darkened streets on what will already be a typically wild Friday night in Cardiff.

Sports.title: Scotland dealt harsh lesson by Switzerland as new boss Sebastien Pocognoli's home bow ends in 3-0 defeat: Moment of madness proves costly on another sobering night
Sports.content:
Scotland dealt harsh lesson by Switzerland as new boss Sebastien Pocognoli's home bow ends in 3-0 defeat: Moment of madness proves costly on another sobering night

To borrow an old line from Mike Tyson, everyone has a plan until they get punched in the face. Just eight minutes into his first match in charge at Hampden, Sebastien Pocognoli took one flush on the chin.

Whatever designs Scotland’s new head coach may have had on causing an upset against Switzerland in this Nations League clash, it all went to pot in double-quick time.

A moment of utter madness from Jack Hendry, with a crude and brainless last-man foul on Switzerland striker Dan Ndoye, saw Pocognoli’s side reduced to ten men.

Switzerland boss Murat Yakin had missed his pre-match media conference on Monday due to hearing problems caused by cabin pressure on the flight into Glasgow.

Hendry looked like he was towing a Boeing 747 in his efforts to run back and chase the jet-heeled Ndoye as he raced through on goal.

The fact that Switzerland defender Ricardo Rodriguez, a free-kick expert throughout his career, then curled one into the top corner from the subsequent set-piece poured salt into Scottish wounds.

Elvedi slides home the second goal at the near post in Switzerland's 3-0 victory at Hampden

Ricardo Rodriguez (far left) celebrates his free-kick opener against Scotland

Up against a slick and stylish Swiss side, this was always likely to be a tough assignment even with 11 players on the field.

Playing 82 minutes with a numerical disadvantage? Mission impossible. Scotland deserve credit for sticking to the task and not just capitulating after that horror start.

They briefly threatened an equaliser at times midway through the first half and the Hampden crowd were clearly appreciative of the effort.

But, ultimately, this was a damp squib. On what was supposed to be a thunderous Hampden bow for Pocognoli and his new-look Scots, it turned into a training exercise for Switzerland.

As such, it was impossible to properly gauge Pocognoli and the performance from his team. They spent the majority of the night operating with one hand tied behind their back.

They must now lick their wounds and dust themselves down ahead of a trip to face North Macedonia in Skopje on Saturday night.

A total of 123 days had passed since Scotland set sail for the World Cup with a 4-1 victory over Curacao in their Hampden send-off.

It doesn’t sound all that long ago when you put it like that. But the scale of the changes — both in terms of the players and a new head coach — have been significant.

As they made their way back to Mount Florida, the Tartan Army were probably still familiarising themselves with some of the new faces in Pocognoli’s squad.

Luis Binks was the latest player to be handed a debut, the Brondby captain coming in to replace Stephen Welsh in central defence.

That was one of three changes made by Pocognoli from the 0-0 draw away in Slovenia last Saturday, with Nathan Patterson and Kieron Bowie also coming in to replace Aaron Hickey and Robbie Ure.

Jack Hendry was given his marching orders early on and left Scotland with a mountain to climb

The first half in Ljubljana had been an eyesore, but Scotland were vastly improved in a dominant second half. On a different day, they could — and perhaps *should* — have won by two or three goals.

This was always likely to be a far stiffer test. Over the past 20 years or so, Switzerland have been a model of consistency in international football.

Back in the summer, they pushed Argentina all the way to extra-time in the quarter-finals of the World Cup and were unlucky to lose in the end.

Even without their captain Granit Xhaka, who withdrew from the squad due to an investigation into a fake Covid vaccine certificate, they were still expected to be formidable opposition.

The Swiss had opened their Nations League campaign with an emphatic 3-0 win over North Macedonia in Skopje, with Zeki Amdouni scoring two of their three goals.

Scotland were clearly intent on pressing the Swiss high up the pitch in the early stages. Picking up where he left off in Ljubljana, Billy Gilmour glided past a couple of red jerseys and fed a through ball for Bowie to chase.

The big striker outmuscled Leeds United defender Nico Elvedi and fired the ball across the face of goal before the visitors managed to clear the danger.

But the air of optimism around Hampden was soon shattered by a rapier-like attack from Switzerland right through the centre of the pitch that would ultimately see the home side reduced to ten men.

After a neat combination in midfield, the ball was played through for Ndoye to chase. One-on-one in a foot race with Hendry, there was only ever likely to be one winner.

Zeki Amdouni fires home the third goal as Switzerland cruised to a comfortable success

Ndoye was racing clear only to be clumsily hauled down just as he could see the whites of Angus Gunn’s eyes and was about to pull the trigger.

Serbian referee Nenad Minakovic initially gave a penalty-kick and booked Hendry. The fact he was blatantly the last man was offset by the double jeopardy law.

But when TV replays showed that the contact had initially started outside the box? Hendry was a dead man walking.

Red card. All day long and twice on Sundays. As he jogged off the field and headed for the tunnel, there was no acknowledgement from Pocognoli.

It was thoroughly dim-witted from Hendry. What on earth was he thinking? The smart play would have been either to let Ndoye shoot and potentially score, or make sure the contact was inside the box.

Either way, Scotland would have kept 11 men on the pitch in their efforts to mount a comeback. When Ricardo Rodriguez then curled a peach of a free-kick into Gunn’s top corner, it was the ultimate double whammy.

Open the touchline, Pocognoli urgently tried to reshuffle the pack. Off came Bowie and on came Welsh. It became a sort of 5-3-1 shape.

Gilmour was still having some excellent moments, drifting away from another challenge before firing the ball out wide to Andy Robertson.

Robertson’s low ball in was intended for Oli McBurnie, only for Elvedi to intervene at the near post. McBurnie also tangled with Remo Freuler on the edge of the box but threw himself to the ground too easily.

Against all the odds, another promising Scotland attack was undone by a clumsy touch from Robertson. Nonetheless, the Tartan Army roared their approval. There was still a game on here.

At the other end, Gunn made a good low save one-handed to deny Ndoye after a clever dummy from Amdouni on the edge of the box.

It became a bruising night for Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli in the Hampden dugout

Switzerland just had so much class and control, capable of flicking a switch and moving up through the gears at any moment.

The referee was needlessly picky at times and Pocognoli, decked out in a dark suit and shirt à la Diego Simeone, was booked towards the end of the first half for some fiery protestations on the touchline.

The mood of the new Scotland head coach wouldn’t have improved much when Switzerland doubled their lead just 10 minutes after the break, Elvedi converting an Ndoye cross from close range.

For Scotland, the final half-hour or so became an exercise in damage limitation. The game was gone. Switzerland continued to threaten, with Ndoye and Amdouni again going close.

The outstanding Amdouni rifled one into the top corner for 3-0 with just under ten minutes left to play. In the end, Scotland were soundly beaten.

That may well have been the outcome had they kept 11 players on the pitch for 90 minutes. We’ll never know. But this was a sobering night.

Sports.title: Roy Keane claims Man City stars should BIN their medals won during period of 'cheating' and hits out at owners after club found guilty of £900m 'sham' in seismic Premier League verdict
Sports.content:
Roy Keane says he would bin his medals if he was a Manchester City player after they were found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules for nine seasons.

The Manchester United legend fears it will be hard for the current crop under Enzo Maresca to maintain their elite levels of performance under the cloud of 'cheating owners'.

The Premier League has condemned City for making 'sham' agreements to manipulate their financial accounts to the tune of £900million over a nine-season period which saw them win eight trophies.

'They knew it would hurt a lot of people but they've still done it,' Keane told ITV Sport after England's 2-0 win over Czechia in the Nations League.

'If I was a player, I'd be 100 per cent sticking those medals in the bin. Of course you would, it's cheating.

'They won it on the pitch because cheating was going on.

Roy Keane has claimed he would throw away his medals if he was a Manchester City player

The Premier League have confirmed that Manchester City are guilty of the most serious financial rule breaches

'I think it's going to be very difficult for the players and the manager, the club, what they stand for, when you've got owners who are happy cheating. It's hard to maintain a level of excellence.'

Ian Wright added: 'They told them nothing bad is going on. If you're a player, something is not right.

'It's very unprecedented and sad for everybody. The owners and what they've done, terrible.'

Before the match, Wright had said: 'Unprecedented punishment is required here. It's a massive day for the Premier League.

'Very messy. It's a problem for them to be going to Liverpool (in their next fixture). In their real time, Liverpool were the team chasing them down. Look at what Jurgen Klopp went through to break them - it probably broke him.'

On Friday, Daily Mail Sport reported how City had been found guilty of 114 of 115 charges against them.

However, there had been no official comment from the Premier League on the findings of an independent panel who oversaw a hearing that concluded in December 2024.

That has now dramatically changed. In a lengthy statement, the Premier League say City arranged 'sham contracts (which misrepresented the true agreement between the parties) with a number of its commercial partners, as well as relying on "sham" agreements with others, to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs'.

It also says the club falsely altered the financial picture at the Etihad to the tune of £900m. The club had agreed exorbitant sponsorship deals with a number of companies, but those sponsors only paid part of the fee.

The rest was propped up by the Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club.

Premier League CEO Richard Masters claimed that the commission's verdict had 'vindicated' the league's decision to pursue the charges

As the Premier League note, this allowed City to 'artificially inflate the club’s revenues' and therefore spend more under Premier League rules. The higher the revenue a club records, the more they are permitted to spend.

Moreover, further 'sham' deals, funded by ADUG, allowed the club to 'record lower operating expenses than it actually incurred'.

The Premier League say that revenues were inflated and costs reduced to the tune of £900m in an attempt to comply with spending rules. The result was that the club 'filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators'.

It added that the club was 'significantly in breach of both the Premier League's and UEFA's spending limits' during the time period in question, 2009-2018 when it won eight major trophies.

Had City reported accurately 'it would have been in breach of both the League's and UEFA's spending limits by a very substantial amount'.

The panel also found that City committed multiple breaches of its duties of co-operation and good faith in that it failed to assist the Premier League's four-year investigation, triggered by the emergence of club emails obtained by a hacker.

Indeed, City had 'made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the PL investigation'.

Richard Masters, Chief Executive of the Premier League, said: 'The core decision establishes the facts of what happened at Manchester City during this period. It details how the club systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade.

'It also vindicates the Premier League's decision to pursue this case against Manchester City. While the process to date has been both long and difficult, the League has remained determined that the facts be established independently.

'It is a key responsibility of the Premier League to ensure that the Rules, approved by the clubs themselves, are upheld to protect the integrity of the competition. It is paramount that the League remains competitive and fair for all clubs and for the fans. We take that role extremely seriously.

'This disciplinary case, and this decision, are the most significant in Premier League history. There are elements of the case that remain to be decided, including, importantly, what sanction must follow for these breaches. Now we have the Commission's decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the League, our clubs and fans.'

Manchester City have insisted on their innocence throughout the saga (Pep Guardiola pictured with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak)

In a statement released a short time later, City said it was ‘disappointed and surprised’ and referred to the ‘opinion of the Premier League Commission’.

It added: ‘The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.

‘The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

‘The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.

‘The club is obviously restricted in what it can say further until all future proceedings are complete.’

City have until Friday to appeal.

Man City were first charged with the 115 breaches in February 2023. While that totemic number stuck, the figure – as they subsequently corrected – was actually 130.

Of those, 54 were charges of ‘failure to provide accurate and up-to-date financial information’ while there were 14 charges of ‘failure to provide accurate financial reports for player and manager compensation’.

Both sets related to alleged offences between 2009 and 2018 (2009-2018), an eight-year period which saw the club win four Premier League titles, the FA Cup, and three League Cup competitions.

There were also five charges of ‘failure to comply with UEFA’s regulations, including Financial Fair Play Regulations’ and seven charges of breaching the Premier League’s profit and sustainability regulations (PSR) between 2015 and 2018.

There were also 35 counts of failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations between 2018 and 2023.

The hearing into the 130 breaches began last September at London’s International Dispute Resolution Centre, with the Premier League sparing no expense and enlisting KCs Adam Lewis and Andrew Hunter to take its case.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.

This article originally appeared in The Athletic.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
