29th Tuesday, September 2026 - 21:37 UTC Full article

“Men don't like to have the prostate test. They don't like the touch. Women learn to receive touch from a young age. Men don't, they're full of hang-ups,” he said

A remark by Brazilian President and re-election candidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva about men's reluctance to undergo prostate examinations has sparked a controversy in the final stretch of the campaign, after opposition figures linked it to child sexual abuse. Lula's campaign has taken the matter to the Superior Electoral Court.

Lula spoke on Monday at an event in Belém, capital of Pará state, after the first robotic prostate surgery carried out by the public health system in the country's north. “Men don't like to have the prostate test. They don't like the touch. Women learn to receive touch from a young age. Men don't, they're full of hang-ups. They don't know that when they get prostate cancer, they'll be touched a lot,” he said. In the same speech he recalled that his mother died of cancer.

Liberal Party deputy Nikolas Ferreira responded on X: “A little girl doesn't learn to receive any touch, Lula!” Other figures from the party, whose candidate is Flávio Bolsonaro, joined the criticism, and messages linking the remark to the abuse of minors spread on the platform.

Lula's coalition filed an action on Tuesday with the Superior Electoral Court against Ferreira's posts, accusing him of attributing a sexual connotation to the statement. According to the campaign, the president was speaking about public health and comparing male reluctance over prostate exams with the gynaecological check-ups women undergo from puberty.

The first round of Brazil's election takes place on Sunday, October 4.

World.title: A falsehood about Brazil's patron saint pits Supreme Court justices against each other mid-campaign
World.content:
A falsehood about Brazil's patron saint pits Supreme Court justices against each other mid-campaign

29th Tuesday, September 2026 - 21:00 UTC Full article

Bolsonaro accused members of the National Conference of Bishops of Brazil of helping the Workers' Party spread the falsehood

A false report that presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro backed stripping Our Lady of Aparecida of her title as Brazil's patron saint has produced contradictory rulings from three Supreme Federal Court justices, a clash with the Catholic bishops' conference and a dispute dominating the final week of campaigning before Sunday's vote.

The claim has no basis. It rests on a bill introduced in 2007 by an evangelical deputy, which was shelved the following year. Bolsonaro, a Liberal Party senator and an evangelical, denied supporting any such initiative and released several videos to that effect. “It is the biggest fake news of this campaign,” he said.

The episode was amplified by a post from comedian Antonio Tabet which, without naming the candidate, associated his family with a supposed attack on the patron saint. At Bolsonaro's request, Justice André Mendonça ordered it removed; on Sunday, Justice Flávio Dino suspended that order and restored the content; Justice Luiz Fux again ordered its removal, and the case went to the full court. The Superior Electoral Court had also ordered posts on the subject taken down.

Bolsonaro accused members of the National Conference of Bishops of Brazil of helping the Workers' Party spread the falsehood. The body denied it in a note stating that “a lie is not fought with another lie”. The candidate later said the text confirmed the report was false and thanked the bishops.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, seeking re-election, said on Monday at a rally in Belém: “As long as I am president of the Republic, no one will dishonour Our Lady of Aparecida,” and called for respect for all religions, including those of African origin. His running mate, Geraldo Alckmin, and other allied candidates released messages aimed at Catholic voters.

The use of religious falsehoods is not new in Brazilian campaigns. Folha de S.Paulo columnist Hélio Schwartsman recalled that in 2018 a claim circulated that Workers' Party candidate Fernando Haddad would distribute material on sexual diversity in schools, and in 2022 that Lula would close churches; in both cases the party went to the electoral courts to have them removed. “Campaigns do not hesitate to embrace the fake news that favours them,” he wrote.

The Quaest poll published on Monday gave Lula 39% and Bolsonaro 34% in the first round, and a 42% tie in a prospective October 25 runoff. The only debate planned with both candidates would take place on Thursday on TV Globo; Bolsonaro confirmed his attendance and Lula had not formally responded.

World.title: Chile's defence minister backs trade between Punta Arenas and the Falklands
World.content:
Chile's defence minister backs trade between Punta Arenas and the Falklands

29th Tuesday, September 2026 - 09:02 UTC Full article

Asked how closer trade ties would fit with regional commitments, Barros said the “potentially most contentious” point is oil and mining exploration

Chile's Defence Minister Fernando Barros Tocornal has backed the development of commercial activity between the Magallanes region and the Falklands, saying his country's support for Argentina's sovereignty claim does not imply restrictions on trade with the archipelago. He made the remarks in an interview with Radio Polar in Punta Arenas during a visit to the region on September 24 and 25.

According to his comments, reported on Sunday by the Argentine daily La Nación, the Magallanes community has “the right to trade” and the minister sees “no impediments to those activities going ahead” within the legal framework.

Barros reiterated Chile's support for Buenos Aires, though with a nuance. “Chile has expressed its support for the Argentine claim, its sovereignty claim over the Malvinas or Falklands, but there is a fact: a friendly country has exercised sovereignty over the islands for 200 years,” he said, referring to the United Kingdom, which has administered the archipelago since 1833, with the 1982 interruption. He added that such support must be expressed in line with international law, “respecting the will and interest of the people involved and by peaceful means”. Argentina's position holds that the will of the archipelago's residents is not decisive in resolving the dispute. La Nación described the remarks as “at the very least confusing”.

The minister's words do not formally alter Chile's diplomatic position. On September 3, Presidents José Antonio Kast and Javier Milei signed a joint declaration in Santiago in which Chile reiterated its support for the sovereign rights Argentina claims over the islands, South Georgia, the South Sandwich Islands and their corresponding maritime areas.

Asked how closer trade ties would fit with regional commitments, Barros said the “potentially most contentious” point is oil and mining exploration, “which will have to be assessed in due course”, and noted that Chile's commitments in Mercosur and Unasur are “political and not legally binding”. In 2011, Mercosur members and associate states, including Chile, agreed measures concerning vessels flying the archipelago's flag.

The remarks come as a project for a sea link between Punta Arenas and Stanley advances. The Falkland Islands Development Corporation, the archipelago's economic development agency, has signed a contract with Easter Island Naviera, a Chilean company operating mainly between Valparaíso and Easter Island. According to Chilean media, the first voyage is planned for November. Some Argentine outlets present the route as an alternative to the supplies that currently reach the islands from Montevideo, some 2,000 kilometres away.

Argentina has 60 administrative proceedings open, with no penalty applied, and three criminal complaints covering ten companies and their directors over hydrocarbon exploration in waters near the archipelago. None of the allegations has been proven. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters chose, on a 92% turnout, to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

World.title: Latin American airports will need US$178 billion to nearly double their traffic
World.content:
Latin American airports will need US$178 billion to nearly double their traffic

29th Tuesday, September 2026 - 07:30 UTC Full article

The organisation also argued that airport charges, set by each country's regulators rather than by the airports themselves, account for a small share of airline costs

Airports in Latin America and the Caribbean will require investment of around US$178 billion over the next thirty years to handle demand that would rise from 809 million passengers this year to around 1.5 billion in 2045, according to projections presented in Lima at the annual assembly of Airports Council International.

The director general of the organisation's regional branch, ACI-LAC, Rafael Echevarne, estimated long-term growth of 3.1% a year and said annual infrastructure spending would need to rise from about US$3.4 billion to between US$8.6 and 8.7 billion by mid-century. In the first half of 2026, regional passenger traffic grew 1.9% and cargo 3.6%. The gathering this week brings together more than 600 executives, officials and specialists from the sector.

Globally, ACI estimates the sector will need around US$4.6 trillion in investment through 2055, after a record 9.8 billion passengers in 2025 and 4.7 billion in the first half of this year. “What really matters now is how we make sure our industry is ready for this growth,” said ACI World director general Justin Erbacci.

Echevarne warned that connectivity within the region has not recovered since the pandemic. “We have lost 20% of the city pairs we had connected,” he said, placing the loss mainly at regional airports in Peru, Ecuador and Chile. He put forward liberalisation of air transport as the main tool to reverse it: “We need to move from signing treaties of good intentions to putting that opening into practice.”

The organisation also argued that airport charges, set by each country's regulators rather than by the airports themselves, account for a small share of airline costs. According to IATA figures cited at the meeting, they represent 4.3% of operating costs globally and 5.5% in the region when air traffic control fees are included. The average charge is around US$9 per passenger.

Brazil leads regional traffic with 235 million passengers in 2025, followed by Mexico with 191 million, Colombia with 100, Argentina with 50, Peru with 43 and Chile with 36. In international trips per inhabitant, Uruguay ranks third among the Latin American countries surveyed, at 0.67, behind the Dominican Republic and Costa Rica, and nearly double Argentina's 0.34. Panama leads in total traffic per inhabitant, at 4.59.

In Argentina, the government on Monday formalised the extension to 2049 of the concession for 35 airports held by Aeropuertos Argentina, part of the Corporación América group, with an option to extend to 2056. The original concession was due to expire in 2038. The company will invest US$600 million, three quarters of it before the end of 2031, with no tariff increases and a reference internal rate of return of 14.3%, below the 17% it had sought.

World.title: Milei orders arbitration proceedings against the UK over the Sea Lion project
World.content:
Milei orders arbitration proceedings against the UK over the Sea Lion project

29th Tuesday, September 2026 - 07:30 UTC Full article

Argentina demanded that the United Kingdom take the necessary measures within that period to prevent the start or continuation of hydrocarbon exploitation and refrain from granting new permits

Argentine President Javier Milei on Monday instructed the foreign ministry and the government's legal teams to launch international arbitration proceedings against the United Kingdom over the development of the Sea Lion oil project in the basin north of the Falklands, and gave London two weeks to halt the activity before Argentina turns to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea.

“I instructed the foreign ministry and our legal teams to begin international arbitration against the United Kingdom for the illegal plundering of our resources through the Sea Lion Project in the North Malvinas Basin. If in 2 weeks the United Kingdom does not stop the illegitimate exploitation, we will go to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea,” the president wrote on X.

According to the statement from the Office of the President, the procedure is the one provided for in Annex VII of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, to which both countries are party. Arbitration formally begins with a written notification to the other party setting out the claim and its grounds; there is no record that such notification has been sent. Argentina demanded that the United Kingdom take the necessary measures within that period to prevent the start or continuation of hydrocarbon exploitation and refrain from granting new permits. If it does not, Argentina will ask the Hamburg-based tribunal for provisional measures, which that body can order while an arbitral tribunal is being constituted if it considers the latter would have jurisdiction on a prima facie basis.

The government bases its position on UN General Assembly resolutions 2065 and 31/49, which recognised the existence of a sovereignty dispute, urged both countries to negotiate and called on them to refrain from unilateral modifications. It argues that exploitation causes “irreversible and irreparable harm” to Argentine rights. These resolutions have the status of recommendations.

The chosen route faces a foreseeable legal obstacle. In previous cases, tribunals constituted under the Law of the Sea Convention declined to rule on disputes involving territorial sovereignty, as in the arbitration between Mauritius and the United Kingdom over the Chagos Islands in 2015 and in the dispute between Ukraine and Russia over Crimea in 2020.

The statement also includes a “categorical rejection” of the written statement the United Kingdom entered into the General Assembly record after Milei's speech, and maintains that the British overseas territory designation and the 2013 referendum have no legal validity. London holds that it has no doubt about its sovereignty, that Argentine law does not apply in the archipelago and that hydrocarbon activity is governed by local legislation in accordance with the same Convention. There was no specific British response to the announcement. The companies behind the project, Israel's Navitas and Britain's Rockhopper, have said they expect no change to their timetable, which sets first production for the first half of 2028.

The government also said it had detected operations by Thales UK Limited between the archipelago and Punta Arenas, in Chile, using a UK-registered aircraft without Argentine authorisation, and ordered sanction proceedings and criminal complaints. Argentina has 60 administrative proceedings open with no penalty applied and three criminal complaints against ten companies. None of the allegations has been proven.

World.title: Lula widens his first-round lead to five points, but the runoff remains tied
World.content:
Lula widens his first-round lead to five points, but the runoff remains tied

29th Tuesday, September 2026 - 07:21 UTC Full article

The survey, commissioned by the newspaper O Globo and TV Globo, was carried out from Thursday to Sunday with 2,400 interviews nationwide and a margin of error of two percentage points

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has widened his lead over Senator Flávio Bolsonaro to five points in voting intentions for Sunday's first round, according to a Quaest poll released on Monday, though the two remain tied in a prospective October 25 runoff.

The survey, commissioned by the newspaper O Globo and TV Globo, was carried out from Thursday to Sunday with 2,400 interviews nationwide and a margin of error of two percentage points. Lula takes 39%, two points higher than in the previous round, and Bolsonaro, of the Liberal Party, 34%, up one. The field is completed by Augusto Cury and Ronaldo Caiado on 4% each, Renan Santos on 3% and Romeu Zema on 1%. Undecided voters account for 5%, and 10% say they will vote blank, spoil their ballot or abstain.

In a second round, the poll shows a 42% tie, with Lula up one point on the previous week and his rival unchanged. Some 49% of respondents disapprove of the government's performance and 46% approve.

A second survey, by Nexus for the bank BTG Pactual, conducted from Friday to Sunday, puts Lula on 42% and Bolsonaro on 37% when respondents are shown the list of candidates, with the president up two points and the senator unchanged. In a prospective runoff, Lula takes 46% to 44%, within the margin of error.

Both surveys confirm the trend of those published in previous weeks: neither candidate is close to the 50% plus one of valid votes needed to settle the election in the first round.

The polls were released after Lula signed Provisional Measure 1,394 on Friday, banning nationwide the operation, offering, intermediation and advertising of online sports betting and casinos, including licences granted by state governments. The measure took effect on publication, but Congress must ratify it within 120 days. It marks a reversal from the law the government itself enacted in December 2023 to regulate the sector, in which 85 companies operate legally. Lula described the phenomenon as “a public health problem”. Bolsonaro called the measure electoral, and industry associations asked the Supreme Federal Court to suspend it. According to Quaest, 62% of Brazilians support the ban.

On Sunday, October 4, Brazilian voters will elect the president, all 27 state governors, the entire Chamber of Deputies and two thirds of the Senate.

World.title: Five shipping lines warn Uruguay the port dispute is damaging its international standing
World.content:
Five shipping lines warn Uruguay the port dispute is damaging its international standing

29th Tuesday, September 2026 - 07:17 UTC Full article

The companies describe a situation of “extreme uncertainty and paralysis” at the specialised container terminal and say that so far in 2026 there have been “more than 35 days of” disruption

Five of the main shipping lines operating at the port of Montevideo have warned the Uruguayan government that the labour dispute at the Terminal Cuenca del Plata is causing “severe economic and commercial harm” and has “severely damaged Uruguay's international prestige”, in a letter addressed to six ministers.

The letter, dated September 22 and received by the ministries on September 24, is signed by Maersk Uruguay, Ocean Network Express, CMA CGM Uruguay, Cosco Shipping Lines and Hapag-Lloyd Uruguay. It was first reported by Informativo Carve. It is addressed to Economy Minister Gabriel Oddone, Labour Minister Juan Castillo, Transport and Public Works Minister Lucía Etcheverry, Industry, Energy and Mining Minister Fernanda Cardona, Livestock, Agriculture and Fisheries Minister Alfredo Fratti, and Foreign Minister Mario Lubetkin.

The companies describe a situation of “extreme uncertainty and paralysis” at the specialised container terminal and say that so far in 2026 there have been “more than 35 days of operational disruption of various kinds”. According to the letter, open-ended strikes have forced them to cancel calls and unload imports at other ports in the region, generating unforeseen costs and breaches of commitments to exporters, importers and hauliers. They argue that, because of the loss of transshipments, global operators now see the country “as an unsafe, unstable and commercially unreliable logistics enclave”, and call for “an immediate, substantive solution that restores predictability”.

The Terminal Cuenca del Plata, majority-owned by the Belgian group Katoen Natie, handles around 80% of containers at the port of Montevideo. The dispute with the port workers' union has dragged on for months, following the expiry of the previous collective agreement. The parties agree on most points of the new deal but differ over its duration: the company wants five years, while the union has said it is willing to sign for three and is seeking better terms if the period is longer.

On September 17, the executive issued a resolution declaring essential services to guarantee minimum operation of the terminal. The union rejected it as a restriction on the right to strike and went ahead with the stoppage planned for September 24 in Montevideo and Nueva Palmira. The company has said it will quantify the damage caused by the action, and exporters' and importers' chambers also report losses.

Minister Oddone has argued for reviewing “certain aspects of port regulation” to strengthen the port's competitiveness. A new tripartite meeting was held on Monday at the National Labour Directorate to examine a government proposal; no agreement was reported.

“Our economic scale is smaller than that of the region's coastal countries; therefore, we cannot afford to waste any opportunity by projecting an inappropriate image,” the shipping lines write, also warning of the risk to jobs in the industry.

World.title: Hurricane Polo hits the Sonora coast after making landfall and crossing the Baja Peninsula
World.content:
After lying threateningly off Mexico’s west coast for the better part of a week, a weakened Hurricane Polo finally made landfall in Baja California Sur at 10 p.m. Monday night, dumping 15-30 cm of rain but causing little harm before making its way across the Peninsula and the Gulf of California to the Sonora coast, where it still packed enough power Tuesday morning to lash the beach city of Guaymas.

Guaymas and nearby Empalme suffered flooding, power outages and damage from fallen trees Tuesday, with storm-generated waves crashing over the Guaymas malecón, flooding streets.

The Sonoran state government had announced on Monday the suspension of all “nonessential” activities, including schools, sports, and certain work, in the state capital and more than a dozen municipalities

The Mexican Navy said it had personnel ready along the northern Pacific coast and, as a precaution, deployed three vessels to deliver aid to coastal communities isolated by the storm, while local authorities along the Baja California Peninsula said they had shelters at the ready.

Travel was also suspended where the hurricane was expected to make landfall, and ports across the region were closed.

Polo was expected to weaken later on Tuesday afternoon as it moves inland, according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center. Before it does, however, Mexican authorities urged residents to remain safe indoors either ‌at their homes or in temporary shelters in high-risk areas. Hundreds of people across the region have been evacuated.

Polo has been an oddly behaving hurricane from its formation and continued to be so after landfall. It hit the Sonora coast hard after it weakened to a Category 1 storm. But after it made landfall in Baja California Sur (far north of Los Cabos, almost in the middle of the Peninsula at the level of the Comondú municipality) as a much stronger Category 3, state authorities were breathing a sigh of relief.

A “saldo blanco” for Baja California Sur was reported preliminarily Tuesday morning — no deaths, no injuries. “There was more water than wind,” Governor Víctor Manuel Castro Cosío said. “So there was only minor damage, well within our capacity to deal with it.”

But it was still a hurricane. Mexico’s National Meterological Weather ​Service (SMN) reported that the hurricane brought to the Peninsula sustained winds of 150 to 170 km/h with gusts of 180 to 200 km/h and waves 7 to ⁠9 meters high.

With reports from CNBC, AP News, La Jornada and Once Noticias

World.title: The Herencia de México mariachi group makes history on Monday Night Football
World.content:
A performance of “The Star-Spangled Banner” by the band Mariachi Herencia de México on “Monday Night Football” this week drew cheers and made history, but it also elicited online backlash from some MAGA supporters.

Mariachi Herencia de México — an ensemble that started in Chicago 10 years ago and has been nominated for two Latin Grammys — became the first mariachi group to perform the U.S. national anthem at Soldier Field in Chicago, according to CBS Chicago.

The Mariachi Herencia de México performed the national anthem in Chicago 🎶 pic.twitter.com/6Sv20SBqIr — ESPN (@espn) September 29, 2026

The 14-member group’s all-instrumental rendering aired on ABC and ESPN before the Chicago Bears’ 27-7 victory over the Philadelphia Eagles. It was part of the team’s annual Latino Heritage Month observances.

Mariachi Herencia de México — which roughly translates as Mexico’s Mariachi Heritage — performs mainly in the United States, including a 2017 Mexican Independence Day concert at the Kennedy Center in Washington.

The group emerged from a program providing mariachi instruction and cultural education to Chicago public-school students.

The program eventually reached 2,100 students at eight schools and led to auditions in which 20 students were selected to form the original ensemble.

The group earned Latin Grammy nominations for best ranchero/mariachi album for its debut, “Nuestra Herencia,” in 2017 and for “Herederos” in 2023.

Their appearance was Soldier Field’s first mariachi performance of the U.S. anthem, but not Chicago sports’ first overall. Mariachi Monumental de México, also based in Chicago, played “The Star Spangled Banner” before a Chicago White Sox baseball game on Cinco de Mayo in 2016.

Chicago native Sandra Delgado, who sang at halftime, told CBS Chicago before the game that Mariachi Herencia de México’s performance was going to be “beautiful and meaningful” and that it was “going to bring down the house.”

But it also prompted criticism on social media, including from supporters of President Donald Trump’s “Make America Great Again” movement.

The prominent pro-Trump social-media account Gunther Eagleman wrote on X, “Hearing the American national anthem played mariachi-style on Monday Night Football feels weird. I understand putting your own spin on music, but the national anthem is one of those things that just hits harder when it’s kept traditional.”

Another MAGA supporter on X added in less measured tones, “Last time I checked, Mexicans have their own country and national anthem … it wouldn’t shock me if Democrat Illinois Governor J.B. Pritzker personally requested this disgusting display. These woke people hate America.”

The Bears-Eagles game came during Week 3 of the NFL season. In Week 11, on Nov. 22, the NFL will return to Mexico City when the San Francisco 49ers play the Minnesota Vikings at Estadio Banorte, better known as Estadio Azteca.

The NFL has selected Latin Grammy-nominated Mexican singer Majo Aguilar to perform the Mexican national anthem, while MXKA, a singer-songwriter from San Leandro, California, will perform “The Star-Spangled Banner.” Mexican rock trio The Warning, a sister act from Monterrey, will headline the halftime show.

With reports from La Jornada, LatinUS, N+, Daily Express US and CBS News

World.title: Mexico’s economy grew 3.3% in July, the strongest monthly result of 2026
World.content:
Mexico’s economy grew 3.3% in annual seasonally adjusted terms in July, the strongest growth of any month so far in 2026.

The national statistics agency INEGI reported the annual growth rate last Thursday, one month after it published data showing that Mexico’s economy expanded 1.9% in annual terms in the second quarter of 2026.

Annual growth in Q1 was just 0.4%.

INEGI also reported that month-over-month growth was 0.8% in July, the second-best result this year after a 1.5% sequential expansion in April. Mexico’s economy stagnated on a month-over-month basis in June, recording 0% growth. It contracted 0.3% in May compared to April.

In the first seven months of 2026, Mexico’s economy grew 1.5% annually, according to INEGI.

Andrés Abadía, chief Latin America economist at the British firm Pantheon Economics, said that the growth data for July “puts the third quarter in a much stronger position than expected.”

However, he added that “one month of strong results is not enough to predict a sustained recovery.”

Services sector fuels growth in July

The tertiary or services sector grew 4% annually in July, according to INEGI, while the secondary sector, which includes manufacturing, construction, mining and electricity generation, expanded 2.4%. The primary sector, which includes agriculture and fishing, contracted 0.6% on a year-over-year basis in July.

On a month-over-month basis, the tertiary sector grew 1.2% in July, while the secondary sector expanded 0.5%. The primary sector contracted 1.1% compared to June.

Other need-to-know economic data

The Bank of Mexico reported an end-of-day USD:MXN exchange rate of 18.06 on Tuesday. The Mexican peso has depreciated 5.9% this month after ending August at 16.99 to the US dollar.

Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate in the first half of September was 3.42%, up from 3.26% across August.

Mexico’s export revenue totaled a record US $549.4 billion in the first eight months of 2026, an annual increase of 29.3%.

The Bank of Mexico’s key interest rate is currently set at 6.50%.

With reports from El Economista and La Jornada

World.title: Authorities present 4 new lines of investigation in Ayotzinapa case
World.content:
Twelve years and two days after 43 students disappeared in the southern state of Guerrero, federal officials outlined “four new lines of investigation” in the abduction and presumed homicide case that shocked Mexico and triggered massive protests during the presidency of Enrique Peña Nieto.

At a press conference on Monday, Deputy Interior Minister Arturo Medina and Mauricio Pazarán, the prosecutor heading up the investigation into the Ayotzinapa case, presented the new investigative leads, which are included in a new federal report.

Before we look at each line of investigation presented on Monday, here is a summary of the Ayotzinapa case, one of Mexico’s most notorious criminal cases.

On the night of Sept. 26, 2014, 43 male students from the Ayotzinapa Rural Teachers College were abducted after a bus on which they were traveling to a protest in Mexico City was stopped by municipal police in Iguala, Guerrero.

The students were presumably murdered after their abduction, which was allegedly carried out by members of a Guerrero-based crime gang.

The remains of just three of the students have been found and formally identified.

A total of 168 people are subject to judicial proceedings in connection with the case. Among those people — 130 of whom are in prison — are soldiers, high-ranking members of the Mexican Army, police officers, members of the Guerreros Unidos crime gang and former officials, including Ángel Heladio Aguirre Rivero, governor of Guerrero at the time of the students’ abduction.

No one has been convicted of involvement in the abduction and presumed murder of the students.

The disappearance of the students triggered large protests in Mexico City and other cities across Mexico in late 2014. Countless additional protests have been held since then, including annual marches on the anniversary of the abduction of the 43 young men. “Fue el estado,” or “It was the state,” is a common chant at the protests, as is “¡Vivos se los llevaron, vivos los queremos!” (They were taken alive, we want them back alive!)

Two mothers and six fathers of the 43 students have died in the 12 years since their sons disappeared.

The Ayotzinapa case file runs to more than 5 million pages and is divided into more than 3,000 volumes. It is currently being digitized.

In a 2023 report, the federal government cited three “possible reasons” behind the abduction of the students. Among those possible reasons was that the students were mistaken for rival gangsters by Guerreros Unidos members, and that “drugs, weapons or money” were on buses they had commandeered to travel to a protest in Mexico City.

Jesús Murillo Karam, federal attorney general at the time of the students’ disappearance and a chief architect of the Ayotzinapa case’s so-called “historical truth,” was detained in 2022 on charges of forced disappearance, torture and obstruction of justice in connection with the case. He was released from prison in 2024 after a judge ruled he could await trial under house arrest. The 78-year-old former attorney general suffered a stroke in April.

Line of investigation No. 1 leads to the discovery of human remains at Iguala funeral parlors

In a statement released after Monday’s press conference, the Interior Ministry (SEGOB) said that the “four new lines of investigation” stem from a “reanalysis of documents and telephone records, using a methodology that incorporates technical and scientific elements.”

“… This approach made it possible to organize, correlate, and compare the data collected over 12 years with a new perspective, in order to identify clues that had not previously been noticed or thoroughly investigated,” the ministry said.

The first “new” line of investigation stems from the analysis of telephone communications and allowed authorities to identify 17 new suspects who are now under investigation. The analysis also allowed authorities to “reconstruct links” between members of the Guerreros Unidos crime gang — who allegedly kidnapped the students — municipal and state police, public servants and “people related to funeral parlors,” according to SEGOB.

“Among the findings, calls between members of that criminal organization and staff of funeral establishments and the health sector were detected. One of the people under investigation (Rodolfo Rueda) and his family were owners of funeral parlors, licensees of the [Guerrero government’s] Forensic Medical Service (SEMEFO) in Iguala and participated in the management of a cemetery,” SEGOB said.

“In August 2025, it was established that the owner of the funeral parlor used a telephone belonging to a student [from Ayotzinapa],” the ministry said.

SEGOB said that the discovery that the funeral parlor owner (Rueda) had used an Ayotzinapa student’s phone “motivated various actions” in October 2025, including searches at funeral parlors and SEMEFO facilities in Iguala, during which authorities found a “human femur, a firearm, documents and a crematorium oven without official registration.”

Between March and June 2026, authorities carried out additional searches at SEMEFO facilities attached to an Iguala funeral parlor owned by Rueda, locating hundreds of bone fragments, dental prostheses, “biological remains,” cartridges, bullet casings and documents, according to SEGOB.

The ministry said that the human remains and other items are “under expert analysis to determine their nature and possible match with missing people.”

Line of investigation No. 2 ‘strengthens the hypothesis’ that some students were taken to the Iguala municipal lockup on the night of their disappearance

The second line of investigation stems from an analysis of the phones of three of the Ayotzinapa students.

After the students’ disappearance, authorities established that those phones were used by a municipal official in Iguala, who was arrested in August on forced disappearance charges, a municipal police officer, who is under investigation, and people close to a former public servant in Iguala.

“The review of the third device strengthens the hypothesis that some students were taken to the municipal lockup [on Sept. 26, 2014] as the users [of the phone] after the disappearance were people close to an ex-public servant in Iguala who was assigned to … [the municipal lockup],” SEGOB said.

Authorities suspect that 17 students were taken to the municipal lockup in Iguala on the night of Sept. 26, 2014. In addition to information found on the telephone in question, the lockup “hypothesis” is based on statements made by municipal police officers, two alleged members of the Guerreros Unidos and an Ayotzinapa student.

Line of investigation No. 3 leads to identification of a new suspect who was a minor at the time of the students’ disappearance

The third line of investigation stems from a reanalysis of documents in the Ayotzinapa case file.

The reanalysis allowed authorities to “identify a person who participated in the events,” SEGOB said, adding that the previously unidentified suspect was aged 14 at the time.

“From the statement he gave on July 30, 2026, information was obtained that strengthens the accusations against members of the ‘Guerreros Unidos’ criminal organization,” the ministry said.

Line of investigation No. 4 leads to the arrest of former Guerrero governor

SEGOB said that the fourth line of investigation is related to the “concealment” of video footage captured by security cameras at the Superior Court of Justice in Iguala on the night of Sept. 26, 2014, and in the early hours of the following day.

Federal Attorney General Ernestina Godoy said in August that her office had evidence that former Guerrero Governor Ángel Aguirre ordered the concealment of said video footage, which apparently showed the bus on which the students were traveling at the time it was stopped by police in Iguala. The Federal Attorney General’s Office hasn’t managed to obtain the footage — which was likely destroyed — but is aiming to do so.

SEGOB said that authorities had been able to “reconstruct part of the decisions” high-ranking officials made in relation to the “concealment” of the video footage.

“This led to the arrest of the former presiding judge of the [Superior] Court [in Iguala], as well as the former inspector of the same judicial body, both of whom are currently subject to criminal processes,” the ministry said.

“Based on the statements made by these former public officials and in light of new evidence, the former governor of Guerrero [Ángel Aguirre] was arrested on August 6, 2026, for the crime of forced disappearance of the 43 students.”

Medina addresses allegations of army involvement

Interior Minister Medina, who heads up the government’s Ayotzinapa Truth Commission, said that the Ministry of National Defense, which has direct responsibility for the Mexican Army, provided investigators with all the information it had that is relevant to the Ayotzinapa case.

He said that 17 members of the Mexican Army have been arrested and are subject to ongoing judicial proceedings. Medina stressed that military personnel allegedly involved in the students’ disappearance are accused of acting independently rather than under the auspices of the Mexican Army. He said that the army, as a federal institution, is not accused of involvement in the abduction and presumed murder of the students.

The government’s ‘priority’ is to find the missing students

In its statement, SEGOB said that “for this government, the mothers and fathers of the 43 young men remain at the center of this process” — i.e., the investigation into the Ayotzinapa case and the pursuit of justice.

“The priority is to find them, shed light on what happened and bring to justice those who are responsible,” the Interior Ministry said.

“… The case is not closed and no person is above the law,” SEGOB said.

One suspect who has avoided arrest is Tomás Zerón, the former head of the now-defunct Criminal Investigation Agency (AIC).

As head of the AIC, Zerón — who now lives in Israel — was tasked with investigating the disappearance of the 43 students. Among the charges he faces in connection with the Ayotzinapa case are torture and tampering with evidence. The Mexican government has long sought Zerón’s extradition from Israel, but, to date, Israeli authorities have not arrested him.

With reports from La Jornada, CNN Español and Sin Embargo

World.title: Oaxaca AG launches investigations into 6 municipal presidents with alleged organized crime ties
World.content:
Following the momentous arrest of the mayor of Juchitán on Sept. 23, the Oaxaca Attorney General’s Office (FGEO) announced that it has launched investigations against six other municipal presidents in the southern state.

Attorney General Bernardo Rodríguez confirmed that his office has opened case files against six politicians following the arrest of Miguel Sánchez Altamirano. He also hinted at a possible investigation of the former director of the state’s Institute of Public Education (IEEPO), Emilio Montero, though he declined to offer specifics.

Montero — Sánchez’s predecessor as mayor of Juchitán, a primarily Indigenous city in the Isthmus of Tehuantepec region — resigned as director of the IEEPO last Friday, two days after Sánchez’s arrest.

The Isthmus of Tehuantepec has one of the highest incidence of crime in Oaxaca, with 957 murders since 2022, 70% of which have been linked to the “Los Cromos” crime gang.

All six cases described by Rodríguez are related to Juchitán — the third-largest city in Oaxaca — and feature a wide variety of charges related to alleged organized crime activities.

Rodríguez also confirmed that an arrest warrant had been issued for Mariano Rosado, the former secretary of the Juchitán City Council and Sánchez’s second in command.

Sánchez remains in pretrial detention on charges of aggravated extortion and crimes against the security of the state related to his alleged ties to “Los Cromos” and the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG).

While Sánchez is a member of the ruling Morena party (he has been described as a key operative of both the party and Governor Salomón Jara, also of Morena, in the region), Rodríguez said the six municipal presidents under investigation are from “different political affiliations.”

“This office does not take into consideration partisan distinctions,” he said. “Any official involved in illicit activities will be investigated, regardless of the position they hold or the party to which they belong,” he said.

The FGEO released a bulletin on Monday claiming that as a result of its ongoing investigations dating back to last year, prosecutors have arrested more than 250 people, including Sánchez and members of the “Los Cromos.”

“This has been an effort carried out jointly with the federal government, with the backing of intelligence units from the Security Ministry and the Navy,” Rodríguez said.

With reports from LopezDoriga.com, El Heraldo de México, N+ and El Sol de México

World.title: Mexican exports increased by nearly 30% through August, led by computer equipment
World.content:
Mexican exports grew at an annual rate of 40.4% in August, accumulating an increase of 29.3% through the first eight months of the year, according to the national statistics agency INEGI.

INEGI’s monthly report showed that exports reached a record US $549.4 billion during the January-August period and topped $78 billion in August.

At the same time, imports increased 34.2% in August and 26.8% through the first eight months of 2026, rising to US $77.405 billion and $539.5 billion (a new record), respectively.

As a result, Mexico recorded a surplus of $605.4 million in August, and $9.86 billion on the year through August.

The export sector was led by non-automotive manufacturing exports, up more than 63% in August, primarily due to a continuing surge in sales of computer equipment that began in 2024.

From January through August, manufacturing exports rose 30.8% annually, while non-automotive manufacturing rebounded 45%, the highest since records began in 1994.

Despite the record performance, analysts point out two concerns: the predominance of the U.S. as Mexico’s main buyer and the country’s reliance on Asia as an indispensable supplier for the fast-growing computer industry.

According to INEGI, 84.7% of Mexico’s total non-oil exports went to the U.S., while Mexico’s dependence on the U.S. in the computer sector is even more dramatic.

Mexico exported nearly $83 billion worth of servers, primarily used in data centers and artificial intelligence, and 93.9% of the servers were destined for the United States.

On the import side, processors, memory, cards and other high-value components come primarily from Taiwan, China, Malaysia, South Korea, Vietnam and Thailand with Taiwan alone supplying approximately 44% of the main inputs imported by the computer industry.

El Imparcial columnist Eduardo Ruiz Healy argued that as Mexico imports these components, assembles the equipment, and exports them (mainly to the United States), a significant portion of the value of each server is generated outside the country.

The concern here is that since the U.S. is demanding greater North American content in servers and other artificial intelligence equipment (in its bilateral trade negotiations with Mexico), the inability to produce them here could impact the export sector negatively.

Still, when paired with other data for August — oil exports down 2.8%, agricultural exports down 1.6% and automotive exports down 2.2% — it is apparent that the technological expansion cycle in the United States is supporting the Mexican economy.

With reports from El Financiero and El Economista

World.title: MND Local BCS: Hurricane Polo hits Baja California Sur, plus new regulations for swimming with whale sharks in La Paz
World.content:
On Monday, Sept. 21, Polo was designated a tropical storm off the southwestern coast of Mexico, with wind speeds of approximately 50 miles per hour (mph). Within 24 hours, winds had increased to 160 miles per hour, and Polo was suddenly one of the most terrifying types of natural disasters: a Category 5 hurricane.

The National Hurricane Center characterized the speed of Polo’s intensification as “truly remarkable,” not to mention historic. Indeed, it was one of the most rapid storm intensifications in recorded history, second only to that of Hurricane Patricia in 2015, a monster Category 5 hurricane that reached sustained winds of over 200 miles per hour.

By Tuesday afternoon, Hurricane Polo had reached sustained winds of 180 miles per hour (285 kilometers per hour), making it the third-strongest hurricane by that measure in the history of the Eastern Pacific region.

This rapid intensification was aided by climate change — sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean are the highest they’ve ever been — and an exceptionally strong El Niño weather pattern, which has raised water temperatures even further. Polo’s development, per NASA, occurred over waters with surface temperatures as high as 90 degrees Fahrenheit (32 degrees Celsius).

But despite its supercharged power, Polo remained offshore as it developed, making no landfall along the southwestern coast, but causing at least four deaths in Jalisco, and inflicting property damage across parts of Colima, Guerrero, Jalisco and Michoacán.

Baja California Sur prepares for the arrival of Hurricane Polo

By Sunday, Hurricane Polo had been downgraded to Category 3, with wind speeds of “only” 125 miles per hour as it continued in an arcing, left hook-like path towards Comondú municipality in the center of Baja California Sur — but with effects expected to be felt statewide, since tropical force winds from Polo were extending up to 105 miles (165 kilometers) from the storm’s center.

Hurricane warnings were issued for both the west (between Punta Abreojos and Santa Fe) and east coasts (from Loreto to Santa Rosalía) of the state prior to the arrival of the hurricane on Monday, and the state readied its response efforts, with help from the federal government.

Classes were canceled statewide for schools on Monday, while 1,360 military personnel in engineering groups awaited deployment, in case of need from impacts such as destructive winds, flooding and storm surges. Port activities in Comondú and Los Cabos were closed over the weekend, as were 26 beaches in Los Cabos. Meanwhile, 169 shelters across all five of the state’s municipalities were readied for those potentially displaced or in vulnerable areas.

The aftermath

The most visibly affected as the storm neared was Puerto San Carlos, in the Bahía Magdalena area, where storm-driven waves flooded streets, prompting hundreds of residents to evacuate their homes and seek shelter.

But it was 84 miles farther north, near Las Barrancas, a small fishing community of a little more than 500 residents that also lies in the municipality of Comondú, that Hurricane Polo finally made landfall at 11 p.m. local time on Monday, Sept. 28. By then, it had been downgraded to a Category 2 hurricane, but still a dangerous one, with sustained wind speeds of 110 miles per hour (175 kilometers per hour).

Six hours later, at 5 a.m., Hurricane Polo reached the Gulf of California on its way to Sonora — downgraded to Category 1 — leaving behind power outages, wind damage and flash flooding, but with no reported deaths in Baja California Sur … at least pending official damage assessments.

New rules instituted for swimming with whale sharks tours in La Paz

Bucket list adventures are a big draw in Baja California Sur. There’s whale watching in Los Cabos and in Pacific Coast lagoons, and swimming with whale sharks off the coast of the state’s capital city of La Paz. (Seasonal opportunities to swim with orcas at La Ventana are currently up in the air after a pilot program for 2025-2026 expired at the end of July).

In each case, however, there are regulations in place to protect not only tourists, but also the wildlife at the center of these experiences. In Los Cabos, for example, permitted boats must remain at a minimum distance from whales (60 to 80 meters, depending on the size of the vessel).

But nowhere is the need for caution more urgent than in the state capital, La Paz, where swimming with whale sharks season (Oct. 1 to April 30) has been suspended for parts of each of the last three years (2023 to 2025) due to an insufficient population of whale sharks.

New zones unveiled for 2026

Whale sharks are listed as endangered worldwide by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), and because La Paz is a seasonal feeding ground for juveniles, it should ideally play a key role in helping to replenish and grow the species’ population. Although whale sharks are enormous (they are the “world’s largest fish,” reaching up to 65 feet long and weighing as much as 60,000 pounds), these “gentle giants” are plankton eaters and very safe to swim with — from a human perspective.

From the wildlife perspective, very strict rules are needed to protect whale sharks from injury or undue stress due to tour activities. To this end, Mexico’s Secretariat of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat) has recently published new guidelines for swimming with whale shark tours in La Paz for 2026 through 2029.

The most notable change is the creation of three zones, in only one of which — Zone I, off the northern shore of the El Mogote peninsula — swimming with whale sharks is permitted. Zone II is listed as a conservation area, with Zone III restricted to transit for tour operators, and at slow speeds (7 knots or less).

Cap on boats tied to whale shark population figures

A ceiling of 56 boats per day for swimming with whale sharks is retained from previous regulations, which will be spread across four time periods for 14 boats each. Boats can bring five swimmers only, plus a guide, with encounters limited to 30 minutes. Other boats must keep at least 50 meters’ distance from those that are engaged in whale shark swims, and tourists are prohibited from touching the whale sharks (they can get no closer than two meters from the side of the fish, or three meters from its tail).

However, since the number of boats permitted for such tours (112 this year) exceeds the daily capacity allowed by half, time slots will be eagerly sought after … but closely tied to abundance. Meaning, the number of allowable boats, per the National Commission of Protected Natural Areas (Conanp), will be scaled back if the whale shark population, or lack thereof, warrants it. For instance, no boats will be allowed if there are five or fewer observable whale sharks, with a sliding scale up to the maximum of 56 boats based on closely monitored population figures.

Chris Sands is a writer and editor for Mexico News Daily, and the former Cabo San Lucas local expert for the USA Today travel website 10 Best and writer of Fodor’s Los Cabos travel guidebook. He has also contributed to numerous other websites and publications, including The San Diego Union-Tribune, Marriott Bonvoy Traveler, Forbes Travel Guide, Porthole Cruise and Travel, and Cabo Living.

World.title: Sheinbaum announces security support for Morelos after student murders
World.content:
President Claudia Sheinbaum announced a special security plan for Morelos following the murder of two teenage students who attended High School No. 2 of the Autonomous University of the State of Morelos (UAEM). The incident, which also left another young man injured, took place early on Sunday in Cuernavaca, the state’s capital.

“We are going to coordinate with the governor [Margarita González Saravia] to find out where she needs our support,” President Claudia Sheinbaum said during her Monday morning press conference. Sheinbaum also said that Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez had contacted the head of the UAEM, Viridiana Aydeé León Hernández, to learn more about the needs of the university community.

“We need to get in touch with the rector and the students to see what is happening and implement further preventive measures involving the students,” the president said.

She noted that according to data from the Public Security and Citizen Protection Ministry (SSPC), the number of intentional homicides in Morelos is declining, but crimes such as theft are on the rise.

Seven UAEM-affiliated students have been murdered in Morelos since April 2025, including Claudia Tacoronte, a Spanish student on an academic exchange program in Cuernavaca. The young woman was murdered on the night of Sept. 12 in Cuautla, after falling victim to a robbery.

Meanwhile, Cuernavaca Mayor José Luis Urióstegui Salgado acknowledged that the municipal security strategy has not succeeded.

“The patrols conducted by our police officers are becoming less visible, and criminals are taking advantage of this; that is why I called upon all of our security forces today to redouble their efforts, and I instructed the secretary and the command staff to focus more on providing support to the officers on the ground,” he noted.

Urióstegui stated that he would evaluate reinforcing police operations and warned that, if no results are seen in two weeks, changes to security leadership could occur.

“I deeply regret this situation. There should be no more homicides anywhere,” he said.

With reports from El Financiero and La Jornada

World.title: Mexico: Morena Picks First 2027 Governor Candidates — Clara Luz Flores Wins Nuevo León, Clouthier Concedes
World.content:
Mexico · Politics · Morena

Key Facts —First slate named. Morena has defined its first candidates for the 2027 state elections through internal polling, with Clara Luz Flores winning the party’s nod for governor of Nuevo León. —Clouthier concedes, stays. Tatiana Clouthier, former economy minister and one of the best-known figures of the Fourth Transformation, accepted defeat and ruled out leaving Morena for another party. —Other prominent losers. Senator Andrea Chávez lost the Chihuahua nod to Cruz Pérez Cuéllar, and Acapulco mayor Abelina López was also passed over in Guerrero’s contest. —Sheinbaum’s unity message. President Claudia Sheinbaum said the internal process showed “great unity” and opened the door for the losing aspirants to run for mayoralties, state congress seats or coordination posts. —The stakes. Seventeen governorships are at play in June 2027, and one allied party deputy has publicly warned Morena could lose twelve of them.

Mexico’s ruling party has fired the starting gun on the 2027 state elections — and its first internal verdicts have already humbled some of the movement’s biggest names, above all Tatiana Clouthier in Nuevo León.

Morena’s leadership chose its first 2027 candidates by internal poll rather than open primary. (Photo: The Rio Times archive)

Morena’s First Slate for 2027

The governing party settled its first candidate selections for next year’s state races the way it has settled them since 2023: by internal survey rather than an open vote of the membership. In Nuevo León, the industrial northern powerhouse governed by Movimiento Ciudadano’s Samuel García, the poll delivered the nomination to Clara Luz Flores — the same politician who carried Morena’s banner in the state in 2021 and lost narrowly to García. She now heads toward a rematch for one of the country’s most coveted statehouses.

In Chihuahua, the survey favoured Cruz Pérez Cuéllar over Senator Andrea Chávez, one of the most visible young faces of the movement. In Guerrero, Acapulco mayor Abelina López — who had requested leave from city hall to compete — likewise failed to win the nod. Seventeen of Mexico’s 32 governorships will be elected in June 2027, making the internal exercise the first real test of the party’s post-AMLO machinery.

Clouthier Concedes — and Stays

The biggest casualty was Tatiana Clouthier. The former economy minister under Andrés Manuel López Obrador — and his 2018 campaign coordinator — had resigned in May as head of the Institute for Mexicans Abroad to seek the Nuevo León nomination. On Monday she recognised Clara Luz Flores’s survey victory and shut down the question every defeated aspirant in Mexico is asked: no, she said, she is not leaving Morena and not joining another party. “If I had not decided to respect the results, I would not have entered the contest,” she told reporters, adding that her backing belongs to President Sheinbaum’s project.

Her camp had fought the selection to the end, accusing the Nuevo León state government of running “a campaign of defamation and unfounded accusations” against her — a claim directed at García’s administration rather than at her own party. She pointedly avoided mentioning Clara Luz Flores after the result, saying only that she respected the survey.

A Family Split on Display

The defeat carried an extra edge because of who celebrated it. Manuel Clouthier, her brother and a prominent opposition figure in Sinaloa, publicly mocked the outcome with a sarcastic “a thousand thanks” to Morena for leaving his sister out. The siblings embody one of Mexican politics’ most famous divides: their father, Manuel J. Clouthier — “Maquío” — was the PAN’s presidential candidate in 1988 and remains an icon of the old fight against one-party rule, while Tatiana crossed over to become a founding figure of López Obrador’s movement. Her brother has been one of that movement’s fiercest critics ever since.

Sheinbaum Moves to Bind the Wounds

Speaking at her Tuesday morning press conference, President Sheinbaum insisted the internal process had unfolded with “great unity” and offered the losing aspirants a path back: new calls for candidates will cover mayoralties, state congress seats and party coordination posts, she said, so “whoever did not win the survey can participate”. Andrea Chávez, who has taken indefinite leave from the Senate — she can return to her seat until 2030 — said she will keep touring Chihuahua to help defeat the “PRIAN”, though she stopped short of explicitly endorsing Pérez Cuéllar.

The unity message arrives against a public warning from inside the governing coalition. Reginaldo Sandoval, a deputy for the allied Labour Party (PT), said this week that Morena’s candidate choices could cost it twelve of the seventeen governorships in play next year — an unusually blunt assessment of the movement’s vulnerability after nearly a decade in national power.

What Comes Next

Morena is expected to roll out further candidate definitions state by state in the coming weeks, alongside the secondary contests Sheinbaum announced for municipal and state-congress races. Nuevo León now shapes up as the marquee fight of 2027: Clara Luz Flores gets a second run at Samuel García’s succession in a state where Morena has invested heavily and where the opposition still dominates local institutions. For Clouthier, the party’s door remains open — but for the first time since 2018, one of the Fourth Transformation’s most recognisable figures has no office and no candidacy.

What We Could Not Confirm

Morena does not publish the detailed results of its internal surveys, so vote shares or percentages for Clara Luz Flores and Tatiana Clouthier are not available. The complete list of states where candidates have already been settled — and those still pending — has not been officially itemised. Whether Clouthier has been offered a specific post or future candidacy by the party leadership could not be verified, and the defamation allegations against the Nuevo León government remain claims by her campaign, not established findings.

More: Mexico news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Morena’s candidate for governor of Nuevo León in 2027?

Clara Luz Flores won the party’s internal survey for the Nuevo León nomination, defeating Tatiana Clouthier. It is her second run at the statehouse after losing narrowly to Samuel García in 2021.

Is Tatiana Clouthier leaving Morena?

No. The former economy minister explicitly ruled out leaving Morena or joining another party, saying she respects the survey results and remains committed to President Sheinbaum’s project.

How many governorships does Mexico elect in 2027?

Seventeen of Mexico’s 32 states will elect governors in June 2027. A deputy of the allied Labour Party has warned that Morena could lose twelve of them.

World.title: Mexico: Polo Fades After Two Landfalls — Baja California Sur Escapes Without Deaths, Guaymas Flooded
World.content:
Mexico · Hurricane Polo

Latest — September 29, 2026, 8 p.m. local time (NHC advisory 38 — final) — Polo has dissipated over north-western Mexico: the NHC’s last advisory placed the remnants 245 miles (395 km) north-east of Guaymas with 35 mph (55 km/h) winds, moving north-east at 23 mph. A wind advisory remains for southern New Mexico and far west Texas overnight. This was the final NHC advisory on Polo. Key Facts —Clean bill in Baja. Civil protection reports no deaths in Baja California Sur after Polo’s midnight landfall near Las Barrancas as a Category 2 hurricane; power and water held in Comondú, Mulegé and Loreto. —Second landfall. Polo crossed the Gulf of California and came ashore again near Guaymas, Sonora, around midday with 75 mph winds, flooding the city centre, the malecón and the municipal palace. —The storm’s only victims. Four members of one family died in Talpa de Allende, Jalisco, when a swollen stream swept away their home before Polo reached Baja. —Fading fast. Polo is now a tropical storm with 65 mph winds over the Sierra Madre; all coastal warnings are discontinued and it is forecast to turn post-tropical early Wednesday. —Still to come. Heavy rain spreads toward Chihuahua — on yellow alert — southern New Mexico and far west Texas; Tropical Storm Rachel is spinning off Michoacán behind it.

Hurricane Polo, once the eastern Pacific’s fifth Category 5 monster of the season, is dying over Mexico’s Sierra Madre after two landfalls in fourteen hours — leaving behind a flooded Guaymas, a remarkably unscathed Baja California Sur and one family’s tragedy in Jalisco.

Polo’s passage left flooded roads and downed trees across two Mexican states, though Baja California Sur reported no loss of life. (Photo: The Rio Times archive)

A Hurricane, Twice Ashore

Polo’s first landfall came around midnight local time near Las Barrancas, in the municipality of Comondú, when the hurricane crossed the central spine of Baja California Sur as a Category 2 storm with sustained winds of 175 km/h and gusts to 205 km/h. It was the same system that had stunned forecasters days earlier by exploding into a Category 5 with 165 mph winds — one of the most intense cyclones of the 2026 eastern Pacific season, which has now produced sixteen named storms.

Weakened but not spent, Polo emerged over the Gulf of California on Tuesday morning as a Category 1 hurricane and accelerated north-east. Its second landfall followed near Guaymas, Sonora, around midday: at 11 a.m. the centre was twenty miles east of the city, still carrying 75 mph winds. By 2 p.m., inland over the Sierra Madre foothills 100 miles north-east of Guaymas, Polo had dropped to tropical-storm strength at 65 mph — and Mexico discontinued every remaining coastal warning.

Saldo Blanco: How Baja California Sur Escaped

The headline from the presidential morning conference was the one officials had hoped for: “El saldo es blanco” — a clean bill. National civil protection coordinator Laura Velázquez reported no deaths and no serious injuries in Baja California Sur, and said electricity and water services held through the storm in the three most exposed municipalities: Comondú, Mulegé and Loreto.

The recorded damage reads like a near-miss ledger: flooded road sections and standing water, fallen trees and branches, landslides on the road between Ciudad Insurgentes and Loreto, and swollen arroyos restricting passage in Mulegé and San Javier. Around 700 people who had spent the night in temporary shelters began returning home on Tuesday morning. Some 6,872 public servants from all three levels of government were deployed to prevention and response. BCS governor Víctor Castro summed it up: the storm left rain, but no loss of human life — material damage would be assessed through the day.

Guaymas Counts the Cost

Sonora took the second hit. Heavy rain set in from 3 a.m. as Polo entered through the municipalities of Guaymas and Empalme, and by landfall the water was standing in central Guaymas — flooding streets around the malecón and reaching the municipal palace, according to La Jornada’s reporters on the ground. Sonora’s civil protection agency documented a waterspout forming off the city as the hurricane approached.

The state had prepared for worse: schools in 72 municipalities were closed for Tuesday and Wednesday, ports from Guaymas to Topolobampo were shut to smaller craft, and the hurricane warning stretched from Bahia Kino to Huatabampito until the final hours. With rainfall totals of 4 to 6 inches and isolated maxima of 8 inches forecast across north-west Mexico, flash flooding and mudslides remain the live threat even as the wind field collapses; Chihuahua state is on yellow alert for up to 75 mm of rain and gusts to 80 km/h.

The Jalisco Tragedy

Polo’s only confirmed victims died before the hurricane ever reached Baja. In Talpa de Allende, Jalisco, four members of a single family were killed when their home was swept away by the sudden rise of a stream swollen by Polo’s outer rain bands. State authorities reported the deaths as the cyclone paralleled the coast, a reminder that the storm’s deadliest weapon was never its Category 5 wind core but the water it carried.

What Comes Next

The National Hurricane Center expects Polo to turn post-tropical early Wednesday over the high terrain of the Sierra Madre. Its remnant moisture keeps travelling: strong winds and heavy rain are spreading across north-western Mexico toward southern New Mexico — already under a wind advisory — and far west Texas. Behind Polo, Tropical Storm Rachel is working the same coastline further south, threatening torrential rain over Michoacán and Oaxaca and waves up to seven metres on the Colima, Michoacán and Guerrero coasts.

Mexican meteorologists attribute the season’s ferocious pace — Polo went from tropical storm to Category 5 in under 24 hours — to the El Niño event warming the eastern Pacific. For expats and travellers in the region, the practical advice stands until Wednesday: stay off flooded roads, expect flight and highway disruptions across Sonora and Chihuahua, and follow Protección Civil bulletins.

What We Could Not Confirm

Damage assessments from both states are preliminary: Baja California Sur’s material inventory was still being compiled on Tuesday, and Sonora has published no official damage figure for Guaymas at the time of writing. Rainfall totals are forecasts, not measurements; actual accumulations in the Sierra Madre may exceed them. The fate of specific road closures and port reopenings will be set by state authorities overnight. We could not independently verify the condition of rural communities between Ciudad Insurgentes and Loreto cut by the reported landslides.

More: Mexico news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Hurricane Polo kill anyone in Mexico?

Yes — four members of one family died in Talpa de Allende, Jalisco, when a swollen stream swept away their home. Baja California Sur, where Polo made its first landfall as a Category 2 hurricane, reported no deaths, according to national civil protection coordinator Laura Velázquez.

Where did Hurricane Polo make landfall?

Twice: first around midnight near Las Barrancas in Comondú, Baja California Sur, as a Category 2 hurricane with 175 km/h winds, then around midday near Guaymas, Sonora, as a Category 1 hurricane with 75 mph winds.

Is Hurricane Polo still dangerous?

Polo has weakened to a tropical storm and is forecast to turn post-tropical early Wednesday over the Sierra Madre, but its rain remains the threat: 4 to 6 inches with isolated maxima of 8 inches are forecast across north-west Mexico, with flash flooding and mudslides possible in Sonora and Chihuahua.

World.title: Brazil Election Risk: Stocks and the Real Recover Five Days Before the Vote
World.content:
Markets · Brazil

Key Facts — What happened Brazilian stocks rose 0.46% and the real edged up on Tuesday 29 September 2026, after a weak morning.

— What traders price Rate futures fell as oil eased and investors added risk, which Valor tied to a possible Flávio Bolsonaro win.

— How nervous Brazil’s stock fear gauge, the S&P/B3 Ibovespa VIX, hit a record 31.84 on Monday 28 September.

— The catch Atlas/Bloomberg and Quaest polls show Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro statistically tied in a runoff, so the result is open.

— The pressure from abroad The 10-year US Treasury yield stood at 5.24% on Monday 28 September, its highest since June 2007.

Brazilian stocks and the real ended Tuesday higher after a nervous morning. Behind the swings sit two questions: who wins the presidency, and what the winner then does with the budget.

Brazil election risk set the tone on Tuesday 29 September 2026, five days before Brazilians choose a president. Stocks and the real, Brazil’s currency, lost ground in the morning and recovered by the close.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of the Workers’ Party (PT) is seeking a fourth term. His main rival is Senator Flávio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party (PL), son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

The first round is on Sunday 4 October. If no candidate wins more than half of the valid votes, the top two meet in a runoff on 25 October.

Where Tuesday ended

The Ibovespa, the main index of the São Paulo exchange B3, closed up 0.46% at 183,828 points on Tuesday. Valor and G1 both reported that closing level.

The rise ended four days of losses, Reuters reported. At about 1 p.m. Brasília time (16:00 UTC) the index was down 0.32%, near its low of 181,562 points, Valor reported.

At the close, the dollar was down 0.16% at a rate of 5.2166 against the real, Valor reported.

How the vote is priced in interest rates

The clearest election signal came from DI futures. These contracts, traded on B3, track Brazil’s interbank lending rate and show where traders expect borrowing costs to go.

At Tuesday’s settlement, reported by Valor at 5:34 p.m. Brasília time, the January 2029 contract fell to 13.79% from 13.90%. The January 2028 rate eased to 13.575% from 13.665%.

Valor linked the fall to cheaper oil, softer words from a US Federal Reserve official and investors adding risk. Earlier, it tied that appetite to the prospect of a possible Flávio Bolsonaro victory.

A government bond sale pointed the same way. The National Treasury sold all 900,000 inflation-linked NTN-B bonds on offer, at lower rates than traders had expected.

Investors took only 23.1% of the 500,000 LFT bonds, which pay the floating Selic policy rate. Market participants read that mix as appetite for risk, Valor reported.

Reuters, in a story carried by InfoMoney, said many traders see a Lula re-election as an obstacle to controlling public finances. Poll news that favours Flávio Bolsonaro therefore tends to push the dollar and local rates down, it said.

The government argues the opposite. Finance Minister Dário Durigan defended its record in an article for The Economist, InfoMoney reported.

He wrote that the primary deficit, before interest, fell from just over 2% of GDP in 2023. He projected 0.6% for 2026.

Goldman Sachs holds a more guarded view, Valor reported. It likes options that pay if the dollar falls below 5 against the real within three months.

Even with a Flávio Bolsonaro win, Goldman believes, difficulty implementing a fiscal agenda could slow the real’s gains.

What each outcome could mean for the real

JPMorgan said the real carried no significant election premium, InfoMoney reported on 28 September.

A result seen as bad for the public finances could send the dollar toward 5.50 against the real, the bank said. A result read as favourable could lift the real about 6%, taking the dollar near 4.90.

For a lasting shift, JPMorgan said, the winner needs clear budget commitments and a credible plan to deliver them. In its own model portfolio, the bank keeps a neutral weight on the real and options that gain if it weakens.

Citi is more hopeful, Valor reported. Its strategists, led by Dirk Willer, see a slight edge for Flávio Bolsonaro and opened an options position betting on the real.

Jonathan Joo Young Lee, head of the international desk at the broker Mirae Asset, said caution dominates among foreign investors. He told Valor that Lula’s larger Bolsa Família family payments and a ban on betting sites had raised their budget worries.

JPMorgan’s own investor survey leans one way, InfoMoney reported. Weighted by money managed, 59.7% of respondents expected Flávio Bolsonaro to win and 40.3% Lula.

Polls are tighter: an Atlas/Bloomberg survey released on Tuesday had Lula ahead in the first round, 45.3% to 42.2%, Reuters reported. Atlas interviewed 5,005 people online from 23 to 28 September.

In a runoff it showed Flávio Bolsonaro on 47.7% and Lula on 47.6%, a statistical tie within its one-point margin. A Quaest poll released on Monday tied them at 42% each, G1 reported.

Quaest interviewed 2,004 people from 24 to 27 September, with a two-point margin. Both firms called the runoff a technical tie.

State results can differ from the national picture, as the latest Rio Grande do Sul poll shows. Neither national survey gives either man a clear runoff lead.

The pressure from Washington

The 10-year US Treasury yield stood at 5.24% on Monday, the highest since June 2007, the US Treasury’s daily table shows.

On Tuesday the same table read 5.26%, level with 12 June 2007. The Federal Reserve, the US central bank, raised its key rate by a quarter point to 3.75%–4% on 16 September.

Relief came in the afternoon from John Williams, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. After the September increase, “there is no need for urgency,” he said in prepared remarks in Buffalo, New York.

Brazilian rates then hit their lows of the day and the dollar extended its fall, Valor reported. Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, closed 2.6% lower at US$102.59 a barrel, Reuters reported.

Borrowing is already costly inside Brazil, where the central bank’s Selic rate stands at 13.75%. The strain on companies is the subject of our report on Moody’s 2027 warning for Brazilian corporate debt.

A record fear gauge, in context

The S&P/B3 Ibovespa VIX, a gauge of expected swings built from option prices, hit 31.84 on Monday 28 September. That was its highest since its launch in March 2024, InfoMoney reported.

The longer view is calmer. A Quantum Finance study found the Ibovespa’s daily swings this year far smaller than in the three previous election cycles, Valor reported.

For anyone who earns in dollars and spends in reais, the vote brings exchange-rate risk in both directions. Option prices imply a move of about 6.5% across the two voting days combined, JPMorgan estimated.

What nobody yet knows is how the winner will handle the budget, the core of Brazil election risk. JPMorgan said that clarity had not yet appeared when its report was published.

The bank argues the harder test comes after the count. The winner would need to name an economic team and win support in Congress, especially the Senate, it said.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is Brazil’s 2026 presidential election?

The first round is on Sunday 4 October 2026. If no candidate wins more than half of the valid votes, the top two meet in a runoff on the last Sunday of October, which is 25 October 2026.

What is the Brazil election risk that investors talk about?

It is the chance that the result moves prices sharply, mainly through what the next government does with spending and debt. JPMorgan, in a report covered by InfoMoney on 28 September, said a result seen as bad for the public finances could push the dollar toward 5.50 against the real.

What are DI futures?

DI futures are contracts traded on B3, the São Paulo exchange, that track the average interbank lending rate in Brazil. Traders use them to bet on or protect against changes in interest rates. When their rates fall, traders expect cheaper borrowing ahead.

What is Brazil’s stock fear gauge?

The S&P/B3 Ibovespa VIX was launched by S&P Dow Jones Indices and B3 on 19 March 2024. It measures the swings that options on the Ibovespa index expect over the next 30 days. It reached a record 31.84 on Monday 28 September 2026, InfoMoney reported.

World.title: Mexican Peso Breaks 18 per Dollar as US Yields Hit Their Highest Since 2007
World.content:
Economy · Mexico

Key Facts — What happened The Mexican peso closed at 18.0635 per US dollar on Tuesday 29 September 2026, Banco de México data show.

— How fast On the central bank’s reference rate, the dollar buys about 7 percent more pesos than on 4 September.

— The real story Higher US bond yields and bets on another Fed rate rise are shrinking the reward for holding pesos.

— The catch The peso is only back where it started 2026, and still stronger than in November 2025.

— What comes next The Fed meets on 27 and 28 October; Banco de México’s next scheduled rate decision is on 5 November.

Banco de México’s reference rate and its official close both went above 18 on Tuesday, for the first time since March. Most of the pressure comes from Washington, where bond yields and bets on the Federal Reserve are pulling money toward the dollar.

Mexican Peso Breaks 18 per Dollar as US Yields Hit Their Highest Since 2007
