The Mexican peso has crossed 18 per US dollar for the first time since March. Banco de México’s FIX, the central bank’s official reference rate, came in at 18.0710 on Tuesday 29 September 2026.

Most of the push came from Washington, not Mexico City. Analysts in the Mexican press point to higher US bond yields, bets on a Fed rate rise and a firmer dollar.

How the line was crossed

The first touch came on Monday 28 September, after regular trading had ended. The dollar reached 18.0059 at 3:30 p.m. Mexico City time in electronic trading, the financial daily El Economista reported.

Banco de México’s official close that day, cited by El Economista, was lower at 17.9445. The business outlet Expansión also reported that 18 was touched shortly after the close.

On Tuesday the peso broke through again during the session, and El Economista put the day’s high at 18.1503. The FIX, published from noon, came in at 18.0710.

This time the line held into the close. Banco de México’s official close, set between 1:55 and 2:05 p.m. Mexico City time, was 18.0635.

The peso lost 0.66 percent from Monday’s close, El Economista reported at 3:13 p.m. Mexico City time. El Financiero carried the same close in an update at 2:50 p.m. Mexico City time.

The FIX is a separate figure, not a closing price. Banco de México sets it each banking day as an average of wholesale market quotes.

Electronic trading also carries on after the official close, so later quotes are intraday, not settlement prices. That is why outlets can show different numbers for the same day.

Tuesday’s FIX was the first above 18 since 31 March. By that measure the dollar buys 4.4 percent more pesos than a week earlier.

The dollar also buys 6.2 percent more than at the end of August. Against the FIX of 16.8748 on 4 September, the strongest Mexican peso reading of 2026, the rise is 7.1 percent.

Washington sets the price

The main pressure is the price of money in the United States. The yield on the ten-year US Treasury bond, the benchmark for global borrowing, stood at 5.24 percent on Monday, Treasury data show.

That was its highest level since June 2007, and it rose again to 5.26 percent on Tuesday. Higher safe returns in dollars make riskier currencies such as the peso less attractive.

The Federal Reserve, the US central bank, raised its key rate by a quarter point on 16 September. The new range is 3.75 to 4 percent, and its statement said inflation “remains elevated”.

The median projection of Fed policymakers, published the same day, puts the rate at 4.1 percent at the end of 2026. That implies one more quarter-point rise this year.

Traders expect that rise soon. The CME FedWatch tool put the odds of an October increase at 68.1 percent on Tuesday morning, El Economista reported.

Later that day John Williams, president of the New York Fed, said he saw no urgency for another rise, Reuters reported. El Economista said his remarks trimmed those bets.

Behind the yields sits a larger number. US federal debt stood at US$40.1 trillion on 25 September, according to the Treasury’s daily count.

Expansión described the peso on Monday as caught between the Fed and record US debt. It wrote that investors are demanding ever-higher yields to absorb new US bond sales.

Energy added to the strain. Brent crude, the global benchmark, stayed above US$100 a barrel on Monday, Expansión reported.

The trigger was President Donald Trump’s rejection of an Iranian proposal to end hostilities and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Costlier energy feeds fears of stubborn US inflation, and so of a tighter Fed.

The carry trade loses some of its pull

For much of 2026, analysts say, the peso was lifted by the carry trade. Investors borrow in low-rate currencies such as the Japanese yen and buy higher-yielding Mexican assets.

Banco de México kept its own rate at 6.50 percent on 24 September. After the Fed’s rise, the gap between the two is 2.50 to 2.75 percentage points.

“As that differential narrows, part of the incentive to hold positions in pesos diminishes,” Janneth Quiroz told Expansión. She heads economic analysis at the Mexican financial group Monex.

Ramsé Gutiérrez, co-chief investment officer of Franklin Templeton in Mexico, described the pattern to the same outlet. “When a currency like the peso appreciates, it appreciates slowly, but the day it depreciates, it depreciates fast,” he said.

Speculators are pulling back, but they have not turned against the Mexican peso. Hedge funds and other speculative traders still held a net 79,188 futures contracts favouring the peso on 22 September.

That figure comes from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the US futures regulator. Its next weekly report will show whether the retreat continued.

What is holding the peso up

The rate gap that props up the Mexican peso has narrowed, but it has not closed. Quiroz said contained inflation and fairly solid external accounts could prevent a deeper fall.

Victoria Rodríguez Ceja, governor of Banco de México, said the slide adds no inflation pressure beyond the bank’s forecasts. She spoke to the newspaper El Financiero in an interview published early on Monday.

She pointed to “balanced external accounts” and “an adequate level of international reserves”. She added that the floating exchange rate lets the peso absorb shocks from abroad.

When she spoke, the peso was still stronger than at the start of the year. By Tuesday’s FIX it had given that gain back.

The long view still tempers the headline. Tuesday’s FIX is only 0.4 percent above the last one of 2025, and below the 18.6233 of 6 November 2025.

What Banco de México can and cannot do

Banco de México cannot move US yields, and it has said it will not copy the Fed. Its 24 September statement said Mexican policy “would not have to react mechanically” to expected US rate moves.

It did list a trend of peso depreciation among the risks that could push inflation up. It judged the overall balance of those risks as tilted upward.

Its next scheduled decision is on Thursday 5 November 2026, and minutes of the September meeting are due on 8 October. The bank’s calendar allows it to act on other dates if extraordinary events require it.

What it means for people with money in both currencies

For foreigners in Mexico who earn in dollars, a weaker Mexican peso stretches their income further. For Mexican firms that import goods or owe dollars, the same move raises costs.

Banco Base, a Mexican bank, raised its forecast for the end-2026 rate to 18.20 from 17.80, Expansión reported. It sees possible spells above 18.50 if investors turn more cautious.

Speaking early on Monday, Gutiérrez said the move was still within normal swings for the currency. A similar week, taking the dollar toward 18.50, would open a debate about a disorderly adjustment, he said.

Our Global Economy Briefing follows the US bond moves each morning. For now, the peso’s direction depends less on Mexico than on the next US inflation figures and the Fed’s October meeting.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did the Mexican peso close above 18 per dollar?

Yes, on Tuesday 29 September. Banco de México’s official close, set between 1:55 and 2:05 p.m. Mexico City time, was 18.0635. On Monday it had closed at 17.9445, before touching 18.0059 in electronic trading at 3:30 p.m. Tuesday’s FIX of 18.0710 is a separate midday reference rate, not a close.

Why is the peso weakening?

Analysts point mainly to the United States. The ten-year Treasury yield reached 5.24 percent on 28 September, its highest since 2007, and traders expect another Federal Reserve rate rise. That narrows the gap between Mexican and US interest rates, which had drawn investors into the peso. Higher energy prices linked to the conflict involving Iran have added to US inflation worries.

Will Banco de México raise rates to defend the peso?

The bank has not said so. On 24 September it held its rate at 6.50 percent and said Mexican policy would not have to react mechanically to US rate moves. Its governor said the recent slide adds no inflation pressure beyond the bank’s forecasts. The next scheduled decision is on Thursday 5 November 2026.

What does a weaker peso mean for foreigners living in Mexico?

Anyone paid in US dollars gets more pesos for each dollar, so local costs fall in dollar terms. Families receiving money from the United States also gain. People who owe dollars or buy imported goods face higher costs. Banco Base, a Mexican bank, now forecasts a rate of 18.20 per dollar at the end of 2026.

Argentina’s pension agency ANSES has locked in October’s numbers: a 1.66% inflation-linked rise and a confirmed ARS 70,000 bonus lift the minimum retirement income to ARS 505,748.51 — about US$332 at the official exchange rate.

What ANSES Has Confirmed

Resolution 284/2026, signed by ANSES’s executive directorate and published in the Official Gazette, applies a 1.66% increase to all benefits under the SIPA pension system for the October 2026 accrual period. The adjustment follows the monthly mobility formula established by emergency decree DNU 274/2024, which ties benefits to the consumer price index measured by statistics agency INDEC — in this case August inflation.

The guaranteed minimum pension rises from ARS 428,633.20 to ARS 435,748.51 gross per month. The system’s maximum benefit is fixed at ARS 2,932,174.85 — about US$1,923 at the official rate of roughly 1,524 pesos per dollar — and does not receive extraordinary supplements. The Universal Basic Benefit (PBU), the component rewarding years of contributions, is updated to ARS 199,335.05.

The Pension Universal para el Adulto Mayor (PUAM), the benefit for over-65s without sufficient contribution history, rises to ARS 348,598.81 gross. The resolution also resets payroll contribution bases for employed workers: the taxable floor moves to ARS 146,759.98 and the ceiling to ARS 4,769,631.49 from October.

The US$46 Bonus: Who Gets It

The Executive branch ratified the continuation of the extraordinary fixed-sum pension reinforcement of ARS 70,000 — about US$46 — paid automatically alongside the regular benefit. Recipients of the minimum pension therefore take their total to ARS 505,748.51, roughly US$332. PUAM beneficiaries receive a consolidated ARS 418,598.81, and the bonus also reaches non-contributory pension beneficiaries.

Pensioners whose benefit sits above the minimum but below the absorption ceiling receive a proportional bonus topping them up to ARS 505,748.51. The bonus is non-remunerative and carries no deductions: the 3% health-insurance (PAMI) withholding — ARS 13,072.45 on the minimum — is calculated on the basic benefit only. ANSES estimates the effective take-home for a single minimum benefit at around ARS 492,676, about US$323.

October Payment Calendar

October payments to pensioners and retirees begin on Thursday 8 October and run through Thursday 29 October, staggered by the final digit of the beneficiary’s national ID number (DNI). The schedule applies to SIPA retirement and pension benefits; non-contributory pensions and family allowances follow parallel calendars published on anses.gob.ar.

Beneficiaries can audit their exact October payment before it lands: log in to anses.gob.ar or the Mi ANSES app with a CUIL number and social-security password, open “Jubilaciones y Pensiones” and select “Consultar recibo de haberes” to see the net benefit, the ARS 70,000 supplement and any statutory deductions.

Context: Pensions Against a Weak Peso

The 1.66% rise arrives as household budgets remain under pressure. As The Rio Times reported this week, Argentina’s poverty rate rose to 32.3% in the first half of 2026, and JP Morgan has cut its growth forecast for the country to 1.5%. In dollar terms the minimum pension with bonus — about US$332 — illustrates how peso weakness offsets nominal increases: the official exchange rate has slipped past 1,500 per dollar, with the informal “blue” rate near 1,565.

Monthly mobility adjustments now compound through the year rather than arriving in quarterly jumps, smoothing income for retirees but also tying purchasing power tightly to each month’s inflation reading. September’s CPI figure, due in mid-October, will determine the November adjustment.

What We Could Not Confirm

Net amounts vary by beneficiary: statutory deductions depend on individual circumstances, and the ARS 492,676 take-home estimate applies to a single minimum benefit only. The day-by-day October payment schedule by DNI ending was reported by provincial media but we could not verify every date against the full official table at publication time. Dollar conversions use the Banco Nación official selling rate of about 1,524 pesos per dollar from the last close before publication; the informal blue rate trades weaker, near 1,565. Whether the ARS 70,000 bonus continues beyond October has not been formally announced.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is Argentina’s minimum pension in October 2026?

The guaranteed minimum pension is ARS 435,748.51 gross — about US$286 — after a 1.66% rise. With the extraordinary ARS 70,000 bonus, total income reaches ARS 505,748.51, roughly US$332 at the official exchange rate.

When does ANSES pay pensions in October 2026?

Payments run from Thursday 8 October to Thursday 29 October 2026, staggered by the final digit of the beneficiary’s DNI. Exact dates can be checked via Mi ANSES or anses.gob.ar.

How is the October 2026 pension increase calculated?

The 1.66% rise matches August inflation as measured by INDEC, under the monthly mobility formula of decree DNU 274/2024. It was formalised by ANSES Resolution 284/2026, published in the Official Gazette.

World.title: Colombia Visa Revocations Hit Two People the President Had Publicly Named
World.content:
Politics · Colombia

Key Facts — What happened The Colombia visa revocations of 28 September 2026 cover senator Martha Peralta and businessman Euclides Torres.

— Where the names came from Both had appeared on a list President Abelardo de la Espriella published in June 2026, before he took office.

— The catch Washington published no individual reason for either Colombian, and its statement does not mention the president or his list.

— Who they are Peralta sits in the Senate for the left-wing Pacto Histórico; Torres is a businessman close to former president Gustavo Petro.

— What comes next De la Espriella says more names will follow, and that United States Treasury asset sanctions could come after that.

A senator and a businessman lost their United States visas on Monday. Their names had been on a list the Colombian president published in June.

The Colombia visa revocations announced on Monday 28 September 2026 struck two people the country’s own president had named in public. Their names had been on his list since June.

The United States Department of State revoked the visas of Senator Martha Isabel Peralta Epieyú and the businessman Euclides Antonio Torres Romero. Their immediate families lost theirs as well.

Peralta sits with the left-wing opposition in the Senate. Torres is a businessman investigated over the financing of Gustavo Petro’s 2022 campaign.

The list the president read out himself

In June 2026 Abelardo de la Espriella was still a presidential candidate. In a live broadcast on Monday 8 June he read out names of Colombian politicians he accused of buying votes.

He addressed them to Christopher Landau, the deputy secretary of state and the second-ranking official at the State Department. “Le dejo aquí, subsecretario, unos nombres para que usted los tenga en el radar,” he said.

In English: I leave you some names here, deputy secretary, so you can keep them on your radar. Colombian outlets nickname Landau “el quitavisas”, the visa remover.

Infobae, a Latin American news site, listed 23 names from that broadcast the next day. Peralta and Torres were both on it.

He kept adding names through June in posts on X. La Silla Vacía, an investigative outlet in Bogotá, counts about 26 in all, every one aligned with Gustavo Petro.

La Silla Vacía also notes that he offered no evidence for the vote-buying he alleged. He won the runoff on 21 June 2026 and took office on 7 August 2026.

What Washington said, and what it left out

The Colombia visa revocations came inside a State Department statement of 28 September 2026 announcing a new regional policy. It covers people who undermine a democratically elected government through corruption or drug trafficking.

The statement describes Peralta only as a senator of the Pacto Histórico and of a smaller indigenous party. It describes Torres only as the owner of an energy, traffic-signal and public-lighting group.

It gives no individual reason for either of them. It does not mention the Colombian president, or his list, or any recommendation from Bogotá.

The statement came from Thomas Pigott, the department’s spokesman. It ties the step to a leaders’ statement of 22 September by a group called the Shield of the Americas.

That group is an American-led security pact against drug cartels, founded at a summit in Doral, Florida, on 7 March 2026. Colombia was not invited then, under Petro, and joined in August under De la Espriella.

The same statement covered 26 people in four countries under the new policy. Our report on the wider list sets out Bolivia, Ecuador and Peru.

Who the two Colombians are

Peralta is a senator for La Guajira, the desert department on Colombia’s Caribbean border with Venezuela. The Supreme Court is investigating her over contracts at the national disaster-relief agency, El Heraldo reported.

She has not been convicted of anything, and the case has stalled. Torres is investigated over the financing of Petro’s 2022 campaign, and he has not been convicted either.

El Heraldo reported that Torres has acknowledged giving logistical support to Petro’s pre-campaign. He denies financing the 2022 campaign itself.

Neither faces any charge in the United States. Visa decisions there require no court and no published proof.

“Me enteré por los medios de comunicación de que me habrían retirado la visa,” Peralta told El Heraldo. She learned of it from the press, she said, and had received no official notice.

She added that she would carry on with her work calmly, facing the country and respecting its institutions.

A president who welcomed it

De la Espriella celebrated the revocations on X on Monday evening. “La lucha apenas empieza; pronto se ampliará no solo en número, sino también en decisiones administrativas,” he wrote.

The fight is only beginning, he meant, and it will widen in numbers and in administrative measures. He then pointed at the OFAC list.

OFAC is the United States Treasury office that freezes the assets of sanctioned people and companies. Being placed on its list is far heavier than losing a visa.

Petro himself knows the instrument. Washington revoked his visa in September 2025, after he addressed a protest outside United Nations headquarters in New York.

The reaction in Bogotá

María Fernanda Cabal, a former senator, told Peralta not to expect explanations from Washington. She said the senator should instead account for public money in La Guajira.

Julián Uscátegui, a Bogotá city councillor, said he hoped more names would follow. He added that anyone who had committed crimes should answer to Colombian courts.

Iván Cepeda, the senator De la Espriella beat in the runoff, made a separate claim on Tuesday. He said on X that a plan had been revived to fabricate testimony against him in a United States case.

Cepeda gave no evidence, and Vanguardia said the closeness in time does not by itself show a link. He lost that runoff by about 252,000 votes, or 0.96 of a percentage point.

Why this matters outside Colombia

A visa is cheap for Washington to withdraw and expensive for the person who loses it. No hearing is held, no charge is filed and no evidence is published.

That makes it an attractive tool for any government that wants pressure applied to its rivals. The pressure arrives from abroad, and the domestic courts are never troubled.

Colombian institutions are not being bypassed in a formal sense, because a visa is a foreign sovereign decision. The practical effect is still that a political fight has acquired a second, foreign arena.

For foreign residents and investors, the rules of ordinary travel have not changed. The measures reach named people and their close families only.

The open question is how long the Colombian list turns out to be. De la Espriella says the number will grow; Washington has named no further Colombians so far.

More: Colombia coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who lost their United States visas in Colombia?

The Colombia visa revocations of 28 September 2026 covered Senator Martha Isabel Peralta Epieyú and the businessman Euclides Antonio Torres Romero, together with their immediate families. Peralta sits for the left-wing Pacto Histórico and the Movimiento Alternativo Indígena y Social. Torres owns a group active in energy, traffic signalling and public lighting. Neither has been convicted of any offence, and neither faces charges in the United States.

Did the Colombian president ask for this?

President Abelardo de la Espriella published names in June 2026, while he was still a candidate, and addressed them to the deputy secretary of state, Christopher Landau. Infobae listed 23 names from that broadcast, including Peralta and Torres. The State Department statement of 28 September 2026 makes no mention of the president, his list or any request from Bogotá.

Does this change anything for ordinary travellers?

No. The policy applies to named individuals and their immediate family members, under Section 212(a)(3)(C) of the United States Immigration and Nationality Act. Nothing in the announcement alters visa rules for other Colombians, or for foreign residents living in Colombia. The same announcement also covered 24 people in Bolivia, Ecuador and Peru.

What is the Shield of the Americas?

It is a security grouping led by the United States and aimed at drug cartels and organised crime in the Americas. It was launched at a summit in Doral, Florida, on 7 March 2026, hosted by President Donald Trump. Colombia did not attend that summit, which fell during Gustavo Petro’s presidency. Colombia joined in August 2026, shortly after Abelardo de la Espriella took office.

World.title: Bolivia Attorney General Case Could Lead to US Extradition, Minister Says
World.content:
Politics · Bolivia

Key Facts — What happened Bolivia’s government is asking Washington, through its Foreign Ministry, for the evidence behind the corruption designation of its chief prosecutor.

— How wide it goes The United States named thirteen Bolivians, including Attorney General Roger Mariaca, and made nine more ineligible without naming them.

— The catch No Bolivian court has convicted Mariaca, and Washington has published no evidence beyond the wording of its own release.

— What could follow Defence Minister Ernesto Justiniano said the case could lead to a United States investigation and probably an extradition request.

— What comes next Mariaca refuses to step aside, and Congress meets on 5 October to consider the American list and possible inquiries.

Washington has barred Bolivia’s chief prosecutor from the United States and accused him of taking bribes to facilitate drug trafficking. His own government now wants to see the file.

The United States has barred Bolivia’s attorney general from its territory. His own government now says it wants to see the case against him.

Ministers in La Paz said on Tuesday 29 September that they were asking Washington for the evidence. They are putting the request through the Foreign Ministry.

The man at the centre is Roger Mariaca Montenegro. He is the Fiscal General del Estado, the prosecutor who heads Bolivia’s Public Prosecutor’s Office.

What Washington actually did

The US Department of State published its decision on Monday 28 September. It announced a new visa restriction policy for the Western Hemisphere.

The policy rests on Section 212(a)(3)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act. That clause bars foreigners whose entry could seriously damage United States foreign policy.

Under it, Washington revoked the visas of twelve named Bolivians and their families. Nine more Bolivians who hold no visa were made generally ineligible for one.

The twelve include three prosecutors, three judges and two magistrates. The rest are a former justice minister, a former head of the national customs service, a police colonel and a businessman.

Mariaca was handled by a second and different instrument. The department publicly designated him for what it called significant corruption.

That designation is made under Section 7031(c) of the State Department’s 2026 appropriations act. The law requires the secretary of state to designate foreign officials where there is credible information of significant corruption.

The department said Mariaca solicited and accepted bribes to facilitate drug trafficking. It added that he helped violent criminals evade justice.

The designation makes him and his immediate family ineligible to enter the United States. Bolivia’s attorney general has rejected the accusations in full.

The measure is about entry, not money. The State Department announced no freezing of assets, and the full list across four countries ran in our earlier report.

La Paz asks for the file

Ernesto Justiniano Urenda has been Bolivia’s defence minister since June 2026. On Monday he said the government took the American statements with complete seriousness.

The government would ask for supplementary information and supporting evidence, he said. Bolivia wants to know what the American decision rests on.

“What we are doing at this moment is making the inquiries through the Foreign Ministry,” he said. The Bolivian state news agency ABI published the remarks on Tuesday.

Fernando Aramayo, the minister of the presidency, spoke on Monday at the Casa Grande del Pueblo, the seat of government. He called the situation a test of Bolivia’s democratic institutions.

He promised cooperation with whatever investigations Bolivian bodies decide to open. He also said the executive would not comment on any specific investigation.

Plaza Murillo in La Paz, with the Legislative Palace on the square and the glass tower of the Casa Grande del Pueblo, the seat of government, behind it. File photograph. (Photo: Parallelepiped09, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0)

The word extradition enters the debate

On Tuesday the defence minister was asked how far the matter could go. He did not rule anything out.

“Yes, this could lead to an investigation, a judicial step in the United States, probably an extradition request,” he said. He added that any such decision belonged to American authorities.

He asked for caution about the others named in the American measures. He said the government had no further information about their cases.

The accusations are those of a foreign government. The Bolivian state news agency noted in its report that they do not by themselves amount to a conviction.

The Bolivian government has announced no charge against Mariaca. No Bolivian court has convicted him, and Washington has published no evidence beyond the wording of its release.

Congress takes the file

Vice-President Edmand Lara presides over the Plurinational Legislative Assembly. He has called a session for Monday 5 October to consider the American list.

His written convocation says the Assembly may form a parliamentary commission of inquiry. It also says a foreign state’s immigration measures do not by themselves establish criminal responsibility in Bolivia.

The heads of both chambers had already asked the prosecutor to step aside, as we reported on Tuesday. Lara has rejected removing him over a list issued abroad.

Mariaca refuses to go. “I will not retreat even one centimetre,” he said in a video message released by the Public Prosecutor’s Office.

He said Bolivia respects the sovereign decisions of other states and expects the same respect for its own institutions. He said his office would carry on with the cases already under way.

Bolivia’s attorney general is chosen by Congress, not by the president. The Plurinational Legislative Assembly elected Mariaca on 21 October 2024, with 115 votes of the 161 cast, for a six-year term.

That is why removing him is a parliamentary matter. Any dismissal would run through a juicio de responsabilidades, the impeachment-style process Congress uses against high officials.

What it changes for people in Bolivia

For residents, travellers and businesses, nothing changes at any border. The measures reach named individuals and their immediate families, not Bolivian citizens in general.

Bolivia takes part in the Shield of the Americas, a United States-backed regional effort against organised crime. Washington tied Monday’s announcement to a statement by that group’s leaders on 22 September.

The calmer reading is that Bolivian institutions are engaging rather than refusing. The government has asked for evidence, Congress has asked for documents, and the prosecutor has answered in public.

The unsettled part is the sequence. Bolivia has asked for the file, and no answer from Washington has been reported.

A dissenting voice from the regions

Leonardo Loza, the governor of Cochabamba, rejected the American step on Tuesday. He called it a “judicial invasion” and said Bolivia was being made to look subordinate.

“I do not defend anyone, I do not justify anyone,” he told reporters. He added that those named should be investigated, without breaking the country’s sovereignty.

The government is also answering questions about the president’s recent trip to the United States. President Rodrigo Paz has governed Bolivia since November 2025.

Nothing in the American measure obliges Bolivia to act against its own prosecutor. What follows depends on whether Washington hands over its file, and on what the Assembly then does with it.

More: Bolivia coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Roger Mariaca?

Roger Mariaca Montenegro is Bolivia’s Fiscal General del Estado, the prosecutor who heads the Public Prosecutor’s Office. The Plurinational Legislative Assembly, Bolivia’s Congress, elected him on 21 October 2024 with 115 of the 161 votes cast, for a six-year term. He was sworn in two days later. Before that he was a departmental prosecutor in Santa Cruz.

What exactly did the United States do?

Two separate things on 28 September 2026. It announced a visa restriction policy under Section 212(a)(3)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, and used it to revoke the visas of twelve Bolivians and to make nine more ineligible. Separately it publicly designated Mariaca for significant corruption under Section 7031(c) of the State Department’s 2026 appropriations act. Both are entry measures; no financial sanctions were announced.

Has Bolivia’s attorney general been charged or convicted?

No Bolivian court has convicted him, and the government has announced no charge against him. Ministers say the competent Bolivian bodies will carry out whatever investigations are needed once Washington shares its material. A designation by a foreign government is an accusation, not a finding by a Bolivian judge.

Does this change anything for foreigners in Bolivia?

No. The measures apply to named individuals and their immediate families, and they concern entry to the United States. Visa rules for other Bolivians, and entry rules for foreigners going to Bolivia, are untouched by the announcement.

World.title: Bahamas Beach Access Row: Party Leader Arrested After Fence Pulled Down
World.content:
Politics · Bahamas

Key Facts — What happened Police arrested Coalition of Independents leader Lincoln Bain on Monday 28 September 2026 as he pulled down a beach fence.

— What the fight is about A US$550 million Four Seasons project has fenced part of Cabbage Beach, on the resort island across the harbour from Nassau.

— The catch Bain was released the same morning and says police laid no charge against him.

— Why a beach turned political A 60-year-old American visitor nearly drowned on Sunday after walking into the water to get around the fence.

— What comes next The environment minister says the Ministry of Works will remove the fence if the developer does not.

Police handcuffed a party leader on a Nassau resort beach and let him go the same morning. The Bahamas beach access row now has an arrest in it.

The Bahamas beach access row stopped being an argument on Monday 28 September 2026. Police handcuffed Lincoln Bain on Cabbage Beach as he and other protesters pulled a fence out of the sand.

Bain leads the Coalition of Independents, the Bahamian party known as the COI, which holds no seat in parliament. Officers in tactical gear walked him off the beach and drove him to the island police station.

He was released the same morning. Bain told The Tribune that police let him go without charge, and no charge against him has been reported since.

Why there is a fence on Cabbage Beach

Cabbage Beach runs along the resort island that faces Nassau across the harbour. The Atlantis and Riu resorts sit on it, and Bahamian vendors have worked the sand for decades.

Part of that sand is now fenced off for the Four Seasons Ocean Club Residences. The Tribune puts the project at US$550 million.

The Bahamian dollar trades at a rate of one to one with the US dollar. The Central Bank of The Bahamas says that parity has held since 1973.

The developers are Access Industries, which owns the existing Ocean Club, and the Florida firm Two Roads Development. The Four Seasons brand is the third partner, and its representatives did not answer messages from The Tribune.

The government did approve a temporary fence for erosion and beach restoration works. Zane Lightbourne, the minister of the environment and natural resources, says its conditions were not met.

“The Government of The Bahamas has an uncompromising position on Bahamians’ access to their beaches,” Lightbourne said. “The position applies to every developer operating in our country.”

His written statement said advance notice to government authorities was required before the fence went up. A public advisory process was required too, and he said neither happened.

The rescue that changed the temperature

On Sunday 27 September 2026 a 60-year-old American visitor was pulled into rough seas at Cabbage Beach. She had stepped into the water to get around the fence, on the eve of her birthday.

Lifeguards, vendors and protesters swam out and brought her ashore, and an ambulance took her to hospital. Among the rescuers was Lincoln Deal, an opposition member of parliament for the Free National Movement.

“We could’ve lost a life,” Deal told The Tribune. “That could happen to Bahamians, children, tourists.”

The Senate Building and the Queen Victoria statue on Parliament Square in Nassau, seat of the Bahamian Parliament. File photograph (Photo: Larry Syverson, CC BY-SA 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Who the Coalition of Independents are

The Coalition of Independents was launched in 2021 by independents and small parties who chose Bain as leader. Its platform calls for a sovereign wealth fund, tighter immigration rules and more open government.

At the general election on Tuesday 12 May 2026 the party took 17,095 votes and won no seats. That was about 12 percent of the votes counted, according to official results reported by The Nassau Guardian.

Bain came second in his own seat, Pinewood, with 1,137 votes. He finished ahead of the Free National Movement candidate, from the party that forms the official opposition.

That is the weight behind the man the police led off the beach. He speaks for a bloc of voters with no seat in the 41-member House of Assembly.

What each side is asking for

Bain told The Nassau Guardian that the fence stood in the sea rather than on land. “This isn’t a land dispute; someone put trash in the water, and we have a right to remove it,” he said.

Lightbourne says the restoration work can go ahead once the process is put right. He says the Ministry of Works will remove the fence if the developer does not, but he could not say when.

Dis We Beach, a campaign group for beach users and vendors, wants the surveyed fence line published. It also wants that line shown against the mean high-water mark, the average line the tide reaches.

The developer’s own environmental study promises public access through the three-and-a-half-year construction period. It promises a walkway 4.6 metres (15 feet) wide afterwards, with vendor kiosks leased at a nominal US$1 a month.

Why a fence matters to the whole country

The Bahamas earns its living from visitors and from financial services sold to foreigners. A confrontation on a resort beach touches the first of those directly.

The Central Bank reported 8.5 million visitor arrivals in the seven months to the end of July 2026. That was 14.8 percent more than a year earlier.

The same bank expects 2026 growth to moderately exceed the country’s medium-term potential of 1.5 to 1.9 percent. Beaches are the product, which is why a fence on one becomes a national argument.

What is still unsettled

No count of the protesters has been published. The Royal Bahamas Police Force has posted nothing about the arrest on its own news page.

The Bahamas beach access fight has run for a month at this one stretch of sand. This is the second fence, and the first came down on Sunday 30 August 2026.

The Department of Environmental Planning and Protection stepped in that time. The government later said the department had advised that work was needed against severe beach erosion.

Bain went into a meeting with the developer within hours of walking out of the police station. Who decides where a fence may stand on a Bahamian beach is the question nobody has answered.

More: Bahamas coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does COI stand for in the Bahamas?

COI stands for the Coalition of Independents. It is a Bahamian political party, not a commission or an inquiry. Independents and small parties founded it in 2021 and chose Lincoln Bain as leader. At the general election on 12 May 2026 it took 17,095 votes, about 12 percent of those counted, and won no seats in the 41-member House of Assembly.

Has Lincoln Bain been charged over the fence?

No charge has been reported. Bain told The Tribune that police released him without charge after taking him to the island police station on Monday 28 September 2026. No court appearance has been reported. The Royal Bahamas Police Force has posted nothing about the arrest on its own news page.

Can visitors still walk on Cabbage Beach?

The Bahamas beach access row is about a fence, not about whether the beach is public. Part of the sand is fenced for construction and beach restoration linked to the Four Seasons Ocean Club Residences. The environment minister has ordered that fence removed. The developer’s environmental study promises access during the three-and-a-half-year build and a walkway afterwards.

Where exactly is Cabbage Beach?

Cabbage Beach is not in Nassau itself. It lies on the resort island on the far side of Nassau Harbour, joined to the city by bridges. The Atlantis and Riu resorts front the beach, and Bahamian vendors have hired out chairs, umbrellas and water sports there for decades.

World.title: Murder accused Anthony Carballo Jr. seeks sentencing indication, signaling possible guilty plea
World.content:
Murder accused Anthony Carballo Jr. seeks sentencing indication, signaling possible guilty plea

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Anthony Carballo Jr., one of two men accused of the 2023 murder of Sylvian Nigel Swift, has asked the High Court for a sentencing indication — a move signaling that he is considering a guilty plea.

Carballo Jr. and his co-accused, Christopher Pitts Jr., appeared before Justice Nigel Pilgrim on Tuesday in connection with Swift’s April 27, 2023 murder in Belize City.

During the hearing, Carballo’s attorney, Nazira Myles-Espat, informed the court that she had recently been able to review the complete disclosure and requested a sentencing indication on behalf of her client.

A sentencing indication would give Carballo an idea of the sentence the court could impose should he decide to plead guilty to murder. No guilty plea was entered on Tuesday.

Justice Pilgrim adjourned the matter to October 8, 2026, when he is expected to give the indication. The Crown has been ordered to file agreed facts by October 5.

Pitts, who is represented by attorney Andrew Bennett, remains jointly charged with Carballo.

Swift, 30, was fatally shot on Antelope Street shortly before 8 p.m. on April 27, 2023. Contemporary reports said he was standing near his home when two men on a motorcycle opened fire. Swift was struck in the arm and neck and died from his injuries.

Police pursued the fleeing motorcycle, and a 9mm pistol and the motorcycle were recovered after the suspects reportedly fell from the bike and escaped on foot.

Carballo was arraigned for Swift’s murder on May 2, 2023, while Pitts was charged several days later on May 8. The pair were subsequently indicted jointly for murder before the High Court in 2025 and initially pleaded not guilty.

The case returns to court next week for Carballo’s sentencing indication.

World.title: Dead doctor’s statement sparks legal battle in weed gummies case against former Police Exhibit Keeper
World.content:
Dead doctor’s statement sparks legal battle in weed gummies case against former Police Exhibit Keeper

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The High Court will have to determine whether a statement given by the late Dr. Cecilio Eck can be admitted into evidence in the upcoming trial of former Belize Police Department exhibit keeper Mario Bustillos over the infamous 2023 cannabis-infused gummies incident.

The issue arose during a Case Management Conference before Justice Nigel Pilgrim on Tuesday, September 29.

Bustillos’ attorney, Nazira Myles-Espat, is challenging the contents and reliability of Dr. Eck’s statement. The Crown has indicated that a voir dire, or hearing within the trial to determine the admissibility of disputed evidence, will therefore be required.

Prosecutors will have to establish that Dr. Eck, who died earlier this year, is deceased and provide the circumstances under which his statement was obtained before seeking to rely on it at trial.

Dr. Eck reportedly treated two of the minors affected after cannabis-infused candies made their way into public circulation in April 2023. His medical evidence forms part of the Crown’s case against Bustillos.

Bustillos is accused of acting in excess of his authority as the Police Department’s exhibit keeper on April 21, 2023, by allegedly disposing of bags containing cannabis-infused gummies that had been placed in the police exhibit room for safekeeping.

Police previously said the gummies had been seized after entering Belize and were later discarded in a garbage trailer at the Queen Street Police Station compound before being taken to the Belize City transfer station. Some subsequently made their way back into circulation and were sold to members of the public. More than 30 children and several adults were hospitalized after consuming the marijuana-laced sweets.

Bustillos was initially charged with 10 counts of negligent harm involving minors affected by the incident. Those charges were later discontinued and he was subsequently charged with willful oppression.

The Crown is expected to call more than 20 witnesses when the matter goes to trial. Bustillos remains on bail and on interdiction from the Police Department.

His trial, which had been scheduled to begin in September, has since been pushed back to March 9, 2027, because of the High Court’s trial calendar.

World.title: Evan Gillett fined $6,000 for almost 3lbs of weed; Pleads guilty so father-in-law isn’t charged
World.content:
Evan Gillett fined $6,000 for almost 3lbs of weed; Pleads guilty so father-in-law isn’t charged

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 46-year-old Belize City businessman has avoided immediate jail time after pleading guilty to possession of 1,295 grams of marijuana with intent to supply.

Evan Michael Gillett appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday alongside his 69-year-old father-in-law, Bert Foreman, following a police search conducted on Sunday, September 27.

Gillett pleaded guilty to possession of a controlled drug with intent to supply, while Foreman pleaded not guilty.

According to the facts presented in court, police received information from the Fusion Center about a vehicle suspected of transporting drugs. Officers were later directed to a residence on Nurse Seay Street, where they allegedly saw Gillett running from the house.

Police say that after he was detained, Gillett told officers that marijuana was inside a drum and expressed concern that his father-in-law could be taken to jail. A search reportedly led to the discovery of a yellow bag containing suspected cannabis weighing 1,295 grams.

In court, Gillett accepted responsibility but disputed the allegation that he had run from police. He also told the court that he had not intended to supply the marijuana to anyone.

The Magistrate initially considered a starting sentence of two years’ imprisonment and an $8,000 fine. Gillett’s previous drug conviction was treated as an aggravating factor, increasing the prospective sentence to two years and six months and the fine to $9,000.

However, a one-third reduction was applied for his early guilty plea.

Gillett was ultimately sentenced to one year and nine months in prison, suspended for two years, and fined $6,000. He was ordered to pay $2,000 immediately, with the remaining $4,000 due by June 30, 2027.

The court explained that the suspended sentence means Gillett will not immediately serve the one-year-nine-month prison term, but it remains hanging over him during the two-year suspension period and could be activated if he is convicted of another offence.

Following Gillett’s guilty plea, the prosecution withdrew the charge against Foreman, who was free to leave the court.

World.title: Nicaraguan woman charged for presenting fake driver’s license at Cemetery Road checkpoint
World.content:
Nicaraguan woman charged for presenting fake driver’s license at Cemetery Road checkpoint

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 35-year-old Nicaraguan woman has been charged after police say she presented a Belize driver’s licence that appeared to have been tampered with and could not be verified in official records.

Yadira De Los Angeles Aldana, a permanent resident of Belize, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday, September 28, where she was arraigned on a single charge of uttering upon a false document.

Police allege that on September 24, Aldana was driving a gold Chrysler Aspen SUV when she was stopped at a vehicular checkpoint on Cemetery Road near Constitution Park.

An enforcement officer reportedly inspected the licence Aldana presented and noticed several inconsistencies. Checks were then made with internal records and the Transport Department, but police were reportedly unable to locate any record of a driver’s licence issued in Aldana’s name.

Aldana was subsequently detained and charged.

No plea was taken during Monday’s arraignment after the police prosecutor informed the court that instructions are being sought from the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions on whether the matter will proceed summarily in the Magistrate’s Court or on indictment before the High Court.

Aldana’s attorney, Leeroy Banner, told the court that his client has lived in Belize for approximately 23 years and holds permanent resident status. He also said she had travelled to Belize City to make funeral arrangements for her father when she was detained.

Banner raised concern about the length of time Aldana remained in police custody before she was formally charged.

The prosecution did not object to bail, and Aldana was granted bail in the sum of $2,000 with one surety in the same amount, which she met.

She is scheduled to return to court on November 26, 2026, when disclosure is expected to be provided.

World.title: Magistrate dismisses aggravated assault charge against interdicted cop
World.content:
Magistrate dismisses aggravated assault charge against interdicted cop

By Breaking Belize News Staff: An aggravated assault charge against Police Constable Luwis Pascascio has been dismissed after the prosecution was unable to produce a case file in the matter.

Pascascio, who had been placed on interdiction following his arraignment in May, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday, September 28, where the sitting Magistrate dismissed the charge. Public reporting confirms that the court was informed that no case file had been produced.

The 31-year-old officer had been charged with aggravated assault upon fellow police officer PC Jose Mejia following an incident at the Puma Gas Station on Freetown Road in May.

Police alleged that Mejia and PC Mario Coye were on motorcycle patrol when they observed a vehicle run a red light at the intersection of St. Thomas and St. Joseph streets. The vehicle was followed to the gas station, where Mejia approached it with his service firearm drawn because its windows were heavily tinted.

Police alleged that Pascascio exited the vehicle and continued advancing toward Mejia after being ordered to stop. Mejia alleged that Pascascio later slapped him across the face, causing a small cut to his lower lip. Pascascio was subsequently detained and charged. He was granted bail with a condition that he remain at least 100 feet away from Mejia.

Speaking following Monday’s dismissal, Pascascio said he had appeared in court about five times since May but had never been provided with disclosure.

He complained that police “can’t get their act together” and said he and his attorney, Oscar Selgado, will now discuss pursuing legal action following the dismissal.

Pascascio has previously faced another aggravated assault allegation. In September 2024, he was charged with aggravated assault with a firearm involving Belizean athlete Shaun Christopher Gill after Gill alleged that an officer assaulted him with a firearm. That case was subsequently withdrawn after Gill requested no further court action.

Monday’s dismissal means Pascascio no longer faces the aggravated assault charge arising from the May incident with his fellow officer.

World.title: Nearly four years after guilty pleas, two men still awaiting sentence for 2018 manslaughter killing of PC Osbourne Martinez
World.content:
Nearly four years after guilty pleas, two men still awaiting sentence for 2018 manslaughter killing of PC Osbourne Martinez

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Nearly four years after pleading guilty to manslaughter in the killing of Police Constable Osbourne Martinez, two Belize City men are still waiting to be sentenced.

Tyrique Myles and Glen Lopez appeared before Justice Nigel Pilgrim in the High Court this week as the court moved to finally conclude sentencing proceedings stemming from the November 2, 2018 killing of the 27-year-old police officer.

The two men pleaded guilty to the lesser charge of manslaughter in November 2022 after initially being charged jointly with murder alongside Rayford Mejia. At the time, Justice Ricardo O’Neil Sandcroft had been presiding over the matter.

Justice Pilgrim reportedly acknowledged the lengthy delay and indicated that the court does not want the matter prolonged any further. The Crown, represented by Senior Crown Counsel Riis Cattouse, and defence attorneys Norman Rodriguez and Orson “OJ” Elrington have been instructed to put together the material necessary for sentencing, including an agreed statement of facts and mitigation submissions.

The matter has now been adjourned to October 8, 2026, for sentencing.

The case dates back almost eight years. Martinez was shot while responding to an armed robbery at the Belcove Hotel on Regent Street West in downtown Belize City. Police reports at the time said three armed men entered the hotel and robbed persons inside before officers arrived. Martinez was shot in the abdomen and later died while undergoing treatment at the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital.

Myles, Lopez and Mejia were subsequently arrested and jointly charged with murder and robbery-related offences. Police also recovered firearms following the confrontation near the Haulover Creek.

While Myles and Lopez opted to plead guilty to manslaughter, Mejia maintained his innocence and went to trial. In May 2023, Justice Sandcroft found Mejia guilty of murder after accepting prosecution evidence that he had fired the shot that killed Martinez.

On June 29, 2023, Mejia was sentenced to life imprisonment and ordered to serve 25 years before becoming eligible for parole, with time already spent on remand deducted from that period.

During sentencing, Sandcroft stressed the seriousness of killing a police officer in the execution of his duties and noted that Martinez had lost his life while responding to an emergency and attempting to protect members of the public.

Nearly three years after Mejia was sentenced — and almost four years after their own guilty pleas — Myles and Lopez are now expected to learn their sentences when the matter returns to court on October 8.

World.title: High Court finds Rupert Codd guilty of raping sick woman on picnic table outside KHMH
World.content:
High Court finds Rupert Codd guilty of raping sick woman on picnic table outside KHMH

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Rupert Codd, a 25-year-old resident of Mile 5 on the Philip Goldson Highway, was found guilty of rape on Tuesday, September 29, 2026, by High Court Justice Derick F. Sylvester.

The verdict was handed down at 9:30 a.m. following a bench trial in the High Court of Belize. Codd was accused of raping a 35-year-old woman on picnic table in the early morning hours of April 2, 2023, outside the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital (KHMH).

According to the evidence presented in court, the victim was unwell and walking to KHMH to seek medical attention around 3:00 a.m. when she was accosted before entering the facility. Codd physically assaulted her, dragged her onto a nearby picnic table, and raped her.

During the trial, Crown Prosecutor Maria Santana Nembhard called 11 witnesses and submitted key evidence, including a 37-second video showing a man in yellow shorts and red sneakers walking near Brad’s Store toward Freetown Road. A police officer who attended primary school with Codd positively identified him from the footage.

Codd, who was represented by attorney Michael Peyrefitte, admitted to being at the scene and physically assaulting the woman, but denied having sex with her. He claimed he had left a nightclub, stopped to urinate behind a building near the Belcan area, and placed his wallet and phone on a picnic table. Codd alleged that when he returned, his items were missing and he confronted the woman, claiming he found his missing belongings inside her bosom. In his 30-page judgment, Justice Sylvester rejected Codd’s narrative as a fabricated story concocted to explain his presence at the crime scene.

Although there was no DNA testing linking hair found on Codd’s clothing to the victim, Justice Sylvester concluded that the Crown successfully proved all essential elements of the crime: that penetration occurred, that it was committed by Codd, and that it was without consent. Justice Sylvester noted minor inconsistencies in the victim’s testimony but deemed them irrelevant to the charge, finding her account credible and reliable while rejecting Codd’s defense.

Following the verdict, Codd was remanded back into custody until his sentencing hearing on November 9, 2026, when Justice Sylvester will consider a mitigation plea on his behalf. Prior to sentencing, the court ordered a Social Inquiry Report, a Victim Impact Statement, an Antecedent Report detailing Codd’s criminal history, and a Prison Report. Under Belizean law, Codd faces a minimum penalty of eight years up to life imprisonment.

World.title: Minister of Health calls for renewed CARICOM action on Non-Communicable Diseases
World.content:
Minister of Health calls for renewed CARICOM action on Non-Communicable Diseases

By Zoila Palma: Minister of Health and Wellness Kevin Bernard is calling for renewed regional action to address non-communicable diseases (NCDs) as CARICOM prepares to mark the 20th anniversary of the Port-of-Spain Declaration in 2027.

The declaration was adopted by CARICOM Heads of Government in 2007, committing the region to bold action against NCDs.

Bernard highlighted the upcoming anniversary during the 53rd Meeting of the CARICOM Council for Human and Social Development (COHSOD) – Health.

The Minister said the milestone should serve not only as an opportunity to reflect on progress but also as a call for stronger engagement beyond the health sector and greater accountability for results.

He also emphasized the need for continued regional cooperation to strengthen health systems against infectious disease outbreaks and climate-related shocks, while protecting the health and resilience of Caribbean communities.

World.title: St Elizabeth student injured by falling boulder still unconscious at UHWI
World.content:
A loosened boulder on the train track in St Elizabeth where three students were injured, one of whom remains unconscious.

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The young schoolgirl, Kendra Rose, who was one of three students injured by a falling boulder as they made their way to Merrywood Primary School in St Elizabeth earlier this month, remains hospitalised in an unconscious state at the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI).

Member of Parliament for St Elizabeth North West, Andrew Morris, provided the update on Tuesday during his contribution to the State of the Constituency Debate in the House of Representatives. He also shared that all medical fees for Rose’s treatment have been waived.

Morris noted that the “heartbreaking incident” occurred on the Merrywood to Breadnut Walk stretch. “Three children were severely injured by falling boulders while forced to use an abandoned train track as an alternative route to get to Merrywood Primary School. No child should risk life and limb just to seek an education,” he said.

READ: Three children injured after being hit by boulder in St Elizabeth

The first-term MP told the House that following dialogue with Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon and Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton and his team, “I am relieved to announce that all medical fees related to care for Kendra Rose have been waived…,” Morris said.

He also shared that the other two children were treated and released from hospital but are still undergoing treatment.

“I have made visits to the hospital and their homes and offered support to the families. Furthermore, I have engaged in constructive dialogue with the Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries, Minister Floyd Green, concerning the rehabilitation of the road from Merrywood to Breadnut Walk under the Farm Road Programme to ensure this tragedy is never repeated,” Morris said.

He also pointed out that his constituents face dangerous roadway breakaways that threaten to cut off entire communities, specifically in Ginger Hill, Pisgah, Cornwall, Retirement and Jointwood.

— Lynford Simpson

World.title: US Supreme Court lifts limits on third-country deportations
World.content:
This image released by the Department of Defense shows US Northern Command supporting Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportation flights via military airlift, at Fort Bliss, Texas, February 7, 2025. (Photo: AFP)

WASHINGTON, United States (AFP) — The United States (US) Supreme Court on Tuesday lifted restrictions until further notice on the deportation of undocumented immigrants to third countries.

The high court granted a request from the Trump administration to suspend a lower court ruling that restricted a policy of deporting undocumented immigrants to countries that are not their own.

In a brief statement, the court ruled that it will hear the case on its merits in December.

World.title: Profound sorrow
World.content:
A police vehicle seen on the campus of Wolmer’s Boys’ School on Monday after the death of a fourth-form student. Photo: Joseph wellington

DEEP sorrow and grief shrouded Wolmer’s Boys’ School on Monday after a fourth-form student collapsed in class and died.

“I don’t think we’ve ever had such a situation; meaning, it’s typical for us to have students fall ill, we take them for medical attention, and we see them back in school. It’s the first that we’re having an experience where a student has been taken for medical attention and will not be back with us,” Principal Dwight Pennycooke told journalists at the school in the Corporate Area.

The principal said he was unable to give a detailed account of the school’s initial reaction to the incident, as, after receiving the call from the school nurse informing him of the situation, he had been at Medical Associates Hospital where the student was rushed.

However, he shared that his students were compassionate and empathetic and he expected that the school would be in a period of mourning for quite some time.

“I know over the next few days it’s going to be a difficult one for his peers, his teachers, and for us the administration. We’ve never had to walk through something like this, but we will, through the grace of God, and the help of the support, walk through this and ensure that we provide the necessary support to his peers as well,” said Pennycooke.

He added that, in his absence, vice-principals had been ensuring that the school remained settled, while an early dismissal gave students and staff time to “decompress and to process” what had happened.

He further noted that he could not speak to the specifics surrounding the medical emergency, but recalled seeing the school nurse’s urgent response after receiving her call.

“I saw her running. She’s heavily pregnant, and you see her running, and so I think you would appreciate that she had the sense that this is an emergency, and so she dealt with whatever the call was… in that moment. So that is all I’m aware of,” he said.

Pennycooke reiterated that the school would continue to provide necessary support to those in mourning, noting that the Ministry of Education responded to the incident, and that counsellors were immediately deployed.

“Our young men are quite sensitive, and when it comes down to empathy and compassion, I know I’m going to have to support them quite a bit over the next couple of days… We had a counselling team here earlier. We had our women’s girls’ school counsellors come over. Now we have persons from the Ministry of Education, and no doubt we will have them again for the next couple of days,” he said.

The principal’s update followed a statement released by Wolmer’s Joint Board of Management, which detailed that the student was rushed to hospital where he was later pronounced dead after he collapsed at school.

The board expressed profound sorrow for the loss of the student and further extended its condolence to his parents, relatives, friends, classmates, teachers, and all whose lives he touched.

The board also said that affected peers and staff were being provided with emotional support and asked that the privacy of the student’s family and the school community be respected at this time.

“We also urge the public to refrain from speculation or the circulation of unverified information concerning the circumstances of his passing. The Wolmer’s family stands together in grief and will continue to support the student’s loved ones in the days ahead,” the board said.

World.title: ‘We are not breaking ranks’
World.content:
TWO defence lawyers representing murder accused Andre Ruddock appeared in court on Monday as his trial continued, despite colleagues maintaining a pledge to withdraw legal services from all criminal matters islandwide in pursuit of amendments to the Firearms Prohibition Restriction and Regulation Act 2022.

But according to attorney Anthony Williams, he and fellow counsel Venice Brown did not break ranks with their colleagues. Instead they had a duty to their client which had to be fulfilled.

“We want to make it very clear that we are not breaking ranks with our colleagues. Myself and Miss Brown are 150 per cent in support of our colleagues. However, there is a difference — the Jamaica Bar Association knows about it and they also sanctioned it. The difference is that when you are in a part-heard matter you can’t just go and strike like that. You have to seek the permission of your client in writing,” Williams told the Jamaica Observer.

“If you don’t seek the permission of your client in writing, then you can be deemed to have neglected your client and you can be sanctioned as well. Also, the court can proceed with the matter and the judge can possibly cite you for contempt of court,” Williams explained.

He added that in the absence of defence attorneys a judge may decide to proceed in a part-heard matter because lawyers are expected to be present. He said that if they don’t turn up, they do so at their own peril.

“The situation is different when you are in a part-heard matter, and the lawyer, whoever he or she is, cannot just abandon their client just like that; they have to seek the client’s permission. And in this particular case our client said, ‘Run with it.’ There are many other lawyers who are in the same position, but we have not abandoned our colleagues,” Williams stressed.

In addition to Williams and Brown, a number of attorneys showed up for their clients on Monday at the Home Circuit Court for various reasons, including that some were not in agreement with the protest action.

Essentially, the defence lawyers are arguing that the Act removes discretionary powers from judges, as it mandates a 15-year minimum sentence for an illegal gun possession conviction.

Williams’ client, Ruddock, is being tried in relation to the October 17, 2021 killing of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner in what has been described as a human sacrifice ritual at Pathways International Restoration Ministries in Albion St James. Ruddock allegedly cut Gardner’s throat on the instruction of his now deceased pastor, Kevin Smith.

Smith died in a car crash in St Catherine a few days later while being transported to Kingston to be charged with the incident.

On Monday the fourth witness in the case, a police sergeant based in St James, returned to complete his testimony which he started last week.

He described the scene at the church as “evil, fluid and chaotic”.

“People were moving from one direction to the next. One body was seen close to the pool area,” the witness recalled.

He explained that members of the Jamaica Defence Force (JDF) made their way through barbed wires to gain access to the compound of the church where three people, including Gardner and two male members of the church, lay dead.

One of the men was allegedly killed by Smith, while the police were said to have shot dead the other man who had rushed toward them with a knife. Based on the sustained gunfire and the sacrificial-type activities that were taking place at the church, the security forces had to call for adequate back-up, which included support from the military.

“The soldiers got to the barbed wire. I saw them climbing over and onto the church premises. On reaching the premises I shouted out to them. Police, accompanied by army personnel, proceeded towards a person who was kneeling behind the column at the entrance gate. I observed them accosting this person. They arrested him and carried out a search of him. The police and soldiers then forced open the big entrance gate,” the witness said.

“When they got there, the man was still in the kneeling position with white cloth over his head. He stood up and the officers searched him. When he stood up, from where I was standing [on the roof] I couldn’t see his face. I could only see the height of the person who was about 5 feet two or three inches tall. At that time there were a lot of police personnel and soldiers around this man. They took him on[to] the roadway and I couldn’t see what took place from there,” the witness said, without being able to say who the man was.

World.title: Stitchie: A legacy that connected dancehall, gospel
World.content:
Lieutenant Stitchie at the 2019 Sterling Gospel Music Awards

Lieutenant Stitchie’s voice may have fallen silent, but the influence of the veteran deejay — who commanded respect in both secular dancehall and gospel music spheres — is expected to continue reverberating across generations.

The veteran artiste, whose given name was Cleveland “Cleve” Laing, died at Kingston Public Hospital on Monday morning, one day shy of his 61st birthday.

The news comes less than 24 hours after his wife, Sophia Laing, confirmed that the entertainer had been hospitalised with a low blood count and was receiving treatment.

His passing closes a remarkable chapter in Jamaican music — one that began in dancehall and found a path to gospel.

For distinguished cultural analyst, Professor Donna Hope, Lieutenant Stitchie’s ability to remain loved across musical boundaries was rooted not only in his talent, but also in his personality that endeared him to audiences.

“Stitchie was loved because a lot of his songs were humorous. They were fun and they made people happy,” Hope said. She pointed to his enduring early hit Wear Yu Size, noting that the song was “digestible”, catchy and non-combative — qualities that helped establish his connection with listeners.

“Stitchie had an excellent career in dancehall and that followed him into gospel,” Hope continued. “I saw Mr Vegas made a post and I’m sure several others will as the news spreads because a lot of the artistes he would have came up with in that era were still close to him even though they were doing different genres.”

Entertainers and government officials took to social media to pay tribute to the deejay. Among them Prime Minister Andrew Holness, Tarrus Riley and Chevelle Franklyn (who also transitioned from dancehall to gospel).

Professor Hope shared that Stitchie’s significance extended beyond his music.

“Having a relationship with secular artistes was something Stitchie did well because he understood that it was important to minister to the sheep that ought to be brought into the fold,” she said. “This loss will be felt across genres and eras. He is a part of the industry in a way few artistes were, and so he will never be forgotten.”

Basillia Barnaby-Cuff, founder and director of Sterling Gospel Music Awards, agreed.

“I think Stitchie set a beautiful example of how you can remain an influence with people even when you’re in a different season of your life,” she said. “He was able to bridge the gap between the secular and gospel. He was still able to be on stage with secular artistes, singing gospel without compromising his walk with Christ.”

For Barnaby-Cuff, that was the essence of Stitchie’s ministry — not simply preaching to people already inside the church, but allowing his life and testimony to reach those outside it.

“It is about allowing your life to minister to those you wish will come over to Christianity,” she said.

The Sterling Gospel Music Awards family shared a particularly close connection with the artiste in his later years. A few years ago, Stitchie was honoured at the awards with the KFC Big Deal Award, an occasion Barnaby-Cuff now views with gratitude.

“I am just so happy we were able to give him his flowers while he was alive,” she said. “The gospel fraternity and we here at the Sterling Gospel Music Awards are really saddened by this news.”

Even as his health deteriorated, the organisation continued to support him, raising funds towards his care in the hope that his condition would improve.

“As the body of Christ, we are so grateful that he used the latter part of his years in ministry, and that he brought so many other persons to Christ,” she said. “He truly lived a full life and, as children of God, we don’t mourn as if we don’t have hope, and so that hope is something we hold on to and that one day we will see him again in the great resurrection.

Stitchie emerged from the competitive sound-system culture of Spanish Town in the early 1980s, working alongside artistes including Papa San and Wickerman. His breakthrough came in 1986 with the humorous Wear Yu Size, followed by songs such as Natty Dread, as his distinctive delivery and ability to connect with audiences propelled him beyond Jamaica. In 1988, he secured a recording deal with Atlantic Records, marking another significant milestone in a career that was increasingly taking him onto the international stage.

But it was his decision to walk away from secular music and embrace Christianity in 1997 that would ultimately redefine his legacy.

In 2014 he published his autobiography and among his accolades was honoured with the Order of Distinction in the rank of Officer in 2021 for his contribution to music.

World.title: Debutants Tru-Juice remaining calm despite table-topping JPL start
World.content:
Tru-Juice FC striker Daniel Roberts celebrates after scoring the winning goal in the club’s 1-0 victory over Molynes United in the Jamaica Premier League at Stadium East on Sunday. (Photo: JPL)

DESPITE Tru-Juice FC’s strong start to their debut Jamaica Premier League (JPL) season, Assistant Coach Craig Richards says it’s too early to be thinking about the play-offs.

The newly promoted club lead the JPL stadings on seven points after a 1-0 win over Molynes United at Stadium East on Sunday. Striker Daniel Roberts’s 62nd-minute strike was enough as Tru-Juice stay unbeaten after their first three games. They also join Montego Bay United and Waterhouse as the only two clubs who have yet to concede.

Richards says he was pleased with the team’s execution, after nearly a week of preparation.

“We knew that it was going to be a tough-fought game. We know how the Molynes team plays and we’ve been training all week to nullify them — and we also worked on ways to hurt them and it paid dividends,” he said.

“When we play against certain teams, we really assess them and train accordingly, so I’m very pleased. There are parts of the game that I’m disappointed with but there are aspects that I’m very pleased [about], and that’s football. I’m pleased we got three points on the board, and we look forward to the next game.”

Tru-Juice have attracted several top players to join their inaugural season, including Reggae Boyz Alex Marshall, Gadail Irving, and Tafari Chambers.

The Linstead based-club caught the eyes of many during their opening game when they thrashed reigning Caribbean Cup champions Mount Pleasant FA 4-0 and held last season’s semi-finalists, Montego Bay United, to a goalless draw.

Although starting on a positive note, Richards says they’re not placing too much pressure on themselves.

“Our objective is to play quality football and maximise on the points and [see] wherever that leads us,” he said. “Our aim is to compete. And competing can lead us to good places but as it relates to [the] objective [of] top six or whatever, if that should come then we are very welcoming for that but for now we’re taking it three games at a time.

“This is our first season. There are quite a number of teams that have been competing in this competition for some time so they have some experience. While we have experienced players, the club itself is in its first season so we continue to set different objectives at different points of the season, and we’ll see where that leads us.”

Mount Pleasant Head Coach Theodore Whitmore was pleased his team got off the mark after their 2-0 win over Dunbeholden at the Dunbeholden Sports Complex.

After losing their first two games of the season, goals from Trayvone Reid and Nicholas Nelson ensured the St Ann-based club picked up all three points.

“It doesn’t feel like three, it feels like six points,” Whitmore said. “I think we would have met our objective when we got two goals this afternoon; we didn’t concede, we kept a clean sheet, so I think it’s something that we can build on.

“When you look at the table and see Mount Peasant at the foot, nobody expects that. It wasn’t pleasing even for the fans that travel with us every Sunday, so it’s very pleasing [to beat Dunbeholden]. We look forward to the next one; and it gives us now a momentum going into the next game and into the semi-final of the Caribbean Cup.”
