World.title: ALL THE KING’S MEN
World.content:
Hunain Shah (second right) of Jamaica Kingsmen celebrates with teammates (from left) Keemo Paul, Andre Russell, and Vitel Lawes after getting the wicket of Roston Chase during their Republic Bank Caribbean Premier League T20 match with St Lucia Kings in Gros Islet, St Lucia, on Friday, August 21. (PHOTO: CPLT20)

JAMAICA Kingsmen Head of Operations Atishai Mansingh says a strong collective effort will be needed to continue cricket’s revival on the island.

The Kingsmen finished runners-up of the recently concluded Republic Bank Caribbean Premier League (CPL), after losing to the Antigua and Barbuda Falcons in the final in Barbados.

It was a remarkable run for the Jamaican franchise in their first season as the Kingsmen, having been inactive for the 2024 and 2025 seasons after former owner Kris Persaud sold the franchise and moved on to the now-champions Falcons.

This season also saw the return of CPL to Sabina Park for the first time since 2019, with four games hosted in Kingston.

While pleased with the franchise’s start, Mansingh says he’s focused on helping to grow the sport locally.

“CPL coming back is not going to solve all of the issues that we have in Jamaica cricket,” he said. “It’s a spark, and what we do with that spark is what will determine whether this moment becomes a temporary celebration or the beginning of a genuine revival — and the revival is going to start from the top down.

“We want to encourage all of public and corporate Jamaica to see the highest-paying sport for what it is. The fact is, we’re not going to fill Sabina Park this year, we’re not going to fill Sabina Park next year, but we have to work towards filling Sabina Park in the years coming, because if this park is seen as a football park, as an entertainment park, for the history that it holds, every single one of us are failing. Filling Sabina Park is not about the Kingsmen putting on social media s and giving away tickets. It’s about the teamwork [and] the support which is needed to to build these cricket structures in Jamaica.”

Mansingh says cricket’s development locally cannot be driven solely by finances but must also be fuelled by passion for the sport.

“Players cannot rebuild it alone. The Government and sponsors, though we always request them, also cannot build it alone. Clubs, schools, families, businesses and supporters must all play a part,” he said.

“If we don’t put the love into the sport, who’s going to? [People] say, ‘Who’s going to fix cricket?’ ‘CPL come, they have money, they’re going to fix it’, ‘This person have money so they’re going to fix it’. Money is not going to fix this; it’s the love that we all possess for the sport that’s going to bring the happiness back to the sport.”

Mansingh says more emphasis needs to be placed on women’s cricket as well, with the debut of the Jamaica Empress team in the Women’s CPL providing a good starting point.

“Cricket is not just about a man with a ball and a man with a bat,” he said. “The women are equally important for this sport’s growth. The Kingsmen launched the first-ever Jamaica women’s CPL franchise, the Jamaica Empress. It has given an opportunity to women to see the sport as a way of employment. A sport that was always seen as a gentleman’s sport has now been seen as just simply a sport.

“That is very crucial, because when the likes of Hayley Matthews, Stafanie Taylor, Chinelle Henry are able to go to tournaments across the world and earn US$250,000 [$38 million] for a six-week tournament, that is eye-opening to state that this sport is not just going to fill the pockets of men any more but it’s going to create structures and systems for young girls to say, ‘I want to be like them when I’m older.’ ”

World.title: Labour conference special: Manchester’s new mayor
World.content:
On a special edition of Westminster Insider from Labour Party conference, Pat and Sascha sat down with the new Mayor of Greater Manchester, Bev Craig, at the POLITICO Pub in Liverpool.

In a conversation recorded in front of a live audience on Tuesday, shortly before Andy Burnham’s conference speech, Craig opened up about what it’s really like taking over from her predecessor — and how she plans to make the job her own.

Fresh from a trip to New York, she revealed what she learned from Mayor Zohran Mamdani and what Greater Manchester might borrow from his playbook.

World.title: Labour picks a side on Gaza — and cheers the party faithful
World.content:
But in addressing one of the most difficult fault lines in the party membership, Miliband has also sparked deep anger among some of his colleagues, particularly some Jewish Labour members, and charges of diplomatic recklessness. Miliband’s team has yet to respond to a request for comment on this piece.

Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, was seen as flat-footed in his support for Gaza as Israel responded with force to the Oct. 7 2023 attacks, and slow in his decision to recognize Palestine. Under his leadership, constituencies with high Muslim populations turned away from the Labour Party in large numbers, either electing independents or preferring the Greens.

But one of Miliband’s first acts as Burnham’s foreign secretary was to announce the sanctions — and accuse Israel’s government of turning a blind eye to the “ethnic cleansing” of Palestinians by settlers. It was a dramatic escalation of the British government’s rhetoric.

Jess Phillips, a Labour former minister who is the MP for Birmingham Yardley, said: “I think it’s a beginning of building back trust with the vast majority.

“I wouldn’t say there is a ticker tape parade or anything but an opportunity for a fair hearing.”

Emily Thornberry, the Labour chair of the cross-party Foreign Affairs Committee, said: “As far as I’m concerned, the only important consideration is that the government has finally done the right thing.” She told at the POLITICO Pub at party conference in Liverpool Tuesday: “If you’re a grown-up politician, you can say sometimes: ‘Well, we were wrong about that. We wished we’d listened to you.'”

World.title: Family first: Le Pen clan tightens its grip as Bardella hits trouble
World.content:
Le Pen has so far backed Bardella, offering her protégé an emphatic public defense. “The system will do anything — including the most disgusting things — to try to hinder this momentum,” she said, sitting next to him as they addressed reporters in the National Assembly Tuesday.

But Bardella’s difficulties inside the party predate the allegations — and the latest controversy now threatens to amplify them. His standing inside the National Rally had already grown precarious, with Le Pen drawing relatives and longtime loyalists closer as she prepares for next year’s presidential election.

Le Pen’s 27-year-old niece Nolwenn Olivier, Bardella’s former girlfriend, has been promoted to communications director. Another niece, Marion Maréchal, who broke with the party during the last presidential election, is back in favor and expected to play a frontline role. And Le Pen’s own brother-in-law, Philippe Olivier, an unofficial chief adviser, is taking part in many top campaign meetings.

At the same time, several figures associated with Bardella have been sidelined, passed over for promotion, or even ejected from the party. Once touted as a possible replacement for Le Pen, Bardella was not invited to speak at a recent National Rally parliamentary gathering, despite being party president and Le Pen’s presumptive choice for prime minister.

There is no indication Le Pen is preparing to cast Bardella aside. And yet, she has shown before that protecting the party can trump even the closest personal ties. In 2015, amid another controversy over antisemitic remarks, she backed the expulsion of the party’s founder — her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen.

That history leaves Bardella with little room for error as Marine Le Pen prepares for her fourth attempt at the presidency — and increasingly surrounds herself with people whose loyalty she has little reason to question.

World.title: Gordon Brown can’t stop talking to Andy Burnham’s team
World.content:
“As Gordon Brown has said, we can be the world’s innovation nation, and he’s right, we can,” Burnham told Labour’s conference on Tuesday, saying the U.K. could be “an honest broker” in the debate on regulating AI. “Just as Gordon did in the financial crisis in 2008, so Britain will do it again — step forward, and bring people together around what’s right for the future — securing our prosperity, but also our safety.”

Burnham served in Brown’s government as health secretary until Labour lost power in 2010. He has picked colleagues who served with him in Brown’s ministerial team for key jobs in government — including Ed Miliband, the new foreign secretary, Chancellor John Healey, and Douglas Alexander, the Scotland secretary.

In interviews at the POLITICO Pub during Labour’s conference in Liverpool this week, the extent of Brown’s contacts became clear. Miliband, who was an adviser to Brown during his time in the Treasury, said they had spoken by phone while he was in New York at the U.N. General Assembly earlier this month. “I had a late-night phone call with him actually last week,” Miliband said. “They come thick and fast. It’s a great email to get, honestly.”

Healey, the chancellor, disclosed in an interview with the Sunday Times that he receives emails in bold capitals from Brown, who was Britain’s longest-serving chancellor of modern times, before he became prime ministers in 2007.

Alexander, the Scotland secretary, told POLITICO he, too, was the recipient of messages from Brown, who represented a Scottish constituency during his time in parliament.

“Yes, it took me great restraint when John Healey revealed that he was receiving emails in Bold Helvetica 14, as I remember, from Gordon Brown, not to send him a message saying ‘the first 35 years is the worst, and then you get over it.’”

World.title: Governments brace for €100B cut to EU budget proposal
World.content:
“If the Irish negotiating box [the next budget proposal] is to serve as the basis for further discussions, it must set out an overall volume that can realistically be financed by those who carry the main financial burden,” the leaders of Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands, Austria, Sweden and Finland wrote in a letter to Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin.

Such a reduction is opposed by a camp of 17 countries known as the "Friends of Cohesion," including Italy, Spain and Poland, that favors a bigger budget. The group is working on a joint statement to warn against the potential cuts and respond to the letter by Berlin and its allies.

“I expect that there will be cuts that will make Friends of Cohesion unhappy,” said one of the diplomats. They were granted anonymity, like others, to discuss the sensitive negotiations.

In its role as a neutral broker in the discussions, Ireland hasn't publicly revealed its intentions. "We haven't even come to any considerations about cuts or increases," Ireland's Europe minister Thomas Byrne said last week.

Parliament’s budget mess

In a further challenge to the budget talks, the European Parliament’s parallel negotiations risk being delayed by turf wars and political fighting among different political groups.

“We’re so far behind that we won’t even have a Parliament position by the end of next year if we continue at the same pace,” Damian Boeselager, one of the Greens’ negotiators on the budget, told POLITICO.

World.title: Bruxelles veut clarifier les responsabilités des autorités face aux catastrophes climatiques
World.content:
“Ceci étant dit, a-t-il ajouté, nous devons veiller à ce que tout soit parfaitement clair […] Qui est responsable de quoi ? Qui est chargé de la lutte contre les incendies ? Qui est responsable du financement ? Qui est chargé de la plantation d’arbres dans les villes ? Qui est responsable des mesures de santé destinées aux personnes âgées ? Et ainsi de suite.”

Pourquoi c’est important

Attribuer la responsabilité des risques peut sembler n’être qu’un détail technique. Mais lorsque ce n’est pas fait, la gestion et la prévention des catastrophes climatiques peuvent devenir confuses.

Le feu de forêt qui a causé des dégâts d’une ampleur inédite le mois dernier dans la réserve naturelle des Hautes Fagnes, en Belgique, en est un bon exemple. D’après les enquêtes menées par les médias locaux, l’incendie aurait été provoqué par des étincelles provenant de machines agricoles qui fauchait des terres complètement desséchées — et personne n’était chargé de prévenir les risques d’incendie.

Le gouvernement fédéral belge est chargé de coordonner la préparation du pays aux effets du changement climatique, mais la gestion des terres est une compétence régionale, et différentes autorités peuvent prononcer des interdictions de fauchage. Une province située près des Hautes Fagnes a imposé une telle interdiction, mais aucune autre ne l’a fait. Et un organisme régional du gouvernement wallon a chargé un prestataire de procéder au fauchage dans la réserve naturelle au plus fort de la sécheresse.

Une zone forestière calcinée à la suite d’un incendie de forêt dans la réserve naturelle des Hautes Fagnes, près de Baraque Michel, dans l’est de la Belgique, le 9 septembre 2026. | ERIC Lalmand/AFP via Getty Images

Les responsables politiques d’opposition se sont appuyés sur l’incendie des Hautes Fagnes pour réclamer de centraliser cette compétence en créant une cellule interfédérale chargée du climat. Lors d’un événement organisé en septembre, le directeur général de la DG Clima de la Commission, Kurt Vandenberghe, a estimé que la gestion de l’incendie en Belgique illustrait pourquoi l’exécutif européen cherche à clarifier les responsabilités des risques : “Cela montre clairement qu’il reste beaucoup à faire.”

Si personne ne se charge de la prévention, les gouvernements ne peuvent que réagir face à l’aggravation des catastrophes, préviennent les experts.

World.title: Tax cuts, handouts and blind hope: Europe finds few tools to fight a coming energy crunch
World.content:
"We see more EVs than ever sold in Europe now, we see electric heat pumps replacing gas boilers and oil boilers than ever before — so yes, there are actually a lot of positive things happening," EU energy chief Dan Jørgensen told reporters in a response to a question from POLITICO. "Many times, one of the best things we can do in these situations that also works in the short term is active electrification."

He added that he was "in no way implying that that is enough," and there were "many big structural things that we need to do that will not help consumers tomorrow or even this year, but there are actually also things that member states can do."

Irish Energy Minister Darragh O'Brien, whose government holds the EU's six-month rotating presidency, also described the deployment of renewables as the main way to address rising costs, emphasizing that Dublin was working to hasten the adoption of a new EU law aimed at strengthening the bloc's electricity grids.

But he said the EU's ability to address the current rise in costs was limited.

"There are flexibilities that member states have at our disposal around taxation, but I think our citizens are aware that there's no government in Europe that is going to be able to protect their citizens from every single price increase," he told reporters. "The fundamental reason for that," he said, was "our over-dependence in the European Union on imported fossil fuel."

Discussions were dominated by the question of where responsibility for addressing rising prices ought to lie. Member countries called on the Commission to institute a windfall tax on energy companies making bumper profits, while the EU executive said it was up to individual countries to decide.

World.title: Top AI and tech firms sign 'morally binding' accord to 'self-police' development after meeting at White House
World.content:
US President Donald Trump said that he and a large group of leaders of artificial intelligence companies signed a voluntary accord on Tuesday that will include internal and external reviews during a meeting aimed at addressing Americans' fears about the technology and its risks on humanity.

 

“I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police,” Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference outside the West Wing.

Trump and US House Speaker Mike Johnson met with leading executives from top tech and AI firms at the White House that are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build out AI infrastructure, including data centres in communities across the country, which have sparked grassroots, bipartisan opposition.

US President Donald Trump speaks in the East Room of the White House during a meeting and luncheon on artificial intelligence (AI), Tuesday Sept. 29, 2026 Jacquelyn Martin/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

The accord was signed by Trump, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Elon Musk, CEO of Tesla, SpaceX, X and xAI – now part of SpaceX.

The accord, which Trump posted on his social media site, Truth Social, late on Tuesday, opened the door to future regulation but focused on four voluntary steps for the companies to take.

It said the companies would implement “robust internal controls,” partner with an “independent external auditor” to assess whether the controls are working, and establish a committee within each company's board of directors to evaluate reports from internal and external auditors.

US President Donald Trump posts copy of the document signed by AI and tech executives to self-police on Truth Social, Tuesday, 29 Sept. 2026 @realDonaldTrump/TruthSocial

“Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws and regulations,” the accord said.

Trump repeatedly praised the business executives for developing a technology that he said would produce “unbelievable growth."

Investment in data centres and the accompanying computer equipment has accelerated the economy and boosted the stock market, which has swelled investment accounts for higher-income Americans and lifted their spending.

Yet there were some notes of caution Tuesday. Amodei, who has been one of the most outspoken voices calling for a slowdown in AI development, said, “The technology has very real risks.”

President Trump speaks to reporters at the White House after meeting with top executives of AI firms and House Speaker Mike Johnson in Washington, Tuesday Sept. 29, 2026 Jacquelyn Martin/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

“And, you know, the mechanism, how we address those risks is still under discussion,” he added.

Trump suggested that about 10 people would be named to a committee to “watch over the whole enterprise” and said the accord would be “morally binding.” He also said he would name someone to oversee the agreement in coming days after consulting with industry.

Some of the actions outlined in the accord are measures these companies are already taking in some form or have previously committed to doing.

The accord however does not introduce a set of legislation that introduces robust legal liability and regulation to guide the technology, which some in the industry have blown the whistle on, saying there is a chance it could outsmart humans and cause their extinction within a decade.

President Trump listens after meeting with top executives of AI firms as Google CEO Sundar Pichai speaks to reporters at the White House in Washington, Tuesday Sept. 29, 2026 Alex Brandon/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

Trump, who has always vocally opposed instating such measures, said before the meeting that the US government wouldn't limit the development of artificial intelligence or support calls for “guardrails” or other restrictions.

“I will never stifle the growth of a technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution,” Trump said at the unveiling of an AI chatbot, America.gov, intended to help Americans navigate government services. “We can’t stifle it, and we’re leading by a lot.”

Trump also said the executives had agreed to assuage the bipartisan opposition to data centres cropping up in local communities across the country by providing more financial support to local schools or taking steps to reduce energy costs.

“You’re going to see, data centres are going to be very popular," Trump said. If the opposition continued, Trump suggested, “they’ll be forced to go overseas or other locations.”

US President Donald Trump on stage at the Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026, in Washington Alex Brandon/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

Trump on Tuesday portrayed the race to develop AI as largely a global competition between the United States and China. He said there would be a winner and a loser, with no “second place.”

The two countries agreed last week to establish a channel for handling AI-related incidents during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington, but Trump underscored on Tuesday that he didn't want to cooperate too much with China.

"I didn’t want to do anything, because we’re leading. Why would I want to do anything?,” he said.

World.title: A little known greenhouse gas is quietly harming half of Europeans. This Italian city is hit hardest
World.content:
Half of Europeans were exposed to a little-known greenhouse gas during this summer’s record breaking heatwaves and wildfires.

 

Ground-level ozone is an air pollutant that can “penetrate deep into the respiratory system and enter the bloodstream, allowing it to reach almost all organs within the body.” People who suffer from asthma are the most at risk.

Ozone forms from thousands of chemical reactions, triggered by sunlight and high temperatures. So the record-breaking heatwaves that gripped Europe from June to August this year led to ozone levels dangerous to human health. During this period, 50 per cent of Europe’s population was exposed to poor, very poor or extremely poor ozone levels, according to the European Commission’s Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS).

“Ozone pollution is a stark reminder of how interconnected our atmosphere, climate, health, and livelihoods really are, with pollution and our changing climate impacting the chemistry of the air we breathe, determining the health of our ecosystems, and even governing our ability to grow food,” says Laurence Rouil, Director of CAMS.

The good news is that EU efforts to combat other air pollutants are making a difference, so it is hoped that ozone levels can also be brought down with sustained effort.

Ozone illustrates the close relationship between air pollution and climate change

Air pollution, often called an invisible killer, causes more than four million premature deaths worldwide, according to the World Health Organization. In 2025, 56 deaths per 100,000 people in Europe and Central Asia were attributable to air pollution.

It is made up of many different gases. Ground-level ozone, not to be confused with upper atmospheric ozone which protects us from UV, is not as well known as others but it is especially concerning because of its close links with climate change.

“Ground-level ozone illustrates the close relationship between air pollution and climate change – a key societal challenge – due to its formation under high temperatures,” according to Atmosphere Watch, the first edition of a new report from CAMS on air quality.

Global temperatures are increasing and heatwaves are becoming more frequent and more extreme due to human-caused climate change. As ozone formation is triggered by high temperatures, the increase in heatwaves means more ozone.

Nitrogen oxides are part of the chemical reactions which lead to the formation of ozone and these, the report explains, are “mainly produced by the combustion of fossil fuels”. It names industry, solvents and road transport as sources of ozone, as well as biomass burning “further compounding the influence of climate change, with more extreme fires occurring under hotter and drier conditions”.

As a greenhouse gas, ozone is responsible for approximately 0.23°C of present-day warming, according to UK charity Clean Air Fund. It calls ground-level ozone a “super pollutant”.

How the EU has reduced levels of other air pollutants

Atmosphere Watch highlights that “air quality in Europe improved significantly regarding all pollutants regulated by the European Air Quality Directive.” Known as one of the most progressive air quality laws in the world, the 2024 directive requires EU countries to monitor pollutant limits and act when safe levels are exceeded.

A 2025 Copernicus report said: “Over the past decade, emissions of sulphur oxides and nitrogen oxides have fallen by approximately three-to-five per cent per year across the European Union. The most significant reductions have been achieved in industry and road transport. Since 2015, industrial emissions of sulphur oxides have fallen by 59 per cent, while nitrogen oxide emissions from industry have declined by 39 per cent. Road transport emissions have also fallen substantially, with reductions of 40 per cent for nitrogen oxides and 34 per cent for fine particulate matter (PM2.5).”

Improving public transport, implementing low or zero emission zones for traffic, switching from fossil fuels to clean energy sources and consuming less meat are seen as some of the most successful ways to reduce air pollutants.

But, Atmosphere Watch says, “ozone shows no clear downward trend and remains an issue.”

Peak-season surface ozone is highest across southern Europe CAMS Atmosphere Watch

Under the EU Ambient Air Quality Directive, the maximum eight-hour daily average ozone concentration should not exceed 120 μg/ m3 more than 18 days per year, with a long-term objective of 100 μg/m3 compliant with the WHO guidelines. The map above shows how much of Europe exceeded these levels during 2026 so far. It shows how levels get worse the further south you go on the continent – the areas where heatwaves were the hottest and most prolonged.

The extreme weather and unprecedented wildfires led to worse air pollution across the whole continent, not just in directly affected areas.

“Atmosphere Watch shows that air pollution knows no border. Wildfire smoke, ozone and dust can travel thousands of kilometres, affecting communities far from their source,” says Florian Pappenberger, Director-General of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.

As an example, in August 2026 Belgium experienced its worst wildfire in 100 years. “The intense smoke columns travelled all the way through Germany, reaching Poland.”

Milan has some of the worst ozone levels in the world

While 50 per cent of Europeans were exposed to unsafe levels of ozone during the summer months, the exposure levels are even higher in other parts of the world.

So far in 2026, almost 40 per cent of the world’s total population has been exposed to extremely high levels of ozone, including 60 per cent of Asian citizens. Oceania was the least affected continent during the first eight months of the year – this is partly because the Northern Hemisphere is more sensitive to ground-level ozone pollution due to the higher landmass and population.

Roughly 50 per cent of the global population was exposed to very or extremely poor air quality due to ozone concentrations in 2026. Milan, Rio de Janeiro, Mexico City, Delhi and Cairo are the cities with some of the highest exposures. Only five per cent of the global population was exposed to ‘good’ long-term ozone levels and 15 per cent to ‘fair’ levels during 2026, according to the analysis.

“Ozone concentrations in all continents are likely to be affected by climate change: ground-level, and more generally, tropospheric ozone formation, is triggered by warm temperatures and sunlight. Therefore, in areas experiencing more heatwaves, local ozone concentrations will increase, partly offsetting the benefits of the mitigation strategies designed to reduce precursor pollutant emissions.”

Surface ozone exposure varies widely across the world CAMS Atmosphere Watch

How can ozone levels be reduced?

Ultimately responsibility for and power over ozone levels rests with governments. Experts recommend much better monitoring and reporting of ozone levels, as is done for other air pollutants. At the moment in the EU, only Croatia, France and Spain have developed or implemented air quality plans explicitly focused on ozone.

Countries and cities that are doing the best on limiting ozone are focused on improving forecasting for ozone concentration and understanding how ozone forms and its main sources, according to the European Environment Agency.

Making the public more aware of ozone and how it forms can also be helpful. On an individual level, we can all help to reduce ozone levels by walking or cycling rather than driving. If you must drive, adjust your habits so as to reduce emissions by lowering your speed and avoiding hard braking or rapid acceleration. Use environmentally safe paints and cleaning products whenever possible.

World.title: Man City found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of financial rules, Premier League says
World.content:
Manchester City have been found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, the league announced on Tuesday.

 

In a statement, the Premier League said an independent commission found that the English club had arranged "sham contracts" with commercial partners to "artificially inflate the club’s revenues and reduce its costs."

City has continued to deny any wrongdoing and issued a statement later on Tuesday saying it was "disappointed and surprised" by the commission's opinion. The club has until 2 October to lodge an appeal, which it has said it will do.

The commission found that City had arranged "sham" commercial deals with sponsors as part of a "disguised funding scheme," in which companies were only required to pay part of the relevant sponsorship fees.

"The remainder was funded by Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club," the league said in its statement.

Further "sham arrangements" funded by the ADUG enabling the club to record lower operating expenses were also identified.

The league said the schemes inflated City's revenues and reduced its costs by more than £900 million (roughly €1.05 billion) over the affected period.

"Manchester City failed to accurately report its income and expenditure for the purposes of the Premier League’s Profitability and Sustainability Rules and UEFA’s Club Licensing and Financial Fair Play Rules," the statement continued.

Had the relevant agreements been reported accurately, the commission found that the club "would have been in breach of both the League’s and UEFA’s spending limits by a very substantial amount."

The league added that City had also been found guilty on the majority of charges relating to its failure to cooperate with the investigation.

A general view of the Etihad Stadium. Copyright 2025 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

The Premier League launched the investigation into City's finances in late 2018, and charges were filed in 2023.

Richard Masters, the chief executive of the Premier League, called the case and the decision "the most significant in Premier League history" but said certain elements, including sanctions, were yet to be resolved.

"The core decision establishes the facts of what happened at Manchester City during this period. It details how the club systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade," he added.

In its response, Manchester City said it was "innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League" and that a "comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case."

"Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe," it added.

Ferran Soriano, City's CEO, also hit out what he dubbed the "Premier League's conspiracy theory" as he insisted the club would be "vindicated."

"Very soon, we will look back at this and recognise as another time in our history when we dealt with adversity and overcame it together," he said in a message to club staff.

World.title: Ukraine pushes for 'bold action' on Russian assets to plug $78 billion gap in 2027
World.content:
Ukraine has urged the European Union to tap into the immobilised Russian assets to help plug the country's financial and military shortfall next year, which could hit a staggering $78 billion (€68.77 billion) if allies fail to step up their contributions.

 

Sergii Marchenko, Ukraine's finance minister, made the push on Tuesday as he met with representatives from international donors and financial institutions in Brussels.

During the gathering, Marchenko argued that using the pool of Russian assets would be both a practical and fair solution to meet Ukraine's extraordinary wartime costs, protect its debt sustainability and ensure accountability for Moscow's aggression, according to officials with knowledge of the private discussions.

The EU holds €210 billion of these assets, most of it in Euroclear, a depository in Brussels.

The minister recognised the topic was politically difficult and encouraged the bloc to consider a centralised, legally sound framework.

Marchenko delivered a similar message on Monday at a panel hosted by the European Policy Centre (EPC) that examined the idea of transferring the assets from Euroclear into an EU-owned custodian to mitigate risks for Belgium.

"We need our friends, our European politicians, to be brave enough and to make some bold actions," the minister said in his remarks.

"Unfortunately, the war is longer, the war is harder, and we need to provide some resolution of frozen Russian assets or provide other means for us to survive."

Marchenko provided an overview of the dire financial situation that Ukraine faces in 2027.

From the $52.6 billion in financial aid needed from donors, only $20 billion has been covered so far, leaving a $32.6 billion gap. Meanwhile, there is roughly $45 billion in defence expenditure for which allies have not provided guarantees.

Altogether, this creates a $78 billion hole.

The budget crunch, Marchenko explained, is further aggravated by Russia's non-stop attacks, which have severely disrupted ordinary activity, crippled power grids, destroyed factories and impeded tax collection. Moscow has recently begun to target Ukraine's data centres to impair its digital economy and communications system.

At the same time, the blockade in the Black Sea has left Ukrainian farmers without the sea routes they need to sell their grain to clients worldwide. Losses mount with each day maritime trade remains closed off.

"It's the first time since 2022 we realised that we have underperformance in our tax and customs administrations," the minister said.

Loan under pressure

This is not the first time that the assets of the Russian Central Bank, immobilised since February 2022, have come under scrutiny.

Last year, the European Commission tried to channel the assets into a zero-interest credit line for Ukraine. The inventive proposal fell apart in December at a dramatic summit, where Belgium, the chief opponent, mobilised a majority against it.

As a Plan B, EU leaders agreed to set up a €90 billion support loan based on joint debt. The loan has been evenly halved: €45 billion for 2026 and €45 billion for 2027.

But Russia's escalation has rapidly added to the bill.

"We're very happy with the €90 billion," Marchenko said. "But it's not sufficient."

Sweden, the Netherlands, Spain and Poland, backed by the Baltics, have also warned the loan would not be enough and called for "new options" to tap the Russian assets.

Belgium immediately pushed back against the move. Italy and France, two key votes, remain sceptical about touching the sovereign funds, according to diplomats.

The Commission is keen to avoid another defeat and insists the "primary focus" is the disbursement of the €90 billion loan, which has been hampered by the slow pace of reforms in the Ukrainian parliament.

EU officials are frustrated that Ukraine is asking for fresh money when it is not doing the necessary work to unlock the assistance already agreed.

Marta Kos, the European Commissioner for Enlargement, drove the point home during Tuesday's donors' conference.

"Our message to our Ukrainian friends is clear: deliver the agreed reforms, so we can continue supporting you financially," she said in her opening remarks.

"The government, the Rada and institutions across Ukraine need to unite around this collective effort and act with determination to deliver the reforms."

For the past month, the Commission has engaged in intense talks with Ukraine and the International Monetary Fund to pin down the exact scope of the financial shortfall.

The country initially flagged a $27 billion gap in its Ministry of Defence for this year, but this figure has since been downgraded. Marchenko focused his intervention on the needs for 2027, rather than 2026.

The Commission is yet to validate the numbers shared by Kyiv.

World.title: No energy shortages, but a painful winter looms for Europe, top EU energy leader warns
World.content:
European Union Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen said the EU is not facing an imminent energy-supply crisis, but warned that high prices could have a similar impact on households unable to afford heating or travel to work.

 

The Danish Commissioner said nearly 50 million Europeans were already unable to adequately heat their homes in a normal winter, underscoring the social risks of another price shock.

"We are looking into all ideas of how we can make rules more flexible, be more efficient in our implementation, do what we can, both on the supply and the demand side," Jørgensen told reporters on the sidelines of an informal gathering of energy ministers in Dublin on Tuesday.

Jørgensen welcomed French President Emmanuel Macron's ask for a temporary relaxation of some fuel rules to help refineries produce more diesel and other products in view of increasing domestic supply.

Asked whether another emergency oil release was in the cards, Fatih Birol, the International Energy Agency's (IEA) leader, who also attended the meeting in Dublin, did not consider it a top priority.

Related EU tells countries to curb energy demand as gas prices face winter squeeze

Countries have so far released about 20% of their strategic stocks, leaving roughly 80% available if supply disruptions become significantly worse and governments agree to further action, Birol noted.

The EU's top energy leader also confirmed that the European Commission plans to delay by one year the enforcement of parts of the EU methane rules covering imports, arguing that this could ease pressure on energy markets while keeping the bloc's longer-term climate goals intact.

"We stick to the objectives, we stick to our ambitions, but I'm proposing now that we take part of it, the parts that are connected to imports, and postpone the set and force date by one year," Jørgensen said.

Despite the current high energy prices, Jørgensen focused on the need to accelerate the EU's exit from fossil fuels by investing in more renewables, electrification and energy efficiency.

“Our answer is twofold: doubling down on the green transition and being flexible and pragmatic in this very difficult transition period. We must help member states, citizens and companies to help this crisis,” he added.

Nonetheless, efforts to prevent skyrocketing energy prices won't include an EU-wide windfall tax, Jørgensen said, leaving EU countries to introduce national schemes within EU rules. Several EU countries have called on the Commission to propose such a target, as it did in 2022.

Jørgensen acknowledged that political pressure could push governments to subsidise fossil fuels, but urged them to keep such measures targeted and temporary to avoid undermining the bloc’s energy transition through tax policy.

Jørgensen and Birol urged countries to reconsider tax systems that heavily tax electricity while imposing lower taxes on gas. If governments want households and industry to switch from gas and oil to electricity, they need to make electricity affordable, particularly during a period of high energy prices, the pair warned. The topic is currently under discussion between the EU co-legislators, the European Council and the Parliament, with Germany showing reservations.

Gas storage remains another concern in the bloc's energy equation. EU rules now require an 80% storage target, down from 90%, but Jørgensen said countries still need to meet it. Falling significantly short this winter could leave the EU starting the next refill season with less gas in reserve, creating what he described as a potentially damaging cycle.

Birol stressed that cooperation between gas-producing and consuming countries will also be critical, pointing to Norway, Canada and even Nigeria as examples of suppliers that can help Europe manage disruptions.

World.title: Pressure grows within EPP to expel Vučić’s SNS party over Mladić funeral
World.content:
Frustration within the European People’s Party is growing over Aleksandar Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), with senior lawmakers urging the party presidency to consider suspending or expelling it from the EPP.

 

Gathered in Toulouse for their political assembly on Tuesday, EPP senior members expressed deep concern over events at the funeral of Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladić, known as the Butcher of Bosnia, who died in late August aged 84 in a UN detention facility in The Hague.

They concluded that state honours and the participation of senior Serbian officials at the funeral “cannot be ignored” in the party's ongoing scrutiny of SNS.

“There is not an inch of Vučić's policies that would fit into the EPP universe. EPP is for the people, not for autocrats,” senior EPP MEP Lukas Mandl told Euronews. Vučić served as SNS president from 2012 to 2023, when he handed over the leadership to Miloš Vučević, but he is still widely considered the party’s de facto leader.

Mandl argued that the Serbian party should be expelled, pointing to the “terrible misbehaviour around the funeral of one of the last European war criminals of the 20th century."

The presence of senior Serbian officials at the funeral of the convicted war criminal already prompted a flow of condemnations from the heads of the EU's institutions.

The EPP's scrutiny process of SNS was launched a year ago, after the Serbian government's crackdown on demonstrations against corruption, and is expected to conclude by the end of this year.

However, no decision will be taken before the Serbian elections, scheduled for 25 October, according to an EPP official. Vučić, who resigned as president last Sunday, is currently standing as SNS’s candidate for prime minister.

EPP leader Manfred Weber has also been critical of the Serbian government’s involvement in Mladić’s funeral, but has so far stopped short of proposing that SNS be stripped of its membership.

According to EPP rules, a suspension or exclusion should be proposed by the Presidency or by seven other parties coming from at least five different countries, and ultimately decided by the Political Assembly.

The scrutiny process has neither a specific timeline nor a predefined outcome.

SNS has been an EPP associated member party since 2016. The Serbian party has so far declined to comment on the matter.

World.title: With two Orbán-era ministers detained, Magyar's 'Operation Purge' takes shape
World.content:
Hungarian prosecutors on Monday detained two former ministers over corruption and abuse-of-office allegations after parliament lifted their immunity.

 

The detention of Miklós Seszták and Balázs Hankó is a significant development in Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s efforts to hold officials from his predecessor Viktor Orbán’s era to account. The campaign has been dubbed “Operation Purge.”

Magyar, whose Tisza Party won April’s parliamentary election, has accused Orbán of running a “mafia state” that channelled billions of euros in public funds to his business associates. Tisza campaigned on a “Road to Jail” programme, and after forming a government, Magyar announced Operation Purge in June, aimed at dismantling what he described as state capture.

"We are launching Operation Purge, which will close those long decades when Hungary could be held hostage by organised political and economic criminal groups," Magyar told parliament.

Prosecutors accelerated several investigations into the Orbán era over the summer.

On Monday morning, parliament, where Tisza holds a majority, lifted the immunity of the two former politicians. Seszták, who served as development minister from 2014 to 2018, is suspected of taking around €30 million in bribes linked to bus tenders. Hankó is being investigated over the disbursement of €46 million in cultural funds to public figures, which the authorities largely regard as campaign financing.

Both men remain in custody as suspects and deny any wrongdoing.

"After decades of lies, millions of Hungarians experienced for the first time what real regime change and equality before the law really mean. Hungary is finally not a country without consequences," Magyar wrote on social media after the detentions. He added that "Operation Purge" would accelerate.

Political analyst Szabolcs Dull said the issue resonates with voters, arguing that accountability is central to Péter Magyar’s political message.

"This is the core issue of Péter Magyar's politics. He always had the greatest success in the campaign by promising accountability, confrontation and consequences. One of these elements is that he will hold those responsible for the past period to criminal proceedings and even send them to prison. The promise of handcuffs and bars, many times," Dull said.

Investigations could reach key allies, or Orbán himself

At the centre of the purge is the newly established National Asset Recovery and Protection Office, an anti-corruption body that can take over investigations from prosecutors, launch new proceedings and issue warrants. The Public Prosecutor's Office and the National Tax Authority are also involved in some cases.

Several other high-profile figures are also under investigation. György Matolcsy, the former governor of the Hungarian National Bank, has been questioned as a suspect in a blackmail case linked to the removal of a manager at Erste Bank Hungary.

Parliament's National Security Committee also invited summoned Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó to a hearing on the investment agreement with Chinese carmaker BYD in Hungary. After the election, Szijjártó took a management position at BYD, prompting concerns over a potential conflict of interest. No official investigation has been opened against him.

Orbán himself could also eventually be drawn in. Lawyers say his possible criminal liability arises in the case of the Ukrainian cash convoy.

In March, at the height of the election campaign, two Ukrainian cash couriers carrying regular transfers from Vienna to Kyiv were stopped near Budapest.

The couriers were detained and a large amount of cash and gold was confiscated. The authorities consider the raid and detentions unlawful and are investigating Orbán's role. According to a former chief prosecutor, Orbán personally gave instructions to the anti-terrorist police.

"Authorities must decide whether there was a legal abuse in the Golden Convoy case or not. If Viktor Orbán is legally punished here, people will want to see it as political accountability for his responsibility for other corruption cases," Dull said.

Fidesz warns of political revenge

On Monday evening, MPs from Orbán's Fidesz party accompanied Hankó to the prosecutor's office in a show of support. They portrayed the investigations as politically motivated and accused Magyar of acting like a tyrant.

"Arbitrariness needs new victims every day. Today it's them, tomorrow it's you," Orbán wrote on social media.

"We send a message to all Hungarians: the Tisza tyrants will not break the community of the national side; we will not let them! They cannot imprison half the country!" he added.

Fidesz has also accused Magyar of dismantling the rule of law, including by removing former President Tamás Sulyok through a constitutional amendment. The party argues that Magyar’s repeated calls to punish former officials threaten judicial independence.

Dull said Fidesz was under pressure to respond constantly to voters. "Fidesz has to react to those investigations every hour to explain to its own voters why its politicians, now former ministers, are being taken into custody one by one. For this, Fidesz has built a narrative of arbitrariness, giving its voters a story that a political showdown is taking place, to keep its base together," he said.

Magyar also faces investigation

Hungary's parliament on Monday also lifted Magyar's immunity at the request of the Prosecutor's Office, in connection with a theft case. The case stems from an incident in May 2024, when Magyar confronted a man who had filmed him dancing in a nightclub and threw the man’s phone into the Danube.

Magyar sharply criticised prosecutors for pursuing the case alongside two corruption investigations involving millions of euros in public funds.

"By placing these three cases side by side without any reasonable explanation, they made it clearer than ever for every Hungarian citizen who the Prosecutor General's Office has served and with what means over the past decade and a half," Magyar said. He added that he was ready to face justice.

World.title: Houthi attacks put Turkey’s new Saudi defence pact to the test
World.content:
Attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia are putting Turkey's new defence pact with the kingdom to its first major test – forcing Ankara to weigh support for its ally against the risk of being drawn deeper into the conflict.

Advertising

Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on 7 August, committing themselves to the principle that an attack on one is an attack on all.

The three countries' military chiefs met in the Saudi capital on Friday, a day after the Iran-backed Houthis launched their latest barrage of missiles targeting Riyadh and Saudi Aramco oil facilities in Yanbu.

In recent weeks, Saudi Arabia has reported intercepting numerous Houthi drone and ballistic missile attacks from neighbouring Yemen.

The military chiefs discussed intelligence sharing, military coordination and integrating their capabilities, Saudi and Pakistani statements said. Turkey's defence ministry did not comment on the meeting.

Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies

Saudi expectations

Turkey has so far stopped short of committing itself to military action.

Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said this month that Ankara was looking into providing what he called “technical support”, without elaborating on what that could involve.

Saudi Arabia could look to Turkey for air defence systems, counter-drone technology, radars and maritime security, given the expertise and capabilities of the Turkish military and defence industry, said Amed Khuzaie of the Washington-based think tank N7 Foundation.

“The Mecca Agreement pact will prove its vitality and importance only if it's deemed to be functional,” Khuzaie told RFI.

The Riyadh meeting followed talks in New York on Thursday involving the Saudi and Turkish foreign ministers and Pakistan's deputy prime minister and foreign minister on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

Turkish media citing foreign ministry sources said the meeting focused on ongoing “technical negotiations”.

But providing support to Saudi Arabia could expose Turkey to retaliation from the Houthis.

“By God, if Turkey and Pakistan become involved, we will strike them with an iron fist,” Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a senior member of the Houthis, said in an Iraqi television interview.

Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade

Risk of retaliation

The warning should be taken seriously given the Houthis' military presence around the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical waterway linking the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, explained Amed Nagi, a Yemen expert at the International Crisis Group.

“[The Houthis] targeted US and UK shipping in the Red Sea,” Nagi said. “They could do the same beyond [that] to the Gulf of Aden, because we know Turkey is very active in the Horn of Africa.

"So I think these are the areas that the Houthis will think about if there is any sort of retaliation against Turkey.”

In 2024, the Houthis attacked US military and commercial shipping in the Red Sea, damaging the Gibraltar Eagle bulk carrier with a cruise missile and sinking the British-linked cargo ship MV Rubymar.

Saudi Arabia could also look to Israel for support if its new partners do not provide what it needs, Khuzaie said.

“Who has better intelligence in the region than the Israelis today?” he said. “Diversifying resources, if one fails you, you have another side that could assist.”

The risks for Ankara go beyond possible Houthi retaliation. Turkey must also manage its relationship with Iran, which backs the Yemeni group.

“It is not in the interest of Turkey to have a direct confrontation with any actor in the region, and the Houthis have become a proxy of Iran; Turkey doesn't want a confrontation with Iran directly," said Bilgehan Alagoz, an international relations professor at Istanbul's Marmara University.

"Turkey is trying to solve the issue from a diplomatic point of view.”

In a joint statement last week, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt said that dialogue and diplomacy were the only sustainable way to resolve the region's conflicts, while affirming Saudi Arabia's right to defend itself under international law.

Fidan met his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in New York on Friday.

Fidan later said they discussed Iran's negotiations with the United States and conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, but that diplomatic efforts had yet to produce a breakthrough.

What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey

Iran balancing act

The diplomatic efforts come as Turkey's relationship with Iran faces other strains.

Turkey-based international relations analyst Soli Ozel said Ankara has for decades walked a “fine line” between rivalry and cooperation with Tehran while balancing its relationships with Iran and Western allies, particularly the United States.

Turkey's banking regulator recently revoked the operating licence of Iran's Bank Mellat branch in Istanbul, although the official notice did not say the move was intended to enforce US sanctions.

The US Treasury also said Ankara had agreed after talks with Washington to stop flights by Iran's Mahan Air as part of efforts to comply with US measures against Tehran. Three Turkish airlines also suspended flights to Iran.

Turkish authorities have also repeatedly accused Iran of hostile operations inside the country, including assassinations and abductions of Iranian dissidents.

In January, security forces arrested six people suspected of spying for Iran and gathering information about the Incirlik air base, which is used by US forces.

Becoming involved in the conflict against the Houthis could upset Ankara's already delicate relationship with Tehran, Ozel told RFI.

“The Iranians who actually have a lot of [intelligence] capabilities in Turkey, we’ve seen that before, then you find yourself in a hot or cold war,” he said.

World.title: Trump says AI companies agree to 'self-police'
World.content:
Donald Trump said the US won't "stifle" the development of AI, which he sees as "bigger than the Industrial Revolution." The agreement comes amid mounting concerns over AI safety after recent hacking incidents.

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said a group of CEOs of Artificial Intelligence (AI) companies had signed an accord to "self-police" the technology's development.

Trump met with AI leaders at the White House, where he doubled down on his support for the technology.

The agreement comes as public scrutiny has grown over the risks posed by the emerging technology, following reports that OpenAI and Anthropic's AI agents had gone rogue and hacked into other companies' systems.

Concerns are also mounting over the industry's growing footprint in communities, particularly with the growth of data centers.

Prior to the meeting, Trump had reiterated that his government would not limit the development of AI or support calls for "guardrails" or other restrictions on the sector.

"I will never stifle the growth of a technology that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution," Trump said. "We can't stifle it, and we're leading by a lot."

Trump also announced that he would officially rename the technology "super intelligence" because "it's not artificial."

Which AI leaders were at the White House meeting?

House Speaker Mike Johnson joined the meeting, which included top AI executives like Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI president Greg Brockman, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, and Elon Musk, whose X social media platform includes its own AI model, Grok.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella also attended.

Data centers face backlash from US communities To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police," Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference outside the West Wing.

Later, the US president posted a copy of the "White House Accord on Super Intelligence" on his Truth Social platform.

What does the AI accord say?

"Every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that builds trust with customers and the public," the accord begins.

The document affirms that tech companies will implement "robust internal controls to ensure all of the controls, monitoring, and detection are operating as intended, and that any issues are remediated."

They are to "empower an internal team" to ensure "control, monitoring, and detection" are working as intended.

AI companies are also expected to "partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator to carry out independent assessments," as well as "designate an independent committee of the board of directors" to oversee and receive reports.

Trump said the agreement is "morally binding" but not legally enforceable.

The accord does, however, leave the door open "to codify these steps into laws or regulations."

World.title: Morocco: King appoints first woman prime minister
World.content:
The appointment of Fatima Zahra Mansouri comes after her center-right party won last week's parliamentary elections in Morocco. She had previously served as mayor of the city of Marrakesh.

Fatima Zahra Mansouri became Morocco's first female prime minister, the country's royal cabinet announced on Tuesday. King Mohammed VI has tasked her with forming the next government.

Under the Moroccan constitution, the country's king has the power to appoint the prime minister, but he must choose someone from the party that wins the most seats in parliamentary elections.

Mansouri's appointment comes after her center-right Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) won last week's parliamentary elections.

PAM raked in 97 out of 395 seats in the House of Representatives, 31 more than the next closest competitor. The vote was, however, marred by the lowest turnout in two decades.

"For the first time in our country's history, a woman is taking on the responsibility of leading the government," Mansouri said. "This is a source of pride not only for me but for all Moroccan women."

Mansouri is now the second woman in the Arab world to serve as prime minister, after Najla Bouden, who served in that position in Tunisia from 2021 to 2023.

Moroccans head to the polls amid rising voter apathy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

First female mayor of Marrakesh

Mansouri's government will now need to deliver on voter's most important issues, such as fighting inflation, raising wages and creating jobs. At the same time, she is expected to oversee billions of dollars in investments linked to Morocco co-hosting the 2030 FIFA World Cup during her tenure.

"We are fully aware that this period will be significant and marked by high expectations from Moroccans, particularly young people," Mansouri said. "That is why we will have a program offering concrete and realistic solutions to citizens' concerns," she added.

Mansouri was the first woman to serve as mayor of Marrakesh. She was elected mayor in 2009 and served for six years. She retook the job again in 2021. In addition to her mayorship, she has also been a member of parliament.

The 50-year-old has been a member of PAM since 2008, the year the party was founded by current royal adviser Fouad Ali El Himma. PAM was formed to serve as a counterweight to the country's Islamist movement.

By 2024, Mansouri was one of the party's top leaders.

Her task now will be to form a government and for that, PAM has expressed willingness to work with all parties. Some, however, including the moderate Islamist Justice and Development party and left-wing Federation of Democratic Left, have said they plan to remain in the opposition.

World.title: Estonia blames Russia for arson attack on defense company
World.content:
The Estonian government accused Moscow of an "act of sabotage" that is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe. The Baltic state has received support from EU and NATO leaders.

NATO and EU leaders rallied behind Estonia on Tuesday, after the Baltic country accused Russia of being behind an arson attack in its capital Tallinn.

Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said Moscow was found responsible for the August 15 arson attack against defense company Milrem Robotics, after the government conducted an investigation into the incident.

Milrem Robotics develops ground drones that are used in Ukraine.

"We can conclude with certainty that the arson attack... was an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation," Tsahkna said on X, adding that the perpetrators had been arrested, and Russia's ambassador had been summoned.

"This act of sabotage is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe, aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine," Tsahkna said.

NATO chief Mark Rutte backed Estonia, accusing Russia of furthering "its reckless campaign of hostile actions against NATO allies."

Rutte also said Russia was "failing on the battlefield in Ukraine " while also failing to undermine NATO's unity.

Kremlin says links to arson are "baseless"

Estonia, an EU and NATO member, has a population of 1.3 million and borders Russia to the east.

The incident took place on the night of August 15, when a fire broke out in a building used by Milrem Robotics in Tallinn. According to a statement from the Estonian government, authorities were on the scene right away and no injuries were reported.

Three suspects were later detained in Latvia in connection with the arson attack and were handed over to Estonia this month.

The Kremlin responded to the arson investigation findings by dismissing them as "baseless" and with "absolutely no relation to reality."

"We cannot and will not take such statements seriously," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow.

How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

EU and NATO leaders rally behind Estonia

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul pledged Germany's "full solidarity" with Estonia. "Russia's reckless hostilities will not divide us. They only strengthen our resolve to bolster NATO deterrence and support Ukraine," Wadephul wrote on X.

The EU said it stood by Estonia, saying the arson attack was "reckless" and would not deter the bloc in its support for Ukraine.

"Moscow is trying to scare Europe into winding down its support for Ukraine. This will not happen," European Commission spokesman Christian Wigand said.

French President Emmanuel Macron labeled the attack a "dangerous escalation" by Russia. He said it represented another in a "multiplication of these hostile acts."

"Russia needs to know that it will not overcome our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine," Macron wrote on X.

Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said "Russia's fingerprints are all over" the arson attack, adding that it was proof that Moscow's "hostile activities do not stop at Ukraine's borders."

Neighboring Latvia's President Edgars Rinkevics said in response to the incident that "more support for Ukraine... will be needed and must be provided."

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson also commented ont he matter, saying attribution of the arson attack was "extremely serious" and "directed against Europe as a whole."

World.title: Germany news: Bremerhaven port to receive defense boost
World.content:
The center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz's party has seen better days: Most recently, it suffered unprecedented defeats in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and Berlin. At this time of voter disenchantment, two prominent CDU politicians have come under fire on social media: Jens Spahn and Philipp Amthor have been facing accusation of being out of touch and self-absorbed.

Jens Spahn has faced a series of controversies in recent months Image: Lars Berg/dpa/picture alliance

A few weeks ago, Spahn resigned from his powerful position as parliamentary group leader of the CDU and CSU bloc in the Bundestag after Spahn had announced that had become a parent with the help of a surrogate mother in the United States. He was accused of hypocrisy because surrogacy is banned in Germany and the CDU and Spahn himself had repeatedly voted to uphold this ban.

Spahn was then given a seat on the influential Budget Committee. He called in sick for a meeting, but at the same time the tabloid BILD published a photograph of him vacationing in Sardinia with his young son. Spahn immediately resigned that post as well.

The CDU's Philipp Amthor has only recently become Minister of State for Federal-State Cooperation in the Chancellor’s Office. There, he placed a beach chair on the balcony of his new office and proudly showed it to a TV reporter. As a reminder: His party has just been voted out of the state parliament in his home state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on the Baltic Sea coast. But that didn't seem to have dampened the minister's good spirits.

The CDU's Philipp Amthor has drawn some unwanted attention at a precarious time for the CDU Image: Michael Brandt/dpa/picture alliance

Once again, social media reactions were fierce: This time with criticism of the young government official’s alleged arrogance. Amthor swiftly had the beach chair removed.

As the German saying goes, "Wer den Schaden hat, braucht für den Spott nicht zu Sorgen" (He who suffers the loss need not worry about the ridicule). That is seen to apply quite accurately to the CDU at the moment.

World.title: Ethiopia: No regard for civilians as fighting in Ethiopia's Tigray region continues
World.content:
Fighting has returned to northern Ethiopia, shattering a fragile peace in the region. DW spoke to civilians caught in the crossfire amid communication blackouts, as rebel and federal forces keep battling for territory.

As fighting keeps spreading across northern Ethiopia, civilians find themselves caught in the crossfire between opposing forces. Little information is emerging from the affected area as the internet and other communication services remain largely disrupted.

However, DW managed to speak to eyewitnesses whose accounts point to a growing toll on civilians.

A 22-year-old woman from the small town of Selenwuha told DW that her relatives were sheltering at home when heavy weaponry shelling struck their residences.

"I have lost six family members," she said. "Those who survived the attack, including the wounded, are currently confined to their homes.

"They have no access to medical facilities or vehicles, and the nearest treatment center is far away."

Strategic town of Alamata reported taken by ENDF

According to local residents, several violent incidents took place in recent days, especially in the border region between the Tigray and Amhara regions, with multiple further reports of civilians being killed by artillery fire.

The overall strategic situation on the ground meanwhile remains difficult to assess, with both rebel and federal forces reportedly making advances in different areas.

DW heard from a source in Tigray that the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) keeps advancing towards the regional capital Mekelle. The ENDDF is the country's official military force.

Tigrayan forces are reportedly fighting to defend other towns, including Mekoni and Maychew in southern Tigray, the source told DW on the strict condition of anonymity.

TPLF fighters are patroling Mekelle — far from the frontline of the present conflict Image: AFP

Pro-government militia and affiliated media outlets in the country had reported earlier that the ENDF had made significant progress by seizing control of Alamata in southern Tigray on September 27.

The purported takeover was also recorded by the US-based conflict-monitoring organization ACLED (Armed Conflict Location & Event Data).

Located about 120 kilometers south of the regional capital Mekelle, the strategically important town is situated on a major highway.

During the 2020-2022 war, Alamata changed hands several times between the two warring parties.

Residents accuse federal forces of deliberate attacks

A 40-year-old resident of Alamata told DW that civilians had deliberately been targeted, citing the account shared by militia members in the region.

"The attacks… were acts of retaliation against the people of Alamata," the local said. "The militias told us that government forces had fired the artillery at us."

Another resident, aged 45, said he believed the attack had deliberately been timed to maximize civilian casualties during the opening hours of a market, "when large numbers of people would be gathered there."

"At the Saturday market in Alamata, 11 people were killed and 15 others were wounded", he told DW.

Alamata has changed hands several times during the 2020-22 civil war (archive picture from January 2021) Image: Alemnew Mekonnen/DW

It's important to note that these claims could not be independently verified.

An ENDF spokesperson was also contacted by DW for comment; by the time of the publishing of this article, the spokesperson had not responded to the request.

Shifting alliances and mutual blame

Large-scale fighting erupted on September 23, when Tigrayan forces seized the airports of the regional capital Mekele as well as the regional hubs of Aksum and Shire.

Three days earlier, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and six other armed groups had announced a new alliance aimed at overthrowing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.

Unexpectedly, the alliance was joined by the Amhara Fano National Movement, which had supported federal forces against the TPLF during the 2020-2022 war, but has since then switched side and turned to fighting the federal government.

The federal government and Tigrayan forces meanwhile have accused each other of starting the latest escalation, both sides portraying their military actions as defensive in nature.

The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The unraveling of Ethiopia's fragile peace accord

Depending on the source, between 162,000 and 600,000 people were killed in the brutal 2020-2022 war, which was fought over the political status of the northern province of Tigray.

The war ended in November 2022 with the Pretoria Agreement, under which the TPLF agreed to the disarmament, demobilization and reintegration of its combatants, and to respect the federal government's constitutional authority.

However, key provisions remained unimplemented and major disputes unresolved, including the status of contested territories, the return of displaced people and the full demobilization of Tigrayan forces.

Meanwhile, a power struggle within the TPLF ended with the more hardline faction around Debretsion Gebremichael reasserting control in Tigray, further straining relations with Addis Ababa.

The TPLF also reinstated Tigray's pre-war regional council, a move the federal government viewed as a violation of the Pretoria framework.

Concerns mounted even further when the TPLF lost its legal party legislation, thus excluding the party from participating in national elections in June this year.

Tensions steadily increased, culminating in renewed clashes between Tigrayan and federal forces beginning in August 2026.

The headquarter of Tigray's state broadcaster was reportedly hit in a drone strike earlier in September Image: AFP

Fears grow over civilian toll and rights violations

Local residents meanwhile are bracing for further fighting, as organizations like the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) have managed to evacuate only few people caught up in the conflict.

According to the ICRC, the global NGO got to evacuate only around 160 individuals from Tigray, including Ethiopian Federal Police personnel, Ethiopian Airlines staff and African Union monitors.

With reports of damage to civilian infrastructure, disruptions to essential services and interrupted communication and transport routes, observers are worried about the situation of residents not only in Tigray but all across northern Ethiopia.

Amdegebreal Admassu, an Ethiopian lawyer focused on political and legal affairs, told DW he had received reports of fighters impacting public facilities including hospitals, schools and religious institutions.

"We observe instances where these facilities — which also serve as shelters for residents — are either accidentally hit or deliberately targeted.

"Under both international law and our country's penal code, such actions are classified as war crimes," Amdegebreal further explained.

Nearly everyone in Tigray impacted by fighting

Mebrihi Birhane, vice director for the NGO Human Rights First Ethiopia, told DW that many of those civilian facilities had already been impacted during the 2020-22 war.

"The population must have access to essential services even in times of war. Ensuring this is an obligation for all armed forces involved in the conflict," he said.

Meanwhile, the prices of goods are reported to be increasing dramatically, as supply routes are disrupted, affecting residents of Tigray whose communities had so far been spared from the direct fighting.

According to local journalists, residents of Tigray have rushed to buy flour and other products Image: AFP

The latest reports indicate that Tigrayan forces have advanced into the Afar region and were said to be controling the area around Erebti.

Analysts say this advance could be aimed at threatening Ethiopia's main trade corridor — a vital route used for imports and exports and a lifeline for the country's economy.

The renewed conflict meanwhile could spread beyond the confines of Ethiopia to the Horn of Africa and beyond, as Prime Minister Abiy has already accused neighboring countries of picking sides and supporting rebel forces.

Several DW journalists contributed to this report.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: TV journalist is crowned king of Uganda's Tooro Kingdom
World.content:
Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma has ascended to the throne after King Oyo died at the age of 34 due to a cancer battle. He previously worked for Ugandan broadcaster UBC as a TV anchor and editor.

A TV journalist on Tuesday was crowned king of Uganda's Tooro Kingdom.

What do we know so far?

Edward Rukidi Kiganangoma has ascended to the thrown after his predecessor, King Oyo Kyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, died unexpectedly last month.

King Oyo was only 34 and had lost his cancer battle while receiving treatment in the US. Oyo had became king at only three years of age.

Oyo's death sparked a succession battle in Uganda, with Oyo's mother pushing for the late king's undisclosed son to be the next monarch.

King Oyo was laid to rest earlier this month after a nine-day period of mourning [FILE: September 10, 2026] Image: Michael Muhati/REUTERS

However, the royal Babito clan chose Kiganangoma, now Nyabongo I, as the heir to the throne out of a group of eligible princes.

Kiganangoma took part in a coronation ceremony in the remote town of Fort Portal in western Uganda to ascend to the throne.

Coronation rituals included a mock battle and animal sacrifices. The ceremony in Fort Portal was televised and attended by thousands of people.

Kiganangoma, who is 56 years old, had worked as a journalist and editor for Ugandan public broadcaster UBC.

Tooro's new king vows to 'protect our culture, our traditions and customs'

"We have a big task to protect our culture, our traditions and customs and good conduct among our people," the new king said in his maiden speech. He had also told the New Vision newspaper: "My family never let me treat royal descent as an entitlement."

Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni was present for the coronation ceremony of the new king.

While expressing sadness over King Oyo's passing, Museveni also said he congratulates "his Highness Nyabongo. I have been watching him on the news and he is a good newsreader. I am sure he will do a good job."

Uganda is a constitutional republic with a president voted in democratically.

However, the country's four major precolonial kingdoms still hold cultural influence over the East African nation, despite not wielding any political power. The kings are involved in maintaining social order and safeguarding the heritage of their respective kingdoms.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko
