We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland is changing the procedures under which its military can fire upon foreign aircraft, citing the “growing threat from Russia”. Visual identification of targets will no longer be required, with other forms of data to be used instead. The move follows a series of violations of Polish airspace over the last year by Russian drones, a missile and a helicopter, as well as Russia’s increasing use of jet-powered drones to attack targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border. Polska zmienia procedury użycia uzbrojenia dla lotnictwa w przypadku zwalczania obcych statków powietrznych. To wnioski Dowódcy Operacyjnego generała Ireneusza Nowaka z ostatnich tygodni. To także odpowiedź na rosnące zagrożenie ze strony Rosji, doświadczenia wojny w Ukrainie… — Cezary Tomczyk (@CTomczyk) September 28, 2026 “In the coming days, the defence minister will change the procedures for firing by Polish planes and helicopters at objects flying to us from the direction of Russia,” announced deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk on Monday, quoted by news service Defence24. The change, as Tomczyk explained in a statement later issued on social media, will shift requirements away from requiring visual identification of foreign aerial objects and towards so-called “positive identification”. The latter involves identifying an object based on a combination of several other, non-visual sources of information, such as using radar and other sensors to determine its speed, altitude, trajectory and flight parameters, as well as a lack of IFF (identification friend or foe) from an object. Tomczyk said that the change was being made based on the “conclusions from recent weeks” made by the operational commander of Poland’s armed forces, General Ireneusz Nowak. It is a “response to the growing threat from Russia, experiences from the war in Ukraine, and the emergence of new air attack means – primarily fast jet drones and cruise missiles in the case of which the time for reaction is very brief”, added Tomczyk. The minister said that positive identification would only be issued when there is a “sufficiently high degree of certainty in determining what we are dealing with”. He noted that accurate target identification is particularly crucial in peacetime, when there are civilian aircraft in Polish airspace. The change will mean “not less identification, but a different way of conducting it: faster and based on data from multiple sources”. Poland's government has issued public guidance on how to act in the case of airborne attacks, amid growing concerns over the threat from Russia. It is also preparing evacuation plans and clearer markings for 85,000 shelters across the countryhttps://t.co/vMEMU6mlRx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 25, 2026 Defence24 reports that the government, military and many experts have found current rules of engagement to be overly restrictive and not suited to meeting the scale and type of threat facing Poland today. It points to last week’s violation of Polish airspace by a Russian helicopter, which crossed the border from Kaliningrad and spent around 42 seconds in Poland before returning. The website also notes that Russia’s growing use of jet-powered drones, which are able to travel much faster than traditional unmanned aerial vehicles, is a further threat. Such drones have recently been used to attack targets along the Ukrainian side of the border with Poland, including a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw. A drone has struck a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw, around 2 km from the Polish border, amid the latest mass Russian attacks on Ukraine. Separately, a truck around 800 metres from a border crossing with Poland was also hit last night https://t.co/ZbfE2iDLOk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 13, 2026 “Until now, we have not utilised these [non-visual identification] capabilities because they are typically reserved for a state of war or martial law,” said Tomczyk. “However, given the threat, and the fact that Poland today struggles daily with the possibility of drones entering our country, we must implement these changes for the benefit of both pilots and national security.” In July this year, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile also entered Polish airspace before landing in a field. On one night last year, around 20 Russian drones crossed Poland’s eastern borders. Some were shot down but many struck the ground. Earlier this month, Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental. Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental, says Polish Prime Minister @donaldtusk, citing intelligence sources. The aim would be to create a sense of "NATO's helplessness", he says https://t.co/9MFPiEEkIV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 18, 2026 Poland has invested heavily in its air defences in recent years, including buying Patriot batteries and fighter aircraft from the United States, as well as developing a new anti-drone system with Norway’s Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace. The government has also recently moved to expand the network of warning sirens along the Ukrainian border, launched a campaign informing the public how to respond to aerial threats, and started more clearly marking bomb shelters. World.title: Ninth-century Arabic silver coins found near Viking trading centre in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Several early medieval Arabic silver coins have been found in a forest near Elbląg in northern Poland. Experts believe they may have belonged to merchants travelling to or from the Viking Age port of Truso, which was situated nearby. The silver dirhams date back around 1,200 years, to the first half of the ninth century, before the founding of the Polish state. They may have remained in circulation until the turn of the 10th/11th century, the time of the settlement’s collapse. The discovery of the “new treasure” was announced last week by the Archaeological and Historical Museum in Elbląg. It did not reveal who had unearthed them, but said that the find had taken place during a legal search in a forest near the town of Młynary, just east of Elbląg. After conservation and processing work, the coins will be included in the collection of the museum, whose archaeologists will also visit the site hoping for further finds. The museum’s Jakub Jagodziński told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that the find consists of “six early medieval Arabic dirhams and two fragments of these silver coins”. He said that they are provisionally dated to the first half of the 9th century, but a more precise estimate will be possible after they are processed. The coins could have belonged to merchants travelling along the routes leading to or from Truso or to Prussian guards who later collected tolls on these routes, Jagodziński explained. Truso was a Viking Age port of trade set up by the Scandinavians on the shores of lake Druzno near the Vistula river delta. Established by the late 7th century and active until the early 11th century, its location enabled trade extending towards Kyivan Rus, Byzantium and the Islamic world. Historians knew of Truso’s existence because of the account of the Anglo-Saxon traveller Wulfstan of Hedeby. Centuries-long efforts to find the precise site proved fruitless until it was finally discovered in the early 1980s by the young archaeologist Marek Jagodziński, Jakub’s father. Finds of Arab coins in Poland are not unprecedented. A silver deposit was discovered in 1986 on the site of Truso itself, consisting of 11 complete coins and five fragments. Coins found there were minted in places including Baghdad and Damascus, according to the Medievalists.net website. More recently, in 2024, a fragment of an early medieval Arabic dirham was found during renovations of an old manor house on the Baltic coast in northwestern Poland. In transactions involving dirhams, it was the value of the silver that mattered, so the coins were often broken into pieces, archaeologist Grzegorz Kurka told PAP. “Therefore, when hoards of Arab coins are discovered in Poland, they are divided into several pieces. Whole coins are also found, but much less frequently,” he explained. World.title: Poland offers to host facility producing Patriot missiles for Ukraine
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has proposed that, if the United States grants Ukraine permission to produce its own missiles for Patriot air-defence systems, the factory could be located on Polish territory to ensure its security. The news was revealed by deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who also confirmed that Poland would seek to establish a Patriot servicing and production facility even if it does not host Ukraine’s. Poland wants to host Patriot production Poland has proposed that the US and Ukraine launch joint production of Patriot missiles. Warsaw is citing security concerns and is proposing to host the facility in Poland instead of Ukraine: “If such a factory is planned to be built in… pic.twitter.com/syCkNt0o0V — Belsat in English (@Belsat_Eng) September 27, 2026 Patriot missile systems have been a key part of Ukraine’s defence against Russian aerial attacks. However, Kyiv has suffered from a shortage of missiles used in the system, prompting President Volodymyr Zelensky to appeal to allies to transfer their interceptors as well as to allow Ukraine to produce them itself. US President Donald Trump initially told Zelensky at a meeting in July that “we are gonna give you a licence to make Patriots”. However, he then backtracked on that offer later the same month. But, following weeks of uncertainty, on Friday last week Zelensky claimed that Trump had personally told him he had made a “final decision” to approve a licence for Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles. Washington has not confirmed that development. Asked about the issue on Saturday, Sobkowiak-Czarnecka told broadcaster TVN, “let’s see if it happens”. However, she added that, “we proposed that, if such a factory is planned to be built in Ukraine, we propose building it in Poland, so that it would be in the so-called safe territory”. Poland is already the primary hub for military equipment, goods and people being transported in and out of its eastern neighbour. Sobkowiak-Czarnecka added that, regardless of where the plant serving Ukraine is located, Poland would also still seek to establish a facility for servicing and, eventually, production of Patriots. “What my interlocutors in Washington confirmed is that, even if such a decision is made regarding Ukraine, it does not change our efforts and does not rule out consent for Poland,” she said. Sobkowiak-Czarnecka was in Washington last week for talks with US officials. In May this year, another deputy defence minister, Cezary Tomczyk, told TVN that Poland had “received preliminary approval from the US State Department to produce missiles for Patriot systems”. The Polish government has confirmed that it has transferred Patriot missiles to Ukraine following opposition criticism It also released a list of all military donations to Ukraine since 2022, showing that the former PiS government gave much more equipment https://t.co/8BmDy5BjiB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026 In 2018, as part of its Wisła air defence programme, Poland signed a $4.75bn contract to purchase Patriot launchers and missiles from the US. In October 2023, the first Patriot systems procured from the US were deployed at Warsaw Babice airport. In December 2025, Poland announced full operational readiness of its US-supplied Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS), an air-defence network that includes Patriot missile batteries. Poland also has an agreement to domestically produce launchers for Patriot systems through cooperation between Polish state-owned defence contractor Huta Stalowa Wola SA and US defence giant Raytheon. Poland has announced a $1.2bn deal that will see a Polish state-owned defence firm manufacture 48 launchers for Patriot missile systems domestically in cooperation with US defence giant Raytheon https://t.co/PQOjKvhqYM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2024 The issue of Ukraine’s need for more Patriot missiles caused domestic political controversy in Poland earlier this year, when the right-wing opposition reacted angrily to reports that the government had handed over some interceptors to Ukraine. In July, the government confirmed that it had done so. However, Prime Minister Donald Tusk later revealed that only five missiles had been transferred to Ukraine. In late July, the Center for Strategic and International Studies reported that the Iran war had depleted America’s stockpile of Patriot missiles to 800 interceptors from roughly 2,300 before the war began. Last week, Germany’s defence minister, Boris Pistorius, confirmed that his country has also proposed that it could manufacture interceptors and perhaps even entire Patriot systems. World.title: “Don’t blame Ukrainian nation,” says Polish priest injured in deadly knife attack
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. One of the priests injured in a knife attack by a Ukrainian man at a Catholic abbey in Poland last week – which left one of his colleagues dead and another fighting for his life in hospital – has delivered a homily calling for people to forgive the attacker and not to blame Ukrainians as a whole for his actions. “I ask you not to repay evil with evil, but with love, support, understanding and care,” said a visibly injured Father Adrian Mantykiewicz. “I ask you to respect and support each other as two brotherly nations.” 🙏 Poruszające słowa ks. Adriana po ataku nożownika w Opactwie w Jarosławiu. W swojej pierwszej homilii po napaści duchowny mówił o przebaczeniu, miłości do bliźniego i odpowiadaniu dobrem nawet na doznaną krzywdę. pic.twitter.com/zGEGvC5meB — Goniec.pl (@GoniecPL) September 28, 2026 On Thursday last week, a 31-year-old Ukrainian man, who can be named only as Ihor H. under Polish privacy law, entered the grounds of the Benedictine abbey in the town of Jarosław. Using a knife he took from a kitchen, he attacked five people before he was stopped. One priest, Stanisław Zbojnowicz, died from his injuries shortly afterwards. Another, Marek Pieńkowski, is still being treated in hospital. Ihor H. was arrested at the scene and, on Saturday, a court approved a request from prosecutors for him to be placed in detention for three months. For now, he is being held in a psychiatric facility, with prosecutors saying that he “displayed symptoms of mental illness”. President @Zelensky has condemned an "evil" knife attack by a Ukrainian man at a Catholic abbey in Poland today, which left a priest dead and others injured Polish Prime Minister @donaldtusk says the perpetrator will face the “full severity of Polish law” https://t.co/SIonlR4JpJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026 On Saturday, in a church that is part of the Benedictine abbey complex, Mantykiewicz celebrated the Eucharist for Zbojnowicz. With bruising under his left eye and bandages on his head and hand, he delivered a homily in which he addressed the attack, its victims, and the perpetrator. “I am a disciple of my master, a disciple of my lord, and Christ teaches me love,” he said. “And from this place, as a disciple of Jesus Christ, I wish to say very clearly in my name, in the name of Father Marek, and in the name of Father Stanisław, that we forgive.” “I ask you to pray for our tormentor,” he continued. “He needs this prayer most of all. Because no matter what happened, we must overcome the evil that occurred here in our abbey with goodness, love, and forgiveness.” Mantykiewicz also appealed for people not to blame Ukrainians more broadly for the incident. There have been fears that the attack could prompt a backlash against Ukrainians, Poland’s largest immigrant group, who have already been experiencing a growing number of hate crimes this year. “I also want to ask you not to blame the nation from which the perpetrator came,” said the priest. “The evil was committed by a specific person…responsible for their own actions. It was not done by other people. It was one person, one person alone.” “Let us be disciples of Christ. Disciples who help others with love, care, respect, help and kindness,” he continued. “It does not matter who they are, what nation they come from, what religion they are, or what colour their skin is; they are human beings…and we must not deprive anyone of their dignity.” On Friday, the head of the Polish Catholic church’s council for migrants and refugees, Bishop Krzysztof Zadarko, gave a press conference at which he condemned the “outpouring of aggression and artificially stoked hatred towards Ukrainians that this event [in Jarosław] has fuelled”. “The church can only appeal to the consciences, primarily of Catholics and Christians, but also of all people, that this is not the right response; it is downright reprehensible, and incompatible with the Gospel,” he added, quoted by broadcaster RMF. “We are dealing with a tremendous tragedy, but shifting the blame of one person onto an entire society, ethnic group, or nationality is wrong,” he added. Agresja i niechęć do kogokolwiek jest nie do pogodzenia z wiarą chrześcijańską – mówił przewodniczący Rady KEP ds. Migrantów i Uchodźców bp Krzysztof Zadarko podczas konferencji prasowej przed 112. Światowym Dniem Migranta i Uchodźcy.https://t.co/M46RXggVTR pic.twitter.com/uZWodfR7sG — EpiskopatNews (@EpiskopatNews) September 25, 2026 Thursday’s attack caused widespread shock and mourning in Poland, and also prompted condolences from Ukraine, including President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said that “we are shocked by this evil”. On Saturday, Ukraine’s ambassador to Poland, Vasyl Bodnar, told broadcaster TVN that he had spoken with Ihor M.’s mother and was able to provide more information about him. He confirmed that the man had left Ukraine in 2022 and lived in Germany. Bodnar, however, said that media reports claiming Ihor M. had served in the Ukrainian military were false. Regarding the motive, Bodnar said that it appears Ihor M. “had some kind of mental illness”. He pledged that the Ukrainian authorities would cooperate and were “working on all the information we can provide to the Polish side”. World.title: Russia condemns Polish city’s “barbaric” removal of Monument of Gratitude to the Red Army
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Russia has criticised the removal of a monument in the Polish city of Rzeszów expressing “gratitude” to the Soviet Red Army. It called the move “barbaric” and “sacrilegious”. The monument – part of which will be moved to a nearby Soviet cemetery and another to a museum – has been the subject of a long-running legal and political battle, amid wider debate in Poland about “decommunising” public spaces, especially in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. ⚡️Komentarz Ambasady Rosji w Polsce 23 września 2026 r. w Rzeszowie (województwo podkarpackie), decyzją władz polskich i z naruszeniem dokumentów rosyjsko-polskich dotyczących ochrony obiektów dziedzictwa memorialnego, rozpoczęto proces demontażu pomnika wdzięczności żołnierzom… pic.twitter.com/HYuNeLG5dy — Russian Embassy, PL (@rusemb_pl) September 24, 2026 The Monument of Gratitude to the Red Army, standing 8.5 metres tall and weighing 6.6 tons, was erected in Rzeszów, southeastern Poland, shortly after the end of World War Two, when the Soviets had pushed Nazi Germany out of Poland and then installed their own communist government. It is located on Ghetto Victims Square, a public space also created after the war on the grounds of the city’s former Jewish cemetery, which had been destroyed by the German occupiers in 1942. Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance, a state historical body, notes that the monument was erected just a few metres from where two Polish anti-communist resistance fighters who had been members of the wartime Home Army (AK) had been publicly hanged by the communists. The monument’s plinth featured bas-relief sculptures depicting Red Army Generals Ivan Konev and Karol Świerczewski, soldiers, and industrial and agricultural workers carrying a hammer and sickle. At the top of the 8.5-metre column was a statue of a woman and child. In 2016, the then-ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government introduced a law requiring local authorities to “decommunise” public spaces by removing objects and names that “propagate communism”. That triggered a legal battle over the monument in Rzeszów. The government-appointed provincial governor and the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical body, moved to have it dismantled, arguing that the monument glorified communism. But city hall – led by left-wing mayor Tadeusz Ferenc, who had been a member of the communist party before 1989 – challenged the decision. It argued that the monument did not promote communism and noted that its name, referring to gratitude to the Red Army, was not an official one. In 2019, the provincial administrative court sided with the city and overturned the decision to remove the monument. However, Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 prompted many Polish municipalities that had not removed Soviet-era monuments to begin doing so. In April 2022, Rzeszów’s current mayor, Konrad Fijołek, announced that his city’s monument would be taken from its current location and placed in a Soviet soldiers’ cemetery elsewhere in the city. “In principle, I am not in favour of dismantling or demolishing monuments, as they are a testament to history,” said the mayor. “But in light of the current wartime reality, this monument should not remain in its current location. But we are not barbarians; we will not demolish the monument, but relocate it.” However, the IPN opposed the idea of relocating the monument and refused to cover the costs of doing so. It wanted it to be eliminated entirely. Another Soviet memorial has been demolished in Poland – the 43rd since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. "We say ‘no’ to Russians who believe these lands somehow belong to their sphere of influence,” declared the Institute of National Remembrance https://t.co/aG9VQVlUQI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 12, 2025 As a result, the city is paying 156,000 zloty (€35,700) for the monument to be taken away, reports news website Wirtualna Polska. The bas-reliefs will go to the Soviet cemetery while the statue of mother and child will go to the city’s Museum of Technology and the Military. Work to remove the monument began this week and is expected to last until November. Once the above-ground section has been removed, a special conservation committee, including a representative of Poland’s Rabbinical Commission for Cemeteries, will determine how to proceed with the monument’s foundation. The beginning of the removal work prompted anger from Moscow, with the Russian embassy in Warsaw issuing a statement that called it a “sacrilegious step”. It demanded “the immediate cessation of work” and restoration of the monument to its previous state. “With regret, we must state once again: the barbaric policy of the Polish authorities, consisting of destroying everything that serves as evidence of the invaluable feat of the soldiers and officers of the Red Army in liberating Poland from Nazi occupation, is being continued at an ever faster pace,” they continued. Russia regards the Soviet Union’s driving Nazi Germany out of Central and Eastern Europe at the end of World War Two as a “liberation”. However, many in the region reject that term, given that it involved bringing their countries under brutal Soviet domination instead. In its statement, the Russian embassy also claimed that the actions in Rzeszów are a “violation of Russian-Polish documents concerning the protection of memorial heritage sites”. Moscow regularly claims that Poland’s removal of Soviet memorials violates a 1994 agreement between the two countries on respect for graves and other places of memory. It did so in August this year, when protesting the demolition of a monument in the town of Pyrzyce. However, Poland points out that the agreement relates to graves and war cemeteries, not separate monuments and symbols, which can be legally removed. Russia has criticised the "sacrilegious" demolition of a Soviet monument in Poland, calling it a “flagrant violation” of a bilateral agreement. But Poland's @ipngovpl says it was a "propaganda object" that had to be removed under a "decommunisation" law https://t.co/73T99ZlPqU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Rzeszów is also home to one of the famous – or infamous, depending on one’s perspective – communist-era monuments in Poland, the 38-metre-tall Monument to the Revolutionary Struggle. It has become a landmark of the city. In 2017, the IPN recommended that it be removed under the “decommunisation” law. The owners of the land upon which it sits also wanted to demolish it. However, mayors Ferenc and Fijołek sought to protect the monument, and their efforts succeeded last year, when it was added to Poland’s list of protected monuments, preventing it from being destroyed. World.title: Techno, Art and Live Performance Come Together at Strahov on October 10
World.content:
On October 10, the Prague electronic music collective EDEN will bring Rotten To The Core to Stadion Strahov for one of the collective’s largest and most ambitious events to date.

Running from 10pm until 7am, the night will bring together international and local DJs, dancers and visual artists for an event built around music, performance and visual art.



The lineup includes VLACE, SCHELLT, RiVid, 2NDRA and Mila (5), with the programme focused on techno and acid.

Among the artists, 2NDRA is a Prague-based schranz and techno producer and performer and one of the founders of EDEN Collective. RiVid, meanwhile, is a Czech-Japanese hard techno duo.

The event takes a broader approach to the club experience, combining the music programme with visual elements, art installations and live performances.

That approach comes at a time when electronic music events are becoming increasingly commercialised, while promoters and venues face rising production costs and growing regulatory pressures.

The event will take place beneath Strahov Stadium in Prague 6, continuing EDEN’s connection with unconventional venues and large-scale rave productions.

The collective previously hosted its 40-hour ALT BABYLON weekender in Prague in August, featuring dozens of local and international artists.

The event is for ages 18 and over, with tickets starting at CZK 300.

World.title: Václav Havel Would Be 90 This Year: From Playwright to President
World.content:
Václav Havel was one of the defining figures of modern Czech history.

Playwright, writer, dissident, political prisoner and, ultimately, the last president of Czechoslovakia and the first president of the Czech Republic, his life reflected some of the country’s most dramatic changes of the 20th century.

Born into a prominent Prague family, Havel experienced both privilege and political persecution. He became one of the leading voices of the opposition to communist rule and played a central role in the Velvet Revolution of 1989.



On October 5th, 2026, Havel would have turned 90. Here is a look at his life, political career and some of the places in Prague and beyond connected to him.

From a privileged Prague family to a banned writer

Havel was born in Prague on October 5, 1936, into a wealthy and well-connected family. His uncle, Miloš Havel, founded Barrandov Studios, while his grandfather was involved in construction and real estate.

His family’s position changed dramatically after the Communist Party took power in Czechoslovakia in 1948. Their property was confiscated, and Havel faced restrictions on his education and career because of his family background.

During the political liberalisation of the 1960s, Havel became increasingly involved in Prague’s theatre scene. He worked as a stagehand and later as a dramaturge, while also establishing himself as a playwright. His plays often explored power, bureaucracy and the absurdity of life under an authoritarian system.

The hopes of 1968

The Prague Spring of 1968 brought a period of political and cultural liberalisation to Czechoslovakia. Censorship was abolished, previously banned books began appearing in print and films that had been restricted were shown in cinemas again.

Havel embraced the new atmosphere and became increasingly active in public life. But the reforms ended abruptly when Warsaw Pact troops invaded Czechoslovakia on August 21, 1968.

Havel opposed the occupation and the return to political repression. He was subsequently banned from publishing and working in the theatre. For a period, he worked as a manual labourer at a brewery in Trutnov.

He later became one of the most prominent figures of the Czechoslovak dissident movement. He was a signatory of Charter 77, a civic initiative calling on the communist government to respect human rights, and was repeatedly arrested and imprisoned.

From dissident to president

The communist regime collapsed in November 1989 following mass demonstrations across Czechoslovakia. Havel was one of the leading figures of the Civic Forum, the opposition movement that helped negotiate the peaceful transfer of power.

On December 29, 1989, he was elected president of Czechoslovakia.

Havel remained in office after the country split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia in 1993, becoming the first president of the newly independent Czech Republic. During his political career, he supported the country’s integration into Western institutions, including NATO, and advocated closer ties with the European Union.

His presidency also left a visible mark on Prague Castle. Parts of the complex were opened to the public, while the South Gardens were restored following their pre-war design.

Life after Prague Castle

Havel left the presidency in 2003 but remained active as a writer and public figure. He continued to comment on political and social issues and maintained friendships with artists, intellectuals and international figures.

Among them was the Dalai Lama, who visited Havel in Prague on several occasions. Havel died on December 18, 2011, at his country house in Hrádeček, near the Krkonoše mountains.

Places connected to Václav Havel in Prague

Several Prague locations are closely connected to Havel and his family.

One is Lucerna Palace on Wenceslas Square, built by Havel’s grandfather. The complex includes the historic Lucerna Cinema, which has been operating for more than a century, as well as the famous Lucerna Café.

Prague Castle is another essential stop. Havel lived and worked there during his years as president and initiated several changes that made parts of the complex more accessible to the public.

Outside Prague, Havel was also closely associated with Lány Chateau, the traditional summer residence of Czech presidents. During his time there, he was known to visit the local pub and meet residents without the formality normally associated with a head of state.

World.title: Prague’s Kramář Villa to Open for Free Visits on October 3
World.content:
Prague’s Kramář Villa will open to the public on October 3, giving visitors a chance to see inside one of the Czech government’s official residences.

Admission will be free.

The villa, located on Gogolova Street in Prague’s Letná district, is the official residence of the Czech prime minister. It was also the home of Karel Kramář, Czechoslovakia’s first prime minister, and his wife, Nadezhda.



Visitors during the open house will be able to take guided tours of the building and learn about its history, architecture and former residents. The tour will include parts of the villa that are normally closed to the public, including its living quarters and ceremonial rooms.

Built with a combination of Neo-Baroque and Art Nouveau influences, Kramář Villa has been one of Prague’s government residences since the early 20th century.

Its history is closely linked to Karel Kramář, who became the first prime minister of Czechoslovakia following the country’s establishment in 1918.

The open house will also include access to the villa’s garden. Located above the city, the grounds provide views across Prague and will remain open for longer than the villa itself.

The villa will welcome visitors from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. on October 3. The garden will be open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

World.title: Czech Study Finds Supporting Homeless People Can Save Public Money
World.content:
A Czech experiment in which homeless people received CZK 100,000 with no conditions attached suggests that early financial support can reduce some of the costs associated with homelessness.

The project, known as New Leaf, was carried out by the Czech organization Neposeda in cooperation with researchers from Charles University.



The findings indicate that the state spends an average of about CZK 200,000 a year on each person experiencing homelessness, with healthcare, social services and police work accounting for a significant share of the total.

The researchers concluded that leaving people without support can ultimately be more expensive for public finances than providing targeted assistance.

How the New Leaf experiment worked

The project ran from summer 2024 until the end of 2025 and was inspired by a similar initiative in Canada.

Researchers focused on people who had been living on the streets for no more than two and a half years. The aim was to examine whether intervention at an earlier stage of homelessness could prevent longer-term problems.

Participants were divided into several groups. Forty people received CZK 100,000 without restrictions on how the money could be used. Another 20 were offered the support of a personal social worker instead, while 40 people formed a control group and received no additional assistance.

The study initially involved 100 people. One participant died from a serious illness shortly after the project began, leaving 99 participants in the final research sample.

The researchers tracked participants’ use of public services and their contact with state authorities, including emergency medical services, hospitals, outpatient healthcare, social services and police.

Healthcare accounts for the largest share

The study estimates that the state spends around CZK 200,000 annually on each homeless person.

Healthcare represented almost 43% of the estimated expenditure. Low-threshold services, which provide basic support and a safe place for people experiencing homelessness, accounted for around a quarter of the total.

Police work represented another 9%, or more than 18,000 crowns per person each year.

The wider cost to public finances

Data from the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs recorded 11,641 homeless people in the Czech Republic in the previous year.

Based on the estimated annual cost per person, direct public expenditure associated with homelessness amounts to roughly 2.33 billion crowns a year.

World.title: Smartwings Cuts Prague Flights as Winter Schedule Shrinks
World.content:
Smartwings is reducing its winter flight schedule from Prague, with several routes being cancelled, frequencies cut and new connections postponed until spring 2027.

The biggest changes will affect Spain, a popular choice for Czech travelers looking for warmer weather during the autumn and winter months.

The airline will suspend flights between Prague and Valencia from November 2 until the beginning of March.

Flights to several other Spanish destinations will also be reduced. Smartwings will cut its Málaga service from two flights a day to one, while Barcelona will move from daily flights to four to six services a week.

Flights to Mallorca will be reduced from four per week to two. The Prague–Madrid route will continue, but flights will operate on an irregular schedule.

Smartwings is also suspending flights from Prague to Nice until early March.

New Prague routes pushed back

Several routes that were expected to launch this year will now have to wait until spring 2027.

The postponed connections include new services to Venice and Bergen, Norway. Smartwings has also delayed the return of flights to Brussels and Bucharest.

Both Brussels and Bucharest were suspended in the spring, with Smartwings originally planning to restore the routes in October.

Eurowings also reduces Prague services

Eurowings is making changes to its Prague schedule as well. The German carrier has cancelled its planned winter flights to Madeira, Portugal.

The route had been scheduled to return for the winter season, but Eurowings will instead offer tickets to Madeira through a partnership with Smartwings, which continues to operate flights to the Portuguese island.

Eurowings will also suspend its Prague–Stockholm service for most of January.

Higher fuel costs affect airline schedules

The changes come as airlines face higher operating costs linked to fuel prices.

According to Eurocontrol, the European organization responsible for coordinating air traffic management, jet fuel prices in Europe more than doubled between the beginning of the year and mid-September.

Airlines around the world have been adjusting schedules as fuel costs fluctuate amid the conflict in the Middle East. Route cancellations and reduced frequencies are among the measures carriers are using to adapt to changing market conditions.

World.title: Home Baking Returns to Czech Kitchens as Flour Sales Rise
World.content:
Home baking is gaining momentum in the Czech Republic, with online supermarket Rohlik.cz reporting a sharp increase in demand for baking ingredients this year.

Flour has been at the center of the trend. Sales of organic flour have risen by almost 72 percent compared with the previous year, while conventional flour sales increased by around 23 percent.



The change has also affected the balance of sales. Organic flour previously accounted for about 19 percent of flour purchases at Rohlik.cz. That figure has now climbed to almost 25 percent.

The figures suggest that customers are not simply buying more flour but are also paying greater attention to the type and quality of the ingredients they use.

Rohlik.cz CEO Miroslava Vopatová says baking continues to play a role in family life, particularly as an activity shared across generations. The supermarket has responded by offering products at different price points, from private-label options to organic and farm-produced ingredients.

Yeast sales tell a different story

The increase in demand for flour has not been mirrored by yeast.

Sales of yeast have been gradually falling since the surge in home baking during the coronavirus pandemic. One shift remains noticeable, however: shoppers are increasingly choosing fresh yeast rather than dried yeast.

Home baking in the Czech Republic is also strongly seasonal. Christmas remains the busiest period of the year, while a smaller increase usually occurs in March and April. Demand drops during the summer months.

For experienced bakers, the quality of the final product often depends on relatively simple details. Yeast dough needs enough time and warmth to rise properly, while rushing the process can affect the result.

The preparation of the filling matters as well. Curd cheese should be drained thoroughly before being added to a cake or pastry, reducing the risk of excess moisture making the dough soggy. Fruit fillings should also be sufficiently thick rather than watery.

These practical details can make a noticeable difference, particularly in traditional Czech pastries whose recipes are often passed down through families.

World.title: New Flights from Prague to Asia Boost Competition on Airfares
World.content:
Travelers flying from Prague this autumn have more options as airlines add capacity and new direct connections, particularly to Asia.

At the same time, increased competition is putting pressure on carriers to keep fares under control, according to data from Czech booking portal Letuška.cz.



The biggest changes are visible on long-haul routes. New services from Prague are making destinations in Asia more accessible, while airlines already serving the Czech market are responding with promotional fares.

“Thanks to high competition and new capacity from Prague, the autumn flight market offers very favorable travel conditions,” said Josef Trejbal, commercial director of Letuška.cz. He said the arrival of new Asian connections has helped revive demand for long-haul travel and encouraged established airlines to introduce more competitive offers.

Direct flights strengthen Prague’s links with Asia

Asia is once again attracting greater interest from Czech travelers. One factor is the growing number of direct or more convenient connections from Prague, which can reduce the need for lengthy transfers through major Middle Eastern hubs.

STARLUX Airlines, for example, is offering flights from Prague to Taipei from around CZK 21,000. The direct service provides an alternative to itineraries involving a stopover and can save travelers both time and, depending on the itinerary, money.

Another new option will be available from October 10, when flights to Hanoi are scheduled to begin on the Prague–Almaty–Hanoi route. Tickets listed through Letuška.cz start at around CZK 18,000.

The expansion comes as airlines compete more aggressively for passengers on long-haul routes departing from Prague.

Caribbean and Latin America see strong growth

Europe remains the most popular region for Czech travelers, but demand for long-haul destinations is also changing. According to Letuška.cz, Latin America and the Caribbean have recorded the sharpest year-on-year increases, with demand growing by hundreds of percent in some cases.

The Caribbean in particular has benefited from rising interest among travelers looking beyond Europe. Latin American destinations have also seen a significant increase in bookings compared with the same period last year.

The stronger demand is coinciding with changes in the competitive landscape. New routes from Prague are challenging airlines that have traditionally carried passengers to Asia and Australia through Middle Eastern hubs.

Major Gulf carriers including Emirates, Qatar Airways and Etihad are responding with promotional fares, adding further pressure to ticket prices.

World.title: Five Free Things to Do in Prague This October
World.content:
Prague will offer a range of free cultural events in October, from exhibitions and science films to family entertainment and hands-on craft workshops.

Several major institutions will also open their doors to the public on October 28, Czech Independence Day.



Here are five events where the main program is free, followed by a guide to some of the places that can be visited without charge on the October 28 public holiday.

Free admission at the National Gallery

October 3–4 and October 28, 10:00 AM–6:00 PM

The National Gallery Prague will offer free access to selected exhibitions on two occasions in October.

On October 3 and 4, visitors can see 1956–1989: Architecture for Everyone at the Trade Fair Palace (Veletržní palác) without paying an entrance fee. The offer forms part of Architecture Day, this year’s festival built around the theme “I Dwell, Therefore I Am.”

The Architecture Day program will also include free tours and workshops at several National Gallery sites, including the Trade Fair Palace, the Convent of St. Agnes of Bohemia and Schwarzenberg Palace. Some activities require advance registration.

Another opportunity comes on October 28, when the National Gallery will waive admission to its eight permanent exhibitions. The program includes medieval and Old Master collections as well as exhibitions covering the First Republic, the period from 1939 to 2021 and Asian art.

The free admission applies to the specified permanent collections and does not cover all temporary exhibitions. The gallery is also preparing additional activities for the public holiday.

Midnight Circus brings family entertainment to Prague 8

October 3, 10:00 AM–7:00 PM and October 4, 10:00 AM–12:00 PM – DDM Prague 8 – Spirála, Přemyšlenská 15

The Spirála Children and Youth Center in Kobylisy will become a temporary circus venue during the first weekend of October.

Midnight Circus will feature clowns, fortune tellers, a storyteller and a House of Horrors, alongside other attractions aimed at families. Visitors can also enter a themed bathhouse.

The daytime program is free and does not require advance registration. Instead of paying directly for individual attractions, visitors receive “Principálky” at the entrance, a special circus currency that can also be earned through activities during the event.

An evening show on Saturday will feature a UV light performance followed by a fire show. Unlike the daytime program, this performance requires a ticket costing CZK 50, payable in cash at the venue. It is not recommended for children younger than five.

Try traditional crafts at the New Town Hall

October 13–14, 8:00 AM–4:00 PM – New Town Hall, Karlovo náměstí 1/23, Prague 2

The New Town Hall will host the 13th edition of Crafts Live (Řemesla živě), an event designed to introduce visitors to traditional and practical trades and the schools where they can be studied.

Visitors will have the opportunity to try different crafts for themselves and speak directly with representatives of vocational schools about their courses and study programs.

Admission to the event is free, although some individual workshops may charge a fee.

Science documentaries come to Suchdol

October 19–22 – Czech University of Life Sciences Prague, Suchdol

The Prague Science Film Fest returns with a program of international science documentaries, including several Czech premieres.

The films explore subjects ranging from the way the human brain can mislead us to the role of fungi and the behavior of otters. Among the scheduled titles are How the Brain Tricks Us, My Otter Diary and The Kingdom of Fungi.

Film screenings will be accompanied by discussions with scientists, filmmakers and other experts, giving visitors an opportunity to explore the topics beyond the films themselves.

The festival will also include an outdoor screening of the Oscar-nominated documentary Fire of Love, an exhibition focused on antelope conservation in Africa and a filmmaking workshop.

Admission is free, and this year’s program does not require registration.

Where to go for free on October 28

October 28 is a public holiday in Czechia, marking the establishment of the independent Czechoslovak state in 1918. Several important Prague buildings traditionally open to visitors on the day.

Straka Academy

The seat of the Czech government will open its meeting rooms, press rooms and garden to the public. The exact visiting hours had not yet been announced at the time of publication.

Wallenstein Palace and Kolowrat Palace

The Czech Senate will open both buildings from 7:30 AM to 5:00 PM. Visitors will be able to see, among other areas, the Senate meeting hall.

Thun Palace

The Chamber of Deputies will open Thun Palace on Sněmovní Street from 9:00 AM to 4:00 PM. Tours start at the main entrance at Sněmovní 4.

Municipal House

The representative rooms on the first floor, including Smetana Hall and the Mayor’s Hall, will be accessible free of charge from 9:00 AM to 3:00 PM. Guided commentary in Smetana Hall will be available every 15 minutes.

World.title: China’s Ambassador Gong Tao: 77 years on a shared journey – Setting out anew with mutual understanding and friendship
World.content:
The past 77 years have witnessed China’s relentless pursuit of progress through trials and triumphs. Under the leadership of the Communist Party of China (CPC), the Chinese people have opened a path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, achieving the historic transformation from national independence to prosperity and strength, while sustaining rapid economic growth and maintaining long-term social stability. The year 2026 marks the 105th anniversary of the founding of the CPC and the opening year of China’s 15th Five-Year Plan. We are advancing Chinese modernization on all fronts through high-quality development, striving unremittingly for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and for the building of a community with a shared future for humanity.

Author: His Excellency Gong Tao, Ambassador of the People’s Republic of China to Hungary

China’s high-quality development is people-centered. In December 2025, the Tianshan Shengli Tunnel in Xinjiang was opened to traffic. With an investment of RMB 6.08 billion and a total length of 22.13 kilometers, the tunnel cuts through the Tianshan Mountains at an elevation of more than 3,000 meters above sea level, closely linking northern and southern Xinjiang. A journey that once took seven hours now takes no more than 30 minutes, making travel and logistics much easier. As a local tour guide put it when introducing the tunnel: “Because the people need a good road like this, the motherland can make the mountains bow and the rivers yield. It is not that piercing through the Tianshan Mountains is easy; it is that the people are on the other side.” These words capture the underlying logic of Chinese modernization and the commitment of the CPC and the Chinese government to ensuring that development truly delivers for the people.

Photo: Embassy of the People’s Republic of China to Hungary

China’s high-quality development is driven by innovation. In 2026, China continues making fresh progress in artificial intelligence, embodied robotics, computing power and commercial spaceflight, among other areas of innovation. Behind these remarkable achievements lies sustained investment in science and technology and a dynamic innovation ecosystem. China’s R&D intensity has surpassed the OECD average, with 77 percent of R&D investment coming from businesses. We have built an innovation ecosystem that is deeply integrated, open, inclusive and full of vitality. In Shenzhen’s Robot Valley, more than 200 robotics companies have gathered within a half-hour radius. It has become clear that decoupling benefits no one, and that a “small yard, high fence” strategy cannot hold back China’s technological innovation. China has always based its development on the strength and ingenuity of its people, while remaining open to international cooperation in science and technology.

Photo: Embassy of the People’s Republic of China to Hungary

China’s high-quality development creates opportunities for the rest of the world. What China pursues has never been self-interest alone, but a community with a shared future for humanity in which all countries can thrive together. Committed to world peace, China has always approached international issues on their merits, acted on the principles of objectivity and justice, and actively explored solutions to hot-spot issues with Chinese characteristics. In September this year, President Xi Jinping put forward a four-point initiative on building a security architecture in the Middle East, contributing China’s solution to lasting stability in the region. On the Ukraine crisis, China remains committed to promoting peace talks and playing a constructive role in advancing a political settlement. Committed to global development, what China brings to the world is not shocks, but opportunities. By opening its vast market, driving industrial innovation, and maintaining stable supply chains, China is bringing greater certainty to the sluggish global economy. China’s economy continues to grow steadily—supported by the world’s largest and one of its most dynamic middle-income groups—making China an increasingly attractive market. In the first eight months of 2026 alone, China’s imports grew by more than 22 percent. Committed to upholding the international order, China has put forward the Global AI Governance Initiative and helped establish World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization in Shanghai, the first intergovernmental organization dedicated to AI, in an effort to bridge the global digital divide and promote fairer AI governance.

Photo: Embassy of the People’s Republic of China to Hungary

This year marks the 77th anniversary of diplomatic relations between China and Hungary, with Hungary being one of the first countries to recognize the PRC. Having stood the test of time, China-Hungary relations have continued to grow in a sound and steady manner. Deepening our friendship and mutually beneficial cooperation has become a shared aspiration and consensus of our peoples.

Mutual respect is the political foundation of our bilateral relations. Despite our different histories, cultures and political systems, China and Hungary have always treated each other with mutual respect, understanding and trust, and regarded each other as reliable partners. China respects the choice of the Hungarian people, never interferes in Hungary’s internal affairs, and appreciates the adoption of friendly policies toward China by successive Hungarian governments, including their adherence to the One-China principle. Following the formation of Hungary’s new government and National Assembly, the leaders of our two countries have maintained friendly exchanges, charting the course for the future development of bilateral relations.

Photo: Embassy of the People’s Republic of China to Hungary

Mutual benefit and win-win outcomes are defining features of our cooperation. Chinese businesses have invested in a wide range of areas in Hungary, creating tens of thousands of jobs and becoming an important force in driving local industrial upgrading, green development and economic growth. Chinese companies operating in Hungary are also contributing to local innovation, R&D and talent development, building close partnerships with universities such as the University of Debrecen and the University of Szeged. It is hoped that the Hungarian government will continue providing a sound business environment for Chinese businesses. Connectivity between our two countries has continued to improve, with 22 direct passenger flights per week connecting Budapest with seven Chinese cities and further strengthening Budapest’s role as an important hub between China and Europe. At the Budapest AI Summit earlier this month, leading Chinese AI companies, research institutes and universities took part, opening new opportunities for AI exchanges and cooperation between our two countries. Last week, the Hungarian side sent a delegation to the 5th Global Digital Trade Expo in Hangzhou. Eleven Hungarian businesses as well as the Hungarian Innovation Agency participated in the event. I am confident that our two countries will achieve even greater results in emerging fields such as the digital economy and green trade.

Photo: Embassy of the People’s Republic of China to Hungary

The deep roots of China-Hungary friendship among our peoples are one of its distinctive hallmarks. In November last year, I visited Perkáta in Fejér County, which forged friendly ties with Huaxiang in Beijing as early as 1960, becoming the first Hungarian township to establish a sister relationship with a Chinese counterpart. More than six decades on, the two sides have preserved this longstanding friendship and maintained close exchanges, writing a new and inspiring chapter in the history of China-Hungary friendship. To this day, Perkáta still has a Beijing Road, while its Hungary-China Friendship Agricultural Company has been operating for more than 50 years. Mr. Oláh István, mayor of Perkáta, will soon lead a delegation to visit Beijing, to renew cooperation in the new era. I would like to express my sincere appreciation to all friends who have supported and contributed to the China-Hungary friendship.

Photo: Embassy of the People’s Republic of China to Hungary

Looking back, the friendship between China and Hungary is deeply rooted in the mutual understanding and affinity between our peoples. Looking ahead, the greatest opportunities for our cooperation stem from our shared pursuit of development. Under the strategic guidance of our leaders, I am confident that China and Hungary will carry forward our traditional friendship, deepen political mutual trust and practical cooperation, strengthen people-to-people exchanges, and maintain close communication on international affairs. Together, we will keep our all-weather comprehensive strategic partnership in the new era strong and enduring, bringing greater benefits to our two peoples.

World.title: Georgian and Bulgarian nationals arrested: International burglary gang caught after targeting homes across Budapest – video
World.content:
Three Georgian and Bulgarian nationals have been arrested in Budapest after police linked them to nine daytime burglaries across six districts, with nearly HUF 17 million in suspected losses.

Police tracked suspicious Ukrainian-registered car

The three men — two Georgian nationals aged 28 and 30 and a 30-year-old Bulgarian citizen — were arrested in Budapest’s District V on 25 September by officers from the Budapest Police Headquarters (BRFK), with assistance from the Counter Terrorism Centre (TEK).

According to police, the men are suspected of committing burglaries on a commercial basis. They were questioned and taken into custody, while prosecutors requested their pre-trial detention. BRFK’s head of the Investigation Department, Lieutenant Colonel Sándor Gál, said the suspects had entered Hungary from Slovakia and carried out nine residential burglaries between 15 and 25 September.

The break-ins took place in six Budapest districts: I, II, III and XI on the Buda side, and XIII and XIV on the Pest side.

Police said the cases were linked by several similarities. All the burglaries took place during the daytime, and the suspects allegedly opened the entrance doors without causing visible damage. The stolen property included cash, jewellery, expensive watches and electronic devices. Police estimate the total damage at almost HUF 17 million.

CCTV footage led police to the suspects

Investigators suspected that the burglars were using a car to move around Budapest and transport the stolen goods. After reviewing CCTV footage from the areas around the burglaries, they noticed a dark blue Toyota RAV4 with Ukrainian registration plates, carrying three men.

On 25 September, police launched a targeted patrol operation in central Budapest to locate the vehicle. They eventually found the Toyota and, with the assistance of TEK officers, arrested the three suspects.

During searches of the men and the vehicle, investigators found specialised tools allegedly used for breaking into properties and opening locks, as well as substances suspected to be drugs. Some of the stolen items and cash were also recovered.

Police said the men had been staying in Hungary since 28 August.

Police suspect ‘travelling criminals’

According to Gál, investigators suspect the men may be so-called “travelling criminals” who enter a country, commit several offences and then move on. Police believe two of the three men actively participated in the burglaries, while the third acted as the driver.

The suspects refused to make statements or cooperate with investigators during questioning. A court has since ordered their detention for 30 days. Gál said police will also contact authorities in the suspects’ home countries and neighbouring states to establish whether they may have been involved in offences elsewhere.

He added that residential burglaries are not currently unusually common in Budapest, with statistics showing broadly stable numbers in recent years.

World.title: Busy autumn at Kempinski: ÉS Bisztró launches Sunday brunch as hotel spa wins prestigious award
World.content:
Autumn has brought several new developments to Kempinski Hotel Corvinus Budapest, with ÉS Bisztró launching a new Sunday brunch concept and Kempinski The Spa being named Hungary’s Best Hotel Spa at the 2026 World Spa Awards.

New Sunday tradition at ÉS Bisztró

Since 20 September, ÉS Bisztró has been serving its new Sunday Brunch every Sunday from 11:30am to 4pm, offering guests a relaxed alternative to the traditional Sunday lunch.

The concept combines an à la carte brunch menu with some of the restaurant’s signature dishes, giving guests the freedom to put together their own Sunday meal. Options range from Eggs Benedict and oysters to Beef Wellington, Sunday roast and the restaurant’s iconic Tafelspitz.

The brunch is designed for a variety of occasions, whether it is a family lunch, a long gathering with friends or simply a leisurely Sunday afternoon. A live DJ provides the soundtrack throughout the afternoon, adding to the relaxed atmosphere.

Photo: ÉS Bistro, Kempinski Hotel Corvinus Budapest

Guests can also choose from a dedicated drinks menu featuring Bellinis, Bloody Marys, martinis and champagne. Two-hour free-flow beverage packages are available as well, alongside soft drinks and mocktails.

The Sunday Brunch will run throughout the autumn-winter season, every Sunday from 11:30 AM to 4 PM. Guests arriving for brunch can also use the hotel’s underground garage free of charge during brunch hours.

Photo: ÉS Bistro, Kempinski Hotel Corvinus Budapest

Kempinski spa takes home another major title

Meanwhile, Kempinski The Spa has once again been recognised at the World Spa Awards, taking the title of ‘Hungary’s Best Hotel Spa’ in the 2026 edition.

The award marks the sixth time the spa has received the distinction, according to Kempinski Hotel Corvinus Budapest.

Spa Manager Katalin O’Nagy said the recognition was a tribute to the work of the spa’s therapists and reception team, highlighting their role in creating a welcoming and relaxing environment for guests.

Kempinski The Spa: Reception. Photo: Kempinski Hotel Corvinus Budapest

The latest award adds another international accolade to Kempinski The Spa’s record and underlines the hotel’s focus on luxury wellness services in the Hungarian capital.

With a new Sunday brunch and another major spa award, Kempinski Hotel Corvinus Budapest is entering the autumn season with both its dining and wellness offerings in the spotlight.

World.title: Budapest police apologise after journalist receives insulting, misogynistic internal email
World.content:
The Budapest Police Headquarters has apologised to an HVG journalist after an internal email describing her as a “screaming blue stocking” was apparently sent to her by mistake.

Journalist had requested interview on street harassment

HVG journalist Noémi Martini first contacted the communications department of the Budapest Police Headquarters (BRFK) in early September to request an interview with Budapest police chief Colonel Norbert Tamás Baricska about street harassment in the capital.

The request was initially turned down. Martini subsequently began collecting accounts from people who had experienced harassment on the streets through an anonymous questionnaire.

According to HVG, more than 300 stories were submitted within a few weeks, 93% of them from women. Most described sexual harassment on Budapest streets or on public transport.

The journalist then contacted the police again, asking whether another representative could discuss the issue, as the responses appeared to point to a broader problem.

BRFK spokesperson Soma Csécsi subsequently called Martini and asked her to send specific questions so that a suitable police representative could be found. The National Police Headquarters (ORFK) later responded in writing, but only answered some of the questions.

Martini then asked why she could not put her questions directly to a police representative and, if written answers were the only option, why only some of her questions had been addressed.

Internal email apparently sent to journalist

According to HVG, an email was sent to Martini a few hours later that appears to have been intended for police staff rather than the journalist herself.

The message began with “Dear Attila!” and included three police employees among the recipients. Discussing Martini’s interview request, it reportedly said that, according to Soma, “a screaming blue stocking” would not be given an interview by the Budapest police chief.

The term “blue stocking” is a derogatory expression traditionally used for a woman portrayed as overly intellectual or opinionated.

BRFK launches internal investigation

In a statement published on Tuesday, BRFK acknowledged the incident and apologised for the tone of the internal correspondence.

The police said the language used was “unacceptable” and did not reflect its communication standards or the ethical requirements associated with them. It stressed that respectful and factual communication is expected when dealing with journalists, members of the public and colleagues alike.

BRFK also addressed the underlying issue raised by the journalist, stating that street harassment of women is a real problem. It said both reported and unreported cases must be taken seriously and that all legally available means should be used to prevent such incidents.

“We apologise to the journalist, everyone affected and the public,” the police said, adding that an internal investigation would be launched into the incident.

The statement did not identify the employee or employees responsible for the wording of the email.

World.title: Fidesz: ‘Ukrainian mafia’ operatives have infiltrated Hungarian state institutions
World.content:
The Fidesz party claims that the “Ukrainian mafia” is paying dozens of people in Hungary who have already infiltrated state institutions. The opposition party also said that people allegedly “paid by Ukrainians” and making false accusations would eventually face legal consequences.

Fidesz made the claims in a statement sent to the Hungarian News Agency (MTI) on Tuesday, accusing the “Ukrainian mafia” of transferring huge amounts of money through Hungary without restraint.

According to the party, Hungarian authorities put an end to this activity under the previous “national government”, and therefore deserve recognition rather than accusations. Fidesz added that the authorities would receive this recognition once the party “restores the rule of law in Hungary”.

USD 40 million and EUR 35 million in cash, plus gold, seized

According to the MTI report, officers from the National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) and the Counter-Terrorism Centre (TEK) seized two vehicles on the M0 motorway on 5 March on suspicion of money laundering.

The vehicles, owned by Ukraine’s Oschadbank, were reportedly transporting USD 40 million and EUR 35 million in cash, as well as 9 kilograms of gold, from Austria’s Raiffeisen Bank to Ukraine.

The seven-member, unarmed crew was questioned the following day and subsequently expelled from Hungary. They later filed complaints alleging inhumane treatment and violations of their rights.

Former prosecutor says ‘gold convoy’ case was politically created

Pál Fürcht, former head of the Central Chief Prosecutor’s Office for Investigations, also commented on the case on Tuesday in an open letter published on the Facebook page of authorised lawyer Lóránt Horváth.

Fürcht wrote that experienced prosecutors at the Budapest Investigative Prosecutor’s Office concluded in May, based on the evidence collected up to that point, that the so-called “gold convoy case” was a case created for political reasons.

According to Fürcht, the investigation at the time indicated that then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán himself had instructed the intelligence services on 3 March to arrest the Ukrainian cash couriers on 5 March. (Read more details HERE.)

He claimed that, while carrying out the task allegedly set by politicians, the intelligence service consulted a department head at the Office of the Prosecutor General on 4 March, as well as the Prosecutor General himself.

Fürcht said that on 5 March, the intelligence service’s criminal complaint reached the investigative authorities within a record four to five hours, instead of the three-day period provided by law. He said this happened with the involvement of the Prosecutor General, the deputy Prosecutor General and another senior prosecutor.

The complaint reportedly came with an instruction from the prosecution service that an investigation had to be launched.

According to Fürcht, even this process was almost too slow, as the operation against the alleged gold convoy was already well underway.

He argued that if the leadership of the Office of the Prosecutor General had sent the instruction to launch the investigation even half a day later, the Ukrainian cash couriers would already have safely returned home and the task allegedly set by the prime minister could not have been carried out.

The Fidesz statement and Fürcht’s open letter offer different interpretations of the background to the case. The claims made public so far do not in themselves establish that “Ukrainian mafia” operatives had infiltrated Hungarian state institutions, or that the people referred to by Fidesz had made false accusations.

World.title: Exclusive interview: “The ‘N’ still stands for non-governmental, doesn’t it?” – Máté Hajba on EU-funded lobbying
World.content:
Máté Hajba is the director of Hungary’s Free Market Foundation, which has published a new report examining what it calls “circular lobbying” in Brussels: public institutions funding NGOs that, among their activities, seek to influence the policies of those same institutions. The report examines nine organisations, identifies roughly €12.8 million in annual public funding, and says around 96.8% of the public funding it identified came from the European Commission. Daily News Hungary spoke with Hajba about whether Brussels has created an echo chamber financed by European taxpayers.

Daily News Hungary: Let’s put this crudely. Brussels gives NGOs taxpayers’ money, some of those NGOs lobby Brussels, and Brussels then hears supposedly independent civil society demanding policies it helped finance. Is that really the system?

Máté Hajba: Put that way, it does sound exceptionally efficient, doesn’t it? You provide the money, help finance the advocacy, receive the advocacy, and then point to civil society as evidence of public demand for the policy. As a Hungarian, I saw how self-servingly such a practice worked in my country under the Orbán regime, which the EU so often and rightly criticised.

Of course, reality in the EU is more complicated, and we should not pretend that every euro in an EU grant is paying somebody to knock on an MEP’s door. Lobbying is legal, advocacy is legitimate, and EU funding does not automatically make an organisation a puppet of the European Commission.

But that is precisely why transparency matters. If these relationships are entirely proper, there should be no problem showing taxpayers exactly where the money goes and what activities it supports. “Trust us, it’s civil society” is not really a substitute for a receipt. This lack of transparency erodes trust in public institutions and NGOs, at a time of global turmoil when justly earned trust is most needed.

Daily News Hungary: You found roughly €12.8 million in annual public funding among just nine organisations, with about 96.8% of the public funding you identified coming from the European Commission. At what point does “independent civil society” start sounding like a rather creative accounting term?

Máté Hajba: The “N” in NGO still stands for “non-governmental,” as far as I am aware. That does not mean an NGO stops being independent the moment it receives a public grant. Plenty of organisations receive government or EU funding for perfectly legitimate work.

But when a public institution becomes a significant financial supporter of organisations that are simultaneously trying to influence public policy, taxpayers are entitled to ask whether the relationship is transparent enough. It is basic due diligence the EU owes to its taxpayers.

And there is a very simple way to test whether people genuinely believe the principle they are defending: reverse the politics. Imagine the Commission giving millions to organisations lobbying against climate regulation, against further tobacco restrictions, or for dramatically tighter migration rules. Would everyone who currently sees no problem suddenly become fascinated by the details of EU grant agreements?

If your standard of transparency changes depending on whether you like the cause, then you do not have a transparency standard. You have a favourite team.

Living, working or doing business in Hungary?
