World.title: Thriving Kids set to begin in Canberra amid waiting-list fears
World.content:
The ACT government says children under the age of nine will not yet be removed from the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) as it begins to roll out the Thriving Kids program.

A federal government initiative, Thriving Kids was announced as a way to better support children experiencing developmental delays.

All states and territories have opted in except for Queensland, but there are concerns it could mean some children will lose vital support.

Today, ACT Disability, Autism and Neurodiversity Minister Suzanne Orr announced Thriving Kids would begin to operate in the ACT from October 1, ahead of its official start date in January 2028.

Suzanne Orr says Thriving Kids offers families an opportunity to ask questions. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

But Ms Orr stressed that those currently accessing the NDIS would not lose that support.

Thriving Kids offers a phone line for parents or guardians to ring if they have questions about their child's development, regardless of whether they have a diagnosis or not.

"If you have a question on your child's development or delay, if you want to check in with an allied health professional, we will have those supports here," Ms Orr said.

'You've got a place to go'

Federal NDIS Minister Mark Butler released the model for Thriving Kids in February as part of a major overhaul of the way disability support is accessed and received in Australia.

Announced without warning last August, it aims to divert children under nine years old with "mild to moderate" developmental delays and autism away from the NDIS.

The first stage of the model centres on identification, where delays or support needs could be identified by a family member, a school or a health professional.

The next stage connects families to the appropriate support, and the later stages focus on providing that care depending on the individual needs of the child.

Some children will fall into categories deemed to be "low", "moderate" or "low to moderate" need.

Children with "significant permanent disability" will remain eligible for the NDIS.

Those on the scheme before 2028 will stay on it, subject to the usual reassessment criteria.

The National Disability Insurance Scheme is being overhauled by the federal government.

"The first phase of the rollout will be a scaling up of our existing services, so we'll have more supports there to assist more people in our community and we'll continue to see that build," Ms Orr said today.

"And if you have a concern, if you just have a question, you've got a place to go."

Ms Orr said the program was "not about moving people off the NDIS".

"This is about meeting that unmet need within our community," she said.

" We'll continue to provide those supports and we'll continue to work through what it looks like for access to the NDIS and how Thriving Kids and the NDIS link. "

Education Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith said the funding would provide a "single point of contact".

"[It's] a clearer pathway for parents, carers and families where they do have concerns about their child's developmental delay or any aspect of their child's development," she said.

'A bit 1980s'

Autism Awareness Australia chief executive Nicole Rogerson told 666 ABC Canberra they still knew little about what the Thriving Kids program would deliver.

"A phone line? Okay, great. It feels a bit 1980s, but sure," she said.

"What are the people on the phone line going to tell the parents when they ring?"

Autism Awareness Australia CEO Nicole Rogerson says they know little detail about Thriving Kids. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Ms Orr said that with early intervention created by Thriving Kids, they would be "getting more people the support they need when they need it, which will actually work in helping to move through the system more seamlessly when you need it as opposed to having to wait".

But Ms Rogerson said with children able to access it without a diagnosis, the service would likely be overwhelmed.

"It's going to capture children with ADHD, children with speech and language delays, it's going to capture children with behavioural issues," she said.

"All I see in the future is wait times.

World.title: DV offender jailed for five years over crash that killed ex-partner
World.content:
The sister of a woman who was killed in a car crash has told the driver in court his "complete lack of regard for human life" led to her "preventable" death.

Rolong Stanley has been sentenced today in the Orange District Court to five years' jail after pleading guilty to aggravated dangerous driving near Orange that killed his ex-partner Justine Hammond on February 9, 2025.

The 32-year-old has been given a non-parole period of three years and seven months, which will expire on May 12, 2029.

Judge Penny Musgrave also took into account that Stanley drove an unregistered car with a defect notice, while he was disqualified from having a licence.

Justine Hammond had an AVO against Stanley at the time of her death. (Supplied: Facebook)

Ms Hammond's sister, Adrienne Hiko, told the court she travelled from New Zealand to "give a voice to my beautiful sister".

"What hurts the most is knowing that Justine's passing was entirely preventable," she said.

"Your choice to disregard the safety of others showed a complete lack of regard for human life.

"We have been handed the life sentence of pain," Ms Hiko told the court.

She described the 42-year-old as a "gentle and deeply compassionate soul," who was a mother, sister, aunt and daughter.

"No amount of time will ever bring Justine back," she said.

AVO breach at apple orchard

Judge Musgrave told the court Stanley should not have been with Ms Hammond at an apple orchard on the Sunday afternoon of February 9, and he should not have been drinking.

Stanley pleaded guilty to aggravated dangerous driving that caused the death of his ex-girlfriend Justine Hammond. (ABC News: Lani Oataway)

Stanley breached an apprehended domestic violence order (AVO) which prohibited him from contacting Ms Hammond or being within 500-metres of her.

He was originally charged with breaching that AVO, which was later dropped.

"He should not have been with the victim, it was a condition of his AVO that he not associate with her," Judge Musgrave said.

Stanley also breached an Intensive Correctional Order (ICO) which banned him from drinking.

Judge Penny Musgrave said Lake Canobolas Road required a driver's "care and attention" due to its condition. (ABC News: Lani Oataway)

He received that ICO as a sentence in December 2024 for other domestic violence offences against Ms Hammond.

He was convicted of being armed with an intent to commit an offence, assault which caused bodily harm and possessing ammunition without a permit.

Judge Musgrave said his willingness to breach court orders placed "upward pressure" on his sentence.

Fatal crash

Judge Musgrave told the court Stanley's dangerous driving on Lake Canobolas Road put other motorists at risk.

After drinking cask wine in his Holden Rodeo at the orchard with Ms Hammond, Stanley drove the pair down the rural road.

Judge Musgrave told the court the route was "well used" by locals frequenting Lake Canobolas and vineyards, but was in poor condition without line markings.

Stanley lost control of his ute on this corner of Lake Canobolas Road. (ABC News: Lani Oataway)

"It is a road requiring the driver's care and attention," Judge Musgrave said.

Stanley lost control when the tyres hit the nature strip, rolled the car, hit an embankment and crashed into a tree.

Ms Hammond suffered fatal injuries including to her head, abdomen, chest and neck, and died at the scene.

Stanley was flown to Westmead Hospital in Sydney for further treatment, where tests found his blood alcohol concentration was four times greater than the legal limit.

Judge Musgrave said she found it "remarkable" that he had previously believed his alcohol consumption was not problematic, given the ICO and other drink driving offences.

She said a psychologists's report determined he had an alcohol use disorder and that he was motivated to engage in treatment.

"The tragedy is that it has come to this point for him to drink and drive as he did," she said.

The Vanuatu national will be eligible for parole in May 2029.

World.title: Mortgage pain hits Tasmanians especially hard
World.content:
Alex Gill and her partner built their family home in Tasmania's south three years ago.

Like a lot of new builds, it ended up costing the family more than they'd budgeted for.

The latest interest rate rise will make things tighter for the family of four.

Tasmanian homeowner Alex Gill says the repeated interest rate rises are definitely having an impact. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

RBA hikes interest rates to 4.6pc The Reserve Bank increases interest rates to 4.6 per cent in its fourth rate rise this year.

Ms Gill said she may have to consider increasing her part-time working hours.

And while on average Tasmania's wages are on average lower than other states, Ms Gill said the family have no plans to move interstate.

"We're just going to have to make it work because we love being here, we love Tasmania," she said.

But, if interest rates continue to climb, the family may need to consider more drastic action.

"It definitely makes us think about maybe selling in the future and not staying in the home that we're in because things are getting up there," she said.

Tasmanian homeowner Ella Tenni is in the process of buying and selling at the moment, and says the interest rate rise does add some uncertainty into the mix. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Ella Tenni, who also lives in Southern Tasmania, is weighing up what the interest rate rise will mean for her family.

"We're in the process of selling and buying at the moment," Ms Tenni said.

"So I did have a bit of a pause, maybe feeling a bit worried about that, but in the scheme of things we're in a position that we'll be able to absorb it."

She said she sometimes worries about further interest rate rises.

"But then I do sometimes put my head in the sand and try not to think about it."

The average new loan size for Tasmania at the start of the year was $505,000. (ABC News: Jacinta Bos )

Lower wages, big mortgages

Consumer research company Canstar has looked at what impact the 0.25 per cent cash rate hike will have on monthly mortgage repayments.

What's impacted in the RBA rate hike While the RBA's decisions are most felt through mortgage repayments, their impact extends well beyond home loans.

For someone who took out the average new loan size for Tasmania at the start of the year of $505,000, the rate hike will translate into an increase to their minimum monthly repayments of $81.

That's based on a 30-year loan at a variable rate of 5.50 per cent.

"While plenty of households might be able to handle this kind of increase in isolation, across what has now been four cash rate hikes in 2026, that same borrower has seen their monthly repayments rise by a total of $322," Canstar's Sally Tindall said.

Sally Tindall says the repeat rate rises are having a compounding impact on households across the country. (Supplied: CANSTAR)

" That's not a one-off expense. That's how much extra they have to pay the bank every month for the foreseeable future. "

On top of that, Tasmania's wages are the lowest in the country.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, Tasmania's average weekly earnings are $1846.30 — compared with a national figure of $2083.70.

The latest figures from Cotality show the median property value in Hobart is over $750 000, while still cheaper than most states and territories, it has been on the rise since the pandemic.

Businesses bracing for belt-tightening

Andrew Turner says the topic of inflation and rate rises is on the minds of customers and staff alike. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Andrew Turner owns a café and brewery in Burnie.

He said every time interest rates rise, there's a change in sentiment among his customers.

"I don't know if we get a huge drop in revenue, but it's definitely something everyone is talking about," he said.

Andrew Turner says he's expecting customers to keep tightening their belt, due to the cost of living. (ABC Northern Tasmania: Monte Bovill)

"Even our staff are talking about now having issues affording their homes."

" I think in north-west Tasmania, because our general mortgage rates aren't as high as some of the big cities, we're still a little bit protected. "

He said he's expecting future rate rises will start to affect customer spending and his business won't be in a position to drop prices.

"All of our costs have gone through the roof as well, and now with the surcharge ban we're looking at absorbing a significant cost as a part of that."

Tips for mortgage holders and advice for government

Canstar's Sally Tindall said it was time the government considered looking at a different way to manage inflation, other than the RBA lifting interest rates.

She said in the last nine months inflation reduction had stalled but at the same time borrowers and renters are paying more.

The Reserve Bank of Australia this week lifted interest rates to the highest level in 15 years. (ABC News: Kylie Silvester)

"But yet savings rates go up for people who are mortgage-free," she said.

"Some people need that extra interest; there's no doubt about it.

" But it does seem crazy that the screws get tighter for, you know, a cohort of borrowers and renters and then the screws get a little bit looser for a different cohort. "

RBA hikes interest rates to 4.6pc The Reserve Bank increases interest rates to 4.6 per cent in its fourth rate rise this year.

Her advice to borrowers is "take a deep breath and get planning".

She said even though rates are on the way up, it's still a good time to find a better home loan deal.

"We've seen a large number of lenders actually cut variable rates — yes, cut.

" In a sea of hikes, we're seeing them cut them, but only for new customers. "

World.title: One EV sold every 100 seconds as Australia catches up to the world
World.content:
An electric car is being sold every 100 seconds in Australia, but there is still a long road ahead to decarbonise the country's transport sector, according to the Electric Vehicle Council.

The 10th anniversary edition of the annual State of Electric Vehicles Report shows how EVs have become mainstream within a decade, making up one in four new cars sold.

Sales have more than doubled within a year and last month, EVs outsold petrol and diesel cars for the first time.

"EVs are being taken up as a cost of living measure by households across Australia," Julie Delvecchio, CEO of the Electric Vehicle Council, said.

Owning an EV is no longer a luxury reserved for well-heeled inner-city dwellers as electric cars come close to price parity with petrol versions. Some are now selling for under $20,000.

Electric cars are no longer more expensive than petrol cars, with some models selling under $20,000. (Facebook: Electric Vehicle Council)

This year's sales boom is being driven by suburban commuters, with the highest EV uptake in Tarneit, about 30 kilometres west of Melbourne.

"It's very much an average Australian suburb with people who have mortgages in the six to seven hundred thousands," Aman Gaur, the EVC's Head of Legal, Policy and Advocacy, said.

"They rely on their cars, they do not have access to three forms of public transport outside their front door, and for them, the sensible economic choice is to get into an EV."

Australians now have access to nearly 200 electric models, and incentives such as the fringe benefit tax exemption have helped to drive uptake.

The beginning of the conflict with Iran in February and the subsequent disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has seen fuel prices to surge this year, helping to further push the number of EVs currently on the road to more than 600,000.

"Australia is an island at the end of a long fuel supply chain, holding weeks' worth of reserves and importing almost all of its fuel," the Electric Vehicle Council (EVC) report said.

"Every car that plugs in instead of filling up is a permanent upgrade to our energy security."

Long road to meet climate goals

While 2026 may well become a turning point for passenger EVs, reaching Australia's climate targets will require a revolution in the national fleet.

There are about 21 million cars on Australian roads, and EVs make up just 3 per cent compared to internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles.

"While the doubling of EV uptake over the last year is great news, Australia needs to maintain this momentum to be on track to reach its climate targets," Helen Rowe, the transport lead at the Monash University's Climateworks Centre, said.

The EVC report notes that Australia's EV uptake is not on track to meet the emission reduction targets of 43 per cent below 2005 levels by 2030, and 62 to 70 per cent by 2035.

"That 2035 target requires 5 million battery electric cars on the road by the middle of the next decade—a significant increase in pace from the current trajectory," the EVC's report said.

All consumers to pay for EV chargers A bitter fight is brewing between EV charging companies and poles-and-wires companies, and now a regulator has weighed in.

The other hurdle is charging infrastructure; it's increasing, but not quite keeping pace, according to the EVC's Aman Gaur.

"We do need to have a coordinated charging plan that will help Australians have confidence that they can get out onto the roads and charge either their car or their truck or their van," he said.

Addicted to diesel

Per capita, Australia uses more diesel than the US, China and Saudi Arabia.

And the biggest user of diesel is the transport and freight sector, which has barely started to electrify.

That's not because there are no electric trucks; while still more expensive, there are a growing number of options.

"China, the undisputed leader on truck electrification, saw monthly sales breach 50 per cent in December 2025 and already appears advanced in meeting its new 2030 target for 40 per cent heavy electric truck sales," The EVC report said.

Most freight operators in Australia are small businesses, running on very tight margins, and according to the EVC's Aman Gaur, the cost of switching to electric trucks was still prohibitive.

"There aren't enough financial incentives to get small mum and dad operators to make the switch to electric, which means that Australia is still importing diesel and our economy is still reliant on those imports," he said.

The EVC report called Australia a "global laggard" when it came to adopting electric trucks, with heavy vehicle rules such as road weight limits "complex and notoriously difficult to reform."

"With almost zero policy support and no dedicated charging infrastructure to speak of, electric trucks are yet to hit even 1 per cent of total truck sales.

"This contrasts with European markets and New Zealand, where strong freight electrification policies are moving heavy EVs beyond the 'early adopter' cohort to everyday trucking fleets.

"Electrifying Australia's heavy freight vehicles is the biggest unseized opportunity in Australia's energy transition."

World.title: 52kg of cocaine stolen from Fiji evidence room, half replaced with flour
World.content:
Fiji Police have confirmed another 12.9 kilograms of cocaine is missing from an evidence room at the country's high court, bringing the total now stolen across Fiji courtrooms to more than 52kg.

Yesterday, Fiji Police revealed 32kg of cocaine stored at the Suva High Court for the long-running trial of Fiji-Canadian national Joshua Aziz Rahman had been replaced with flour and is now effectively missing.

Two weeks ago it was announced 7kg of cocaine had been stolen from the Suva High Court.

Following a public outcry, Fiji Police held a press conference in Suva on Wednesday to update on their investigation.

Cocaine replaced with flour in Fiji drug trial More than $10 million worth of cocaine stored at a Fiji court as evidence in a long-running drug-trafficking trial has been replaced with flour.

Senior Superintendent of Fiji Police Peni Tuivaga confirmed parts of the CCTV at the courthouse's evidence room were not working and the biometric security was faulty during the period when the drugs were stolen, and the 32kg was replaced with flour.

Following further questioning from local media on how widespread the issue has become, Superintendent Tuivaga confirmed 12.9kg seized during a 2018 raid on Australian horse trainer John Nikolic's yacht had also disappeared.

"All the cocaine is stolen," he said.

Nikolic was found guilty in 2019 of two charges of importing illicit drugs and was sentenced to at least 18 years jail.

The drugs were not destroyed as an appeals process was ongoing, as per orders from the country's court.

"In regards to this [Nikolic's] case, the application for destruction [in March] led us to the missing drugs," Fiji Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu said.

" I'm very concerned about it, we all want these drugs to be destroyed after. "

Fiji's Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu says they were conducting the investigation with "utmost urgency". (ABC News)

Depending on the purity of the 52kg of missing cocaine, its street value could be worth more than $20 million.

Commissioner Tudravu said the judiciary, and police, were now conducting a full audit of other exhibits in its possession.

"There is an audit team going around all police stations, focusing [on] drugs and cash," he said.

Flour swapped for cocaine

Commissioner Tudravu said there were six people of interest who had access to the evidence room that Fiji Police were focusing on, with one person currently overseas.

However he confirmed that the cocaine in the court evidence room was the responsibility of the judiciary.

"Once it is deposited in the Suva High Court exhibit room, we are not there to guard it," he said.

"They [the court] have their own arrangements.

" It's like your home, you're the boss of your home, I cannot come in and tell you I'll guard your home. "

In a statement released on Wednesday, Fiji's Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions said its policies around drug destruction had changed since the establishment of the country's anti-narcotics division in 2024.

It said it was now "prioritising applications" for destruction of drug exhibits.

Fiji is ground zero in the Pacific's drugs crisis Watch part one of Foreign Correspondent's special investigation.

Fiji has become ground zero in the Pacific's struggle with transnational drug trafficking.

In January, police alleged they seized 2.6 tonnes of cocaine, worth about $780 million, in a raid on a suspected drug operation in the remote north-west of the country's largest island.

That cocaine is due for a destruction order this month.

An ABC investigation earlier this year uncovered widespread Australian connections in the transportation of drugs through the country.

Earlier this month, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced $600 million for a new Pacific-wide initiative to combat the surge of illicit drug smuggling in the region.

World.title: Breaking: Planning decision to extend life of mega coal mine saves 1,500 jobs
World.content:
An estimated 1,500 jobs have been saved after the NSW Independent Planning Commission (IPC) handed down its ruling on the future of a major coal mine near Singleton in the New South Wales Hunter Valley.

The IPC today approved plans that will allow Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) to continue mining at the site until 2045, extracting an estimated 429 million tonnes of coal across its North and South sites.

In April 2025, the mine was given a last-minute extension, which allowed it to continue operating until December this year.

HVO told IPC hearings in July that the mine employed more than 1,500 people, engaged more than 800 suppliers and injected more than $1 billion a year into the economy.

But environmentalists argued the extension would put the NSW government's ability to reach its net-zero targets in jeopardy.

The proposal had backing from Premier Chris Minns and Natural Resources Minister Courtney Houssos, as well as the NSW Coalition.

"Those 1,500 jobs are such a key part of the state's economy, but particularly here in the Hunter Valley," Ms Houssos told ABC Upper Hunter ahead of today's decision.

"We've got legislated net-zero emissions targets and we will adhere to those, but we also understand the important role that coal mining has particularly for the Hunter Valley, but for our entire state's economy," she said.

More than 10,000 public submissions were made to the IPC during its deliberations, with about 60 per cent supporting the project.

The Independent Planning Commission has released its decision on the future of Hunter Valley Operations. (ABC 730)

The IPC released a statement acknowledging the emission of 809 megatonnes (Mt) of greenhouse gases from the mining operations and coal combustion overseas would contribute to climate change impacts across the Hunter, NSW and globally.

But it said those impacts were balanced against the "significant employment, business, social and economic benefits of the mine extension".

The approval comes with conditions, including implementing measures to limit coal exports to jurisdictions that have policies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions consistent with the Paris Agreement, maximising the use of renewable energy at the mine, and purchasing additional carbon offsets.

Georgina Woods from the Lock the Gate Alliance. (ABC Upper Hunter: Courtney Yeandle)

Lock The Gate Alliance national coordinator Georgina Woods said the IPC decision was a "crossroads moment for the Hunter and NSW".

"We are right on this knife edge of dangerous levels of global warming, but obviously also too little has been done to prepare the Hunter region for the closure of mines," she said.

"Every single year, greenhouse gas pollution resulting from this mine will wipe out all the efforts that everyone in Australia and NSW is making to reduce our own pollution.

"That's how stark it is."

Ms Woods said the decision would "unwind all of our good work".

"It's [now] pretty much impossible to avoid that dangerous level of 1.5 degrees of warming, and that will have profound consequences," she said.

"Lost income, lost jobs, lost food production, lost culture, lost lives and livelihoods."

World.title: Minister says Perth barracks sale will not mean bulldozers for heritage sites
World.content:
The planned sale of Perth's Irwin and Leeuwin barracks will free up land in highly desirable suburbs but developers will not have free rein to bulldoze the sites for housing, defence minister Richard Marles has said.

Speaking to Nadia Mitsopoulos on 102.5 ABC Perth, Mr Marles also said the sales were still some way off and would not proceed until the cadets and army reservists who currently use the sites had transitioned to an alternative site.

"This whole exercise is making sure that our Defence estate is more fit for purpose for what Defence does," he said.

"In respect of [Leeuwin and Irwin barracks], what we are thinking mostly about is both reserves and cadets here in Perth and making sure that the outcome here … is better sites.

"That it is ultimately a better outcome for our reservists and for our cadets.

"A lot of the activity that is undertaken by cadets and reserves now, and this would include in respect of these two sites, is happening on old sites which are really not that fit for purpose for what they're doing."

Mr Marles also said the Defence department was working closely with the WA RSL branch to consult on the move of some activity to Palmer Barracks in South Guildford.

Both Irwin and Leeuwin barracks occupy substantial amounts of land in highly desirable residential areas. Irwin Barracks covers 61.5 hectares in the heart of Perth's affluent western suburbs, while Leeuwin occupies 14 hectares on the Swan riverfront at East Fremantle.

Both sites require some remediation and preparation before they will be transferred to the Department of Finance, which will handle the sale.

While he could not say whether any expressions of interest had been received or how much the sites may be worth, Mr Marles said both sites were protected by heritage overlays, which would limit how far they could be developed.

"They are protected by law and they will be protected by law," he said.

"None of these sites are going to be bulldozed.

"In fact, I think what will happen with a lot of these heritage sites is that they will be opened up to the public much more and people will be able to enjoy them."

World.title: Body found in rivulet in Hobart's north by passer-by
World.content:
Tasmanian Police are investigating after a body was found in a rivulet in Hobart's north.

In a statement, police said a person walking in the area contacted police around 10.30 this morning, to report a deceased person in the water at Humphreys Rivulet, near Grove Road, Glenorchy.

Police said "detectives and specialist resources" were at the scene on Wednesday afternoon, and asked that people avoid the area.

An investigation is underway to determine the circumstances of the death.

Anyone with information about this matter is asked to contact Glenorchy Police on 131 444 and quote ESCAD 125-30092026.

Information can also be supplied anonymously to Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or online at crimestopperstas.com.au.

World.title: Why you shouldn’t rush to value your property ahead of 2027 tax change
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingAsk an expert Opinion Why you shouldn’t rush to value your property ahead of 2027 tax change Noel Whittaker Money columnist Updated September 30, 2026 — 2:09pm , first published September 30, 2026 — 5:00am

Updated September 30, 2026 — 2:09pm ,first published September 30, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Under the new capital gains tax rules, some properties may need a market value established at June 30, 2027 so that gains accruing before and after July 1, 2027 can be calculated. Given the huge number of properties potentially involved and the relatively small number of valuers, should property owners arrange a valuation before June 30, or will the tax office accept a retrospective valuation done later? We are confused because we have heard two different views. Furthermore, do we need a registered valuer? An Australian Taxation Office spokesman tells me there is no need to rush out and have your property valued before June 30, 2027. In fact, if you intend to rely on a market valuation, you should not obtain one now. A prospective valuation – one prepared before the specified valuation date – will not be acceptable. A retrospective valuation prepared later can be used and, in many cases, may be preferable because the valuer will then have access to a broader range of records and comparable sales around the relevant date, allowing a more informed assessment. The new rules apply to capital gains accruing from July 1, 2027, but tax is generally not payable until the gain is eventually realised. Suzanne White There is another important point. The new rules apply to capital gains accruing from July 1, 2027, but tax is generally not payable until the gain is eventually realised, such as when the property is sold. If you choose to use a valuation-based method to work out your tax consequences, you will only need the valuation, at June 30, when preparing your tax return in the year of disposal and self-assessing your taxable gain. You may, of course, choose to obtain the valuation earlier. Importantly, not every affected property will necessarily need a formal valuation. Taxpayers may have a choice between establishing the property’s market value immediately before 1 July 2027 and using an alternative apportionment method the Government is developing. The Tax Office says it will provide further guidance, tools and calculators once the legislation and method are settled.



As for whether you need a registered or professional valuer, the tax office says that, for tax purposes, the acceptability of a valuation usually depends on the valuation process and the asset being valued rather than simply on who conducted the valuation. There are exceptions – for example, a professional valuer is required for a market valuation for GST margin scheme purposes. The tax office also points out that valuations undertaken by professional valuers are generally more credible than those prepared by somebody who is not a professional valuer. But engaging a professional does not shift the responsibility. The onus remains on the taxpayer to provide a valuation that is replicable and defensible. The tax office says its forthcoming guidance will give more detail on how market values may be determined for different types of CGT assets, the types of professionals taxpayers may wish to engage, and the documents and records that should be kept. The message is simple: don’t panic and don’t pay for a valuation now. Wolter Peeters Meanwhile, the message is simple: don’t panic and don’t pay for a valuation now. If a market valuation is eventually required, it can be prepared retrospectively for June 30. And before spending money on a professional valuation, wait for the tax office’s detailed guidance on exactly what will be required. Under the proposed capital gains tax changes, I understand that if I buy shares now, they will effectively be treated as having been sold on June 30 and repurchased on July 1. Suppose they have risen in value by June 30, but I have owned them for less than 12 months. Does that mean the gain before July 1 will not qualify for the 50 per cent CGT discount and will ultimately be taxed at my marginal rate when the shares are sold? Given the 12-month rule, could there be a case for delaying some share purchases until after June 30?



Technically, there is “deemed disposal” on June 30 and re-acquisition on July 1, however, any capital gain/loss is disregarded and deferred until when the shares are eventually sold. Related Article Opinion

Ask an expert Ditch the credit card? Why it’s time to switch to debit Noel Whittaker Money columnist The value at that date will be used to calculate the pre-July 1 component of the capital gain when you eventually dispose of the shares. Provided you have owned the shares for at least 12 months by the time you actually dispose of them, the pre-July 1 component will still qualify for the 50 per cent CGT discount. Therefore, the fact that you may have owned the shares for less than 12 months at June 30 does not, by itself, cause you to lose the discount. I am 70, retired and drawing a flexi pension from my UniSuper balance, currently around $975,000. My wife is 63, also retired, and has about $1.35 million in UniSuper. We have decided to preserve her super for as long as possible and live on mine until it is eventually exhausted. We own our home and have no other significant assets.



Given our ages and super balances, could either of us qualify for the age pension or a part pension? How would Centrelink treat my wife’s super while she is still under the pension age, and what happens once she reaches that age? Related Article Opinion

Ask an expert I’ve inherited $400,000 in shares. What should I do with them? Paul Benson Money contributor Your wife’s super will not count for the asset test until she reaches pensionable age, which is 67, unless she starts to draw a pension from it. Depending on your other assets, you may be eligible for a part pension, provided your total assessable assets do not exceed $1,121,000. If your total assessable assets are a little over the cut-off point, you could seek advice about investing in one of those lifetime income-stream products, where generally only 60 per cent of the purchase price is initially counted for the assets test. This could give you a tiny pension, plus an income stream. But they’re highly specialised, so make sure you understand the product if you decide to choose one. You may also be eligible for the Commonwealth seniors health card, subject to the income test. I’m considering giving both my adult children some money to contribute to super. One is a low-income hospitality worker and the other is a stay-at-home mum. They are in their 30s, and I’m thinking of perhaps $10,000 to $20,000 each. I realise they may have more immediate uses for the money, but I’m also conscious of the power of compounding if the money goes into super at their age. Is contributing to their super a worthwhile strategy, and what contribution and tax issues should we consider?



I understand what you mean about compounding. Putting $10,000 or $20,000 into super in their 30s gives the money decades to grow, but the downside is that it will generally be inaccessible until they reach preservation age, which for both of them will be 60, and satisfy a condition of release. However, if they are likely to buy their first home in the future, consider the First Home Super Saver (FHSS) scheme. You could give them the money and they could then make eligible personal voluntary contributions to their own super. This distinction is important because contributions made directly into their super by a parent are not eligible for the FHSS scheme. They can have up to $15,000 of eligible voluntary contributions in any one financial year count towards the scheme, up to $50,000 across all years, plus associated earnings. Putting $10,000 or $20,000 into a super account when the account-holder is in their 30s gives the money decades to grow. Getty Importantly, if they never buy a home, the money is not lost. It simply remains in super under the normal rules and can generally be accessed from age 60 once they retire or otherwise satisfy a condition of release. So the real question is whether they are better off having the money available now or locking it away for either a first home or retirement. Noel Whittaker is the author of Retirement Made Simple and other books on personal finance. Email: noel@noelwhittaker.com.au.



Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: ‘Bludgeoned with platitudes’: Australian politicians lead the English-speaking world in AI speeches
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAI ‘Bludgeoned with platitudes’: Australian politicians lead the English-speaking world in AI speeches Brittany Busch Updated September 30, 2026 — 2:08pm ,first published 11:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Just three years ago, Liberal MP Aaron Violi was the first Australian politician to publicly declare he had used AI to write a speech. Today, Australian politicians lead the English-speaking world for AI use in speeches, according to analysis in The Economist. The findings have sparked a debate around how MPs should be using the technology, as OpenAI apologises for rogue agents that broke into a Medicare portal, the Albanese government races to attract billions of dollars in data centre investment, and tech leaders warn AI could pose an existential threat to humanity. A random sample of speeches made between September 2025-26 found more than 20 per cent of those made in Australia’s House of Representatives were flagged by AI content detector Pangram for AI-generated or AI-assisted text. Just under 15 per cent of Senate speeches were flagged.



Australian MPs were the most prolific users compared to other English-speaking legislatures, just ahead of Canada but triple the rate of the British. In July, a Canadian politician went viral after accidentally reciting AI editing prompts. Bill Oliver was making a speech in the chamber when he said: “Here’s a more natural flowing version of that section that reads like a legislator speech rather than a series of short points.” Loading In 2023, Violi declared that he had used AI to write a speech to highlight the technology’s power. “Since that time, the tools have become more powerful, but the government has still been slow to act,” the opposition spokesman for the digital economy and cybersecurity said.



He said AI was a useful tool, but MPs had to be careful in how they used it to construct a speech. “If an MP is putting a prompt into AI and then using the speech verbatim without checking the source documents, well, I think at some point they’re going to get themselves in trouble.” Shadow minister for cybersecurity Aaron Violi used AI in a speech in 2023 as a call to action. Renee Nowytarger Violi said he encouraged his staff to use AI, but had rules for fact-checking, protecting confidentiality by only entering information that could be made publicly available, and not using AI content word-for-word. He said one of the problems with AI-generated content was that it was predictive, based on other content.



“It’ll give you the average of what everyone does – it’s not going to give you that point of difference to really stand out,” he said. “Personally, most of my speeches, particularly those that are most impactful in parliament, are off the cuff with dot points.” Related Article Updated

OpenAI Australian senators invite OpenAI boss as hack expands beyond Medicare James Button, who was a speechwriter for former prime minister Kevin Rudd and previously a journalist at this masthead, said there was a place for using AI for research, but something was lost when using it to write. “The thing about a speech is that it’s a very human event, right? It’s a person standing up in a room, speaking to others, and seeking a connection with those people,” he said. “You add AI into that, and we are absolutely not getting the thoughts of the human being, the politician … so it’s troubling.” Button said AI was capable of imitating an MP’s preferences and speaking style, but the question remained whether it should.



Another speechwriter for a former prime minister, who requested anonymity to speak freely, said AI was an efficient tool to generate the bulk of a speech that could then be finessed – a process which could otherwise take days. The tradeoff was potentially failing to develop the skill of forming and delivering an argument. “The orators will get better, and those who use the tools appropriately will get sharper and better,” they said. “But there will be others who, maybe they’re using AI and all they did previously was just use the leader’s office talking points. They’ve just substituted one form of artificial intelligence for another.” Senator David Pocock said the prime minister’s slashing of staff for the crossbench and opposition put pressure on offices to become more efficient. Dominic Lorrimer Independent senator David Pocock, who has published his own guidelines for using AI, encouraged MPs to disclose when they used the technology and justify its use to constituents. He said increasing AI use meant a more homogenous output, and politicians “bludgeoning people with platitudes”.



“As an elected representative, you’re elected to represent, not to read out AI speech. It comes down to trust. I think Australians would expect you to be using it to become more efficient. But you can’t lose that human touch.” Related Article Political leadership Shorten’s $310,000-a-year writer behind at least 170 speeches – but no zingers Speaker Milton Dick said there were no rules for how members used AI in House speeches, but that MPs were responsible for what they said. “In speaking, members are aware of their overriding duty to the national interest, and primary duty to represent the interests of their constituents,” he said. Political speechwriters typically write major speeches for MPs on a senior staffer salary that starts at $140,000 before adding loadings for allowances and seniority. However, sometimes politicians will write their own or speak off the cuff, and their speechwriters do not always shape the speeches delivered in parliament that were measured by The Economist. World.title: PLC Resources hits geological sweet spot in emerging WA gold district
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears PLC Resources hits geological sweet spot in emerging WA gold district Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd September 30, 2026 — 1:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

PLC Resources has wrapped up its latest round of drilling at its Rochefort gold prospect in Western Australia’s Murchison region, intersecting the exact geological sweet spot it has been hunting for to prove up a potential virgin gold discovery. The company has completed an eight-hole, 1896-metre reverse circulation (RC) campaign designed to step out from its maiden program earlier this year, with early geological logging confirming the drill bit passed through sheared zones of sulphides within the targeted fractionated dolerite gold target. A drill rig on site at PLC Resources’ Rochefort gold prospect in Western Australia’s Murchison region. The company says early results are a textbook match for its exploration model, which is based on a “sulphidation” process known to be a key ingredient in major Yilgarn gold deposits, including those hosted by the famed Golden Mile Dolerite - host of the famed Kalgoorlie Super Pit. All samples are now at the laboratory, with a four to six-week wait for gold assays.



‘Our follow-up drilling at Rochefort, and the logging shows the geology we set out to find.’ PLC Resources executive director Simon Phillips The latest program was designed to test for extensions of a fractionated dolerite unit that delivered low-level yet consistent gold in the project’s maiden five-hole campaign in May. That initial program picked up geochemical clues suggesting the drilling may have clipped the edge of a larger mineralised system, a theory which is soon to be truth-tested by the lab. PLC’s working theory is that mineralising fluids interacted with the iron-rich dolerite, altering primary sulphides such as pyrrhotite into pyrite and potentially dropping gold out of the solution in the process. The latest visual confirmation of sheared zones, sulphides and magnetite-bearing intervals appears to give the company’s exploration model a significant shot in the arm. PLC Resources executive director Simon Phillips said: “We’ve now completed our follow-up drilling at Rochefort, and the logging shows the geology we set out to find: sheared, sulphide-bearing zones within the fractionated dolerite. That’s encouraging, but the assay results are required to determine whether the system is mineralised with gold. We expect those results within the next four to six weeks.” While the market awaits the lab results from Rochefort, a potentially bigger story is unfolding on the company’s nearby ground.



Independent of the Rochefort target, PLC’s recent airborne magnetic survey may have changed the game for the company at a regional level. The high-resolution data revealed a large-scale fold structure along the eastern margin of the Abbotts Greenstone Belt. Management says the structure is a crustal-level feature that extends for more than 14km of strike and, importantly, continues south into ground held by the $750 million market-capped New Murchison Gold. New Murchison has been moving and shaking in WA’s burgeoning gold sector of late, successfully trucking high-grade discoveries from the region to a toll-treatment facility and generating more than $50 million in cash flow in the last quarter alone. PLC is now moving to ground-truth these newly identified structural corridors and cash in, with geological reconnaissance planned for next month ahead of a maiden regional aircore drilling campaign on its untested targets. With Rochefort assays now pending and a second discovery front taking shape, PLC is building some serious momentum across its Murchison ground. A clear path to drill a major structure apparently shared with a highly profitable neighbour gives the company two shots at uncovering a new gold system. World.title: Shoebridge says Greens must ‘replace’ Labor in first speech as leader
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Shoebridge says Greens must ‘replace’ Labor in first speech as leader Nick Newling Updated September 30, 2026 — 1:47pm ,first published September 30, 2026 — 8:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Newly elected Greens leader David Shoebridge has vowed to take the fight to both Labor and One Nation and cast the left-wing party as the best alternative for a growing base of disaffected voters. The former barrister and staunch AUKUS opponent was elected on a joint ticket with new Victorian senator Steph Hodgins-May as his deputy on Wednesday, following the shock resignation of former leader Larissa Waters due to worsening chronic kidney disease. New federal Greens leader David Shoebridge, left, with deputy Steph Hodgins-May. Sam Mooy “This is an extraordinary moment in politics and we can all feel it. Politics, as usual, is not providing the answers that people are desperately calling for,” Shoebridge told a Sydney press conference after his election. “Things have got harder, much, much harder, for ordinary Australians. What has become so clear after four years of this government, and years before, is that we are not here to make the Labor Party any better. The Greens are here to replace them.”



Shoebridge was elected in a rare contested vote for a party that typically seeks consensus before leadership elections, receiving seven votes to NSW senator Mehreen Faruqi’s four on a two-candidate preferred count. Hodgins-May was elected deputy with six votes to Tasmanian senator Vanessa Bleyer’s five. Bleyer has sat in the Senate for just over two months. In a statement posted to social media, Faruqi, the former deputy leader, said she was disappointed to have not been elected and called for party members to have the right to vote in leadership elections moving forward. Faruqi ran on a joint ticket with Tasmanian senator Nick McKim as deputy candidate.

Loading Fallen Queensland MP Max Chandler-Mather made a similar request in a letter sent to Greens parliamentarians on Tuesday. Shoebridge said both he and Hodgins-May were committed to the “democratisation” of the party, and that conversations on the matter were ongoing.



Veteran South Australian senator Sarah Hanson-Young was the third contender for leadership, running on a solo ticket. The senator was knocked out in the first round after receiving only two votes from the 11-person caucus. Addressing the media after his election, Shoebridge said One Nation was gaining traction in the polls because Labor had facilitated its growth, and that the Greens were the only party capable of combating Pauline Hanson. Shoebridge highlighted that One Nation was polling around 7 per cent early last year, before significant increases in its popularity over the past year to a high of 29 per cent in this masthead’s Resolve Political Monitor. New leader of the Greens David Shoebridge at a press conference in Sydney. Sam Mooy “What we need to do is bridge that gap … with hope. With a sense of political momentum and positivity,” Shoebridge said.



The Greens have maintained a steady support of between 11 and 12 per cent over the past year in polls published by this masthead. Speaking immediately after Shoebridge’s election, Treasurer Jim Chalmers urged the new Greens leader to “focus on the risks posed to workers and to our economy by One Nation, the Liberal Party and the National Party”. The vote took place during a pre-planned “retreat” in Sydney this week, in which matters of policy and strategy were also set to be discussed. Shoebridge has been in politics for 22 years, serving on the inner-Sydney Woollahra Council from 2004 to 2012, and in the NSW state parliament from 2010, until he transitioned to the Senate in 2022. Before entering state parliament Shoebridge was a barrister at Denman Chambers in Sydney. The 55-year-old is currently the party’s spokesman on foreign affairs, defence and immigration, and has established himself as a fierce combatant in Senate estimates hearings.

Five people have been arrested after Geraldton man Ashley Wayne Cameron was shot in the leg in the early hours of Wednesday. Cameron was taken to Geraldton Regional Hospital about 1am on Wednesday, after he was allegedly shot in the leg by a person known to him. His injuries were not life-threatening. Ashley Cameron. Facebook A WA Police spokesperson said officers responded to a report of a firearm incident on Allen Road in Moonyoonooka, which is about 12 kilometres outside the Geraldton town centre. They arrived to find 32-year-old Cameron with a wound to his leg. The incident sparked a public safety warning in the early hours of Wednesday as a precaution.



“While this incident involves a firearm, there is no information to suggest an ongoing threat to the wider community”, a WA Police spokesperson said. “Members of the public are not being asked to be alarmed, however they should remain vigilant and report any suspicious activity to police.” Ashley Cameron is in hospital recovering. Facebook Cameron is a Geraldton man and often travels between the state’s Pilbara, Goldfields and Mid West regions. He is a father and an artist.



The police spokesperson said five people were arrested on Hart Street in Utakarra about 10.30am on Wednesday, and were helping police with their inquiries. On Wednesday, WA Attorney-General Tony Buti, who did not speak about Cameron’s identity, said it seemed he had been shot by “pellets” to his leg, rather than a bullet. “All I know is that there was one person that was injured. Pellets, I think were shot,” he said. “I think there are three offenders, and the police will provide a [later] update, I’m sure.” Significant police resources have been deployed to the area, including the tactical response group.



Police advised extra resources had also been sent to nearby Utakarra. However, all roads remain open as normal, and the area is not considered to be in lockdown. Related Article Missing person Shot partner of Mullewa fugitive makes plea for her ‘sexy bush critter’ to come home “Members of the public are asked to stay away from the area while police continue to respond to the incident,” a WA Police spokesperson said. It is the second shooting incident in the Mid West this year. In January, Kenneth Giles allegedly shot his partner in the hand in Mullewa and sparked an active shooting incident.



As of September, the 58-year-old remains on the run despite intense searches by WA police. His car was found in February, but there has been no sign of him despite a desperate plea from his partner.

World.title: There’s a reason why The Turn of the Screw is both feared and revered
World.content:
Key points OPERA: Victorian Opera take on Benjamin Britten’s The Turn of The Screw

THEATRE: Koreaboo at Malthouse draws from lived experience

OPERA

The Turn of the Screw ★★★

Palais Theatre, until October 1 Operatic takes on the supernatural span the centuries, but no modern work is more revered and feared than Benjamin Britten’s The Turn of the Screw. The 1954 opera follows a governess who takes up residence at an English country house, only to find the spirits of two dead servants are haunting the children now in her care. Rachelle Durkin, Genevieve Gray and Oliver Thadoe Naing in a scene from The Turn of the Screw. Jeff Busby Finally, an opera where the muffled screams drifting in from Luna Park next door actually add to the drama, rather than detract! This is a piece that has potential to be The Shining-level unnerving. When staged up close and creepy, the eerie singing and sinister spectacle can captivate like a demonic spirit itself. Here, the huge set and vast stage dwarf the drama – in pivotal moments, the singers are far away from each other; we are far away from them. Detachment creates a disconnect that does not serve some excellent performances.



It is, after all, a chamber opera. Britten scored it for just 13 instruments. Perhaps no Australian conductor knows more about the English composer than Paul Kildea, and the reduced Orchestra Victoria was guided superbly by him. Rachelle Durkin (Governess) was more maternal than hysterical, with a self-assured, impressive vocal performance to match. His voice sharp and cold, Kanen Breen uses his lithe physicality to intensify Peter Quint’s menace, despite donning the most unflattering wig anyone’s ever been cursed to wear (it’s a confusing choice, when it’s clearly mentioned how handsome Quint is). Rachelle Durkin, Michaela Cadwgan and Kanen Breen. Photo Jeff Busby One exceptional discovery to come from this production is soprano Genevieve Gray (currently a university student), who sings the older child, Flora. Gray possesses a vocal evenness and an array of colour that belies her youth. Neither a spook nor a snore, though with moments of satisfaction, this production feels like a missed opportunity to bewitch more people with the mystery and magic of operatic storytelling.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies



THEATRE

Koreaboo ★★★

Malthouse, until October 10 Inspired by playwright Michelle Lim Davidson’s own experiences and directed by Jessica Arthur, Koreaboo is a two-hander that surveys contentious issues of race, diaspora and belonging, with a light touch. Heather Jeong and Michelle Lim Davidson in a scene from Koreaboo Gianna Rizzo Davidson herself plays Hannah, a young Australian who travels to Seoul in an attempt to reconnect with her estranged birth mother, Umma (Heather Jeong). It’s only their second meeting. We learn that although she was born in Korea, Hannah was adopted as a baby and grew up in Newcastle, NSW. At the start, the two women fail and flail in communication. Hannah was expecting a summer-long stay – a long enough period, perhaps, for meaningful reconnection; Umma (mother in Korean), however, believed it was just going to be a short vacation. Her behaviour toward her daughter thrums with wariness, as though one were greeting a stranger. Maybe, she suggests, Hannah should be visiting Seoul’s touristy spots instead.



The entire performance is staged in a small convenience store run by Umma, lovingly decked out in all manner of brightly coloured snacks, and with harsh fluorescent lighting thanks to designer Mel Page. The two women move within the space as they interrogate, parry, and deflect. Davidson explores a raft of issues, including the question of identity. Hannah’s hyphenated background (Korean-Australian) means she’s part of both cultures and wholly of neither, and at first, Umma’s brusque criticism of Hannah’s language skills feels like a wholesale rejection of her daughter’s “Koreanness”. Seeking both maternal and cultural acceptance, Hannah feels crushed to receive neither. Koreaboo Gianna Rizzo Their common language – and one that helps them move toward connection and bridge distance, it turns out – is K-pop. The title actually refers to someone who’s not of Korean heritage but who is obsessed with Korean pop culture. Koreaboo swerves to the unexpected and surreal when both performers begin to sing and dance. There is a talent show in the offing to prepare for, and a chance for Hannah to become more Korean. It’s all surface-level cultural appropriation, though, much in the same way that Umma learned English by watching TV, becoming so familiar with the lives of the characters in Sex and the City that she can quote from them.



After a shaky start, Jeong and Davidson become good sparring partners and friends as they navigate the tricky mother-and-daughter relationship anew after years apart. Umma’s backstory is revealed: the reasons behind Hannah’s adoption and how her yearnings for a singing career were quashed because of filial obedience to her own mother. Korean culture is not just skincare and pop music, but, like a lot of Asian countries, there’s an expectation to conform to parental demands. Related Article Performing arts Star of ABC hit The Newsreader mines real-life family drama for new project Koreaboo packs in a lot during its hour-and-a-half stage time – maybe too much, as there is a lot of jumping about trying to cover a lot of ground. The beginning set-up takes a while to develop and can be tightened, and the ending feels rushed. And although the singing and dance sequences are overextended and as distracting as they are humorous, the play’s value is drawn from highlighting the possible consequences of adopting a child, removing them from their motherland, and raising them in an entirely foreign environment. Even if they embrace the riches of a new life in their host country, there are always losses to be reckoned with.

Reviewed by Thuy On The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.content:

The Age is seeking aspiring and early-career journalists for 12-month traineeships in its Melbourne newsroom. It is a rare opportunity for the next generation of journalists to hone their craft alongside award-winning reporters and editors, with a strong focus on developing breaking news and digital skills. Age reporters Angus Delaney and Hannah Kennelly. Reaching 5.28 million readers each month, The Age is Victoria’s most widely read masthead and a leader in digital innovation, delivering trusted journalism across politics, sport, business, and culture. Traineeship applications are open here and close on Sunday, October 18. The program will begin in February, with the potential to secure a permanent role when it concludes.



Age editor Patrick Elligett said The Age takes its responsibility to nurture the next generation of journalistic talent seriously. “It’s important for our masthead, our industry and our society that we continue to produce reporters with the standards of rigour and quality The Age strives to uphold,” he said. Angus Delaney, who was appointed state political reporter in July, was one of five trainees at The Age in 2024. He said the traineeship helped him develop the skills he needed to pursue his interest in political journalism. The 2024 Age trainees (from left): Brittany Busch, Hannah Hammoud, Hannah Kennelly, Angus Delaney and Gemma Grant. Simon Schluter “It was an opportunity to learn from the best journalists and editors in Australia, and build my experience on how to break news stories across a wide range of departments in the newsroom,” Delaney said. “The Age is very supportive of hungry, young journalists wanting to build their core skills to make it in this industry.” A highlight for him was being assigned to Parliament House in Canberra during last year’s federal election campaign. “The Age has really allowed me to pursue my passions, and now I get to report on the biggest issues affecting our state.”



Related Article Media & marketing Meet the future of The Age as we welcome five talented new trainees Hannah Kennelly was a trainee in the same 2024 intake and now works as a sports reporter with The Age. She was sent to cover the Commonwealth Games in Scotland this year. “The traineeship was incredibly comprehensive and allowed me to experience different sections of journalism, under the fantastic mentorship of senior reporters in the newsroom,” Kennelly said. “My career highlight so far would be travelling to Belgium to attend the Spa Grand Prix to interview Oscar Piastri.” The newsroom is looking for sharp, curious individuals with exceptional writing skills, strong news judgment and a genuine passion for Age journalism. Candidates with skills in breaking news, data journalism, multimedia production and visual storytelling are encouraged to apply. Cover letters and story pitches must be original and written by the applicants. To be considered, you must already have the right to work and live in Australia lawfully. World.title: Why you shouldn’t rush to value your property ahead of 2027 tax change
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingAsk an expert Opinion Why you shouldn’t rush to value your property ahead of 2027 tax change Noel Whittaker Money columnist Updated September 30, 2026 — 2:09pm , first published September 30, 2026 — 5:00am

Updated September 30, 2026 — 2:09pm ,first published September 30, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Under the new capital gains tax rules, some properties may need a market value established at June 30, 2027 so that gains accruing before and after July 1, 2027 can be calculated. Given the huge number of properties potentially involved and the relatively small number of valuers, should property owners arrange a valuation before June 30, or will the tax office accept a retrospective valuation done later? We are confused because we have heard two different views. Furthermore, do we need a registered valuer? An Australian Taxation Office spokesman tells me there is no need to rush out and have your property valued before June 30, 2027. In fact, if you intend to rely on a market valuation, you should not obtain one now. A prospective valuation – one prepared before the specified valuation date – will not be acceptable. A retrospective valuation prepared later can be used and, in many cases, may be preferable because the valuer will then have access to a broader range of records and comparable sales around the relevant date, allowing a more informed assessment. The new rules apply to capital gains accruing from July 1, 2027, but tax is generally not payable until the gain is eventually realised. Suzanne White There is another important point. The new rules apply to capital gains accruing from July 1, 2027, but tax is generally not payable until the gain is eventually realised, such as when the property is sold. If you choose to use a valuation-based method to work out your tax consequences, you will only need the valuation, at June 30, when preparing your tax return in the year of disposal and self-assessing your taxable gain. You may, of course, choose to obtain the valuation earlier. Importantly, not every affected property will necessarily need a formal valuation. Taxpayers may have a choice between establishing the property’s market value immediately before 1 July 2027 and using an alternative apportionment method the Government is developing. The Tax Office says it will provide further guidance, tools and calculators once the legislation and method are settled.



As for whether you need a registered or professional valuer, the tax office says that, for tax purposes, the acceptability of a valuation usually depends on the valuation process and the asset being valued rather than simply on who conducted the valuation. There are exceptions – for example, a professional valuer is required for a market valuation for GST margin scheme purposes. The tax office also points out that valuations undertaken by professional valuers are generally more credible than those prepared by somebody who is not a professional valuer. But engaging a professional does not shift the responsibility. The onus remains on the taxpayer to provide a valuation that is replicable and defensible. The tax office says its forthcoming guidance will give more detail on how market values may be determined for different types of CGT assets, the types of professionals taxpayers may wish to engage, and the documents and records that should be kept. The message is simple: don’t panic and don’t pay for a valuation now. Wolter Peeters Meanwhile, the message is simple: don’t panic and don’t pay for a valuation now. If a market valuation is eventually required, it can be prepared retrospectively for June 30. And before spending money on a professional valuation, wait for the tax office’s detailed guidance on exactly what will be required. Under the proposed capital gains tax changes, I understand that if I buy shares now, they will effectively be treated as having been sold on June 30 and repurchased on July 1. Suppose they have risen in value by June 30, but I have owned them for less than 12 months. Does that mean the gain before July 1 will not qualify for the 50 per cent CGT discount and will ultimately be taxed at my marginal rate when the shares are sold? Given the 12-month rule, could there be a case for delaying some share purchases until after June 30?



Technically, there is “deemed disposal” on June 30 and re-acquisition on July 1, however, any capital gain/loss is disregarded and deferred until when the shares are eventually sold. Related Article Opinion

Ask an expert Ditch the credit card? Why it’s time to switch to debit Noel Whittaker Money columnist The value at that date will be used to calculate the pre-July 1 component of the capital gain when you eventually dispose of the shares. Provided you have owned the shares for at least 12 months by the time you actually dispose of them, the pre-July 1 component will still qualify for the 50 per cent CGT discount. Therefore, the fact that you may have owned the shares for less than 12 months at June 30 does not, by itself, cause you to lose the discount. I am 70, retired and drawing a flexi pension from my UniSuper balance, currently around $975,000. My wife is 63, also retired, and has about $1.35 million in UniSuper. We have decided to preserve her super for as long as possible and live on mine until it is eventually exhausted. We own our home and have no other significant assets.



Given our ages and super balances, could either of us qualify for the age pension or a part pension? How would Centrelink treat my wife’s super while she is still under the pension age, and what happens once she reaches that age? Related Article Opinion

Ask an expert I’ve inherited $400,000 in shares. What should I do with them? Paul Benson Money contributor Your wife’s super will not count for the asset test until she reaches pensionable age, which is 67, unless she starts to draw a pension from it. Depending on your other assets, you may be eligible for a part pension, provided your total assessable assets do not exceed $1,121,000. If your total assessable assets are a little over the cut-off point, you could seek advice about investing in one of those lifetime income-stream products, where generally only 60 per cent of the purchase price is initially counted for the assets test. This could give you a tiny pension, plus an income stream. But they’re highly specialised, so make sure you understand the product if you decide to choose one. You may also be eligible for the Commonwealth seniors health card, subject to the income test. I’m considering giving both my adult children some money to contribute to super. One is a low-income hospitality worker and the other is a stay-at-home mum. They are in their 30s, and I’m thinking of perhaps $10,000 to $20,000 each. I realise they may have more immediate uses for the money, but I’m also conscious of the power of compounding if the money goes into super at their age. Is contributing to their super a worthwhile strategy, and what contribution and tax issues should we consider?



I understand what you mean about compounding. Putting $10,000 or $20,000 into super in their 30s gives the money decades to grow, but the downside is that it will generally be inaccessible until they reach preservation age, which for both of them will be 60, and satisfy a condition of release. However, if they are likely to buy their first home in the future, consider the First Home Super Saver (FHSS) scheme. You could give them the money and they could then make eligible personal voluntary contributions to their own super. This distinction is important because contributions made directly into their super by a parent are not eligible for the FHSS scheme. They can have up to $15,000 of eligible voluntary contributions in any one financial year count towards the scheme, up to $50,000 across all years, plus associated earnings. Putting $10,000 or $20,000 into a super account when the account-holder is in their 30s gives the money decades to grow. Getty Importantly, if they never buy a home, the money is not lost. It simply remains in super under the normal rules and can generally be accessed from age 60 once they retire or otherwise satisfy a condition of release. So the real question is whether they are better off having the money available now or locking it away for either a first home or retirement. Noel Whittaker is the author of Retirement Made Simple and other books on personal finance. Email: noel@noelwhittaker.com.au.



Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions.
