World.title: ‘Bludgeoned with platitudes’: Australian politicians lead the English-speaking world in AI speeches
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAI ‘Bludgeoned with platitudes’: Australian politicians lead the English-speaking world in AI speeches Brittany Busch Updated September 30, 2026 — 2:08pm ,first published 11:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Just three years ago, Liberal MP Aaron Violi was the first Australian politician to publicly declare he had used AI to write a speech. Today, Australian politicians lead the English-speaking world for AI use in speeches, according to analysis in The Economist. The findings have sparked a debate around how MPs should be using the technology, as OpenAI apologises for rogue agents that broke into a Medicare portal, the Albanese government races to attract billions of dollars in data centre investment, and tech leaders warn AI could pose an existential threat to humanity. A random sample of speeches made between September 2025-26 found more than 20 per cent of those made in Australia’s House of Representatives were flagged by AI content detector Pangram for AI-generated or AI-assisted text. Just under 15 per cent of Senate speeches were flagged.



Australian MPs were the most prolific users compared to other English-speaking legislatures, just ahead of Canada but triple the rate of the British. In July, a Canadian politician went viral after accidentally reciting AI editing prompts. Bill Oliver was making a speech in the chamber when he said: “Here’s a more natural flowing version of that section that reads like a legislator speech rather than a series of short points.” Loading In 2023, Violi declared that he had used AI to write a speech to highlight the technology’s power. “Since that time, the tools have become more powerful, but the government has still been slow to act,” the opposition spokesman for the digital economy and cybersecurity said.



He said AI was a useful tool, but MPs had to be careful in how they used it to construct a speech. “If an MP is putting a prompt into AI and then using the speech verbatim without checking the source documents, well, I think at some point they’re going to get themselves in trouble.” Shadow minister for cybersecurity Aaron Violi used AI in a speech in 2023 as a call to action. Renee Nowytarger Violi said he encouraged his staff to use AI, but had rules for fact-checking, protecting confidentiality by only entering information that could be made publicly available, and not using AI content word-for-word. He said one of the problems with AI-generated content was that it was predictive, based on other content.



“It’ll give you the average of what everyone does – it’s not going to give you that point of difference to really stand out,” he said. “Personally, most of my speeches, particularly those that are most impactful in parliament, are off the cuff with dot points.” Related Article Updated

OpenAI Australian senators invite OpenAI boss as hack expands beyond Medicare James Button, who was a speechwriter for former prime minister Kevin Rudd and previously a journalist at this masthead, said there was a place for using AI for research, but something was lost when using it to write. “The thing about a speech is that it’s a very human event, right? It’s a person standing up in a room, speaking to others, and seeking a connection with those people,” he said. “You add AI into that, and we are absolutely not getting the thoughts of the human being, the politician … so it’s troubling.” Button said AI was capable of imitating an MP’s preferences and speaking style, but the question remained whether it should.



Another speechwriter for a former prime minister, who requested anonymity to speak freely, said AI was an efficient tool to generate the bulk of a speech that could then be finessed – a process which could otherwise take days. The tradeoff was potentially failing to develop the skill of forming and delivering an argument. “The orators will get better, and those who use the tools appropriately will get sharper and better,” they said. “But there will be others who, maybe they’re using AI and all they did previously was just use the leader’s office talking points. They’ve just substituted one form of artificial intelligence for another.” Senator David Pocock said the prime minister’s slashing of staff for the crossbench and opposition put pressure on offices to become more efficient. Dominic Lorrimer Independent senator David Pocock, who has published his own guidelines for using AI, encouraged MPs to disclose when they used the technology and justify its use to constituents. He said increasing AI use meant a more homogenous output, and politicians “bludgeoning people with platitudes”.



“As an elected representative, you’re elected to represent, not to read out AI speech. It comes down to trust. I think Australians would expect you to be using it to become more efficient. But you can’t lose that human touch.” Related Article Political leadership Shorten’s $310,000-a-year writer behind at least 170 speeches – but no zingers Speaker Milton Dick said there were no rules for how members used AI in House speeches, but that MPs were responsible for what they said. “In speaking, members are aware of their overriding duty to the national interest, and primary duty to represent the interests of their constituents,” he said. Political speechwriters typically write major speeches for MPs on a senior staffer salary that starts at $140,000 before adding loadings for allowances and seniority. However, sometimes politicians will write their own or speak off the cuff, and their speechwriters do not always shape the speeches delivered in parliament that were measured by The Economist. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: PLC Resources hits geological sweet spot in emerging WA gold district
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears PLC Resources hits geological sweet spot in emerging WA gold district Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd September 30, 2026 — 1:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

PLC Resources has wrapped up its latest round of drilling at its Rochefort gold prospect in Western Australia’s Murchison region, intersecting the exact geological sweet spot it has been hunting for to prove up a potential virgin gold discovery. The company has completed an eight-hole, 1896-metre reverse circulation (RC) campaign designed to step out from its maiden program earlier this year, with early geological logging confirming the drill bit passed through sheared zones of sulphides within the targeted fractionated dolerite gold target. A drill rig on site at PLC Resources’ Rochefort gold prospect in Western Australia’s Murchison region. The company says early results are a textbook match for its exploration model, which is based on a “sulphidation” process known to be a key ingredient in major Yilgarn gold deposits, including those hosted by the famed Golden Mile Dolerite - host of the famed Kalgoorlie Super Pit. All samples are now at the laboratory, with a four to six-week wait for gold assays.



‘Our follow-up drilling at Rochefort, and the logging shows the geology we set out to find.’ PLC Resources executive director Simon Phillips The latest program was designed to test for extensions of a fractionated dolerite unit that delivered low-level yet consistent gold in the project’s maiden five-hole campaign in May. That initial program picked up geochemical clues suggesting the drilling may have clipped the edge of a larger mineralised system, a theory which is soon to be truth-tested by the lab. PLC’s working theory is that mineralising fluids interacted with the iron-rich dolerite, altering primary sulphides such as pyrrhotite into pyrite and potentially dropping gold out of the solution in the process. The latest visual confirmation of sheared zones, sulphides and magnetite-bearing intervals appears to give the company’s exploration model a significant shot in the arm. PLC Resources executive director Simon Phillips said: “We’ve now completed our follow-up drilling at Rochefort, and the logging shows the geology we set out to find: sheared, sulphide-bearing zones within the fractionated dolerite. That’s encouraging, but the assay results are required to determine whether the system is mineralised with gold. We expect those results within the next four to six weeks.” While the market awaits the lab results from Rochefort, a potentially bigger story is unfolding on the company’s nearby ground.



Independent of the Rochefort target, PLC’s recent airborne magnetic survey may have changed the game for the company at a regional level. The high-resolution data revealed a large-scale fold structure along the eastern margin of the Abbotts Greenstone Belt. Management says the structure is a crustal-level feature that extends for more than 14km of strike and, importantly, continues south into ground held by the $750 million market-capped New Murchison Gold. New Murchison has been moving and shaking in WA’s burgeoning gold sector of late, successfully trucking high-grade discoveries from the region to a toll-treatment facility and generating more than $50 million in cash flow in the last quarter alone. PLC is now moving to ground-truth these newly identified structural corridors and cash in, with geological reconnaissance planned for next month ahead of a maiden regional aircore drilling campaign on its untested targets. With Rochefort assays now pending and a second discovery front taking shape, PLC is building some serious momentum across its Murchison ground. A clear path to drill a major structure apparently shared with a highly profitable neighbour gives the company two shots at uncovering a new gold system. World.title: Shoebridge says Greens must ‘replace’ Labor in first speech as leader
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Shoebridge says Greens must ‘replace’ Labor in first speech as leader Nick Newling Updated September 30, 2026 — 1:47pm ,first published September 30, 2026 — 8:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Newly elected Greens leader David Shoebridge has vowed to take the fight to both Labor and One Nation and cast the left-wing party as the best alternative for a growing base of disaffected voters. The former barrister and staunch AUKUS opponent was elected on a joint ticket with new Victorian senator Steph Hodgins-May as his deputy on Wednesday, following the shock resignation of former leader Larissa Waters due to worsening chronic kidney disease. New federal Greens leader David Shoebridge, left, with deputy Steph Hodgins-May. Sam Mooy “This is an extraordinary moment in politics and we can all feel it. Politics, as usual, is not providing the answers that people are desperately calling for,” Shoebridge told a Sydney press conference after his election. “Things have got harder, much, much harder, for ordinary Australians. What has become so clear after four years of this government, and years before, is that we are not here to make the Labor Party any better. The Greens are here to replace them.”



Shoebridge was elected in a rare contested vote for a party that typically seeks consensus before leadership elections, receiving seven votes to NSW senator Mehreen Faruqi’s four on a two-candidate preferred count. Hodgins-May was elected deputy with six votes to Tasmanian senator Vanessa Bleyer’s five. Bleyer has sat in the Senate for just over two months. In a statement posted to social media, Faruqi, the former deputy leader, said she was disappointed to have not been elected and called for party members to have the right to vote in leadership elections moving forward. Faruqi ran on a joint ticket with Tasmanian senator Nick McKim as deputy candidate.

Loading Fallen Queensland MP Max Chandler-Mather made a similar request in a letter sent to Greens parliamentarians on Tuesday. Shoebridge said both he and Hodgins-May were committed to the “democratisation” of the party, and that conversations on the matter were ongoing.



Veteran South Australian senator Sarah Hanson-Young was the third contender for leadership, running on a solo ticket. The senator was knocked out in the first round after receiving only two votes from the 11-person caucus. Addressing the media after his election, Shoebridge said One Nation was gaining traction in the polls because Labor had facilitated its growth, and that the Greens were the only party capable of combating Pauline Hanson. Shoebridge highlighted that One Nation was polling around 7 per cent early last year, before significant increases in its popularity over the past year to a high of 29 per cent in this masthead’s Resolve Political Monitor. New leader of the Greens David Shoebridge at a press conference in Sydney. Sam Mooy “What we need to do is bridge that gap … with hope. With a sense of political momentum and positivity,” Shoebridge said.



The Greens have maintained a steady support of between 11 and 12 per cent over the past year in polls published by this masthead. Speaking immediately after Shoebridge’s election, Treasurer Jim Chalmers urged the new Greens leader to “focus on the risks posed to workers and to our economy by One Nation, the Liberal Party and the National Party”. The vote took place during a pre-planned “retreat” in Sydney this week, in which matters of policy and strategy were also set to be discussed. Shoebridge has been in politics for 22 years, serving on the inner-Sydney Woollahra Council from 2004 to 2012, and in the NSW state parliament from 2010, until he transitioned to the Senate in 2022. Before entering state parliament Shoebridge was a barrister at Denman Chambers in Sydney. The 55-year-old is currently the party’s spokesman on foreign affairs, defence and immigration, and has established himself as a fierce combatant in Senate estimates hearings.

Exclusive NationalWAPolice Victim in Geraldton shooting that sparked manhunt identified Hannah Murphy and Heather McNeill Updated September 30, 2026 — 1:20pm ,first published September 30, 2026 — 8:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Five people have been arrested after Geraldton man Ashley Wayne Cameron was shot in the leg in the early hours of Wednesday. Cameron was taken to Geraldton Regional Hospital about 1am on Wednesday, after he was allegedly shot in the leg by a person known to him. His injuries were not life-threatening. Ashley Cameron. Facebook A WA Police spokesperson said officers responded to a report of a firearm incident on Allen Road in Moonyoonooka, which is about 12 kilometres outside the Geraldton town centre. They arrived to find 32-year-old Cameron with a wound to his leg. The incident sparked a public safety warning in the early hours of Wednesday as a precaution.



“While this incident involves a firearm, there is no information to suggest an ongoing threat to the wider community”, a WA Police spokesperson said. “Members of the public are not being asked to be alarmed, however they should remain vigilant and report any suspicious activity to police.” Ashley Cameron is in hospital recovering. Facebook Cameron is a Geraldton man and often travels between the state’s Pilbara, Goldfields and Mid West regions. He is a father and an artist.



The police spokesperson said five people were arrested on Hart Street in Utakarra about 10.30am on Wednesday, and were helping police with their inquiries. On Wednesday, WA Attorney-General Tony Buti, who did not speak about Cameron’s identity, said it seemed he had been shot by “pellets” to his leg, rather than a bullet. “All I know is that there was one person that was injured. Pellets, I think were shot,” he said. “I think there are three offenders, and the police will provide a [later] update, I’m sure.” Significant police resources have been deployed to the area, including the tactical response group.



Police advised extra resources had also been sent to nearby Utakarra. However, all roads remain open as normal, and the area is not considered to be in lockdown. Related Article Missing person Shot partner of Mullewa fugitive makes plea for her ‘sexy bush critter’ to come home “Members of the public are asked to stay away from the area while police continue to respond to the incident,” a WA Police spokesperson said. It is the second shooting incident in the Mid West this year. In January, Kenneth Giles allegedly shot his partner in the hand in Mullewa and sparked an active shooting incident.



As of September, the 58-year-old remains on the run despite intense searches by WA police. His car was found in February, but there has been no sign of him despite a desperate plea from his partner.

World.title: There’s a reason why The Turn of the Screw is both feared and revered
World.content:
Key points OPERA: Victorian Opera take on Benjamin Britten’s The Turn of The Screw

THEATRE: Koreaboo at Malthouse draws from lived experience

OPERA

The Turn of the Screw ★★★

Palais Theatre, until October 1 Operatic takes on the supernatural span the centuries, but no modern work is more revered and feared than Benjamin Britten’s The Turn of the Screw. The 1954 opera follows a governess who takes up residence at an English country house, only to find the spirits of two dead servants are haunting the children now in her care. Rachelle Durkin, Genevieve Gray and Oliver Thadoe Naing in a scene from The Turn of the Screw. Jeff Busby Finally, an opera where the muffled screams drifting in from Luna Park next door actually add to the drama, rather than detract! This is a piece that has potential to be The Shining-level unnerving. When staged up close and creepy, the eerie singing and sinister spectacle can captivate like a demonic spirit itself. Here, the huge set and vast stage dwarf the drama – in pivotal moments, the singers are far away from each other; we are far away from them. Detachment creates a disconnect that does not serve some excellent performances.



It is, after all, a chamber opera. Britten scored it for just 13 instruments. Perhaps no Australian conductor knows more about the English composer than Paul Kildea, and the reduced Orchestra Victoria was guided superbly by him. Rachelle Durkin (Governess) was more maternal than hysterical, with a self-assured, impressive vocal performance to match. His voice sharp and cold, Kanen Breen uses his lithe physicality to intensify Peter Quint’s menace, despite donning the most unflattering wig anyone’s ever been cursed to wear (it’s a confusing choice, when it’s clearly mentioned how handsome Quint is). Rachelle Durkin, Michaela Cadwgan and Kanen Breen. Photo Jeff Busby One exceptional discovery to come from this production is soprano Genevieve Gray (currently a university student), who sings the older child, Flora. Gray possesses a vocal evenness and an array of colour that belies her youth. Neither a spook nor a snore, though with moments of satisfaction, this production feels like a missed opportunity to bewitch more people with the mystery and magic of operatic storytelling.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies



THEATRE

Koreaboo ★★★

Malthouse, until October 10 Inspired by playwright Michelle Lim Davidson’s own experiences and directed by Jessica Arthur, Koreaboo is a two-hander that surveys contentious issues of race, diaspora and belonging, with a light touch. Heather Jeong and Michelle Lim Davidson in a scene from Koreaboo Gianna Rizzo Davidson herself plays Hannah, a young Australian who travels to Seoul in an attempt to reconnect with her estranged birth mother, Umma (Heather Jeong). It’s only their second meeting. We learn that although she was born in Korea, Hannah was adopted as a baby and grew up in Newcastle, NSW. At the start, the two women fail and flail in communication. Hannah was expecting a summer-long stay – a long enough period, perhaps, for meaningful reconnection; Umma (mother in Korean), however, believed it was just going to be a short vacation. Her behaviour toward her daughter thrums with wariness, as though one were greeting a stranger. Maybe, she suggests, Hannah should be visiting Seoul’s touristy spots instead.



The entire performance is staged in a small convenience store run by Umma, lovingly decked out in all manner of brightly coloured snacks, and with harsh fluorescent lighting thanks to designer Mel Page. The two women move within the space as they interrogate, parry, and deflect. Davidson explores a raft of issues, including the question of identity. Hannah’s hyphenated background (Korean-Australian) means she’s part of both cultures and wholly of neither, and at first, Umma’s brusque criticism of Hannah’s language skills feels like a wholesale rejection of her daughter’s “Koreanness”. Seeking both maternal and cultural acceptance, Hannah feels crushed to receive neither. Koreaboo Gianna Rizzo Their common language – and one that helps them move toward connection and bridge distance, it turns out – is K-pop. The title actually refers to someone who’s not of Korean heritage but who is obsessed with Korean pop culture. Koreaboo swerves to the unexpected and surreal when both performers begin to sing and dance. There is a talent show in the offing to prepare for, and a chance for Hannah to become more Korean. It’s all surface-level cultural appropriation, though, much in the same way that Umma learned English by watching TV, becoming so familiar with the lives of the characters in Sex and the City that she can quote from them.



After a shaky start, Jeong and Davidson become good sparring partners and friends as they navigate the tricky mother-and-daughter relationship anew after years apart. Umma’s backstory is revealed: the reasons behind Hannah’s adoption and how her yearnings for a singing career were quashed because of filial obedience to her own mother. Korean culture is not just skincare and pop music, but, like a lot of Asian countries, there’s an expectation to conform to parental demands. Related Article Performing arts Star of ABC hit The Newsreader mines real-life family drama for new project Koreaboo packs in a lot during its hour-and-a-half stage time – maybe too much, as there is a lot of jumping about trying to cover a lot of ground. The beginning set-up takes a while to develop and can be tightened, and the ending feels rushed. And although the singing and dance sequences are overextended and as distracting as they are humorous, the play’s value is drawn from highlighting the possible consequences of adopting a child, removing them from their motherland, and raising them in an entirely foreign environment. Even if they embrace the riches of a new life in their host country, there are always losses to be reckoned with.

Reviewed by Thuy On The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: The Age on the hunt for the next generation of passionate journalists
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaMedia & marketing The Age on the hunt for the next generation of passionate journalists Updated September 30, 2026 — 12:46pm ,first published 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Age is seeking aspiring and early-career journalists for 12-month traineeships in its Melbourne newsroom. It is a rare opportunity for the next generation of journalists to hone their craft alongside award-winning reporters and editors, with a strong focus on developing breaking news and digital skills. Age reporters Angus Delaney and Hannah Kennelly. Reaching 5.28 million readers each month, The Age is Victoria’s most widely read masthead and a leader in digital innovation, delivering trusted journalism across politics, sport, business, and culture. Traineeship applications are open here and close on Sunday, October 18. The program will begin in February, with the potential to secure a permanent role when it concludes.



Age editor Patrick Elligett said The Age takes its responsibility to nurture the next generation of journalistic talent seriously. “It’s important for our masthead, our industry and our society that we continue to produce reporters with the standards of rigour and quality The Age strives to uphold,” he said. Angus Delaney, who was appointed state political reporter in July, was one of five trainees at The Age in 2024. He said the traineeship helped him develop the skills he needed to pursue his interest in political journalism. The 2024 Age trainees (from left): Brittany Busch, Hannah Hammoud, Hannah Kennelly, Angus Delaney and Gemma Grant. Simon Schluter “It was an opportunity to learn from the best journalists and editors in Australia, and build my experience on how to break news stories across a wide range of departments in the newsroom,” Delaney said. “The Age is very supportive of hungry, young journalists wanting to build their core skills to make it in this industry.” A highlight for him was being assigned to Parliament House in Canberra during last year’s federal election campaign. “The Age has really allowed me to pursue my passions, and now I get to report on the biggest issues affecting our state.”



Related Article Media & marketing Meet the future of The Age as we welcome five talented new trainees Hannah Kennelly was a trainee in the same 2024 intake and now works as a sports reporter with The Age. She was sent to cover the Commonwealth Games in Scotland this year. “The traineeship was incredibly comprehensive and allowed me to experience different sections of journalism, under the fantastic mentorship of senior reporters in the newsroom,” Kennelly said. “My career highlight so far would be travelling to Belgium to attend the Spa Grand Prix to interview Oscar Piastri.” The newsroom is looking for sharp, curious individuals with exceptional writing skills, strong news judgment and a genuine passion for Age journalism. Candidates with skills in breaking news, data journalism, multimedia production and visual storytelling are encouraged to apply. Cover letters and story pitches must be original and written by the applicants. To be considered, you must already have the right to work and live in Australia lawfully. World.title: Lakapi Samoa unhappy with Oceania Sevens cancellation
World.content:
Lakapi Samoa is disappointed that the Oceania 7s rugby tournament has been cancelled.

Chief executive Seumanu Douglas Ngau Chun told the Samoa Observer in Apia on Tuesday the cancellation will affect the Samoan national sevens teams' preparation for World Rugby qualification series next year.

Ngau Chun said both the Manu Samoa 7s and Manusina 7s teams were training in Apia for the Rotorua event, initially scheduled for October 31 and November 1.

Oceania Rugby cancelled the event last Friday, pointing to lack of funding as the main reason for the decision.

"Both teams had already started training and were preparing for the tournament when we were informed of its cancellation," Ngau Chun told the Samoa Observer.

"It is disappointing for our players, as the tournament would have given them much needed game time against international teams.

"The coaches will now revise their training plans while we look for other matches or tournaments for both teams."

Both teams are overseen by Lakapi Samoa, which remains listed as Samoa's member union by World Rugby despite its ongoing dispute with the government and the government's recognition of a new union.

The event was scheduled for 31 October to 1 November in Rotorua, but Oceania Rugby announced its cancellation last week, two weeks after it had initially announced that the event was being hosted in Rotorua by Bay of Plenty Rugby, in association with New Zealand Rugby.

Oceania Rugby general manager Frank Puletua said in the statement they could not secure funding for the event.

That is despite having 12 months to prepare for the event, as the Oceania 7s is an annual event on the calendar of the regional rugby body.

RNZ Pacific reached out to Puletua today to find out why the organisation had failed to gather funding support when they have had the last 12 months to do that.

Puletua acknowledged in his statement last week that all the other stakeholders such as World Rugby had made its commitments in full, with only Oceania Rugby being unable to live up to its side of the bargain.

Miss out

The event was to have featured eight teams in the Men's Cup - Fiji, New Zealand, Australia, Samoa, Tonga, Tuvalu, Cook Islands and Niue.

Five of those unions, Samoa, Tonga, Tuvalu, Cook Islands and Niue, were also going to compete for Oceania's SVNS 3 qualification places.

The women's competition had lined up two sections, the Oceania 7s Women's Cup, doubling as the SVNS 3 qualifier, featuring Samoa, Tonga, Cook Islands, Niue and Solomon Islands, while a six-team International Women's Invitational would have featured Fiji, New Zealand and Australia together with France, Japan and the United States.

The cancellation now means the teams that need to qualify for the SVNS 3 competition will have to find another way of doing that.

Samoa, Tonga, Cook Islands, Niue and Solomon Islands will also need to qualify for the 2028 Olympic Games, through the Oceania event.

That process will be decided at next year's Oceania 7s, which Puletua and Oceania Rugby are hoping can be staged in Rotorua.

World.title: Explainer: What you need to know about road rules changing on 1 October
World.content:
Explainer - Road rules are changing tomorrow. Here's what you need to know.

Four new rules that come into effect on 1 October include changes to overtaking, where e-scooters can travel and where children can ride their bikes.

"These changes are about fixing the basics: safer streets, clearer rules, and less bureaucracy getting in the way of everyday travel," Transport Minister Chris Bishop said in announcing the changes earlier this year.

Okay, what are the changes?

The new rules:

require a minimum passing gap of 1.5 metres when drivers pass other road users who are not driving a motor vehicle

allow children up to 12 years old to ride bikes on footpaths and allow parents or caregivers to ride with them

allow people to ride e-scooters in cycle lanes

require road users to give way to buses leaving bus stops

The Government sought feedback from the public on possible transport changes earlier this year, Bishop said, and received about 6000 responses.

There are changes for bike lanes. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Changes for families biking together

One big change is for families who go cycling with young children.

Originally, it was proposed children 12 and under only could use footpaths, but that has been extended to allow their parents or caregivers to accompany them.

"One of the strongest messages we heard was that allowing children to ride on footpaths only solves half the problem if the grown-up riding with them still has to use the road," Bishop said.

"That's why we've adapted the proposal to allow parents and caregivers to ride alongside children on the footpath.

"Keeping kids safe while they're learning to ride is common sense. This change strikes the right balance between protecting young cyclists and ensuring footpaths remain safe for everyone who uses them."

Some submitters to the proposal have worried about possible impacts on pedestrian safety, especially for the elderly or disabled.

Overtaking gap rule simplified

The changes also simplified overtaking-gap rules when passing cyclists, pedestrians, horse riders and any other road users who are not driving a motor vehicle.

NZTA says that drivers must leave a distance of at least 1.5 metres when passing those other road users who are travelling in the same direction as them, in the same lane.

"If you can't pass safely, slow down and wait behind them until you can," NZTA notes on its website. "Take extra care when passing them as the wind gust from your vehicle could affect their balance."

"Instead of different distances in different circumstances, drivers will be required to leave a minimum gap of 1.5 metres when overtaking," Bishop said.

"That's clearer for drivers and safer for everyone."

E-scooters can now use bicycle lanes. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

New rules for e-scooters and bus stops

E-scooters will now be allowed to use cycle lanes.

E-scooters have been allowed to ride on the footpath and the road, but it has been illegal to ride in the cycle lanes.

This only applies to e-scooters that are not considered a motor vehicle, NZTA says. (You can get in the weeds of the details about how exactly that is decided here.)

A fourth rule also clarifies when drivers must give way to buses, which hadn't previously been laid out.

On roads with a 60km/h or lower speed limit, if bus drivers are leaving a bus stop, the side of the road or moving out of a bus lane, other drivers must give way to the bus.

The bus driver must indicate their intention to move for at least three seconds, giving other drivers time to react and bus drivers time to check the way is clear, NZTA says.

One change that was mooted but did not go forward was to give councils more power to fine people for parking on grass berms.

"We also heard strong views on the proposal relating to parking on berms, which would have given councils greater powers to fine the owners of vehicles parked on berms," Bishop said.

"After considering the feedback, we've decided not to proceed because it became clear the proposal wouldn't solve the underlying problem."

World.title: Fuel contained during boat salvage in Marlborough Sounds
World.content:
A boat that sunk in the Marlborough Sounds with 2000 litres of diesel onboard has been refloated, with only a small amount of fuel spilt.

The 56-foot boat, named the Padrone, sunk near Waitaria Bay jetty in Kenepuru Sound on yesterday.

It was carrying 2000 litres of diesel and 60 litres of engine oil which prompted an oil spill response from the harbourmaster.

On-scene commander Pete Hamill said less than five litres of oil had leaked out, and containment bunds placed around the vessel were able to stop it from spreading any further.

The vessel sunk in quite shallow water. Marlborough District Council

"We were very lucky that the depth of the water here meant that the breather pipes for the tanks didn't get submerged when she sat on the bottom, so we've only had a small amount of oil, mainly from the engine and bilge, enter the water."

Divers and a salvage team had refloated the boat on Wednesday afternoon using lift bags and water pumps and the diesel would be transferred off the boat, before it was moved.

Once the fuel was off the boat, it would be up to the owner to make plans for it.

Hamill cause of the sinking was not yet known.

World.title: Naked residents and dangerous dogs: The perils of the political door knock
World.content:
There are just 38 days to go until the general election and until then, you can be sure that political candidates will be pounding the pavement and knocking on thousands of doors as they seek to win votes.

While they might be able to reach far greater numbers of potential people through advertising or social media campaigns, the candidates that RNZ spoke to are adamant there is nothing quite like a face-to-face conversation to try and gain votes.

The political door-knock is also the source of countless memorable yarns - from dangerous dogs to constituents answering the door in various states of undress.

Audio player for " Politcal candidates go door-knocking in hunt for support " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1663770%2Fnaked-residents-and-dangerous-dogs-the-perils-of-the-political-door-knock

Politcal candidates go door-knocking in hunt for support Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

Despite the miserable weather, ACT Party leader David Seymour set a ferocious pace as went door-to-door through Auckland's Mission Bay to endorse his new candidate for the Tāmaki electorate James Christmas on Saturday.

On a good day, he said people will answer the door half the time, that the hit rate is about one in four. But the responses were largely positive.

"It's a real antidote to social media. When you get out and talk to people, even today, we've had pretty good political support, but even if they're not hanging out to vote for us, they're still very positive and friendly," Seymour said.

"I think that's a really nice thing that more people need to see. Because you go on a Facebook comment section, bloody hell, it makes you fear for humanity and democracy."

Seymour reckoned he had knocked on about 15,000 doors during the course of his political career, and he said he had become an expert in all manner of latches, door knobs, knockers and doorbells.

"This is an old tactic - I always go to the very back first so that if someone did want to cause trouble, you haven't alerted them to your presence and then left them between you and the road."

Another thing he has learned: never assume how people might vote based on their place of residence.

"When I was first door knocking down the bottom of Baradine College, I knocked on the nunnery and I found three hardcore ACT voting nuns. So you should never judge a book by its cover."

While he found the experience of door-knocking overwhelmingly positive, Seymour has had a few close scrapes.

"I was knocking on a door with this huge front yard and a big stone wall and I heard this ferocious dog coming so I hoofed it, leapt the fence, tore my pants and then I looked around and despite the huge noise it was a tiny little thing."

On the other side of the political divide, Labour's deputy leader Carmel Sepuloni was equally adamant about the importance of door knocking.

"I think you shouldn't underestimate the importance of face to face - kanohi ki te kanohi - New Zealanders still appreciate it. And there's nothing more persuasive than having someone in front of you having a genuine conversation talking about things that matter to you."

Even if they made it clear they were not going to give her their vote, people were by and large very polite, although not always entirely presentable.

"We had to walk past a bedroom window to get to the main entrance and unfortunately the window was open and someone was putting their pants on.

"In that situation I said to my volunteer with me, 'just pretend you didn't see that and to save embarrassment for that person and also ourselves'."

National MP Cameron Brewer door-knocking in Greenhithe. RNZ / Matthew Theunissen

Catching someone just after they have hopped out of the shower is another occupational hazard for the door knocker, as National Party MP Cameron Brewer discovered when RNZ joined him on a door-knock on the streets of Greenhithe in his Upper Harbour electorate.

Nonetheless, a key advantage that door knocking had over other forms of campaigning was that people remembered, said Brewer.

"I remember at primary school - or even in adulthood - who came to my place of business, who came to my primary school, and you never forget.

"People still say to me, 'you knocked on my door, remember what we talked about?' And I'm like, 'yes, I do'. And they say, 'so what have you done about it?' I said, 'we're looking into that issue. Just give it to me again. Was it traffic?' 'No, it wasn't traffic!'."

Brewer had also had his fare share of awkward encounters.

"Sometimes there's a bit of cuddling on the couch watching Netflix. One's kind of in a bit of a predicament there as to whether they kind of try to tiptoe away, which might even look worse - a peeping tom kind of comes to mind - or whether you just kind of back yourself and knock on the door and look the other way."

Brewer said campaigners were also being briefed about the potential perils of "smart doorbells".

"Normally these days when you push them, they start recording and... sometimes someone might be in Singapore listening and watching," he said.

"If you're an ill-disciplined candidate that has big opinions about people's gardens or wants to exchange a bad taste joke with the volunteer or whatever, that quip could be recorded. And so smart doorbells are a bit of an occupational hazard."

Not that he would ever say a bad word about one of his constituent's gardens. "My constituents are world class and we know that because they vote very well every election."

He said some of his colleagues had not quite finessed the art of the door-knock. He recounted a story that John Banks told him about a door-knock he did with his then-colleague Paul Goldsmith.

"Banksy rang me up and he said, 'Cam, he knocked on this door and it was quite a challenging neighbourhood and this young woman came to the door and she was holding a crying baby and had a toddler kind of wrapped around her leg and she was very busy and looked exhausted'."

Goldsmith reportedly said: "'Would you like to eradicate socialism?' That's typical Goldie," said Brewer.

Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said relationships developed on doorsteps were vital for good politics.

"One of my favourite things is talking to people who think that they hate me," she laughed.

"I think when you wear away the concept of each other that we may be holding in our minds and you come back down to the brass tacks of the things that we have in common, you'll find most New Zealanders want more affordable lives, not just for themselves, but for their fellow New Zealanders.

"They want greater job opportunities for all of us. They want healthy nature and they want honest politics.

World.title: Pacific leaders unite on climate at UNGA: 'Think of the children'
World.content:
Audio player for " Pacific leaders urge for more global action on climate issues " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/pacific/1659474%2Fpacific-leaders-unite-on-climate-at-unga-think-of-the-children

Pacific leaders urge for more global action on climate issues Pacific Waves Download MP3 4m

Pacific leaders pulled no punches in their climate messaging at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York this month.

Countries from all three regions - Melanesia, Micronesia and Polynesia - have called on the international community to do far more on climate action.

They say climate change is not merely an environmental concern, but an existential problem of planetary proportion.

Tonga's Prime Minister Lord Fatafehi Fakafanua questioned why the Pacific's climate concerns are still a reccuring theme at the UNGA.

Lord Fakafanua was among several other Pacific leaders who pointed out that the nations doing the least climate damage are left to deal with the worst impacts.

But it is a message they have been conveying for years.

"I stand here mindful that Pacific leaders have come before me, raising the same warnings, making the same appeals," Lord Fakafanua said during his UNGA address.

"Today, I'm compelled to make them again. The question before us is not whether the world has heard our message, but why has it still not acted?"

Federated States of Micronesia's Vice-President Aren Palik warned that global climate action is not progressing fast enough.

Palik reminded world leaders there are less than five years to achieve the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, which are global objectives to end poverty, protect the planet and ensure prosperity for all by 2030.

He said the international community must scale up efforts or small island nations will be the ones left burdened with the cost - financial and physical.

"The recent typhoon, and severe flooding in our states, and more frequent king tides affecting our low-lying islands, demonstrate that these are no longer isolated events, but recurring pressures that test the resilience of our communities on the front line of climate crisis."

Samoa's Deputy Prime Minister Mulipola Anarosa Ale Molioo said global climate financing needs to be scaled up to better support the needs of the most heavily affected.

Mulipola shared how climate adaptation is taking money away from other development needs.

"Resources intended for education, health, water, and social protection are now diverted to disaster recovery," she said.

"Small nations are being asked to finance both development and survival. No nation should have to borrow its way out of a crisis it did so little to create."

Palau's President Surangel Whipps Jr said the region needs financing that reaches communities without adding debt.

He told leaders these countries are already bearing the cost of problems they did not create.

"Those who contributed the least to this climate crisis, yet confront the worst threats of rising sea levels must not be burdened with debt simply to purchase a life jacket for their survival."

Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine reiterated that these smaller nations affected by climate change deserve proper compensation.

She shared how schools are being destroyed by rising seas, salt water is poisoning wells and disease outbreaks have been linked to environmental change.

"This injustice must be addressed, our communities deserve restitution. The Marshall Islands and vulnerable people everywhere need sufficient, timely, and accessible finance for adaptation and loss and damage. Those who have profited to the detriment of the many must pay."

PNG's Prime Minister James Marape urged world leaders to think about the needs of the future generation. RNZ Pacific/ Koroi Hawkins

Papua New Guinea's Prime Minister James Marape said countries must always bear in mind the needs of future generations

He urged the international community to put differences aside and work together to protect the planet.

"It is where we live, it is where we grow our food, it is where we fish, it is the inheritance we will pass on to our children. In our interconnected world, decisions made in one country can affect people thousands of kilometres away."

Marape urged other countries to prioritise humanity ahead of war - reminding them that decisions made today will shape tomorrow.

"Think of the children. A child born today did not create climate change," he said.

"That child did not choose the worst of this generation. That child did not create pollution or the environmental destructions.

World.title: Tauranga City Council CEO's resignation highlights NZ’s weak safety culture - employment lawyer
World.content:
Audio player for " Marty Grenfell steps down after Tauranga landslide review " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics/1663671%2Ftauranga-city-council-ceo-s-resignation-highlights-nz-s-weak-safety-culture-employment-lawyer

Marty Grenfell steps down after Tauranga landslide review Morning Report Download MP3 5m

An employment lawyer says New Zealand needs a stronger culture of accountability for safety, following the resignation of Tauranga City Council's chief executive.

Marty Grenfell suddenly stepped down yesterday, a month and a half after a damning review found January's Mauao landslide in which six people died, could have been prevented.

Safety and employment lawyer Hazel Armstrong told Morning Report it was about time.

"He's taken eight months to decide that he needed to be accountable. So I think it's the least that could have happened."

Armstrong said a litany of safety incidents in New Zealand including the Pike River Mine disaster, and Whakaari/White island, showed the country had systemic issues with safety.

Because there was generally no right to sue for accidents or injuries in New Zealand, due to ACC, Armstrong said organisations didn't take safety seriously enough.

"I do think it's had a big impact on how we regard risk, and how the organisations who should be managing the risk just... put the reports into a nice neat file and move on."

Regulations were needed to put external pressure on organisations to keep people safe, she said.

Armstrong called out the ACT party for cutting safety regulations and said it would be responsible for more deaths like those in the Mt Maunganui landslide.

"We've got a campaign against regulation, well that campaign results in these deaths. There is a direct line between them."

The coalition government has made changes aimed at cutting back red tape in health and safety laws, led by workplace safety minister and ACT MP Brooke Van Velden.

In a statement, van Velden said Armstrong's claims were "wrong" and "deeply insensitive".

"The loss of life from the landslides at the Mount are tragic and my thoughts go out to the family and wider community.

World.title: 'It gives you that willpower to face the world' - the magic behind an eye prosthesis
World.content:
Leith Freeman has just got a new eye made for her.

Her last prosthetic eye no longer fits and no longer matches the changing colour of her healthy eye. This is her fourth one since one eye was removed 14 years ago after a melanoma diagnosis.

It took a while for her to be comfortable with the eye, and it took longer for her to comfortably talk about it.

"I couldn't talk about it for quite some time. It was too hard. But now it's not so difficult. I find it quite easy to talk about. Interesting for people, I guess, because you never think you're going to have an eye that you can just take out."

Audio player for " Prosthetic eyes bringing self-confidence to wearers " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/health/1663534%2Fit-gives-you-that-willpower-to-face-the-world-the-magic-behind-an-eye-prosthesis

Prosthetic eyes bringing self-confidence to wearers First Up Download MP3 5m

Research in 2012 estimated that there were more than 3000 artificial eye wearers in New Zealand.

Health New Zealand told RNZ it did not routinely collect national data on the number of people living with an artificial eye, but 143 people accessed Health NZ's artificial eyes subsidy in 2025.

Freeman received her latest eye at Dr Keith Pine's clinic in Auckland's Takapuna.

To get a new eye made, Freeman sat through four sessions in one day, which involved getting the impression of her socket taken, and watching Dr Pine meticulously paint the iris and sclera to match the colour of her healthy eye.

Leith Freeman sits through four sessions in one day to have her prosthetic eye made and fitted. Ke-Xin Li/RNZ

"Once I start talking about eyes I never stop," Dr Pine warned RNZ.

Having written the first comprehensive textbook on ocular prosthetics, Dr Pine had a lot of thoughts about eyes.

Prosthetic eyes come in many forms, picture shows Dr Keith Pine holding an orbital prosthesis that includes the eyelid and eyebrow. Ke-Xin Li/RNZ

He explained how the pupil should be at the upward centre of the iris, how making eyes bluer made them look more vital, and how to use cotton thread to recreate veins on the sclera.

Painting a prosthetic eye to match the natural eye is a delicate process. Ke-Xin Li/RNZ

He also spoke more about the evolving care for prosthetic eye wearers.

He said for patients like Freeman, prosthetic eyes were not for aesthetics.

"When you talk to somebody, you don't look at their mouth, you look at their face, you don't look at their ears, you look at their eyes. And the non-verbal communication, emotions, attention, interest, all done through the eyes."

Dr Keith Pine polishing a prosthetic eye. Ke-Xin Li/RNZ

Pine said prosthetic eyes helped move a stranger's attention from the eye loss to the person.

"When strangers look at them, that tension is caused by the stranger being curious, something's wrong, and the need to stare to figure it out. And that tension can be interpreted as shock or something different. Family, friends, they're not curious anymore. So they see the person as a whole person, and they don't even see the eye."

A prosthetic eye did not allow a patient to regain vision on their lost eye, but Dr Pine said it helped many people regain confidence in doing everything they loved.

"The prosthetic eye is really just the first step of the journey."

Optometrists, ophthalmologists and psychologists all played an important role.

Dr Keith Pine paints the prosthetic eye. Ke-Xin Li/RNZ

Dr Pine recently researched the psychological experiences of prosthetic eye wearers - work he had proudly done with his daughter Dr Nicola Pine, who is a clinical psychologist.

They found that depression related to eye loss had more to do with social settings, than the disfigurement itself.

"The main defence around that is to have family and friends support the people who have lost an eye."

That social anxiety was top of mind for Kokila Vaidyanathan when she made the decision to remove an eye.

"When I did make a first public appearance to an event, the compliments that I got from people who knew, and people who didn't know really didn't say anything, I thought, oh, this is a good balance. I could live with that."

Kokila Vaidyanathan says she's been adjusting well to her prosthetic eye. Ke-Xin Li/RNZ

She has been wearing a prosthetic eye for a month after losing one eye to a fungal infection.

It had been an adjustment, but she was glad she braved the decision.

"One, it just gives you the confidence, and two, it gives you the will to do anything in life. It just gives you that willpower to face the world."

She has been walking her dog without tripping over, pouring her tea without spilling, and she was planning her favourite activity - travel - very soon.

While she lost an eye, the experience had given Vaidyanathan new vision on life.

"In life, we have to adjust for every little thing, this is one of them as well. This may take a little longer, but we will adjust to it."

Kokila Vaidyanathan has been wearing a prosthetic eye for a month now. Ke-Xin Li/RNZ

Having spent about five decades making eyes, Dr Pine had a lot of hopes and dreams for the field.

He would like to see improvement in 3D printed eyes and digital irises so that they fitted better and looked more realistic, and he would like to see a multi-disciplinary care for prosthetic eye wearers.

"Obviously, for people to drive cars more safely, look after themselves better, go to the doctors, get diagnosed early when it comes to cancer."

For those who did not wear a prosthetic eye, Dr Pine said the advice was to look into their natural eye, if you could figure it out.

World.title: 'Significant change': NZ Film Commission scraps major source of funding for organisations
World.content:
A major source of public funding for film and screen sector organisations is set to end after more than two decades of it being offered.

The New Zealand Film Commission (NZFC) announced on Wednesday that its annual Core Funding Programme would cease when contracts expired on 30 June 2027.

The programme currently provided over $1 million in support to 10 industry groups, including the Screen Producers Guild and the actors' union Equity.

Film Commission chief executive Annie Murray said the commission would be directing public funding towards fewer, but "higher-impact investments".

"We recognise that this is a significant change for the organisations involved, particularly given the programme's long history. Our responsibility is to regularly review our programmes, carefully prioritise public funding and make deliberate choices about where NZFC investment can have the greatest impact for New Zealand film.

"This decision is about ensuring that NZFC's public investment supports the New Zealand screen industry as effectively as possible, now and into the future."

The commission said its Core Funding Programme had existed in different forms for more than two decades.

World.title: Neale set to join Magpies as Lions confirm exit
World.content:
Collingwood says it "looks forward" to Lachie Neale joining the club in 2027 after it was confirmed the three-time premiership player is leaving the Brisbane Lions.

Neale's departure was no secret, as he revealed he was going to miss the Lions "very much" when speaking immediately after Saturday's AFL grand final at the MCG.

This morning, the Lions confirmed the 33-year-old would leave the club as an unrestricted free agent.

"Lachie has been a great player for the Brisbane Lions, and we thank him for his incredible contribution over his eight seasons," Lions list manager Dom Ambrogio said in a club statement.

"We understand Lachie's reasons for wishing to explore free agency and we wish him all the best for the next chapter of his career."

Lions break Dockers' hearts The Brisbane Lions launch an incredible fightback late in the grand final to edge Fremantle by seven points and win a third consecutive premiership.

The Lions said they would "further celebrate and recognise Neale's contribution to the club in the coming days".

The Magpies did not waste time announcing Neale's intention to move south.

"Three-time premiership player and two-time Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale has decided to exercise his free agency rights with a move to Collingwood," a Magpies statement read.

"The club looks forward to welcoming him … when the AFL trade and free agency period commences on Friday."

The AFL is expected to confirm the suitable free agency compensation the Lions will receive during the trade and free agency period.

Speaking after the Lions clinched a third straight flag with a remarkable seven-point win over Fremantle in the grand final, Neale said he owed the club a lot.

"It doesn't feel real at the moment, but I'm sure it will sink in," Neale said on Saturday.

"I've absolutely loved my time at this footy club, they're an exceptional organisation from top to bottom and I can't thank them enough.

"It's been an incredible ride and the best eight years of my life."

Neale moved to the Lions from the Dockers at the end of the 2018 season.

He won his two Brownlow Medals (2020 and 2023) while playing 186 senior matches for the Lions.

Neale, a four-time All-Australian selection, played 135 matches for the Dockers between 2012-18.

World.title: Why Daniel Tupou is a Sydney Roosters grand final specialist
World.content:
The Roosters boast a galaxy of stars for Sunday's NRL decider against Newcastle, but veteran winger Daniel Tupou might be the only one who can call himself a grand final specialist.

Not that he ever would. The 35-year-old has for many years now been a firm believer that actions speak louder than words, and those actions demand his automatic inclusion in any discussion about an all-time Roosters XVII.

A win over the Knights will make Tupou, already the club's highest-ever tryscorer and only a few games shy of being their most capped player, the first Rooster to win four premierships with the club since the 1940s.

He's the only player to have appeared in all three grand final wins under coach Trent Robinson, although calling what Tupou has done merely "appearing" sells him short.

Back in 2013, in just his second year of first grade, Tupou went skywalking to score a spectacular try in the Tricolours' win over a Manly side containing future teammate Daly Cherry-Evans.

Tupou has been making his mark in grand finals for more than a decade. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Back then, Tupou was like so many of his teammates are now — young and hungry in his first grand final, with everything to prove.

"I can't remember much, to be honest it's a bit of a blur, it was such a long time ago. Most of these boys are where I was in 2013 — I was the same age then as Rob Toia is now," said Tupou.

"He's (Cherry-Evans) has never brought it up. I might not bring it up this week, not until after the game on Sunday at least."

That try was just the 17th of Tupou's career, and his 199th in the preliminary final win over the Dolphins is proof he can still fly.

But that and his calm demeanour are about the only things that are still the same after all this time, with Tupou himself having become one of the best wingers of the modern era in the years since.

His performances in the club's back-to-back premiership wins in 2018-19 are living proof of that transformation from skinny aerial specialist to a truly complete flanker.

In the first victory, a comprehensive win over Melbourne, he scored the opening try and worked like a dog from the backfield, running for the second-most metres of any Roosters player.

In the second, a 14-8 war with Canberra, he was unlucky not to become the first winger to win the Clive Churchill Medal as man of the match.

Tupou ran for a team-high 185 metres from 17 carries and saved several tries with perfect defensive decision-making before making the break and throwing the final pass for James Tedesco's premiership-winning score.

It's as good a game as a winger has ever played in a grand final, but when Tupou explains how he finds his best form on the season's biggest day, he makes it sound maddeningly simple.

"You have to stay calm and collected. Enjoy the week and the hype around it, enjoy the atmosphere once we hit the field but embrace the vibe, embrace the energy," said Tupou.

"There's a lot of stuff to tick off, but you have to enjoy every bit of it.

"Just stay present. Don't overthink, be where your feet are."

It's the advice he'll give the grand final rookies on Sunday, even though the Roosters have plenty of premiership experience on hand.

Victor Radley and James Tedesco both played in 2018-19, Nat Butcher and Angus Crichton were both there for the latter and Spencer Leniu won three titles with Penrith.

This Rooster has been the NRL's best forward in 2026 Fresh off another act of blunt-force artistry, there can be no doubt that Roosters prop Naufahu Whyte has been the best forward in the NRL in 2026.

But given 15 of the 22 players named on Tuesday have yet to play in a grand final, they have a fair share of first-timers.

None could ask for a better example of how to make the most of it than Tupou, whose deeds under the brightest of lights have made him a stone-cold living legend of the club he'll once again try to bring to glory on Sunday.

"It's in the preparation. We've worked so hard during the year to earn this moment," said Tupou.

"It's nothing less than what we've already done, we just have to stay consistent."

World.title: Aussie skipper Molineux a chance to play home series despite injury
World.content:
Australia will give captain Sophie Molineux every chance to play in white-ball matches against Bangladesh and New Zealand, as she battles a hip injury.

Molineux was named to captain Australia's side for one-day internationals against Bangladesh and T20s against New Zealand next month, despite the injury.

Fast bowler Darcie Brown has been sidelined with a back injury that also has her in doubt for the WBBL, while fellow quick Lucy Hamilton will miss the ODIs with a quad strain.

Molineux proves inspired choice Sophie Molineux is praised for her leadership ability after guiding Australia to its Women's T20 World Cup victory.

But it is Molineux's fitness that is of most interest ahead of the opening ODI in Brisbane on October 9.

The Victorian put aside a history of frustrating blows to have a stellar first six months as captain, culminating in Australia's T20 World Cup win in England.

"Sophie has been named in the squad but has been managing a hip injury," chief national selector Shawn Flegler said.

"Her involvement in the series will continue to be assessed over the coming days.

"Lucy suffered a mild quad strain at training, but we're hopeful she'll recover in time to be fit and firing for the T20 series."

If Molineux is ruled out, selectors will have to make a call between vice-captains Tahlia McGrath and Ashleigh Gardner to lead the side.

Australian squad:

Sophie Molineux (c), Ashleigh Gardner (vc), Tahlia McGrath (vc), Nicola Carey, Kim Garth, Lucy Hamilton, Alana King, Phoebe Litchfield, Beth Mooney, Ellyse Perry, Megan Schutt, Annabel Sutherland, Georgia Voll, Georgia Wareham

AAP

World.title: Biles undecided about competing at 2028 LA Olympics
World.content:
Simone Biles understands the constant speculation about whether she will compete at another Olympics.

Mostly because the American gymnastics icon is still kind of wondering about the prospect herself.

So much so, there will be times when the question wakes the two-time Olympic all-around champion up in the middle of the night.

"I don't know what the decision [is) I should make, but I don't necessarily have to make it just yet," Biles said.

"But I feel like it's kind of in the works which way I'm leaning towards."

After competing at the Rio de Janeiro, Tokyo and Paris Olympics, the lure of performing on the world stage at home in Los Angeles in 2028 is real.

Simone Biles has won seven gold medals across her Olympic career. (Getty Images: Tom Weller)

Olympic teammates Suni Lee, Jordan Chiles and Jade Carey are already pointing toward LA.

So is Katelyn Ohashi, who returned to elite competition in July following a staggering 13-year break from the sport's top level.

"I know [athletes] are going a lot longer … It's going to be like a big reunion if I did," Biles said.

"It would be so much fun. But I still have to weigh the options."

Biles, who has won seven Olympic gold medals, will be 31 by the time the flame is lit at the Los Angeles opening ceremony in July 2028.

The sacrifices of trying to make a fourth Olympic team would be far different than what she faced in Rio a decade ago.

Biles and her husband, Indianapolis Colts NFL player Jonathan Owens, would like to start a family at some point.

"I am getting to the age of 30 where we start to talk about, 'What does your reproduction cycle … what's going on in there? Biles said.

" I think these are major things that are on the table at my age that I have to take in consideration and weigh those options and what that looks like and when we want to start a family."

Still, the "FOMO", or fear of missing out, when it comes to LA is only too real.

"Like a home Olympic Games … how could you not?" she said.

"It's absolutely incredible."

AP

World.title: Aussie breaks 24-year-old world record at national short course swimming titles
World.content:
Two-time Paralympic gold medallist Rowan Crothers has set a men's S10 world record for the 200 metres freestyle at the Australian Short Course Championships in Sydney.

Competing in the 200m freestyle multiclass event, Crothers stopped the clock in 1 minute and 49.93 seconds.

Canada's Philippe Gagnon had held the previous world record of 1:52.83 since 2002.

Crothers's Australian teammate Alex Tuckfield also dipped under the mark, swimming 1:50.79 to finish second.

"I did not see that coming at all. Not even close," Crothers said.

"Unfortunately, the 200m freestyle isn't a Paralympic event for my classification (S1), but we're going to keep working on it and keep building on the 200m because it's just great training and it's going to help my 100m massively.

"That swim just gets me really excited for the future."

Tuckfield was full of praise for Crothers.

"Rowan is someone I definitely look up to," Tuckfield said.

"I take every opportunity to race him with heart. He's a lovely, lovely man. I want to be like him when I get to his level, and I will.

"Every time I race him, I get a bit better, and it shows with tonight's PB (personal best) that is under the world record … I couldn't be prouder that we both went under the world record."

Among other results, Maddie McTernan broke her S14 women's 200m freestyle national record, swimming 2:07.68.

Ed Sommerville and Ben Armbruster also set national records in the men's 200m freestyle and 50m butterfly respectively.

Sommerville swam 1:40.16, while Armbruster recorded a time of 21.90, becoming the first Australian to go under 22 seconds for the event.

Lani Pallister continued her outstanding 2026 season with an Australian all-comers record in the women's 1,500m freestyle.

Pallister, who won eight gold medals across the Commonwealth Games and Pan Pacific Championships earlier this year, swam 15:18.68.

She won the 200m freestyle final earlier in the evening, with a time of 1:51.99.

World.title: When are the Dally M Awards? Who is the favourite?
World.content:
The NRL's and NRLW's best gather in Sydney tonight to crown rugby league's biggest stars at the Dally M Awards.

Here is what you need to know.

What time is the Dally M ceremony?

The NRL's Dally M Awards ceremony will start at 6:30pm AEST at The Cutaway in Barangaroo on Sydney Harbour.

Players are set to start arriving on the red carpet at 5:30pm.

How can I watch?

Wednesday's ceremony will be broadcast live on Fox League and Kayo Sports.

ABC Sport will be live-blogging the red carpet and the vote count.

Who are the Dally M favourites?

Brisbane Broncos fullback Tamika Upton is favoured to win her third women's award in four years, while Penrith Panthers halfback Nathan Cleary is the frontrunner for the men's award, which would be his first.

Cleary, who is in hospital after surgery on his badly broken leg, and Upton led the men's and women's counts before voting went behind closed doors earlier in the season.

Cleary led with 38 points after round 12. Warriors prop Jackson Ford was his closest competitor on 35, but suffered a pectoral injury in round 16 and missed the rest of the regular season.

Cleary's next closest competitors are a trio of fullbacks — Penrith's Dylan Edwards (32), North Queensland's Scott Drinkwater (29) and defending winner James Tedesco (27) of the Roosters.

Upton had 12 points from four NRLW games when voting became secret and faces tough competition from Roosters playmaker Tarryn Aiken (11), Raiders fullback Sheridan Gallagher (11), Brisbane halfback Jesse Southwell (10) and rugby sevens star turned Titans five-eighth Teagan Levi (9).

Players can earn a maximum of six points per game, so margins can be closed or extended quickly.

Who are the previous Dally M medallists?

Year Men Women* 2025 James Tedesco Tamika Upton 2024 Jahrome Hughes Olivia Kernick 2023 Kalyn Ponga Tamika Upton 2022 Nicho Hynes Raecene McGregor 2021 Tom Trbojevic Millie Boyle, Emma Tonegato 2020 Jack Wighton Ali Brigginshaw 2019 James Tedesco Jessica Sergis 2018 Roger Tuivasa-Sheck Brittany Breayley

*Before the start of the NRLW in 2018 the best female player was awarded the game's top international women's player.

What other awards will be handed out?

There will be NRL and NRLW Team of the Year named, highlighting the leagues' best in each position, as well as:

Rookie of the Year

Captain of the Year

Coach of the Year

Try of the Year

Tackle of the Year

The Ken Stephen Medal and Veronica White Medal will also be awarded to the men's and women's players who made the biggest contribution to their rugby league communities.

World.title: Crossland to miss NRL grand final with four-game ban for Cleary tackle
World.content:
Newcastle Knights hooker Phoenix Crossland has been suspended for four games by the NRL judiciary for the tackle that left Penrith's Nathan Cleary with a broken leg.

Crossland pleaded guilty to the dangerous contact charge on Tuesday before fronting the judiciary to learn his fate.

He will now miss this Sunday's NRL grand final.

The ban would also rule him out of New Zealand's three World Cup pool games.

Crossland was sent off for a hip drop tackle on Cleary in the 36th minute of Newcastle's preliminary final win over the Panthers.

Cleary suffered a compound fracture and a dislocated ankle.

Crossland was represented by barrister James McLeod, who made the case for his client to receive a two or three-week ban.

Crossland cited his career record, telling the judiciary he had never before been sent off. He admitted he got the execution of the tackle wrong but insisted "wasn't trying to hurt anyone".

Phoenix Crossland said he made a remorseful call to Nathan Cleary after the incident. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Arguing for a four-game suspension, the NRL said Crossland's tackle failed to exercise a proper duty of care and, while accidental, did not show enough caution towards Cleary.

Crossland told the judiciary was deeply remorseful for Cleary's injury and had reached out to the Panthers star.

"I called him yesterday. It was obviously a tough phone call," Crossland said.

"I reached out to his dad [Panthers coach Ivan Cleary] as well.

"Nathan was great, he said not to worry about and he understood it was an accident.

"He was such a gentleman … he told me to stop saying sorry.

"He's my favourite player in the game by a mile," Crossland said.

Crossland added: "He's the best player in the game and I look up to him."

Phoenix Crossland was sent off in the 36th minute of the preliminary final for the tackle. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Crossland described the incident and fallout as a low point in his life. In his submissions, McLeod produced abusive Instagram messages that had been directed towards Crossland in the past 48 hours.

"It's killing me," he said.

Crossland added: "It's been the worst couple of days of my life.

"It's meant to be the best week of my life and it's been far from it."

The verdict sets up a scenario where 19-year-old Knight Diesel Hagan could make his NRL debut in a grand final.

It would be the first time such a debut has taken place in 90 years. Eddie Lockhart was the last to do it in 1936, for Balmain.

Harrison Graham will almost certainly shift to a starting role for Newcastle in the grand final, while other options for the Knights include Thomas Cant and Jermaine McEwen.

World.title: Brazil beat Socceroos in fractious, entertaining clash
World.content:
The Socceroos have fallen to a 4-2 defeat against Brazil in front of 52,423 fans at Lang Park in Brisbane.

Fresh from a superb performance in Townsville on Friday night, the Socceroos will once again take plenty from a contest that ebbed and flowed throughout 90 thoroughly engaging minutes.

With Tony Popovic naming an unchanged team for just the second time in his tenure, it seems likely that this XI is the one that will start the Asian Cup in January.

On the basis of what they showed against the number five team in the world, they should serve Australia very well indeed.

Australia fell behind early to a Brazil team that came out the blocks firing, scoring through a superb Vanderson strike in the opening three minutes.

They could have fallen even further behind when Pat Beach pulled off two sensational saves to twice deny Raphinha just a couple of minutes later.

The Socceroos had barely had control of the ball at that stage, the promised response from a badly burned Brazil team in full evidence.

However, the hosts showed superb composure and self-confidence to hit back, gradually regaining control in the midfield and scoring two goals in the space of four minutes to take the lead mid way through the first half.

Alessandro Circati turned home a corner at the back post, a goal initially ruled out for offside before VAR intervened.

Connor Metcalfe's stunner gave the Socceroos the lead. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

Then, Connor Metcalf prompted an explosion of joy from the home fans in the stands by drilling home a magnificent strike just minutes later, taking a touch and hammering a left-footed shot into the top corner from the edge of the area.

The pressure was clearly getting to Brazil, with the normally Imperturbable Carlo Ancelotti screaming into the face of the assistant referee after Tete Yengi was fouled.

The visitors drew level on the stroke of half time, first of two penalties awarded to the visitors converted by skipper Raphinha after another lengthy VAR review when the referee inexplicably failed to give a penalty after Harry Souttar made a rough challenge.

Tempers threatened to boil over in the second half when Endrick and Souttar clashed, Aziz Behich coming in a sparking a small melee in front of the Socceroos bench.

That finally sparked Brazil, who turned the style back on as Bruno Guimarães finished a sumptuous move from the left to give the visitors the lead.

Vinícius Júnior was then fouled in the penalty area and converted to seal the victory in front of the biggest football crowd ever at Lang Park.

"Honestly, they [the Socceroos] press really well," Ancelotti said.

"They are really well organised, they surprised us in this sense.

"They put much more pressure in the front and we had difficulty to build from the back.

"They are a very good team, in my opinion."

Follow all the action from Lang Park in our live blog.

Tech.title: Sam Altman says OpenAI won’t go public until its models are safe
Tech.content:
is The Verge’s senior AI reporter. An AI beat reporter for more than five years, her work has also appeared in CNBC, MIT Technology Review, Wired UK, and other outlets.

For months, people have wondered when OpenAI will go public. CEO Sam Altman says it won’t happen until the company can make better promises about model safety, with no firm timeline in sight. “We intend to continue with AI progress … but as the models have had this surge forward in capability, and we see more of that ahead of us, we have got to be able to make confident safety claims,” Altman said Tuesday during a Q&A with reporters after his DevDay keynote. At the same time, he said, waiting too long for an IPO would be “bad for the world.”

Altman’s comments come after months of controversy about whether or not OpenAI and its rivals can control their own creations. In July, news broke that an unreleased OpenAI model had hacked into a rival AI lab, Hugging Face, without OpenAI’s knowledge. More cybersecurity incidents soon came to light at OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google. A high-profile resignation letter from an Anthropic employee sparked a public discussion about how risky these systems are for society at large. OpenAI, alongside its rivals, called for regulation and “pacing the frontier.” And earlier this month, Altman said in an interview that the company would likely not go public this year.

At DevDay, Altman was circumspect about what “pacing the frontier” actually meant, refraining from calling it an outright slowdown. “Pacing to us means that we push safety and alignment ahead of capabilities,” Altman said. But he expressed concerns that going public could create the potential to “disappoint Wall Street supporters in the names of safety or whatever else,” and that doing it during a “shift to very capable models and a new kind of safety requirement seems ill-advised.” He said OpenAI would prioritize safety to “confidently scale to the next stage of AI without people debating what percent chance we’re going to do all these bad things,” rather than “barrel, all guns blazing, towards an IPO.”

“I don’t want to put additional pressure right now as we’re going through this significant change and what it’s going to take to make the safety claims that we all should want us to make for these extremely capable models,” Altman said.
